How this handbook worksRatings, the apostolic standard, the map, every section, and the ratings table

A debate-ready handbook: the positive case for the triune God, an internal critique of Islam built on the Islamic Dilemma, and answers to other worldviews and traditions, all tested by Scripture alone. Written at intermediate level; every technical and Arabic term is defined the first time it appears. Qur'an translations follow Sahih International, lightly adapted. Hadith numbers use sunnah.com numbering unless stated otherwise.

How to use this handbook

The apostolic standard. Every theological claim in this handbook is settled by Scripture alone (1D). Church fathers, councils, historians, and the other side's own sources (the Qur'an, hadith, the Catechism, the Nag Hammadi texts) are quoted as historical witnesses or as what the other side claims, never as an authority over the Bible. Cards on Christian doctrine carry a "Scripture alone: the apostolic test" field showing the texts that settle the question.

Ratings. Every argument carries a rating. STRONG means the premises rest on clear primary texts or broad academic consensus, and the standard responses have clear answers. MODERATE means the argument depends on a disputed interpretation, dating, or hadith grading. WEAK means a fringe reading, a weak hadith, or an argument that is easily answered; the card tells you to drop it, and explains why so you can answer a Christian who uses it.

(VERIFY) marks anything not yet checked against a primary source. Check it before you quote it in public. The complete list is in 4C.

Cards open as summaries (on the website): each card first shows its thesis or the objection, and the 30-second version. Tap Open full card for the rest, or choose Full cards in the filter bar to open them all. Every 30-second version has a Copy button, and the row of buttons at the top of an open card jumps straight to its escape routes, trap questions, or any other part.

On the website, start on the home screen. Type what someone just said into What did they just say? and the matching cards come up at once. Or pick who you're talking with (Muslims, Catholics, Orthodox, atheists, Jehovah's Witnesses, Latter-day Saints, Hebrew Israelites, Oneness Pentecostals and unitarians, fellow Christians caught in popular errors, Jewish friends, or spiritual seekers): the app shows that conversation's battle plan first (4D), then only its sections. Search at the top (press / on a keyboard) shows matching cards as you type. Practice quizzes you: it shows an objection or an argument, you answer out loud, then you check the 30-second version. It favors the cards you haven't mastered yet, and Progress shows how many you have mastered for each kind of conversation. Practice this and Spar on this on any card start with that card.

Live: answers while they're talking. Open Live and choose Computer sound (a YouTube debate, a livestream, or a call playing on your computer), Microphone (a conversation in the room), or A recording (a saved audio or video file). Live turns the speech into text and, each time a claim matches a card, shows that card's 30-second reply, the key Scripture, and a question to ask. Listening works in the offline file (Apologetics_Handbook.html) opened in Chrome or Edge on a computer. claude.ai pages can't use the microphone, so there you type what you hear instead. The speech-to-text runs on your computer: the first start downloads a speech model (about 200 MB, or about 40 MB on computers without a capable graphics card), and the audio is never saved or sent anywhere. If you listen to a private call, tell the other people.

Handbook Live (Windows app). To listen while you use other apps, run Handbook Live Setup.exe from your Downloads once; it adds Handbook Live to your Start menu and desktop. In Listen to, choose an app (Discord, Zoom, Teams, or your browser for YouTube and TikTok, and only that app is heard), any speakers or headphones (everything they play), or any microphone or input, including virtual mixers such as Voicemeeter or Wave Link. Scan for sound shows which device actually has the voices. Also listen to adds a second source, such as your own microphone marked as your own words. The answers appear in a small window that stays on top of your other apps.

Video library. All 18,229 videos, livestreams, and Shorts from the 14 channels this handbook draws on (GodLogic Apologetics, A Messenger of Truth, Kyrillos Apologetics, Testify, Apostate Prophet, Taco Talks, Nick Matau, TheArchive, Wes Huff, Give Light (Reese), Grace to You, Towards Jesus, TheChristianKing Apologetics, and Wise Disciple), sorted into this handbook's topics by their titles. Open it from the home screen or the section list, or press ▶ videos on this topic under any section heading. Search and Ask list matching videos too. The full list by topic is also in Video_Library.md in your Downloads. Arguments drawn from these videos are checked against primary sources before they're added to a card, and the card names the video.

Coaching with Claude (on the website at claude.ai). Ask: type what someone just said, and Claude answers from the matching cards with a 30-second reply, key Scripture, and the cards to study. Spar: Claude plays a Muslim, Catholic, atheist, or other opponent at the difficulty you pick; when you end the match, it grades you on accuracy, use of Scripture, handling pushback, clarity, and tone, and lists better replies. Check my answer (in Practice) grades a typed answer against the card. These use your own Claude account, and the page asks your permission the first time. Claude can still make mistakes: trust the cards and the (VERIFY) marks over any single answer. ☆ Save marks a card with a gold ribbon, and ★ Saved shows only your saved cards. To print a cheat sheet, open the offline file (Apologetics_Handbook.html) in your browser, choose who you're talking with, leave the cards as Summaries, and print from the browser.

The map

Part 3 answers other worldviews and traditions, including Roman Catholicism (3J), Eastern Orthodoxy (3K), Gnosticism (3L), the Hebrew Israelites (3M), Oneness Pentecostals and biblical unitarians (3N), and popular errors inside the church: the prosperity gospel, King James Onlyism, and date-setting (3O). The five threads of the Islam section

  1. The hub: the Dilemma (2A). The Qur'an tells Jews and Christians to judge by the Torah and Gospel they have. Those books teach the crucifixion and deity of Jesus, which the Qur'an denies. Everything else either closes an escape route from this or adds a second, independent problem.
  2. Closing the exits (2B-1, 2B-2, 2B-3, 2B-5, 2B-7, 2B-8). The escape is always "the Bible was corrupted." These sections ask when, who first said so, and why Muhammad himself treated the Torah of his day as genuine.
  3. The cross cluster (2B-6, 2B-13, 2B-14, 2D-1). If Jesus was not crucified, God made the event look like a crucifixion to everyone, which undermines eyewitness testimony, history, and the mass transmission Muslims rely on for the Qur'an.
  4. The Qur'an's own reliability (2B-10, 2B-11, 2B-12, 2C-1, 2F, 2G). Here the ratings vary most. Expect several MODERATE cards and a few WEAK ones you'll be told to drop.
  5. God's nature (2D-2, 2D-3, 2D-4, 2H). TAG returns: can a single-person God ground love, communication, morality, and trustworthy revelation?

Suggested study order

  1. 2A → 2B-1 → 2B-6 → 2D-1 → 2B-14: a complete core against Islam.
  2. 1A (the deepest section) → 1C → 1B → 1E → 1F for the objections skeptics raise most.
  3. 2J and 2K, since you'll need them in your first conversations.
  4. 1D before any conversation with Catholic or Orthodox friends, then 3J and 3K.
  5. Then 4A, the ranked battle plan, and everything else.

Part 1

The Case for the Triune God

1A

The Transcendental Argument (TAG)

10 cards4 moderate

New terms

TAG: The Transcendental Argument for God: God must exist because logic, science, morality, and reasoning are impossible without him.

Transcendental argument: An argument from the preconditions of something we already use (thought, experience, argument) to what must be true for it to be possible.

Presuppositionalism: The apologetic method of Van Til and Bahnsen: argue at the level of ultimate commitments (presuppositions), showing that only the Christian worldview makes knowledge possible.

Impossibility of the contrary: Showing that every alternative to a claim is self-defeating or unable to account for what it uses, so the claim must be true.

Uniformity of nature: The assumption that nature behaves consistently, so that the future will resemble the past.

Problem of induction: David Hume's point that we can't justify reasoning from past to future without assuming the very regularity we want to prove.

Normativity: The 'ought' quality of logic and morality: they tell us how we should think and act, not just how we do.

Brute fact: A fact with no explanation; it just is.

The one and the many: The ancient puzzle of how unity (laws, kinds) and diversity (individual things) relate, and which is ultimate.

Unitarian (theism): Belief in a God who is one person only (Judaism, Islam, Jehovah's Witnesses), as opposed to the Trinity.

Aseity: God's existence 'from himself': he depends on nothing for his existence.

Worldview: A person's most basic beliefs about reality, knowledge, and ethics, the lens through which they interpret everything.

Internal critique: Testing a worldview by its own standards, to see whether it is consistent and can account for what it uses.

What a transcendental argument is. Most arguments for God reason from evidence within experience: the universe began, so it has a cause; the universe is fine-tuned, so it has a designer. A transcendental argument asks a different question: what must be true for experience, reasoning, and argument to be possible at all? It reasons from the preconditions of intelligibility. Immanuel Kant made the method famous (Critique of Pure Reason). Cornelius Van Til and Greg Bahnsen turned it into an argument for the God of the Bible.

The core move. The skeptic uses logic, trusts that the future will resemble the past, makes moral judgments, and relies on his own reasoning, in the very act of arguing against God. TAG argues that only the triune God of Scripture makes those things intelligible. So the skeptic's argument presupposes what it denies.

What TAG is not. It is not a "God of the gaps" argument (we don't know X, so God). It is a claim about what a worldview can or cannot account for in principle. It is also not a refusal to use evidence. Bahnsen used evidence constantly; he insisted only that the framework for weighing evidence is itself the point in dispute.

Honest framing. TAG is the deepest argument in this handbook and the most debated among professional philosophers. In conversation it is a superb internal critique: it makes the other person account for the tools he is using. As a deductive proof that only Christianity works, it carries a heavy burden (see the objections below). Present it with confidence, but don't claim more than it shows.

Argument1AMODERATE

The Transcendental Argument for God

as a formal proof; excellent as an internal critique

Name + thesis

Logic, induction, objective morality, and reliable reasoning are possible only if the triune God exists. They are possible, since the skeptic must use them to argue at all. Therefore the triune God exists.

Key texts

  • Prov 1:7: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge."
  • Col 2:3: Christ, "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge."
  • Rom 1:18–21: people "by their unrighteousness suppress the truth... For what can be known about God is plain to them... although they knew God, they did not honor him as God."
  • Col 1:17; Heb 1:3: "in him all things hold together"; he "upholds the universe by the word of his power."
  • Gen 8:22: "While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat... shall not cease." (God's promise as the ground of nature's regularity.)
  • John 1:1: "In the beginning was the Word (Logos)."

Their best case (steelman)

A thoughtful atheist philosopher replies:

  1. Logic needs no grounding. The laws of logic are not things that need a cause; they are necessary truths, true in every possible world. Asking "what grounds logic?" is like asking what grounds the number 2.
  2. Induction is justified pragmatically. Science works. We don't need a metaphysical guarantee that nature is uniform; we bet on it, and the bet keeps paying off.
  3. Morality can be grounded naturally. Moral facts can supervene on facts about well-being (moral realism without God, e.g. Erik Wielenberg, Robust Ethics, 2014), or morality is a useful human construction.
  4. Reason is reliable because evolution selected for it. Creatures with wildly false beliefs died out.
  5. You can't refute every worldview. Even if you defeat naturalism, Islam, and pantheism, there may be an unconsidered option. "Only the Christian God" outruns the evidence.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. If the triune God does not exist, then logic, induction, objective morality, and reliable reasoning are not intelligible (they have no adequate foundation).
  • P2. Logic, induction, objective morality, and reliable reasoning are intelligible: we use them successfully, and the skeptic must use them to argue against P1.
  • C. Therefore the triune God exists.

P1 is defended by the "impossibility of the contrary": an internal critique of each rival worldview (the next three cards). P2 is defended by showing that denying it is self-refuting.

Evidence for each premise

P2 (the preconditions are real). This premise is the easy one. To deny that logic works, you must use logic; to argue that induction is unreliable, you must expect your argument to work tomorrow as it did today. Any argument against P2 assumes P2.

P1 (they need the triune God). The case is built in four parts:

Precondition What it requires Why the triune God supplies it
Logic Laws that are universal, unchanging, necessary, and normative (we ought to reason by them) Laws of thought are best understood as thoughts; necessary, universal thoughts require a necessary, universal mind (James Anderson and Greg Welty, "The Lord of Non-Contradiction," Philosophia Christi 13.2, 2011)
Induction A reason to expect the future to resemble the past A personal God who governs nature and has promised its regularity (Gen 8:22; Col 1:17). Hume showed that induction cannot be justified by induction without circularity (Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, §4).
Objective morality Obligations that bind everyone regardless of opinion, and real moral knowledge A perfectly good, personal lawgiver whose nature is the standard. Even some atheist philosophers concede evolution explains moral beliefs, not moral truth (Sharon Street, "A Darwinian Dilemma for Realist Theories of Value," Philosophical Studies 127, 2006).
Reliable reason Cognitive faculties aimed at truth, not merely at survival Minds made in the image of a rational God (Gen 1:27). On naturalism, see Plantinga's Evolutionary Argument Against Naturalism (1B).

Why "triune"? The argument moves from "a God" to "the triune God" through the problem of the one and the many (see the Trinitarian TAG card below).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Weakest premise: P1, and specifically its word "only." The internal critiques show that naturalism, pantheism, and unitarian theism each struggle to ground the preconditions. They do not, by themselves, show that no possible worldview could. That is the "inductive-survey" objection (answered in the objections below).

Hardest surviving objection: the necessity reply. "Logic is necessary; necessary truths need no ground." Answer: Necessity is not the whole story. Logic is also normative: it tells minds how they ought to think. An abstract, impersonal truth doesn't explain why any mind is obligated to conform to it, or why human minds can know it. Anderson and Welty also argue that propositions (the bearers of truth) are by nature thoughts, so necessary propositions point to a necessary mind. This is a respectable, published argument, but it is still debated. That is the reason for the MODERATE rating.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Logic is just a human convention."

  • Close (R1): Then the law of non-contradiction could have been otherwise, and it would be true only for humans who adopt it. Then your claim "God doesn't exist" could be both true and false.
  • Their comeback: "It's a description of how the universe behaves."
  • Close (R2): Descriptions are general summaries of past observations. They can't tell you that a contradiction is impossible everywhere, including in places and times you'll never observe. You're treating logic as necessary in practice while calling it contingent in theory.

2. "Induction just works. That's justification enough."

  • Close (R1): "It has worked in the past, so it will work in the future" is itself an inductive argument. You are using induction to justify induction. Hume saw this in 1748.
  • Their comeback: "Your view is circular too: you trust God's promise, and you learned it from the Bible."
  • Close (R2): Every ultimate standard is circular in a broad sense, since you can't justify logic without using logic (see the circularity objection below). The question is which circle can account for itself. The Christian worldview contains an explanation of why nature is regular; naturalism treats regularity as an unexplained brute fact.

3. "Morality comes from evolution and well-being."

  • Close (R1): Evolution explains why we feel obligations, not why they are true. If our morals had evolved differently (Darwin himself imagined that creatures raised like hive-bees would develop a very different conscience, in his chapter on the moral sense in The Descent of Man), would those morals be equally right?
  • Their comeback: "Moral facts are brute, necessary facts, like logic" (Wielenberg).
  • Close (R2): Then you have impersonal facts that issue commands. Obligation is something persons owe to persons. And your evolved faculties would have no special reason to track those facts, which is Street's dilemma.

Boomerang check

A. "A Muslim can run TAG too: Allah grounds logic and morality."

  • Answer: That's why TAG continues past theism into the Trinity. A God who is one person alone faces the one-and-many problem and the question of love and communication before creation (see the Trinitarian TAG card and 2D-3). TAG is not just "theism beats atheism."

B. "Christians disagree about TAG. Many Christian philosophers think it fails."

  • Answer: True, and you should say so. Classical apologists (William Lane Craig, for example) doubt TAG's strong form. That's why this handbook also gives a cumulative case (1B). Disagreement among Christians about the best argument is not evidence against the conclusion.

C. "You just assume your worldview."

  • Answer: Everyone reasons from ultimate commitments. TAG doesn't ask anyone to accept Christianity first; it asks both sides to put their commitments on the table and see which one can account for reasoning itself.

Strength rating

Why: P2 is unassailable. P1 is supported by serious, published philosophical work (Bahnsen, Frame, Anderson and Welty), but it is not academic consensus, and the "only" claim faces the inductive-survey objection. In conversation the argument is very effective, because it forces a skeptic to give an account of logic, induction, and morality that most have never thought about.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Popular / street-level atheist Very effective. Most have never been asked to account for logic or induction. Use the questions, not the jargon.
Philosophically trained atheist Will raise necessity, brute facts, and Stroud's objection Use the modest form ("Christian theism best accounts for...") and the objections below.
Agnostic Helps them see that "neutral" is not neutral Pair with 3B.
Muslims (all groups) They already accept God, so the theistic part lands; the force is in the Trinitarian step Skip to the Trinitarian TAG card; see 2D-2 and 2D-3.
Postmodern / relativist Shows that denying objective truth uses objective truth See 3H.

Trap questions

  1. "When you say a contradiction can't be true, do you mean just here and now, or everywhere and always? How do you know that?"
  2. "Why do you expect the sun to rise tomorrow? And can you justify that without assuming the future will be like the past?"
  3. "If our moral sense had evolved differently, would cruelty to children be good?"
  4. "If your thoughts are the product of processes aimed at survival rather than truth, why trust the thought that atheism is true?"

30-second version

"Here's what fascinates me. To argue that God doesn't exist, you have to use logic, trust that nature will behave tomorrow like it did today, and assume your mind is reliable. Those things make perfect sense if a rational God made the world and our minds. What makes sense of them on your view?"

2-minute version

"Can I ask you something deeper than evidence? Before we look at any evidence, we both use tools: logic, the expectation that nature is regular, moral judgments, and trust in our own reasoning. Those tools are interesting. Logic isn't made of matter, yet it holds everywhere and always, and it tells us how we ought to think. The regularity of nature can't be proven by experience without assuming it first; David Hume pointed that out almost 300 years ago. And moral obligations bind people whether they like it or not.

In the Christian view, these things fit. There's a personal, rational God whose thinking is the source of logic, who governs nature faithfully, whose character is the standard of goodness, and who made our minds to know the truth. So when you and I reason together, we're both relying on a world that God made.

My question is, what's your account? If the universe is ultimately matter and energy without purpose, where do universal laws of thought come from? Why should nature be regular? Why are we obligated to anything? I'm not asking to trap you. I think these questions point to God, and ultimately to the God who is one and three, and I'd love to talk about why."

Further reading

Christian

  • Greg L. Bahnsen, Van Til's Apologetic: Readings and Analysis (P&R, 1998)
  • Greg L. Bahnsen, Always Ready: Directions for Defending the Faith (1996): the most accessible introduction
  • John M. Frame, Apologetics: A Justification of Christian Belief (2nd ed., P&R, 2015)
  • K. Scott Oliphint, Covenantal Apologetics (Crossway, 2013)
  • James N. Anderson and Greg Welty, "The Lord of Non-Contradiction: An Argument for God from Logic," Philosophia Christi 13.2 (2011)

Muslim

  • Muslim scholars rarely engage TAG directly; Muslim debaters sometimes adapt it to argue for Allah. Read the unitarian critique below and 2D-3.

Academic / critical

  • Barry Stroud, "Transcendental Arguments," Journal of Philosophy 65 (1968)
  • Erik J. Wielenberg, Robust Ethics (Oxford, 2014): the best atheist account of objective morality
  • David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), §4
Argument1AMODERATE

Internal Critique of Naturalism

premises widely discussed; the critique of induction and normativity is strong

Name + thesis

Naturalism (the view that nature is all there is) cannot account for the universal, normative laws of logic, the uniformity of nature, objective moral obligation, or the reliability of reason. It must borrow them from a theistic worldview.

Key texts

  • Rom 1:21–22: "they became futile in their thinking... Claiming to be wise, they became fools."
  • 1 Cor 1:20: "Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?"
  • 2 Cor 10:5: "We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ."

Their best case (steelman)

The best naturalists don't claim matter creates logic. They say logic is necessary and abstract (a Platonist naturalism), induction is a rational default that science vindicates, morality supervenes on natural facts (Wielenberg, Peter Railton), and evolution, together with cultural learning and the self-correction of science, makes our reasoning reliable enough. Thomas Nagel, an atheist, admits naturalism has serious trouble with mind and reason (Mind and Cosmos, 2012), but says the answer is a better naturalism, not God.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. On naturalism, everything that exists is physical or depends on the physical, and nothing is directed toward purposes.
  • P2. The laws of logic are universal, unchanging, and normative. The uniformity of nature cannot be justified from experience alone. Moral obligations bind persons. Reason must be aimed at truth to be trusted.
  • P3. Physical, purposeless processes can't produce or explain normativity (ought), universality beyond experience, or faculties aimed at truth rather than survival.
  • C. Naturalism cannot account for the preconditions it uses. When the naturalist reasons, he relies on capital borrowed from theism.

Evidence for each premise

  • Logic. Matter is particular and changing; the law of non-contradiction is universal and unchanging. A brain state is not "true" or "valid"; it simply occurs. Validity is a normative relation between propositions, not a physical event.
  • Induction. Hume's problem remains unsolved in its classic form. Most philosophers accept that there is no non-circular justification of induction. Naturalism has nothing to say about why nature should be uniform.
  • Morality. Street's "Darwinian dilemma" (2006): if moral facts are independent of us, evolution gives us no reason to have tracked them. If they aren't, they're not objective.
  • Reason. Plantinga: if our faculties were shaped only for survival, the probability that they are reliable is low or inscrutable, so the naturalist has a defeater for all his beliefs, naturalism included (Where the Conflict Really Lies, 2011, ch. 10; full card in 1B).
  • Concessions. Nagel: "Evolutionary naturalism provides an account of our capacities that undermines their reliability, and in doing so undermines itself" (Mind and Cosmos, 2012, p. 27).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Weakest premise: P3. A Platonist naturalist will say logic and moral facts are abstract, necessary objects, so matter doesn't have to produce them.

Hardest objection: "Abstract objects exist necessarily; no mind required." Answer: (1) That's no longer strict naturalism; it adds a realm of non-physical, eternal, causally inert objects. (2) Causally inert objects can't explain how physical brains come to know them (Paul Benacerraf's problem, "Mathematical Truth," Journal of Philosophy 70, 1973). (3) They can't explain obligation: why is any mind bound by them? A personal God explains all three.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Science is self-correcting, so reason is reliable."

  • Close (R1): Self-correction uses reason to check reason. That's fine if reason is reliable, which is the question.
  • Their comeback: "Evolution selects for true beliefs because they help survival."
  • Close (R2): Behavior is what survives, not belief. Many false beliefs produce useful behavior. And for abstract beliefs (philosophy, mathematics, metaphysics), survival value is almost irrelevant. See the EAAN card in 1B.

2. "Morality is about human flourishing."

  • Close (R1): Why ought I to promote flourishing, especially others', when it costs me?
  • Their comeback: "Because it's rational: cooperation benefits everyone."
  • Close (R2): That makes morality advice for the self-interested, not obligation. What if cruelty benefits me and I won't be caught? On your view, what's wrong with it, beyond being unwise?

Boomerang check

"God is also an unexplained brute fact." Answer: God is not a contingent fact that happens to be so; on classical theism he exists necessarily and of himself (aseity). Ending explanation in a necessary, personal being is different from ending it in contingent, impersonal regularities that might have been otherwise. See the brute-facts objection below.

Strength rating

Why: The internal critique of induction and normativity is widely recognized as a problem for naturalism, even by atheists (Nagel, Street). But sophisticated naturalists have replies (Platonism, robust realism) that keep the debate open. This is a strong conversational tool and a respectable philosophical argument, not a consensus result.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Scientific materialist Strong: often hasn't noticed science presupposes uniformity Start with induction.
Philosophy student Will know Hume, Benacerraf, and Street Lead with normativity.
Muslims Agree with you here; good common ground Use it to build rapport, then move to the Trinity.

Trap questions

  1. "Is a thought true because of the chemicals in your brain, or because it matches reality? How do the chemicals know the difference?"
  2. "Why should nature be uniform tomorrow, on your view?"
  3. "What makes 'you ought to be rational' binding on me?"

30-second version

"If your mind is just chemistry shaped for survival, why trust it to tell you the truth about something as abstract as whether God exists? I trust my reason because a rational God made it. What's your reason for trusting yours?"

2-minute version

"I appreciate how much you value science and reason. I do too. But here's a puzzle. Science assumes nature is uniform: the same causes produce the same effects. You can't prove that by experiment without assuming it first. Reasoning assumes the laws of logic hold everywhere and that we ought to follow them. And trusting your conclusions assumes your brain is aimed at truth.

If nature is all there is, matter in motion, with no purpose, then why would any of that be so? Chemicals don't have obligations. Survival rewards useful behavior, not true beliefs about abstract questions. Even the atheist philosopher Thomas Nagel has said materialism has a serious problem here.

In the Christian view, it all fits: a faithful God governs nature, his mind is the source of logic, and he made our minds to know truth. So you and I can do science together, but I think only one of our worldviews explains why science works."

Further reading

  • Alvin Plantinga, Where the Conflict Really Lies: Science, Religion, and Naturalism (Oxford, 2011)
  • Thomas Nagel, Mind and Cosmos (Oxford, 2012): an atheist's critique of materialism
  • Sharon Street, "A Darwinian Dilemma for Realist Theories of Value," Philosophical Studies 127 (2006)
  • Victor Reppert, C.S. Lewis's Dangerous Idea (IVP, 2003)
  • C.S. Lewis, Miracles (1947), ch. 3
Argument1AMODERATE

Internal Critique of Pantheism and Monism

Name + thesis

If all is one and distinctions are ultimately illusion (as in Advaita Vedanta, much New Age thought, and philosophical pantheism), then logic, which depends on real distinctions (A is not non-A), and morality, which depends on the real distinction between good and evil, are ultimately unreal.

Key texts

  • Gen 1:1, 1:4: "God created the heavens and the earth... God separated the light from the darkness." (Creator and creation are distinct; creation contains real distinctions.)
  • Isa 5:20: "Woe to those who call evil good and good evil."
  • Rom 1:25: "they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator."

Their best case (steelman)

Advaita Vedanta (Shankara, 8th c.) teaches that Brahman alone is ultimately real, and the world of distinctions is maya (appearance). But Advaita distinguishes two levels: on the conventional level (vyavaharika), logic and morality fully apply; only on the ultimate level (paramarthika) do distinctions vanish. So logic is valid where we live. Many Buddhists and New Age thinkers say the same: ultimate reality is beyond concepts, and our categories are useful tools.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Logic and morality require that distinctions (true/false, good/evil, self/other) are real.
  • P2. Monism holds that, ultimately, distinctions are not real.
  • C. On monism, logic and morality are not ultimately real. They are useful illusions, and so is every argument for monism, including the one being offered.

Evidence for each premise

  • The law of non-contradiction is a distinction between a claim and its denial.
  • Shankara's two-level system concedes the point: logic is valid only at a level that is ultimately unreal.
  • Morality: if the distinction between the torturer and the tortured is ultimately illusory, then there is no ultimate wrong done.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: the two-levels reply. "Logic is valid at the level where arguments happen." Answer: Then the claim "ultimately all is one" is itself made at the conventional level, using distinctions it calls unreal. It can't be true in the ultimate sense, because at that level there is no true/false distinction. The view saws off the branch it sits on.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Ultimate reality is beyond logic."

  • Close (R1): Is that statement logical? If it is, it's not beyond logic; if not, I can't evaluate it, and neither can you.
  • Their comeback: "Words point beyond themselves; you need experience, not argument."
  • Close (R2): Then you can't tell me I'm wrong to believe in a personal God, because "wrong" is a distinction. Christianity gives a reality where unity and distinction are both ultimate: one God, three persons.

Boomerang check

"The Trinity is also beyond logic." Answer: The Trinity is above full comprehension but not against logic: one in essence (what God is) and three in persons (who God is). It doesn't affirm and deny the same thing in the same sense. See 2J on "1+1+1=3."

Strength rating

Why: The self-refutation point is strong, but sophisticated Vedantins and Buddhists have long-developed answers (two levels of truth), so the debate is not one-sided. Use it with care and respect.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Popular New Age Strong: "all is one" is often held loosely Ask about evil.
Trained Vedantin / Buddhist Knows the two-levels reply Press on how the ultimate level can be known. See 3D and 3E.

Trap questions

  1. "Is the difference between love and cruelty ultimately real?"
  2. "When you say 'all is one,' is that true and its opposite false?"
  3. "If the self is an illusion, who is having the illusion?"

30-second version

"If all distinctions are ultimately illusions, then so is the distinction between true and false. So the claim 'all is one' can't be ultimately true. Christianity gives you a God in whom unity and distinction are both real."

2-minute version

"I love that you want to see reality as a whole. But if, ultimately, there are no real distinctions, then the difference between kindness and cruelty isn't ultimately real either, and neither is the difference between true and false. That makes your own view impossible to hold as true.

The Christian view keeps both. There is one God, but within God there are real distinctions, Father, Son, and Spirit, who know and love one another. So unity is real and distinction is real, all the way down. That's why logic works and why love is more than an illusion."

Further reading

  • Vishal Mangalwadi, When the New Age Gets Old (IVP, 1992)
  • Harold Netland, Encountering Religious Pluralism (IVP, 2001)
  • Eliot Deutsch, Advaita Vedanta: A Philosophical Reconstruction (1969): a sympathetic academic account
Argument1AMODERATE

Trinitarian TAG: The One and the Many

philosophically contested; very effective with Muslims and unitarians

Name + thesis

Reality contains both unity (laws, kinds, universals) and diversity (particular things), and knowledge requires both. Only a God who is eternally one and many, one being in three persons, makes unity and diversity equally ultimate, and grounds love and communication without needing creation.

Key texts

  • Deut 6:4: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one."
  • Matt 28:19: "baptizing them in the name (singular) of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit."
  • John 1:1: "the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
  • John 17:24: "you loved me before the foundation of the world."
  • 1 John 4:8: "God is love."

Their best case (steelman)

A Muslim scholar (or a Jewish or unitarian philosopher) replies: God is absolutely one (tawhid), and diversity comes from his creative will. God doesn't need others to be loving or speaking. His attributes are eternal, and he expresses love and speech in creation when he chooses. Making love require an eternal other makes God dependent; the Trinity, not unitarianism, is the problem. And the "one and many" problem is a philosopher's puzzle, not a proof.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Human knowledge requires both unity (general categories, laws) and diversity (particulars), with neither reducible to the other.
  • P2. If ultimate reality is a bare unity, diversity is derivative or illusory. If ultimate reality is bare plurality, unity is derivative or arbitrary. Either way, knowledge loses one of its preconditions.
  • P3. Personal attributes such as love and communication require a subject and an object. If God is one person alone, then before creation he had no one to love or speak to, so these attributes were either unexercised (merely potential) or dependent on creation.
  • P4. The triune God is one being (unity) in three persons (real distinction), eternally. Unity and diversity are equally ultimate in him, and love and communication are eternal and complete within God.
  • C. The triune God, and only a God of that kind, grounds the one and the many and eternal personal love.

Evidence for each premise

  • The problem is ancient. Parmenides (all is one) and Heraclitus (all is flux) stand for the two horns. Van Til argued that the Trinity alone resolves it (The Defense of the Faith; see also R.J. Rushdoony, The One and the Many, 1971).
  • Love. "God is love" (1 John 4:8) describes his nature, not a later activity. John 17:24 places the Father's love for the Son "before the foundation of the world."
  • Communication. The Word was with God in the beginning (John 1:1). Speech within God is eternal.
  • The Islamic version of the problem. Sunni theology (Ash'ari and Maturidi) affirms that God's speech (kalam) is eternal, and many affirm that his love is an eternal attribute. That raises the question: eternal love and speech toward whom? (Full card: 2D-3.)

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Weakest premise: P3. A unitarian can say love is a disposition that can exist without being exercised, or that God loves himself.

Hardest objection: "Self-love is enough." Answer: Self-love is the lowest form of love, not the highest. The love the Bible and the Qur'an celebrate is love for another. A God whose only eternal love is self-love is less loving than a mother. And an unexercised "potential" love means God changes when he creates, becoming actually loving only then, which most Muslim theologians deny (God doesn't change).

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "God's love is eternal but directed at creation, which he always knew."

  • Close (R1): Loving an idea of a future creature is not the same as loving a person. And if creation was needed for God's love to be real, God depends on creation.
  • Their comeback: "God needs nothing (al-Ghani, 'the Self-Sufficient,' 2:263). His attributes are perfect in themselves."
  • Close (R2): Exactly. In the Trinity, God is self-sufficient in love: the Father loves the Son in the Spirit, with no need for creation. Only a triune God makes "self-sufficient" and "loving" both fully true.

2. "The Trinity is three gods."

  • Close (R1): Christians confess one God (Deut 6:4; Mark 12:29). The three persons share one divine nature; they are not three beings.
  • Their comeback: "Three persons who each are God equals three gods."
  • Close (R2): Only if "person" means a separate being, as it does for humans. In God, the persons are distinct relations within one undivided being. That is mysterious, but not contradictory. See 2J.

Boomerang check

"Your God needed the Son to be loving, so he is dependent." Answer: The Son is not something outside God that God needs; the Son is God. God's love is complete within his own being. That is the point.

Strength rating

Why: The texts are clear, and the problem it raises for unitarian theism is real and recognized by Muslim theologians (the long debates over eternal speech and attributes). But the "one and many" premise is philosophical and disputed, and Muslims have sophisticated replies. Very effective in conversation; MODERATE as a proof.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Sunni Athari / Salafi Affirm God's attributes literally (love, speech) and that the Qur'an is his eternal speech, so the question "toward whom?" bites Ask about eternal speech.
Ash'ari / Maturidi Have a developed theory of eternal attributes "neither God nor other than God" Engage the essence vs. action distinction (2D-3).
Twelver Shia Tend to identify attributes with the essence (closer to Mu'tazili views) Focus on love as relation.
Cultural Muslims Never considered it Ask simply: "Who did God love before he made anything?"
Jehovah's Witnesses / unitarians Same problem See 3G.

Trap questions

  1. "Was God loving before he created anything? Whom did he love?"
  2. "Was God speaking before creation? To whom?"
  3. "Is self-love the highest kind of love?"
  4. "Does God become more loving after creating?"

30-second version

"The Bible says God is love. But love needs someone to love. Before creation, whom did God love? In the Trinity, the Father has always loved the Son in the Spirit. God didn't need to create in order to love."

2-minute version

"Here's a question I find beautiful. We both believe God is loving. But love is always love for someone. So before God created anything, was he loving? Whom did he love?

If God is a single person alone, there's no one to love until he creates. Then either his love was only potential, or God needed creation to be fully who he is. Neither fits a perfect God.

Christianity says God has always been love, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have always known and loved one another, as one God. Jesus prayed, 'You loved me before the foundation of the world' (John 17:24). God didn't create because he was lonely. He created to share a love he already had. And that's the love he offers you."

Further reading

  • Cornelius Van Til, The Defense of the Faith (4th ed., P&R, 2008)
  • Michael Reeves, Delighting in the Trinity (IVP, 2012)
  • R.J. Rushdoony, The One and the Many (1971)
  • Nabeel Qureshi, No God but One, part 2 (on tawhid and the Trinity)

Conversation script (modeled on the 1985 Bahnsen–Stein debate)

Background: In 1985 Greg Bahnsen debated the atheist Gordon Stein at the University of California, Irvine. Bahnsen didn't trade evidence; he asked Stein to account for logic, science, and morality on atheism. Stein said logic consists of conventions and descriptions of how the world behaves. Bahnsen pressed that conventions and descriptions can't be universal, invariant, and binding. Bahnsen's best-known line, from his opening statement: "The transcendental proof for God's existence is that without Him it is impossible to prove anything" (debate transcript). This script is modeled on that approach; it is not a transcript.

Christian: You said you'd believe in God if there were enough evidence. Can I ask how you'll evaluate the evidence?

Skeptic: Logically. Scientifically.

Christian: Great. Let's start with logic. Is the law of non-contradiction true everywhere, even in parts of the universe no one has observed?

Skeptic: Sure.

Christian: How do you know? You haven't been there.

Skeptic: It's just how reality works.

Christian: I agree. But what is it? It's not made of matter. It's universal and unchanging, and it tells us how we ought to think. What does that fit better: a universe of matter in motion, or a universe made by a rational mind?

Skeptic: Logic is a human convention.

Christian: If it's a convention, a different culture could adopt contradictions. Then "God doesn't exist" could be true and false at once. You don't really think that, do you?

Skeptic: No... Fine, it's a description of how things behave.

Christian: A description of the past. How do you know it'll hold tomorrow?

Skeptic: Because it always has.

Christian: That's using the past to prove the future: induction justifying induction. I believe nature is regular because a faithful God governs it. You use the same regularity every day; I'm asking what your worldview offers to explain it.

Skeptic: I don't need an explanation. It's a brute fact.

Christian: Then nothing on your view tells you it will continue. You live as though the world is orderly, rational, and moral, which is exactly how the Bible describes the world God made. I'd suggest you know God more than you admit (Rom 1:21). Can I tell you who he is?

Lessons from the debate: stay on the preconditions; ask questions instead of lecturing; don't let "brute fact" end the conversation; move from God to the gospel.

Defense1A

"TAG is circular: you assume God to prove God."

The objection (best form)

"You assume the Christian God is the precondition of logic, then use logic to prove the Christian God. That's begging the question."

Answer

Every ultimate standard is circular in a broad sense: you can't justify logic without using logic, or reason without reasoning. John Frame distinguishes narrow circularity ("God exists, therefore God exists"), which is vicious, from broad circularity, where a worldview's ultimate commitment is tested by whether it can account for the evidence and for reasoning itself (Apologetics, ch. 1). TAG doesn't say "God exists because I assume he does." It says: put every worldview's ultimate commitment on the table and see which one makes reasoning possible. The skeptic is in the same position. He assumes the reliability of reason in order to argue for it.

30-second version

"Everyone's ultimate standard is circular at some level; you can't prove logic without logic. The question is which circle makes reasoning possible. I'm asking yours to account for itself, and offering mine for the same test."

Defense1A

"You can't refute every possible worldview" (the inductive-survey problem)

The objection (best form)

"Even if you refute naturalism, pantheism, and Islam, there are infinitely many possible worldviews. You can't show that only Christianity grounds logic without checking them all."

Answer

This is TAG's most serious objection, so answer it honestly.

  1. The classification reply (Van Til, Bahnsen). Worldviews divide by their ultimate reality. It is either an absolute, personal God, or something impersonal or finite (matter, chance, an impersonal one, many finite gods). Refuting the types covers their members. Weakness: the classification itself has to be defended.
  2. The modest reply (James Anderson and others). Treat TAG as showing that Christian theism provides the best account of the preconditions, and that every rival actually on offer fails. That's how all reasoning about worldviews works: you compare live options.
  3. The burden reply. If the skeptic thinks an unconsidered worldview would work, he should name it. "Some unknown view might work" is a hope, not an argument.

Use the modest form in public.

30-second version

"Fair point. I can't test every possible worldview, but no one can do that for any claim. I can test the ones people actually hold, and they fail where Christianity succeeds. If you have a better candidate, tell me and we'll test it."

Defense1A

"Why not another god?"

The objection (best form)

"Even if a God is required, why yours? Why not Allah, Zeus, or a deist god?"

Answer

TAG requires a God who is (1) absolute and personal, the source of logic, order, and morality, not subject to them; (2) one and many, grounding unity and diversity (the Trinitarian card); (3) self-revealing, so that we can know him and his standards. Finite gods like Zeus are themselves subject to fate and logic, so they can't ground them. A deist god doesn't reveal, so it gives no basis for knowing his standards. A unitarian god (Allah, the God of Jehovah's Witnesses) faces the one-and-many problem and the question of eternal love and speech. Only the triune God of Scripture meets all three.

30-second version

"The God who grounds reason has to be absolute, personal, both one and many, and self-revealing. Zeus isn't absolute, the deist god doesn't speak, and a solitary God has no one to love or speak to before creation. The triune God is the only candidate who fits."

Defense1A

"Logic and the uniformity of nature are brute facts."

The objection (best form)

"Some things are just how reality is. Logic and regularity are brute facts that need no explanation. Your God is a brute fact too."

Answer

A brute fact is a fact with no explanation. Three problems:

  1. Brute facts give no reason for expectation. If regularity is brute, there's no reason it should continue tomorrow. So induction is still unjustified.
  2. Brute facts can't be normative. "This is how things are" doesn't yield "this is how you ought to reason."
  3. God is not a brute fact in the same sense. Classical theism holds that God exists necessarily and of himself (aseity). His existence explains itself in a way that contingent regularities can't. Ending explanation in a necessary, rational, personal being is a different kind of stopping point from ending it in impersonal facts that could have been otherwise.

30-second version

"If order is a brute fact, nothing tells you it'll still be there tomorrow, and nothing tells you you ought to reason logically. I end with a necessary, rational God who explains both. You end with an unexplained accident."

Defense1A

Barry Stroud's critique

The objection (best form)

"Barry Stroud showed in 1968 that transcendental arguments only prove what we must believe, or how we must think, not what is actually true. At most TAG shows we must think as if God exists."

Answer

Stroud's point is serious against Kant-style arguments about the structure of our concepts. Three replies:

  1. TAG is about the preconditions of successful reasoning, not just of belief. The skeptic doesn't merely believe logic works; he succeeds in reasoning, predicting, and arguing. If those successes require God, then God is a precondition of real success, not just of belief.
  2. The skeptic's own position is self-refuting. To say "we only must think logic is valid, it may not be" uses logic to separate thought from reality, which assumes that logic is reliable about reality.
  3. Modest TAG survives. Even granting Stroud, TAG shows that the Christian worldview is uniquely able to make sense of our unavoidable practices, a strong reason to believe it.

Know this objection if you debate philosophers; ordinary conversations rarely raise it.

30-second version

"Stroud says transcendental arguments show only how we must think. But you don't just think logic works, you succeed in using it on the real world. I'm asking what makes that success possible."

Defense1A

"TAG is an argument from ignorance."

The objection (best form)

"You're saying 'I can't see how naturalism explains logic, so God did it.' That's just a God of the gaps. Science may explain it someday."

Answer

An argument from ignorance says "we don't know X, therefore God." TAG argues something different: that naturalism, by its nature, lacks the kind of resources needed, regardless of future discoveries. Future science can discover more physical facts, but logic, normativity, and the justification of induction are not physical facts awaiting discovery. And science itself presupposes them, so it can't be the thing that eventually grounds them.

30-second version

"I'm not saying 'we don't know, so God.' I'm saying science uses logic and induction, so it can't be what grounds them. More discoveries about matter won't turn matter into an ought."

1B

Supporting Arsenal

9 cards8 moderate1 weak

New terms

Kalam argument: The argument that the universe began to exist and so has a cause; named after kalam, medieval Islamic rational theology.

Contingent / necessary: A contingent thing could have failed to exist; a necessary thing could not fail to exist.

Principle of Sufficient Reason (PSR): The principle that everything that exists has an explanation of its existence.

Pure act (actus purus): In Aristotelian-Thomist philosophy, a being with no unrealized potential at all: God.

Multiverse: The hypothesis that our universe is one of a vast number of universes with different physical constants.

EAAN: Alvin Plantinga's Evolutionary Argument Against Naturalism: naturalism plus unguided evolution undermines trust in our own reasoning.

Hard problem of consciousness: David Chalmers' name for the puzzle of why physical processes are accompanied by subjective experience at all.

Cumulative case: A case in which several independent arguments together make a conclusion far more probable than any one argument alone.

These arguments reason from evidence within experience. They support TAG (1A) by showing that the same God it requires also explains the universe's beginning, existence, order, morality, minds, and mathematics. Two notes for using them with Muslims: (1) Muslims share almost all of these arguments; the Kalam argument was developed by Muslim theologians. They build common ground but don't distinguish Christianity from Islam. (2) So use them with atheists and agnostics, and with Muslims mainly to establish shared premises before moving to the Trinity, the cross, and the Dilemma.

Argument1BMODERATE

The Kalam Cosmological Argument

premise 2 rests on contested cosmology and philosophy

Name + thesis

Whatever begins to exist has a cause. The universe began to exist. Therefore the universe has a cause, and that cause must be timeless, spaceless, immensely powerful, and personal.

Key texts

  • Gen 1:1: "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth."
  • Heb 11:3: "the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible."
  • Ps 90:2: "from everlasting to everlasting you are God."

Their best case (steelman)

A skeptic replies: (1) "Begins to exist" and "cause" are concepts drawn from inside the universe; we can't apply them to the universe as a whole. (2) Quantum events occur without causes. (3) The Borde–Guth–Vilenkin theorem applies only to classical spacetime; quantum gravity models (Hartle–Hawking, Carroll–Chen) may avoid a beginning, and Alan Guth himself thinks the universe may be eternal. (4) Even if there is a cause, why a personal God?

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Whatever begins to exist has a cause.
  • P2. The universe began to exist.
  • C1. The universe has a cause.
  • C2. That cause is beyond space and time (it created them), enormously powerful, and personal (only a free agent explains a timeless cause producing a temporal effect).

Evidence for each premise

  • P1: Something coming from absolutely nothing, with no cause, is metaphysically absurd. "Nothing" has no properties, no potential, no quantum field. Quantum events happen within a quantum vacuum, which is not nothing.
  • P2 (philosophical): An actually infinite series of past events can't be traversed to reach today (al-Ghazali, The Incoherence of the Philosophers, first discussion; William Lane Craig).
  • P2 (scientific): Big Bang cosmology; the Borde–Guth–Vilenkin theorem (Physical Review Letters 90, 2003): any universe that has on average been expanding cannot be infinitely extended into the past; the second law of thermodynamics.
  • C2 (personal): a timeless, unchanging cause that produces an effect with a beginning implies a free choice. Otherwise an eternal sufficient cause would produce an eternal effect.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Weakest premise: P2's scientific support. Cosmologists debate whether BGV implies an absolute beginning. Sean Carroll argued in his 2014 debate with Craig that quantum cosmologies need not have one.

Answer: Lead with the philosophical argument against an infinite past, and treat the science as confirmation, not proof. Even eternal-inflation models typically require a beginning to inflation (BGV). Models without a beginning remain speculative.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Quantum mechanics shows things can come from nothing."

  • Close (R1): Quantum fluctuations arise within a vacuum governed by physical laws. That's something, not nothing.
  • Their comeback: "The laws themselves could produce the universe" (Lawrence Krauss, A Universe from Nothing, 2012).
  • Close (R2): Laws describe what happens; they don't make things happen. And laws are part of what needs explaining. Even the philosopher of physics David Albert criticized Krauss on exactly this point (New York Times review, March 2012).

2. "Who caused God?"

  • Close (R1): The premise is "whatever begins to exist has a cause." God, by definition, didn't begin.
  • Their comeback: "Then why not say the universe didn't begin?"
  • Close (R2): Because the evidence and the impossibility of an actually infinite past say it did. A timeless, uncaused, personal cause is the conclusion of an argument, not special pleading.

Boomerang check

Muslim use. Muslims (Ash'aris especially) champion this argument; it is called Kalam after Islamic theology. It establishes a Creator, not the Trinity. Don't treat it as an argument against Islam.

Atheist parity charge ("you define God as uncaused to escape the premise"): answered in escape route 2.

Strength rating

Why: P1 is intuitively strong and widely accepted. P2 is supported by good philosophical and scientific arguments but debated among cosmologists. A respectable argument with real force, not a knockout.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Popular atheist Strong; "who made God?" is the usual reply Use escape route 2.
Science-trained skeptic Will raise quantum cosmology Lead with the philosophical argument; keep the science modest.
Muslims They agree Use it to build common ground.

Trap questions

  1. "Do you think something can come from absolutely nothing, with no cause at all?"
  2. "If the past were infinite, how would we ever have arrived at today?"
  3. "What kind of cause could create space and time themselves?"

30-second version

"Everything that begins to exist has a cause, and the evidence says the universe began. So the universe has a cause beyond space and time, extremely powerful, and personal. That sounds a lot like God."

2-minute version

"Here's an old argument, actually developed by Muslim and Christian thinkers together in the Middle Ages. First, whatever begins to exist has a cause; things don't pop into being from absolutely nothing. Second, the universe began. Philosophers point out that an infinite past could never have been crossed to reach today, and modern cosmology points to a beginning too. So the universe has a cause. And think about what that cause must be like: it created space and time, so it's beyond them; it brought the whole universe into being, so it's immensely powerful; and it chose to create, so it's personal. The question isn't whether there's a cause. It's whether you'll get to know him."

Further reading

  • William Lane Craig and James D. Sinclair, "The Kalam Cosmological Argument," in The Blackwell Companion to Natural Theology (2009)
  • Al-Ghazali, The Incoherence of the Philosophers, first discussion
  • Sean Carroll vs. William Lane Craig, "God and Cosmology" debate (2014)
  • Alexander Vilenkin, Many Worlds in One (2006)
Argument1BMODERATE

The Leibnizian Contingency Argument

depends on a version of the Principle of Sufficient Reason

Name + thesis

Everything that exists has an explanation of its existence, either in the necessity of its own nature or in an external cause. The universe doesn't exist by necessity. So it has an external cause, a necessary being, which is God.

Key texts

  • Acts 17:24–25, 28: God "made the world and everything in it... he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything... In him we live and move and have our being."
  • Rev 4:11: "you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created."

Their best case (steelman)

Bertrand Russell, in his 1948 BBC debate with Frederick Copleston: "I should say that the universe is just there, and that's all." Contemporary critics add that the Principle of Sufficient Reason, if fully general, leads to "modal collapse" (everything becomes necessary). And the universe might be a necessary being itself.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Everything that exists has an explanation of its existence, either in the necessity of its own nature or in an external cause (a modest Principle of Sufficient Reason).
  • P2. The universe (the sum of contingent things) doesn't exist by the necessity of its own nature.
  • C1. The universe has an external cause.
  • P3. That cause can't be contingent (or it would be part of what needs explaining), so it is a necessary being.
  • C2. A necessary, transcendent cause of all contingent reality exists, which is what we mean by God.

Evidence for each premise

  • P1 is presupposed in science and daily life: we always look for explanations. Rejecting it only for the universe is arbitrary (the "taxicab fallacy": riding the principle until you reach the destination you want, then dismissing it).
  • P2: every part of the universe could have been otherwise; matter and energy have no feature that makes their non-existence impossible.
  • P3: an infinite chain of contingent explanations still leaves the whole chain unexplained.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "Modal collapse": a strong PSR implies God's choice to create was itself necessary, so everything is necessary. Answer: Use the modest PSR, which applies to the existence of things, not to every fact. Alexander Pruss defends a weaker principle that avoids collapse (The Principle of Sufficient Reason, Cambridge, 2006). Free choices can be explained by an agent's reasons without being necessitated.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "The universe is just there."

  • Close (R1): Would you accept that answer about anything else? If you found a glowing sphere in the woods, would "it's just there" satisfy you?
  • Their comeback: "The universe is different from things in it."
  • Close (R2): Making it bigger doesn't remove the need for an explanation. A bigger sphere still needs one.

2. "The universe itself is necessary."

  • Close (R1): Then nothing about it could have been different, not a single particle. That's very hard to believe.
  • Their comeback: "Maybe the underlying quantum field is necessary."
  • Close (R2): A field with particular properties and values is the paradigm of something that could have been different. Necessity belongs to something more basic than any physical structure.

Boomerang check

Muslims affirm this argument (Ibn Sina's "necessary existent," wajib al-wujud). It supports theism generally.

Strength rating

Why: The modest PSR is reasonable, and the argument is valid. But the PSR is contested among philosophers, and atheists can stop at "brute fact." Good, not decisive.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Philosophically curious Very effective Use the glowing-sphere illustration.
Muslims Agree (Ibn Sina) Common ground.

Trap questions

  1. "Why is there something rather than nothing?"
  2. "Is 'it's just there' an explanation you'd accept for anything else?"
  3. "Could the universe have been different?"

30-second version

"Everything that exists has an explanation. The universe could have been different or not existed at all, so its explanation lies outside it, in a being that exists necessarily. That's God."

2-minute version

"Have you ever wondered why there's something rather than nothing? Everything in the universe could have failed to exist. So could the universe as a whole. Things that might not have existed need an explanation outside themselves. If you trace that back, you can't keep appealing to more things that might not have existed; you have to reach something that exists by its very nature, that can't fail to exist. Christians and philosophers going back centuries have called that God. And the Bible says something more: he isn't just a necessary being, he's a person who 'gives to all mankind life and breath and everything' (Acts 17:25)."

Further reading

  • Alexander R. Pruss, The Principle of Sufficient Reason: A Reassessment (Cambridge, 2006)
  • Edward Feser, Five Proofs of the Existence of God (Ignatius, 2017), ch. 5 (rationalist proof)
  • G.W. Leibniz, Monadology (1714), §§32–38
  • Bertrand Russell and F.C. Copleston, BBC debate (1948), transcript in Russell, Why I Am Not a Christian
Argument1BMODERATE

Aquinas' Five Ways (Feser's Aristotelian Proof)

requires accepting Aristotelian metaphysics

Name + thesis

Change is real. Every change is the actualization of a potential by something already actual. A series of things actualizing each other here and now must terminate in something that is purely actual, with no potential at all: an unchanging, eternal, perfect being, which is God.

Key texts

  • Mal 3:6: "I the LORD do not change."
  • Jas 1:17: "the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change."
  • Exod 3:14: "I AM WHO I AM."

Their best case (steelman)

Modern physics doesn't use "potency and act." Newton's first law says motion continues without a mover. Aristotelian metaphysics is an outdated framework. And even if a "pure act" exists, it's an abstract principle, not the personal God of the Bible.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Change occurs: potentials become actual (water becomes hot, a cup's potential to be on the floor becomes actual).
  • P2. No potential actualizes itself; it is actualized by something already actual.
  • P3. A simultaneous (here-and-now) series of actualizers can't regress infinitely: if every member only passes on actuality, there is none to pass on.
  • C1. There is a first actualizer that is purely actual (actus purus).
  • C2. A purely actual being is unchanging, eternal, immaterial, one, perfect, intelligent, and all-powerful: God (Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 2, a. 3; Feser, Five Proofs, ch. 1).

Evidence for each premise

  • The argument is about hierarchical causes (a cup held by a hand, held by a person, sustained by a floor, sustained by the earth...), not a chain back in time. It does not depend on the universe having a beginning; Aquinas thought that couldn't be proven by reason.
  • Newton's first law is about motion (local change), not about the metaphysics of change. Feser argues inertia is compatible with the Aristotelian principle.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "Aristotelian metaphysics is outdated." Answer: "Potency and act" is a philosophical analysis of change, not a physical theory. It's defended by contemporary philosophers (Feser; David Oderberg, Real Essentialism, 2007). But it does take time to explain, which is why this argument works best in longer conversations.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Things change by themselves, through physical laws."

  • Close (R1): Laws describe how actual things act; they don't supply actuality. The laws themselves exist only as the behavior of actual things.
  • Their comeback: "Then the most basic physical level (fields, particles) is the first actualizer."
  • Close (R2): Fundamental particles and fields have potentials (they can change state), so they are not pure act. Something with no potential at all is still needed.

Boomerang check

Muslims accept versions of this argument; Maturidis and philosophers in the Avicennian tradition especially. Atharis (and Ibn Taymiyya) are wary of "pure act" metaphysics because they think it denies God's real attributes and actions. Expect a mixed reception.

Strength rating

Why: Powerful and rigorous within its framework, but persuasive only to those willing to engage classical metaphysics. Not ideal for short conversations.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Catholic / philosophy-educated Strong Use Feser.
Popular atheist Hard to follow Use Kalam or contingency instead.
Salafi Suspicious of the metaphysics Don't lead with it.

Trap questions

  1. "Can something give itself what it doesn't have?"
  2. "What's holding up the cup right now, and what's holding that up?"
  3. "If every link only passes on power, where does the power come from?"

30-second version

"Things change only when something already actual changes them. Here and now, that chain can't go on forever. It must end in something purely actual, needing nothing, unchanging: God."

2-minute version

"Think of a chandelier hanging by a chain. Each link holds up the one below, but only because it's held up by the one above. If the chain went on forever, with no hook, nothing would hold it up. Change is like that. Everything that changes is being changed, right now, by something else, and that thing depends on something else. The series has to end in something that doesn't depend on anything, that is fully actual, with no unrealized potential at all. Aquinas called it the First Mover, and he said, 'this everyone understands to be God.'"

Further reading

  • Edward Feser, Five Proofs of the Existence of God (Ignatius, 2017)
  • Edward Feser, Aquinas: A Beginner's Guide (Oneworld, 2009)
  • Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 2, a. 3
  • David S. Oderberg, Real Essentialism (Routledge, 2007)
Argument1BWEAK

The Modal Ontological Argument

in public debate; philosophically interesting

Name + thesis

If it is even possible that a maximally great being (all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly good, existing in every possible world) exists, then such a being exists in every possible world, including ours.

Key texts

  • Ps 14:1: "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God.'"
  • Heb 11:6: "whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists."

Their best case (steelman)

The whole argument rests on premise 1 ("it's possible that a maximally great being exists"). In modal logic, that premise is equivalent to the conclusion. So a skeptic who doubts God's existence should doubt the possibility premise too. And the parody works just as well: "It's possible that a maximally great being doesn't exist," which, by the same logic, implies God is impossible.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. It is possible that a maximally great being exists.
  • P2. If that's possible, then a maximally great being exists in some possible world.
  • P3. If it exists in some possible world, it exists in every possible world (that's part of maximal greatness).
  • C. So it exists in the actual world (Alvin Plantinga, The Nature of Necessity, 1974).

Evidence for each premise

  • The logic (system S5 of modal logic) is valid.
  • For P1: the concept of God seems coherent; no contradiction has been shown in it.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Fatal in debate: the parody ("possibly, no maximally great being exists") is just as intuitive, and it proves the opposite. Plantinga himself said the argument shows belief in God is rational, not that it is proven.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "The possibility premise begs the question."

  • Close (R1): Concede it is close to the conclusion. Present the argument as showing that God is either necessary or impossible, so the atheist must claim God is impossible, a heavy burden.
  • Their comeback: "Fine, God is impossible: the problem of evil, divine hiddenness."
  • Close (R2): Now you're debating evil and hiddenness, which is a better use of time. Move to those arguments directly.

Boomerang check

Muslims can use it equally. It doesn't distinguish Christianity.

Strength rating

Why: Valid and philosophically fascinating, but in debate its key premise is no more obvious than its denial. Drop it from public debates. Its one real use is to show that the atheist must argue God is impossible, not just unproven.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Most audiences Feels like a trick Don't use it.
Philosophy students Interesting discussion Use it only to show the necessary-or-impossible point.

Trap questions

  1. "Do you think God is impossible, or just unproven?"
  2. "Is there a contradiction in the idea of a perfect being?"

30-second version

"I don't lead with this one. But it shows something: if God is even possible, he's necessary. So an atheist has to show that God is impossible, not just unproven."

2-minute version

"Philosophers have an argument showing that God, if he exists, exists necessarily, in every possible world. That means God is either necessary or impossible; there's no middle option. So the real question for an atheist isn't 'is God unproven?' but 'is God impossible?' That's a much harder claim to defend. I don't think the argument proves God by itself. But it clarifies what each side has to show."

Further reading

  • Alvin Plantinga, God, Freedom, and Evil (Eerdmans, 1977): the accessible version
  • Alvin Plantinga, The Nature of Necessity (Oxford, 1974), ch. 10
  • Graham Oppy, Ontological Arguments and Belief in God (Cambridge, 1995): the main critic
Argument1BMODERATE

The Fine-Tuning Argument

the fine-tuning data are mainstream physics; the inference to design is debated

Name + thesis

The physical constants and initial conditions of the universe fall within extremely narrow ranges that permit life. This is far more likely if a designer exists than if the universe is the product of chance or necessity.

Key texts

  • Ps 19:1: "The heavens declare the glory of God."
  • Isa 45:18: God "formed the earth... he did not create it empty, he formed it to be inhabited!"
  • Rom 1:20: "his invisible attributes... have been clearly perceived... in the things that have been made."

Their best case (steelman)

(1) The multiverse: if there are countless universes with varying constants, some would be life-permitting, and we necessarily find ourselves in one (the anthropic principle). (2) Future physics may show the constants must take these values. (3) Life could adapt to other conditions. (4) "Who designed the designer?"

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The fine-tuning of the universe for life is due to physical necessity, chance, or design.
  • P2. It is not plausibly due to physical necessity or chance.
  • C. It is due to design.

Evidence for each premise

  • The data are mainstream. Examples: the cosmological constant appears fine-tuned to roughly 1 part in 10^120 relative to natural expectations; small changes to the strong nuclear force or the ratio of electromagnetism to gravity would prevent stable atoms or stars (Martin Rees, Just Six Numbers, 1999; Luke Barnes and Geraint Lewis, A Fortunate Universe, Cambridge, 2016).
  • Against necessity: current physics treats the constants as free parameters, not required values.
  • Against chance: the probabilities are tiny, and the multiverse is (a) speculative and untestable, and (b) itself needs a fine-tuned mechanism to generate universes.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: the multiverse. Answer: (1) There's no direct evidence for it. (2) The mechanisms proposed (eternal inflation, the string landscape) require their own fine-tuned laws. (3) The multiverse predicts we should more likely be "Boltzmann brains" (lone observers fluctuating into existence) than inhabitants of a large, orderly universe. That's a well-known problem in cosmology. Concede that the debate is live.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "If it weren't fine-tuned, we wouldn't be here to notice" (the anthropic principle).

  • Close (R1): True, but it doesn't explain anything. If you survived a firing squad of 100 marksmen, "if they'd hit me, I wouldn't be here" doesn't explain why they all missed (John Leslie's illustration).
  • Their comeback: "Unless there were billions of firing squads (the multiverse)."
  • Close (R2): Then you need evidence of billions of firing squads, and a fine-tuned mechanism that produces them.

2. "Who designed the designer?"

  • Close (R1): To recognize design, you don't need to explain the designer. Archaeologists recognize arrowheads without knowing who made them.
  • Their comeback: "A designer would be more complex than the universe" (Richard Dawkins, The God Delusion, ch. 4).
  • Close (R2): God is a simple, immaterial mind, not a complex physical system. And God is not a contingent being who needs a designer.

Boomerang check

Muslims use this argument too, sometimes alongside "scientific miracles in the Qur'an" claims. Note the difference: fine-tuning is mainstream physics, while "scientific miracle" readings are usually stretched (see 2G).

Strength rating

Why: The fine-tuning data are accepted across physics. The inference to design is debated because of the multiverse. Strong in conversation, MODERATE as a proof.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Science-minded Strong Use the numbers from Barnes and Lewis.
Multiverse fan Will push back Use the firing squad and Boltzmann brains.
Muslims Agree Common ground.

Trap questions

  1. "If you survived a firing squad of 100 marksmen, would you ask why they all missed?"
  2. "Is there any direct evidence of other universes?"
  3. "What produces all those universes, and is it fine-tuned?"

30-second version

"The laws of physics are set to values that permit life, within incredibly narrow ranges. That's what we'd expect if a designer exists. The main alternative, an untestable multiverse, needs fine-tuning of its own."

2-minute version

"Physicists, including many who aren't religious, agree on something striking: the constants of nature fall in a very narrow range that allows life. Change the strength of gravity or the strong force slightly and there are no stable stars or atoms. Why? Necessity doesn't explain it: physics doesn't require these values. Chance is very unlikely. So many physicists turn to a multiverse. But there's no evidence for it, and any machine that makes universes would itself need to be finely tuned. I think the simpler explanation is the one most people see when they look up at the stars: a mind set the dials. 'The heavens declare the glory of God' (Ps 19:1)."

Further reading

  • Luke A. Barnes and Geraint F. Lewis, A Fortunate Universe: Life in a Finely Tuned Cosmos (Cambridge, 2016)
  • Robin Collins, "The Teleological Argument," in The Blackwell Companion to Natural Theology (2009)
  • Martin Rees, Just Six Numbers (1999)
  • Sean Carroll, The Big Picture (2016): a naturalist's reply
Argument1BMODERATE

The Moral Argument

very effective in conversation

Name + thesis

If God does not exist, objective moral values and duties do not exist. Objective moral values and duties do exist. Therefore God exists.

Key texts

  • Rom 2:14–15: the Gentiles "show that the work of the law is written on their hearts."
  • Mic 6:8: "He has told you, O man, what is good."
  • Gen 1:27: humans made "in the image of God," the basis of human dignity.

Their best case (steelman)

(1) Euthyphro: is something good because God commands it (then morality is arbitrary), or does God command it because it's good (then goodness is independent of God)?
