(2) Godless realism: moral facts are necessary truths, like math (Wielenberg). (3) Moral disagreement across cultures shows morality is constructed.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. If God does not exist, objective moral values and duties do not exist.
  • P2. Objective moral values and duties do exist.
  • C. Therefore, God exists.

Evidence for each premise

  • P2: we perceive moral truths as clearly as physical ones. Torturing a child for fun is wrong, whatever anyone thinks. Even critics of religion make objective moral claims against religion.
  • P1: without a personal moral lawgiver, obligations have no source: to whom is the obligation owed? Atheist philosophers have acknowledged this: J.L. Mackie, an atheist, argued that objective values would be "queer," and that if they existed they would make God's existence more likely (The Miracle of Theism, 1982, ch. 6).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: Euthyphro. Answer: A false dilemma. Goodness is grounded in God's nature, not in arbitrary commands or an external standard. God's commands flow from his good character, so they are neither arbitrary nor independent (William Alston; Robert Adams, Finite and Infinite Goods, 1999). For the Islamic version, see 2D-2.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "You don't need God to be good."

  • Close (R1): Agreed. Atheists can be very moral. The argument is about whether morality is grounded, not whether people know or practice it.
  • Their comeback: "Morality is grounded in human well-being."
  • Close (R2): Why is human well-being obligatory rather than just preferred? And on naturalism, why are humans more valuable than other animals?

2. "Morality evolved."

  • Close (R1): Evolution explains moral feelings, not moral truth. If we'd evolved to value cruelty, would cruelty be good?
  • Their comeback: "There is no objective morality, just preferences."
  • Close (R2): Then the Holocaust wasn't wrong, only disliked. Most people can't live with that conclusion, and neither can you when someone wrongs you.

Boomerang check

Atheist: "Your God commanded genocide (the Canaanites)." This is a serious objection; it's addressed in 1F, and in the boomerang check on Old Testament warfare in 2I. Note that it assumes objective morality, which supports P2.

Muslim: agrees with the argument in general, but the Ash'ari version of Islam faces Euthyphro sharply (2D-2).

Strength rating

Why: P2 is widely accepted intuitively; P1 is supported by serious arguments but contested by atheist moral realists. Very effective in ordinary conversation.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Popular atheist Very strong; most hold objective moral beliefs Ask about justice and human rights.
Moral relativist Must be shown P2 first See 3H.
Muslims Agree Use it to set up 2D-2.

Trap questions

  1. "Is torturing a child for fun wrong, even if a whole culture approved of it?"
  2. "To whom do we owe our moral obligations?"
  3. "Why are human beings more valuable than other animals, on your view?"

30-second version

"If there's no God, there's no objective right and wrong, only preferences. But some things really are wrong, like torturing a child for fun, whatever anyone thinks. So there's a moral lawgiver."

2-minute version

"Do you think some things are really wrong, not just disliked, but wrong even if everyone approved? Most of us do. Racism, cruelty to children, betrayal. But if the universe is just matter, with no purpose, where would that kind of objective obligation come from? Molecules don't owe anything to anyone. The best explanation is that there's a moral lawgiver whose character is goodness itself. The Bible says his law is written on our hearts (Rom 2:15). That's why we know right and wrong, and also why we know we fall short. Which is where Jesus comes in."

Further reading

  • C.S. Lewis, Mere Christianity, Book 1
  • Robert M. Adams, Finite and Infinite Goods (Oxford, 1999)
  • Paul Copan, Is God a Moral Monster? (Baker, 2011)
  • Erik Wielenberg, Robust Ethics (Oxford, 2014): the atheist alternative
  • J.L. Mackie, The Miracle of Theism (1982)
Argument1BMODERATE

The Argument from Reason and Plantinga's EAAN

published and debated; a strong internal critique

Name + thesis

If naturalism and unguided evolution are both true, the probability that our cognitive faculties are reliable is low or inscrutable. Then the naturalist has a reason to doubt all his beliefs, including naturalism itself. So naturalism combined with evolution defeats itself.

Key texts

  • Gen 1:27: humans made in God's image, with minds fitted to know truth.
  • Prov 2:6: "the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding."

Their best case (steelman)

Natural selection favors true beliefs, because true beliefs lead to successful action. A creature that believed tigers were cuddly would be eaten. Our faculties are reliable at least for practical matters, and science corrects our errors beyond that.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Evolution selects for adaptive behavior, not for true belief as such.
  • P2. On naturalism plus evolution (N&E), the content of beliefs is either causally irrelevant to behavior, or connected to it in many ways that don't require truth. So the probability that our faculties are reliable, given N&E, is low or inscrutable.
  • P3. Anyone who accepts N&E and sees P2 has a defeater for the belief that his faculties are reliable.
  • P4. A defeater for the reliability of one's faculties is a defeater for every belief produced by them, including N&E.
  • C. N&E is self-defeating (Plantinga, Warrant and Proper Function, 1993, ch. 12; Where the Conflict Really Lies, 2011, ch. 10).

Evidence for each premise

  • P1: many false beliefs can produce adaptive behavior (Plantinga's example of Paul, who wants to be eaten by tigers but believes running away is the best way to get eaten).
  • P2: materialists often hold that beliefs are neural states whose content doesn't do causal work. If content is irrelevant to behavior, selection is blind to truth.
  • Supporting voices: C.S. Lewis, Miracles, ch. 3; Thomas Nagel, Mind and Cosmos (2012); Darwin's own "horrid doubt" whether "the convictions of man's mind, which has been developed from the mind of the lower animals, are of any value" (letter to William Graham, 3 July 1881).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "True beliefs are more adaptive overall; evolution does track truth for ordinary beliefs." Answer: Even granting reliability for practical beliefs, our abstract beliefs (metaphysics, philosophy, whether naturalism is true) have little to do with survival. Naturalism is exactly that kind of belief.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Science corrects our errors."

  • Close (R1): Science uses the same faculties. You can't check the reliability of a ruler with the same ruler.
  • Their comeback: "The success of technology proves our faculties are reliable."
  • Close (R2): Technology shows our faculties work for engineering. It doesn't show they are reliable about whether the universe has a purpose.

Boomerang check

"If God made our minds, why do we make so many mistakes?" Answer: Theism explains general reliability (minds made for truth) and also error (finitude and sin, Rom 1:21). Naturalism can't explain the reliability itself.

Strength rating

Why: Published in top venues, defended and criticized at length (see Naturalism Defeated?, ed. James Beilby, Cornell, 2002). A strong internal critique, but not a consensus result.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Science-minded atheist Surprising and effective Use Darwin's "horrid doubt."
Philosophy student Will know the debate Use the defeater structure.
Muslims Agree Common ground.

Trap questions

  1. "Does natural selection care whether your beliefs are true, or only whether your behavior helps you survive?"
  2. "How would believing in naturalism help a caveman survive?"
  3. "Can you check a ruler using the same ruler?"

30-second version

"If your brain was shaped only for survival, not truth, why trust it on abstract questions like whether God exists? Darwin himself had that 'horrid doubt.' I trust my reason because God made it."

2-minute version

"Here's something Darwin himself worried about. If our minds developed only because they helped our ancestors survive, then evolution cared about behavior, not truth. Useful beliefs survive, true or not. That might be fine for avoiding tigers. But for big abstract questions, like whether the universe is just matter, survival gives no reason to trust our conclusions. So if naturalism is true, we'd have reason to doubt the very reasoning that led us to naturalism. On the Christian view, God made our minds to know truth. That's why reasoning works, and why I think it leads to him."

Further reading

  • Alvin Plantinga, Where the Conflict Really Lies (Oxford, 2011), ch. 10
  • James Beilby, ed., Naturalism Defeated? Essays on Plantinga's Evolutionary Argument Against Naturalism (Cornell, 2002)
  • C.S. Lewis, Miracles (1947), ch. 3
  • Victor Reppert, C.S. Lewis's Dangerous Idea (IVP, 2003)
Argument1BMODERATE

The Argument from Consciousness

Name + thesis

Conscious experience (what it is like to see red or feel pain) is not explained by physical processes alone. It is far less surprising if a conscious God exists who creates conscious beings than if the universe is only matter.

Key texts

  • Gen 2:7: God "breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature."
  • Ps 139:13–14: "you formed my inward parts... I am fearfully and wonderfully made."

Their best case (steelman)

Neuroscience is making steady progress correlating experience with brain states. "We can't explain it yet" is a gap argument. Some philosophers (Daniel Dennett, Consciousness Explained, 1991) say the "hard problem" is an illusion.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Conscious states (subjective experience, intentionality, a unified self) are real.
  • P2. They are not reducible to, or fully explained by, physical states.
  • P3. Their existence is much more probable if a conscious God exists than if naturalism is true.
  • C. Consciousness is evidence for God (J.P. Moreland; Richard Swinburne).

Evidence for each premise

  • P2: David Chalmers (not a theist) named it the "hard problem" ("Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness," Journal of Consciousness Studies 2, 1995). Thomas Nagel, "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" (Philosophical Review, 1974). Correlation is not explanation: knowing every brain fact doesn't tell you what pain feels like.
  • P3: on theism, mind is fundamental, so minds in creation are expected. On naturalism, mind is a late and surprising byproduct of mindless matter.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "Gap argument." Answer: The argument isn't "science hasn't explained it." It's that physical description, by its nature, is third-person and quantitative, while experience is first-person and qualitative. No amount of the first adds up to the second.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Consciousness is just brain activity."

  • Close (R1): Brain activity can be measured from outside. Your pain can't be. How is one identical to the other?
  • Their comeback: "It's an illusion" (Dennett).
  • Close (R2): An illusion is an experience. Calling consciousness an illusion presupposes consciousness.

Boomerang check

Muslims agree (the ruh, 17:85: "the soul is of the affair of my Lord"). Common ground.

Strength rating

Why: The "hard problem" is widely acknowledged, including by non-theists, but its theistic explanation is one option among several (panpsychism, dualism without God). Good supporting evidence.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Materialist Effective Use "what does pain feel like?"
Spiritual-but-not-religious Agree with P2 Steer from "consciousness is God" (3I) to a personal Creator.

Trap questions

  1. "Could a scientist who knows every fact about your brain know what your coffee tastes like to you?"
  2. "If consciousness is an illusion, who is being fooled?"

30-second version

"Your experience, what it's like to see red or feel pain, isn't something brain scans can capture. Mind seems to be more than matter. That fits a world made by a Mind."

2-minute version

"Neuroscience is amazing, but there's a puzzle even atheist philosophers call the 'hard problem.' A scientist can map which neurons fire when you taste coffee. But the taste itself, what it's like for you, isn't in the map. Physics describes things from the outside; experience is from the inside. If the universe is only matter, it's very surprising that inner experience exists at all. If a conscious God made us in his image, it's exactly what you'd expect."

Further reading

  • J.P. Moreland, Consciousness and the Existence of God (Routledge, 2008)
  • David Chalmers, The Conscious Mind (Oxford, 1996)
  • Richard Swinburne, The Existence of God (2nd ed., Oxford, 2004), ch. 9
Argument1BMODERATE

The Applicability of Mathematics

Name + thesis

Abstract mathematics, often developed with no practical purpose, turns out to describe the physical universe with astonishing precision. That is expected if the same rational God who thinks mathematical truths also made the world; on naturalism it is a mystery.

Key texts

  • Prov 3:19: "The LORD by wisdom founded the earth."
  • Job 38:4–5: "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?... Who determined its measurements?"
  • Wisdom of Solomon 11:20 (deuterocanonical): "you have arranged all things by measure and number and weight."

Their best case (steelman)

Mathematics is a human invention, refined because it works. We select the math that fits. Or mathematical structure is physical structure (Max Tegmark's "mathematical universe"), so the fit is no surprise.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Mathematics developed abstractly often applies to physics with remarkable precision (complex numbers in quantum mechanics; non-Euclidean geometry in general relativity).
  • P2. On naturalism there is no reason to expect abstract structures discovered by minds to govern physical reality.
  • P3. On theism, the same divine mind is the source of both mathematical truth and physical order, and made human minds to grasp both.
  • C. The applicability of mathematics is evidence for God.

Evidence for each premise

  • Eugene Wigner, Nobel laureate in physics: "The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences," Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 13 (1960). He called it "a wonderful gift which we neither understand nor deserve."
  • Mark Steiner, The Applicability of Mathematics as a Philosophical Problem (Harvard, 1998): argues the success of mathematics in physics is an "anthropocentric" fact that sits awkwardly with naturalism.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "Selection effect: we notice the math that works." Answer: That doesn't explain why math developed for purely abstract reasons, decades or centuries earlier, should later fit the deepest physical laws. Riemann's geometry (1854) waited sixty years for Einstein.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Math is invented, not discovered."

  • Close (R1): Then why does an invention predict phenomena (the positron, gravitational waves) that no one had observed?
  • Their comeback: "Because physical reality is mathematical."
  • Close (R2): That restates the puzzle. Why is reality mathematical, and why can our minds grasp it?

Boomerang check

Muslims agree. Common ground.

Strength rating

Why: Wigner's puzzle is widely recognized. The theistic explanation is natural but not the only one proposed.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
STEM students Very effective Use the Riemann–Einstein example.
Others Less intuitive Use briefly.

Trap questions

  1. "Why should equations invented on paper predict what happens in distant galaxies?"
  2. "Did Einstein invent the geometry of spacetime, or discover it?"

30-second version

"Mathematicians work out abstract structures on paper, and decades later physicists find the universe runs on them. Wigner called it 'unreasonable.' It's reasonable if the same Mind made both math and matter."

2-minute version

"Here's something that amazed the physicist Eugene Wigner. Mathematicians often develop ideas just for their beauty, with no use in mind. Then, decades later, physicists discover those exact ideas describe the universe. Riemann worked out a strange geometry in 1854; sixty years later Einstein needed it for gravity. Why should the universe follow equations worked out in someone's head? If the universe is a mindless accident, that's a mystery. If a rational God made both the universe and our minds, it's exactly what you'd expect."

Further reading

  • Eugene Wigner, "The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences" (1960)
  • Mark Steiner, The Applicability of Mathematics as a Philosophical Problem (Harvard, 1998)
  • Vern S. Poythress, Redeeming Mathematics (Crossway, 2015)

How it all fits together: one cumulative case with TAG

Think of the arguments as layers, each adding something the others don't:

Layer Argument What it adds
Foundation TAG (1A) Without God you can't reason at all, so the debate itself presupposes him.
Existence Kalam, contingency, Aquinas The universe needs a necessary, timeless, powerful, personal cause.
Order Fine-tuning, mathematics That cause is intelligent and purposeful.
Persons Consciousness, reason (EAAN) That cause is a mind, the source of our minds.
Goodness Moral argument That cause is good and the source of obligation.
Identity Trinitarian TAG + the resurrection (1C) That God is the triune God revealed in Jesus Christ.

How to combine them with TAG. Presuppositionalists and classical apologists debate method. A practical synthesis (close to John Frame's): TAG explains why evidence can be evidence at all; the evidential arguments show that the world looks exactly as the God of TAG would make it. In conversation, start where the person is: evidence for the curious, TAG for the confident skeptic, the resurrection for the person who already believes in God. Always move toward Jesus.

What the arsenal does not do. None of these arguments, except Trinitarian TAG, distinguishes Christianity from Islam or Judaism. With Muslims, they are common ground. The decisive questions are the identity of God (Trinity), the person of Jesus, and the reliability of revelation: 1C and Part 2.

1C

The Case for Christianity

4 cards3 strong1 moderate

New terms

Textual criticism: The scholarly method of reconstructing an original text by comparing its surviving copies.

Minimal facts: Gary Habermas's method: argue for the resurrection only from facts that nearly all critical scholars, including skeptics, accept.

Son of Man: Jesus' favorite self-title, drawn from Daniel 7:13–14, where 'one like a son of man' receives everlasting dominion and worship.

Messiah (Arabic al-Masih): 'Anointed one': the promised king of Israel. The Qur'an also calls Jesus al-Masih (3:45).

Kerygma: The earliest Christian proclamation: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised (1 Cor 15:3–4).

Masoretic Text (MT): The standard Hebrew text of the Old Testament, preserved by Jewish scribes (the Masoretes).

Septuagint (LXX): The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, made by Jews in the 3rd–1st centuries BC.

Theism is not yet Christianity. This section establishes three things: the New Testament is a reliable source, Jesus rose from the dead, and Jesus claimed to be God. It ends with the prophecies that anticipated him. These cards matter for Part 2 too: the Qur'an affirms Jesus as Messiah and prophet but denies his crucifixion and deity, so the historical case here is where most conversations with Muslims eventually land.

Argument1CSTRONG

The Reliability of the New Testament

textual transmission; historical reliability of every detail is more debated

Name + thesis

We can know what the New Testament authors wrote with a high degree of confidence, and those authors wrote within living memory of Jesus, drawing on eyewitness testimony.

Key texts

  • Luke 1:1–4: "just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses... it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account."
  • 1 Cor 15:3–8: "I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received... he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive."
  • 2 Pet 1:16: "we did not follow cleverly devised myths... we were eyewitnesses of his majesty."
  • John 19:35: "He who saw it has borne witness—his testimony is true."

Their best case (steelman)

Bart Ehrman's case (Misquoting Jesus, 2005; Jesus, Interrupted, 2009): we don't have the originals; copies contain hundreds of thousands of variants; the Gospels are anonymous, written 40–65 years after Jesus by non-eyewitnesses in Greek, and they contradict each other. Muslim apologists add: the Bible has had many hands, while the Qur'an was memorized and written in Muhammad's lifetime.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. If a text survives in many early, independent manuscripts across regions, its original wording can be reconstructed with high confidence (the method of textual criticism used for all ancient texts).
  • P2. The NT survives in more and earlier manuscripts than any other ancient text, in several independent lines of transmission.
  • P3. The NT's core documents were written within about 20–65 years of Jesus, in the lifetime of eyewitnesses, and they preserve even earlier oral traditions.
  • C. The NT is a textually reliable record of what its authors wrote, and its authors were in a position to know the events they report.

Evidence for each premise

  • Manuscripts: over 5,000 Greek manuscripts (counts vary, and the popular "5,800" figure needs care; see Peter Gurry in Myths and Mistakes, ch. 2), plus thousands in Latin, Syriac, and Coptic, and an immense body of quotations in early Christian writers. Earliest: fragments from the 2nd–3rd centuries; complete Gospels by the 4th (Codex Vaticanus, c. 300–350; Codex Sinaiticus, c. 330–360).
  • Variants: the large number of variants results from the large number of manuscripts. The great majority are spelling, word order, or obvious slips. Ehrman himself says his position "does not actually stand at odds with" Bruce Metzger's view that "essential Christian beliefs are not affected by textual variants in the manuscript tradition of the New Testament" (Misquoting Jesus, paperback edition, appended interview, p. 252, as cited; VERIFY against the book).
  • Dates: Paul's letters, AD c. 48–64 (undisputed). Mark is usually dated c. 65–70, Matthew and Luke c. 80–90, John c. 90–95 by mainstream critical scholars. Many conservatives date the Synoptics earlier.
  • Early traditions: the creed in 1 Cor 15:3–7 is widely dated to within a few years of the crucifixion; Paul says he "received" it, probably in Jerusalem around AD 35 (Gal 1:18).
  • Eyewitness character: Richard Bauckham, Jesus and the Eyewitnesses (2nd ed., 2017), argues the Gospels preserve named eyewitness testimony.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "Anonymous Gospels written decades later." Answer: (1) Ancient biographies were often formally anonymous; the titles ("according to Mark") are universal in the manuscripts and early writers (Papias c. 110–130, via Eusebius; Irenaeus c. 180). (2) 40–60 years is within living memory, and far closer than most ancient biographies (the earliest biographies of Alexander the Great come over 300 years after him). (3) The argument for the resurrection (1C, next card) doesn't even require the Gospels to be eyewitness accounts; it uses facts accepted by critical scholars.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "We don't have the originals."

  • Close (R1): We don't have the originals of any ancient book, including Plato, Tacitus, or the Qur'an's first written sheets. Scholars reconstruct originals from copies; the NT has more copies than any of them.
  • Their comeback: "But the copies differ."
  • Close (R2): The differences are known and catalogued, which is how we know the original. And no central doctrine depends on a disputed reading.

2. "The Qur'an was preserved better."

  • Close (R1): Apply one standard. The Qur'an's text was standardized by Uthman, who burned other copies (Sahih al-Bukhari 4987, narrated by Anas ibn Malik). The NT was never centrally controlled, so its variants survived and can be compared.
  • Their comeback: "That proves the Qur'an is uniform."
  • Close (R2): It proves the Qur'an's text was made uniform. Uniformity by editorial decision is not the same as perfect preservation of the original. See 2F.

Boomerang check

"Then the Qur'an's early manuscripts also prove it reliable." Answer: Yes, apply the same standard both ways. The Qur'an's text is well preserved from the Uthmanic recension onward, and Christians should say so. The real questions are what came before Uthman (2F), and whether the Qur'an is true. Textual stability proves only that a text was copied well, not that its claims are from God.

Strength rating

Why: The textual reliability of the NT is the consensus of textual critics, including skeptics like Ehrman (on core beliefs). Dating Paul's letters and the 1 Cor 15 creed early is near-consensus. The historical reliability of every Gospel detail is more debated, so don't overclaim it.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Muslims (all groups) They're often told the Bible was "changed many times" Pair with 2B-1. Use one standard (2F).
Quranists Same Stay on the Qur'an's own affirmations (2A).
Atheists who've read Ehrman Know the variant numbers Quote Ehrman's own concession.

Trap questions

  1. "Do we have the originals of any ancient book? How do historians reconstruct them?"
  2. "Which important Christian belief depends on a disputed manuscript reading?"
  3. "Why would the Qur'an tell Christians to judge by their Gospel (5:47) if it was hopelessly corrupted?"

30-second version

"We have more early manuscripts of the New Testament than of any other ancient book, by far. Scholars, including skeptics, agree we can reconstruct what the authors wrote, and no core belief depends on a disputed reading."

2-minute version

"People often say the Bible has been changed so many times we can't trust it. But here's how historians work. We don't have the original of any ancient book. We reconstruct them from copies. For most ancient writers, we have a handful of copies made many centuries later. For the New Testament, we have thousands, some within a couple of centuries of the originals, spread across different regions and languages. That's why scholars, even skeptics like Bart Ehrman, agree that no essential Christian belief depends on an uncertain reading. And the documents were written within living memory of Jesus. Paul quotes a creed about Jesus' death and resurrection that goes back to within a few years of the events."

Further reading

  • Peter J. Gurry and Elijah Hixson (eds.), Myths and Mistakes in New Testament Textual Criticism (IVP Academic, 2019)
  • Richard Bauckham, Jesus and the Eyewitnesses (2nd ed., Eerdmans, 2017)
  • Craig Blomberg, The Historical Reliability of the New Testament (B&H, 2016)
  • Bart D. Ehrman, Misquoting Jesus (HarperOne, 2005): the strongest skeptical case
Argument1CSTRONG

The Resurrection via Minimal Facts

the facts are near-consensus; the inference is what's debated

Name + thesis

A small set of historical facts, granted by nearly all critical scholars (including skeptics), is best explained by Jesus' bodily resurrection. Every naturalistic alternative fails to explain all of them.

Key texts

  • 1 Cor 15:3–8: "Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures... he was buried... he was raised on the third day... he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers... Then he appeared to James... Last of all... he appeared also to me."
  • Mark 16:6: "He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him."
  • Acts 2:32: "This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses."

Their best case (steelman)

A skeptic (Ehrman, Gerd Lüdemann, Dale Allison, who is a Christian but agnostic on some details) says: historians, as historians, can't conclude a miracle, because miracles are by definition the least probable explanation. The appearances were visions, perhaps grief hallucinations or religious experiences; such experiences of the dead are common. The empty tomb story may be a later legend. A Muslim adds a different alternative: God made someone else look like Jesus (4:157), so the disciples sincerely but mistakenly believed.

Premises → conclusion

The minimal facts (Gary Habermas and Michael Licona, The Case for the Resurrection of Jesus, 2004):

  • F1. Jesus died by crucifixion.
  • F2. His disciples sincerely believed that he rose and appeared to them.
  • F3. Paul, a persecutor of the church, was suddenly converted.
  • F4. James, Jesus' skeptical brother, was suddenly converted.

  • F5. The tomb was empty. (Widely but not universally accepted; Habermas estimates roughly 75% of scholars who write on it.)

  • P1. These facts are established by ordinary historical method.

  • P2. The best explanation of all of them together is that God raised Jesus from the dead.
  • C. Jesus rose from the dead.

Evidence for each premise

  • F1: all four Gospels; Paul; Tacitus, Annals 15.44; Josephus, Antiquities 18.63–64 (core authentic in the majority view); the Talmud (b. Sanhedrin 43a, "on the eve of Passover they hanged Yeshu"). John Dominic Crossan (a skeptic): the crucifixion is "as sure as anything historical can ever be" (Jesus: A Revolutionary Biography, 1994). Full card: 2B-14.
  • F2: the 1 Cor 15 creed (within a few years of the events); the disciples' willingness to suffer (Acts; 1 Clement 5; Polycarp). Ehrman: "It is indisputable that some of the followers of Jesus came to think that he had been raised from the dead, and something had to have happened to make them think so" (How Jesus Became God, 2014, pp. 182–183, as quoted by Michael J. Kruger).
  • F3: Paul's own letters (Gal 1:13–16; 1 Cor 15:8–9; Phil 3:4–7).
  • F4: Mark 3:21 and John 7:5 (his family's unbelief); 1 Cor 15:7 (an appearance to James); Josephus, Antiquities 20.200 (James, "the brother of Jesus who was called Christ," was stoned, AD 62).
  • F5: the earliest proclamation was in Jerusalem, where the tomb could be checked; the earliest Jewish counter-claim admits the tomb was empty ("the disciples stole him," Matt 28:13–15); women are named as the first witnesses, an embarrassing detail no one would invent in that culture.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "Historians can't conclude a miracle." Answer: That's a philosophical assumption (methodological naturalism), not a historical finding. If God exists (1A, 1B), a resurrection isn't impossible, and the question becomes which explanation fits the facts. Licona's The Resurrection of Jesus: A New Historiographical Approach (IVP, 2010) treats this at length.

Second hardest: "Group hallucinations." Answer: Hallucinations are private experiences; there is no well-documented case of a group sharing the same hallucination. And hallucinations don't explain F3 or F4 (enemies and skeptics), or F5 (the empty tomb).

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "The disciples hallucinated."

  • Close (R1): Hallucinations don't happen to groups, to skeptics like James, or to enemies like Paul. And they don't empty tombs.
  • Their comeback: "Grief visions of the dead are common, even in groups."
  • Close (R2): Grief visions don't produce the conviction that a dead man has been bodily raised. Jews believed in a general resurrection at the end of time, not a single man raised in the middle of history. The disciples' claim was new and specific.

2. "Legend developed over time."

  • Close (R1): The 1 Cor 15 creed dates within a few years of the events. That's too early for legend to replace the core facts.
  • Their comeback: "The creed only mentions appearances, not an empty tomb."
  • Close (R2): "He was buried... he was raised" implies the body left the grave, for a first-century Jew. And Paul's audience in Corinth included people who could ask the living witnesses ("most of whom are still alive").

3. (Muslim) "Someone else was made to look like him" (4:157).

  • Close (R1): That doesn't explain the appearances after the crucifixion. Who appeared to Peter, James, Paul, and five hundred people?
  • Their comeback: "God raised Jesus to heaven before the crucifixion; the appearances were false or later inventions."
  • Close (R2): Then God caused his own prophet's followers to preach a false message. See 2B-6 and 2D-1.

Boomerang check

"Christians reject other religions' miracle claims (Muhammad splitting the moon) but accept their own." Answer: Apply one standard. The resurrection is supported by sources within a few years of the event and accepted facts granted by skeptics. The moon-splitting reports appear in hadith collections compiled about two centuries later (Sahih al-Bukhari 3636 (in-book 61/140), narrated by Ibn Mas'ud), and no ancient non-Muslim astronomer recorded it. We can evaluate both by the same historical criteria (2G).

Strength rating

Why: F1–F4 are accepted by the vast majority of critical scholars, including skeptics; F5 by a strong majority. The rival theories each fail to explain the full set. The remaining dispute is philosophical (whether miracles can be concluded), not historical.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Atheists Strong; most haven't heard the facts laid out Lead with F1 and F3.
Muslims (all groups) Accept Jesus as Messiah and his miracles; deny the crucifixion Stay on F1 and the appearances; then 2B-14.
Jews Respect the Jewish context Emphasize Jewish expectations of resurrection; see 3C.

Trap questions

  1. "What best explains why Paul, who was killing Christians, suddenly became one?"
  2. "Why would Jesus' own skeptical brother die for the claim that Jesus rose?"
  3. "If the tomb wasn't empty, why didn't the authorities just show the body?"
  4. "Have you ever heard of a group of people having the same hallucination?"

30-second version

"Almost all historians, including skeptics, agree that Jesus died by crucifixion, his disciples believed they saw him alive, and both a persecutor (Paul) and a skeptic (James) became believers. The resurrection explains all of that. Nothing else does."

2-minute version

"I'd like to show you why I believe Jesus rose, using only facts that skeptical historians accept. First, Jesus died by crucifixion; even Roman and Jewish sources say so. Second, his disciples sincerely believed they saw him alive afterward. That belief goes back to a creed Paul quotes, from within a few years of the events. Third, Paul, who was hunting Christians, suddenly became one. Fourth, James, Jesus' brother, who didn't believe in him during his life, became a leader of the church and died for it. And most scholars also accept that the tomb was empty.

Now, what explains all of that together? Hallucinations don't happen to groups or to enemies, and they don't empty tombs. A stolen body wouldn't convince Paul or James. Legend doesn't develop in a few years. The explanation the first witnesses gave is still the best one: God raised him. And if he rose, then what he said about himself, and about you, is true."

Further reading

  • Gary R. Habermas and Michael R. Licona, The Case for the Resurrection of Jesus (Kregel, 2004)
  • Michael R. Licona, The Resurrection of Jesus: A New Historiographical Approach (IVP Academic, 2010)
  • N.T. Wright, The Resurrection of the Son of God (Fortress, 2003)
  • Dale C. Allison Jr., The Resurrection of Jesus: Apologetics, Polemics, History (T&T Clark, 2021): an honest, cautious treatment
  • Bart D. Ehrman, How Jesus Became God (HarperOne, 2014): the skeptical alternative
Argument1CSTRONG

Jesus' Claims to Deity

from the texts; critical scholars debate the authenticity of some sayings

Name + thesis

Jesus claimed the authority and identity of God: to forgive sins against God, to be the divine Son of Man of Daniel 7, to exist before Abraham as "I am," and to receive worship as Lord and God.

Key texts

  • Mark 2:5–10: "'Son, your sins are forgiven.'... 'Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?'... 'that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.'"
  • Mark 14:61–64: "'Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?' And Jesus said, 'I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.' And the high priest tore his garments and said... 'You have heard his blasphemy.'"
  • Dan 7:13–14: "with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man... And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve (Aramaic yiflechun, a verb used of worship) him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion."
  • John 8:58: "Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am." (Then "they picked up stones to throw at him.")
  • John 20:28: "Thomas answered him, 'My Lord and my God!'" Jesus accepts it.

Their best case (steelman)

Muslim debaters (Shabir Ally, the late Ahmed Deedat) ask: "Where did Jesus say 'I am God, worship me'?" They argue: "Son of God" means a righteous servant (Ps 2:7; Luke 3:38 calls Adam a son of God); "Son of Man" means a human being (Ezek 2:1); forgiving sins can be delegated authority (John 20:23, the disciples forgive sins); John's Gospel is late and theological; and Jesus said "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28) and prayed to God. Critical scholars add that Mark 14:62 and John 8:58 may be Christian formulations rather than Jesus' own words.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. In first-century Judaism, forgiving sins against God, sharing God's throne, receiving universal worship, and taking God's name were prerogatives of God alone.
  • P2. Jesus claimed and exercised these prerogatives (Mark 2; Mark 14 with Dan 7; John 8:58; John 20:28).
  • P3. His opponents understood these as claims to deity and charged him with blasphemy.
  • C. Jesus claimed to be God, not merely a prophet.

Evidence for each premise

  • Mark 2: the scribes' objection ("who can forgive sins but God alone?") shows they understood the claim; Jesus doesn't correct them but proves his authority by healing. The forgiveness is of sins against God, not against himself.
  • Mark 14 + Dan 7: Jesus combines Ps 110:1 (seated at God's right hand) and Dan 7:13 (coming on the clouds, a mode of travel the Old Testament ascribes to God: Isa 19:1; Ps 104:3). The high priest's reaction (tearing garments, "blasphemy") shows how it was heard. Mark is our earliest Gospel.
  • John 8:58: "I am" (ego eimi) with no predicate echoes God's self-naming (Exod 3:14; Isa 43:10–13 LXX). The crowd's reaction (stoning, the penalty for blasphemy, Lev 24:16) confirms the meaning.
  • John 20:28: a Jewish disciple calls Jesus "my God"; Jesus accepts it, while angels and apostles refuse worship (Acts 10:25–26; Rev 22:8–9).
  • Earliest worship: Phil 2:6–11 (c. AD 60 or earlier, possibly a pre-Pauline hymn) applies Isa 45:23 ("to me every knee shall bow") to Jesus. Larry Hurtado, Lord Jesus Christ (2003): devotion to Jesus as divine arose very early among Jewish believers.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "Jesus never said the exact words 'I am God; worship me.'" Answer: Neither did he say "I am a prophet only." People in the first century made claims in their own idiom. Jesus claimed God's prerogatives and titles in ways his Jewish hearers understood perfectly; that's why they tried to stone him. See the full defense in 2J.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "'Son of Man' just means human."

  • Close (R1): Sometimes, yes (Ezek 2:1). But Jesus says "the Son of Man... coming with the clouds of heaven," quoting Dan 7, where the figure receives everlasting dominion and the service of all nations.
  • Their comeback: "Daniel's figure is a symbol for Israel (Dan 7:18, 27)."
  • Close (R2): Even so, Jesus identifies himself as that figure, sitting at God's right hand. And the high priest called it blasphemy, not a claim to be Israel.

2. "Forgiving sins was delegated; the disciples did it too" (John 20:23).

  • Close (R1): The disciples announce forgiveness in Jesus' name, after his resurrection, by the Spirit he gives. In Mark 2 Jesus forgives on his own authority.
  • Their comeback: "Jesus said, 'I can do nothing of myself' (John 5:30)."
  • Close (R2): The same chapter says the Son does whatever the Father does, gives life as the Father does, and should be honored "just as they honor the Father" (John 5:19–23). Unity of action is the point.

Boomerang check

"Then who was Jesus praying to? Can God pray to God?" Answer: The Son prays to the Father: distinct persons within one God. Jesus' humanity is real, so he prays, grows, hungers, and dies. Christianity has always confessed Jesus as truly God and truly man. See 2J.

"The Qur'an says Jesus will deny claiming deity (5:116)." Answer: 5:116 has Jesus deny telling people to take him and his mother as gods. No Christian group worshiped Mary as a member of the Trinity. See 2B-10.

Strength rating

Why: The texts are clear, and Mark 2 and 14 are in the earliest Gospel. Some critical scholars doubt the authenticity of particular sayings, but even they agree the earliest Christians worshiped Jesus within a few years (Hurtado). For Muslims, who accept the Injil as revelation, the texts carry special force.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Muslims (all groups) They'll ask "where did he say it?" Start with Mark 2 (the earliest Gospel, no "late John" objection).
Jehovah's Witnesses Will cite John 14:28 and the New World Translation of John 1:1 See 3G.
Jews Will hear "blasphemy" in the Jewish sense Use Dan 7 respectfully.

Trap questions

  1. "In Mark 2, the scribes said 'only God can forgive sins.' Did Jesus correct them, or prove his authority?"
  2. "Why did the high priest tear his robe at Jesus' answer?"
  3. "Why did the crowd pick up stones after 'before Abraham was, I am'?"
  4. "When Thomas called Jesus 'my God,' why didn't Jesus rebuke him?"

30-second version

"Jesus claimed to forgive sins against God, to be Daniel's Son of Man who shares God's throne, and to exist before Abraham as 'I am.' His enemies understood exactly what he meant; that's why they called it blasphemy."

2-minute version

"People often ask, 'Where did Jesus say he's God?' He said it in the language of his time, and his listeners understood. In Mark, the earliest Gospel, he forgives a man's sins. The religious leaders say, 'Only God can forgive sins.' Jesus doesn't say they misunderstood; he heals the man to prove he has that authority. At his trial, asked if he's the Messiah, he says, 'I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven,' claiming to be the figure in Daniel 7 who receives everlasting worship. The high priest tore his robe and called it blasphemy. In John, he says, 'Before Abraham was, I am,' and they tried to stone him. Thomas fell at his feet and said, 'My Lord and my God,' and Jesus accepted it. A prophet would have refused."

Further reading

  • Robert M. Bowman Jr. and J. Ed Komoszewski, Putting Jesus in His Place (Kregel, 2007)
  • Larry W. Hurtado, Lord Jesus Christ: Devotion to Jesus in Earliest Christianity (Eerdmans, 2003)
  • Richard Bauckham, Jesus and the God of Israel (Eerdmans, 2008)
  • Shabir Ally vs. James White, debates on Jesus' deity (watch for the "where did he say it" framing)
  • Bart D. Ehrman, How Jesus Became God (2014), with the reply by Michael Bird et al., How God Became Jesus (Zondervan, 2014)
Argument1CMODERATE

Messianic Prophecy (Isaiah 53, Daniel 9, Psalm 22)

each text has real interpretive and textual debates

Name + thesis

Texts written centuries before Jesus describe a suffering servant who dies for others' sins and is vindicated (Isa 53), a timetable for the Messiah's coming and being "cut off" before the destruction of the Temple (Dan 9), and a righteous sufferer whose hands and feet are pierced (Ps 22). Jesus fits them uniquely.

Key texts

  • Isa 53:5–6, 10–11: "he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities... the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all... when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days... by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous."
  • Dan 9:25–26: "from the going out of the word to restore and build Jerusalem to the coming of an anointed one (mashiach), a prince, there shall be seven weeks. Then for sixty-two weeks... And after the sixty-two weeks, an anointed one shall be cut off... And the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary."
  • Ps 22:1, 16, 18: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?... they have pierced my hands and feet [textual note below]... they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots."

Their best case (steelman)

Jewish interpreters (Rashi, and much Jewish tradition since the Middle Ages) read Isaiah's servant as the nation of Israel (Isa 41:8, 49:3 call Israel "my servant"). Critical scholars date Daniel to c. 165 BC and read Dan 9 as referring to the high priest Onias III (murdered 171 BC) and Antiochus IV. In Ps 22:16 the standard Hebrew text (the Masoretic Text) reads ka'ari, "like a lion, my hands and feet," not "pierced." And the Gospel writers may have shaped their stories to fit the prophecies.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. These texts were written well before Jesus (Isaiah attested in the Great Isaiah Scroll, c. 125 BC; Psalms and Daniel attested among the Dead Sea Scrolls).
  • P2. Isa 53 describes an individual, innocent servant who suffers vicariously, dies, and is vindicated; Dan 9 places an "anointed one" being "cut off" before the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple (AD 70); Ps 22 describes a sufferer mocked, pierced, his garments divided, who then proclaims God's deliverance to the nations.
  • P3. Jesus fits these descriptions in ways that are historically grounded (crucifixion, death before AD 70, the rise of a worldwide community worshiping the God of Israel).
  • C. The prophecies point to Jesus.

Evidence for each premise

  • Isa 53 and an individual: the servant suffers for "my people" (Isa 53:8), so he is distinct from them; he is innocent ("he had done no violence," Isa 53:9), while Israel is repeatedly called sinful in Isaiah (Isa 1:4; 59:2). Some ancient Jewish sources read the passage messianically (Targum Jonathan renders Isa 52:13 "my servant the Messiah," though it reinterprets the suffering).
  • Dan 9: on any reckoning, the "anointed one" is "cut off" before the city and sanctuary are destroyed. The Temple was destroyed in AD 70, so a messiah must have come before it. (The exact chronology is debated even among Christians; avoid precise date calculations in debate.)
  • Ps 22:16 (Ps 22:17 in Hebrew numbering): the oldest Hebrew witness, a Dead Sea Scroll fragment (5/6HevPs), reads ka'aru, written with a final vav (a verb, "they dug/pierced"; Peter Flint's edition in Discoveries in the Judaean Desert 38), though critics note the same scribe sometimes wrote yod like vav; and the Septuagint (Greek, pre-Christian) reads oruxan, "they dug." The garments and lots detail (Ps 22:18) is recorded in all four Gospels and, crucially, Roman soldiers had no motive to fulfill Jewish prophecy.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: the servant is Israel. Answer: Isaiah does call Israel the servant, but in Isa 49:3–6 the servant Israel has a mission to Israel ("to bring Jacob back to him"), so the servant is an individual who embodies Israel. In 53 the servant suffers for the people. Even many Jewish scholars acknowledge the individual reading has early support. Be respectful; see 3C.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "The Gospel writers invented details to fit the prophecies."

  • Close (R1): Some details were beyond anyone's control: the manner of death (crucifixion, a Roman method), the timing before AD 70, and the rise of a global faith in Israel's God.
  • Their comeback: "The garments detail could still be invented."
  • Close (R2): Possibly. That's why the argument should lean on the publicly checkable facts, not on small details. The crucifixion itself is the best-attested fact about Jesus (2B-14).

Boomerang check

Muslim: "Muhammad is prophesied in the Bible too (Deut 18; Song 5:16)." Answer: Apply the same test: specific, written beforehand, fulfilled in checkable ways. Those claims are tested in 2B-4, and most fail on context.

Jewish: "Christians read Jesus into texts that aren't about him." Answer: Take each text in context and admit where readings are contested (as above).

Strength rating

Why: Isa 53 is a powerful text with a good case for the individual reading. Dan 9's chronology is debated, though the "before AD 70" point is solid. Ps 22:16 has a real textual issue. Taken together, MODERATE. Don't present prophecy as mathematical proof.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Jews Isa 53 is sensitive and contested Be respectful; see 3C.
Muslims Accept Jesus as Messiah, so the debate is about how he fulfilled it Isa 53 shows the Messiah suffers and dies for sins, against Qur'an 4:157.
Skeptics Will raise dating and "the Gospels invented it" Lean on the checkable points.

Trap questions

  1. "In Isaiah 53, the servant suffers for 'my people.' Can the people suffer for themselves?"
  2. "Daniel says the anointed one is 'cut off' before the city and sanctuary are destroyed. The Temple fell in AD 70. Who came before that?"
  3. "Why would the Messiah need to suffer for others, if a sinless prophet could just be taken to heaven?"

30-second version

"Seven centuries before Jesus, Isaiah described God's servant 'pierced for our transgressions' who dies and is vindicated. Daniel says the anointed one is 'cut off' before the Temple's destruction in AD 70. Jesus fits both."

2-minute version

"Let me read you something written long before Jesus. Isaiah 53: 'He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities... the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.' This servant is innocent, suffers in the place of others, dies, and then 'sees his offspring' and 'prolongs his days.' We have a copy of Isaiah from about 125 BC, so this isn't a later Christian insertion. Daniel 9 adds a timeline: an anointed one is 'cut off' before the city and sanctuary are destroyed, and the Temple was destroyed in AD 70. If the Messiah was going to come and die before that, who else could it be? This is why Christians say the cross wasn't a defeat. It was the plan all along."

Further reading

  • Michael L. Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vols. 2–3 (Baker, 2000–2003)
  • Kristin M. Swenson, "Psalm 22:17: Circling Around the Problem Again," Journal of Biblical Literature 123.4 (2004)
  • John J. Collins, Daniel (Hermeneia, 1993): the critical view

1D

Scripture Alone: The Apostolic Standard

3 cards1 strong

New terms

Sola scriptura: "Scripture alone": the teaching that Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith, and every other authority must be tested by it.

Apostolic deposit: The faith taught by Christ's apostles, "once for all delivered to the saints" (Jude 3).

Holy Tradition: In Catholic and Orthodox teaching, the apostolic faith handed down in the church's life, councils, liturgy, and fathers, alongside or around Scripture.

Canon: The list of books recognized as Scripture.

This handbook is apostolic in one specific sense: every theological claim is settled by Scripture, and by Scripture alone. Church fathers, councils, creeds, historians, and the other side's sources (the Qur'an, hadith, the Catechism, Nag Hammadi) are quoted as historical witnesses or as the other side's own claims, never as an authority over the Bible. When a card says what Christians believe, the "Scripture alone" field shows where the Bible teaches it. If Scripture doesn't teach something, the handbook doesn't either.

Argument1DSTRONG

Scripture Is the Only Infallible Rule

as "the only infallible rule we can verify today"; the canon question needs preparation

Name + thesis

Scripture alone (sola scriptura). The apostles' teaching is the final authority for the church, and the only place we can be sure we have it today is the written Scripture. Church tradition, councils, and leaders are real and useful, but they are fallible and must be tested by Scripture. They don't stand beside it.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • Scripture is God-breathed and makes the believer "complete, equipped for every good work" (2 Tim 3:16–17).
  • Jesus judged the religious tradition of his day by Scripture and condemned it where it "made void the word of God" (Mark 7:8–13).
  • The Bereans were praised for testing even an apostle's preaching "to see if these things were so" (Acts 17:11).
  • "Do not go beyond what is written" (1 Cor 4:6).
  • The faith was "once for all delivered to the saints" (Jude 3); even an angel preaching another gospel is accursed (Gal 1:8–9).
  • Verdict: Scripture claims final authority for itself and subjects every other teacher to it.

Key texts

  • 2 Tim 3:15–17: "the sacred writings... are able to make you wise for salvation... All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work."
  • Mark 7:13: "...thus making void the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down."
  • Matt 22:29, 31: "You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God... have you not read what was said to you by God?"
  • Isa 8:20: "To the teaching and to the testimony! If they will not speak according to this word, it is because they have no dawn."

Their best case (steelman)

A thoughtful Catholic or Orthodox Christian would say:

  1. The church came first. For decades there was no New Testament. The apostles handed on the faith orally, and Paul tells the Thessalonians to hold to traditions "by word of mouth or by letter" (2 Thess 2:15).
  2. The Bible doesn't list its own books. Someone had to decide which books are Scripture. That was the church, guided by the Spirit. If the church's judgment can be trusted for the canon, it can be trusted for doctrine.
  3. The church is "the pillar and buttress of the truth" (1 Tim 3:15). Jesus promised the gates of hell wouldn't prevail against it (Matt 16:18) and that the Spirit would guide it into all truth (John 16:13).
  4. Scripture alone produces chaos. Without an authoritative interpreter, Protestants split into countless denominations. "No prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation" (2 Pet 1:20).
  5. The Bible never says "Scripture alone." 2 Tim 3:16 says Scripture is profitable, not that it is the only authority.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The final authority for Christian doctrine is the teaching of Christ and his apostles (Eph 2:20; Jude 3).
  • P2. That teaching was delivered "once for all" and is now available to us with certainty only in the inspired writings (2 Tim 3:16; 2 Pet 1:15; 2 Pet 3:1–2).
  • P3. Every other source (tradition, councils, leaders) is fallible and can contradict God's word (Mark 7:8–13; Gal 2:11–14).
  • C. Therefore Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith, and every other authority must be tested by it (Acts 17:11).

Evidence for each premise

P1. Jesus gave the apostles his authority to teach (Matt 28:18–20; John 14:26). The church is "built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone" (Eph 2:20). A foundation is laid once.

P2. The apostles wrote so their teaching would outlast them: "I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things" (2 Pet 1:15). Peter puts the apostles' commands alongside the holy prophets (2 Pet 3:1–2), and he calls Paul's letters "Scriptures" (2 Pet 3:16). 1 Tim 5:18 quotes Luke 10:7 as "Scripture" next to Deut 25:4. No unwritten apostolic teaching can be identified today with the same certainty. The Catholic and Orthodox churches don't agree on a list of unwritten traditions.

P3. Jesus condemned a tradition that was ancient, respected, and claimed to come from Moses (Mark 7:8–13). Peter, an apostle, was publicly wrong in Antioch and was corrected (Gal 2:11–14). If an apostle in person could err in practice, later leaders can err too. Councils have contradicted each other: the Council of Hieria (754), which called itself ecumenical, condemned icons, and the Second Council of Nicaea (787) reversed it. Something above councils has to decide between them.

Old Testament precedent. Israel had no infallible teaching office, and the priests and scribes were often wrong. Yet Jesus held ordinary people responsible to know Scripture: "have you not read?" (Matt 12:3; 19:4; 22:31). God's people were judged by the written word, not by the leaders' interpretation of it.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: the canon. "The Bible doesn't contain a table of contents. You accept 27 New Testament books on the church's authority."

Answer: The church recognized the canon; it didn't create it. The books were authoritative because God inspired them, and the churches received them as such (1 Thess 2:13). Israel recognized the Old Testament books without an infallible council, and Jesus treated that collection as "Scripture" that "cannot be broken" (John 10:35; Luke 24:44). Paul says the Jews were "entrusted with the oracles of God" (Rom 3:2), yet they were not infallible. Being a reliable witness to Scripture doesn't make someone an infallible authority over it. Note too that the Roman Catholic Church didn't dogmatically define its canon until the Council of Trent (1546), and the Orthodox churches still differ on the Old Testament's extent. So "the church settled the canon" isn't a simple fact on their side either.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "2 Thess 2:15 commands oral tradition."

  • Close (R1): Paul is speaking of what he himself taught them in person and by letter, so both are apostolic teaching. Then ask: what specific doctrine, not found in Scripture, can you show came from Paul's spoken word? No church has produced a verified list.
  • Their comeback: "The church's living tradition preserved it."
  • Close (R2): That assumes what's in dispute. Jesus showed that a tradition claiming Mosaic origin can nullify God's word (Mark 7:13). The only way to test a claimed tradition is against the apostolic teaching we can verify, which is Scripture.

2. "1 Tim 3:15 makes the church the pillar of truth."

  • Close (R1): A pillar holds up something above itself. The church supports and proclaims the truth; it isn't its source. The truth in context is the gospel of the next verse (1 Tim 3:16).
  • Their comeback: "So the church is the guarantee of truth."
  • Close (R2): Paul is writing to the church at Ephesus, the very church Jesus later warned would lose its lampstand unless it repented (Rev 2:4–5). A church that can lose its lampstand isn't infallible.

3. "Who interprets? 2 Peter 1:20 forbids private interpretation."

  • Close (R1): Read 2 Pet 1:20–21 to the end. It's about where prophecy came from: no prophecy came from the prophet's own will, but from the Holy Spirit. It isn't about readers.
  • Their comeback: "Then you're your own pope."
  • Close (R2): Every Catholic and Orthodox believer also uses private judgment: to decide which church to trust, and to interpret the councils and Catechism. Scripture assumes ordinary believers can understand it (Ps 19:7; 2 Tim 3:15, where Timothy knew it "from childhood"; Acts 17:11).

4. "The Bible never says 'Scripture alone.'"

  • Close (R1): The doctrine is that Scripture is the only infallible rule, and that is taught: it alone is God-breathed (2 Tim 3:16), and everything else is to be tested by it (Acts 17:11; Isa 8:20; 1 Cor 4:6).
  • Their comeback: "'Profitable' doesn't mean 'sufficient.'"
  • Close (R2): Paul says Scripture makes the man of God "complete, equipped for every good work" (2 Tim 3:17). Nothing needed for faith and godliness is missing.

Boomerang check

"You use church fathers and councils too." Yes, as witnesses. We read Irenaeus and Athanasius the way we read any historian: valuable, but tested by Scripture. The Nicene Creed is accepted because it summarizes Scripture faithfully (John 1:1; Col 2:9), not because a council said so.

"Protestants disagree about baptism and other doctrines." True, but Catholics and Orthodox disagree with each other about the papacy, purgatory, and the Filioque, despite both claiming an authoritative tradition. An infallible interpreter hasn't produced unity either. Disagreement shows that people err, not that Scripture is unclear on the gospel.

Strength rating

STRONG (on the "only infallible rule we can verify" framing). Every premise rests on clear texts, and the main objections have clear answers. The canon objection is the hardest; prepare the answer above before you use this card with a trained Catholic or Orthodox apologist.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Catholic converts / trained apologists Will lead with the canon and 2 Thess 2:15 Use the canon answer and ask which unwritten traditions are verified.
Eastern Orthodox Speak of Scripture within Holy Tradition, not beside it Ask how a council is known to be ecumenical (Hieria vs. Nicaea II).
Cultural Catholics Rarely read the Bible; often assume the church wrote it Start with Mark 7:8–13 and Acts 17:11.
Muslims Agree that a final scripture should judge Use it to frame 2A: the Qur'an itself points back to the earlier Scripture.

Trap questions

  1. "When Jesus disagreed with the Pharisees' tradition, what did he use to correct it?" (Mark 7:8–13)
  2. "Can you name one doctrine that came from the apostles' spoken word, isn't in Scripture, and is verified?"
  3. "When two councils that both claimed to be ecumenical contradicted each other, how did the church decide which one was right?"
  4. "If the Bereans tested Paul by Scripture, can we test anyone by less?" (Acts 17:11)

30-second version

"Jesus judged even ancient religious tradition by Scripture (Mark 7:13), and the Bereans tested Paul himself by Scripture (Acts 17:11). The apostles wrote so their teaching would outlast them (2 Pet 1:15). Today the only place we can be sure we have their teaching is the Bible. Everything else is valuable, but it has to be tested by it."

2-minute version

"I believe the church's final authority is the teaching of Jesus and his apostles. The question is where we find that teaching today. The apostles told us: Peter wrote so that after his death believers could always recall it (2 Pet 1:15), and he called Paul's letters Scripture (2 Pet 3:16).

Jesus showed how to treat tradition. The Pharisees had an ancient tradition they said came from Moses, and Jesus said it 'made void the word of God' (Mark 7:13). The Bereans tested even the apostle Paul's preaching against Scripture and were praised for it (Acts 17:11).

I'm not against tradition. I love the creeds, because they say what Scripture says. But councils have contradicted each other, and leaders, even Peter, have been wrong (Gal 2:11). So something has to be the final judge, and the only thing God breathed out is Scripture (2 Tim 3:16). That's what the apostles left us."

Further reading

  • Keith A. Mathison, The Shape of Sola Scriptura (Canon Press, 2001): distinguishes sola from "solo" scriptura
  • John MacArthur (ed.), The Inerrant Word (Crossway, 2016); and MacArthur, Our Sufficiency in Christ (Word, 1991)
  • Michael J. Kruger, Canon Revisited (Crossway, 2012): how the canon was recognized
  • James R. White, Scripture Alone (Bethany House, 2004)
  • Catholic side: Trent Horn, The Case for Catholicism (Ignatius, 2017); Orthodox side: Timothy (Kallistos) Ware, The Orthodox Church
  • Videos on this topic: Grace to You, "Why You Can Trust Scripture" (Parts 1–2); A Messenger of Truth, "Wait, There Was No Bible in the Early Church…"; Wes Huff, "What really led to the Council of Nicaea?"
Defense1D

"There was no Bible in the early church."

The objection (best form)

"For decades Christians had no New Testament. The church existed and taught before the Bible was finished, so the church, not the Bible, is the authority."

Answer

  • They had Scripture from day one. The early church had the Old Testament, and the apostles preached from it (Acts 17:2–3, 11; Acts 18:28).
  • They had the apostles in person. While the apostles lived, their spoken teaching was the living word of Christ. Sola scriptura applies to the church after the apostles, when that teaching remains only in writing (2 Pet 1:15).
  • The New Testament circulated early. Paul's letters were read aloud and exchanged between churches (Col 4:16; 1 Thess 5:27). Peter already calls Paul's letters "Scriptures" (2 Pet 3:16), and 1 Tim 5:18 quotes Luke's Gospel as Scripture.
  • The objection proves too much. Before the church existed, Israel had Scripture. God's people have always been ruled by his written word (Deut 31:9–13; Matt 22:31).

30-second version

"The early church had the Old Testament, and it had the apostles themselves. As the apostles died, they left their teaching in writing so it would last (2 Pet 1:15). Peter already called Paul's letters Scripture (2 Pet 3:16). So the church was never without God's word. It was built on it."

Defense1D

"Sola scriptura created 40,000 denominations."

The objection (best form)

"Scripture alone leads to endless division. The Catholic (or Orthodox) Church preserves unity."

Answer

  • The number is misleading. The "40,000+" figure comes from the World Christian Encyclopedia method, which counts denominations country by country, so one church present in fifty countries counts fifty times, and which includes Catholic, Orthodox, and independent bodies (the Center for the Study of Global Christianity's method, as explained in Pew Research's appendix on its figures).
  • Most Protestants agree on the core. The Trinity, the deity and resurrection of Christ, salvation by grace through faith, and the authority of Scripture are shared across historic Protestant churches.
  • Infallible interpreters haven't produced unity either. The Catholic and Orthodox churches have been divided since 1054. Both claim an authoritative tradition, and they disagree on the papacy, purgatory, and the Filioque.
  • Division existed in the apostles' time (1 Cor 1:10–13; 1 Cor 11:19). Scripture expects false teaching and tells believers to test it (1 John 4:1).

30-second version

"Catholics and Orthodox both have councils and traditions, and they've been split for almost a thousand years. Division comes from people, not from Scripture. Paul faced it too (1 Cor 1:10–13), and his answer was to call everyone back to the apostolic gospel (1 Cor 15:1–4)."

1E

Answering Atheist Objections

8 cards4 moderate

New terms

Theodicy: An account of why a good and all-powerful God permits evil.

Annihilationism: The view, held by some evangelicals, that the lost are finally destroyed rather than punished consciously forever (also called conditional immortality).

Pseudepigraphy: Writing under someone else's name, such as a later author writing as an apostle.

Methodological naturalism: The working rule of explaining events only by natural causes, which rules out miracle and prophecy from the start.

The objections skeptics raise most often, online and face to face: suffering, animal suffering, hell, and "the scholars say the Bible is unreliable." These are serious questions, often asked out of real pain. Answer the person before you answer the argument. Every card is tested by Scripture alone (1D), and the ratings say honestly where Christian answers are strongest and where the question stays hard.

Argument1EMODERATE

The Problem of Evil

the logical version is widely judged answered; the evidential version remains debated

Name + thesis

The problem of evil. "If God is all-good and all-powerful, why is there so much evil and suffering?" Scripture doesn't hide from the question; it asks it (Ps 13:1; Hab 1:2–3). It answers that evil entered through creatures' rebellion, that God works even through evil for good purposes we often can't see, that he entered our suffering himself on the cross, and that he will end it. And the objection itself depends on objective moral standards that atheism can't ground.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Gen 50:20).
  • Jesus was delivered up "according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God," by lawless men who were still guilty (Acts 2:23).
  • "For we know that for those who love God all things work together for good" (Rom 8:28); present sufferings aren't "worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed" (Rom 8:18).
  • "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more" (Rev 21:4).
  • Verdict: Scripture affirms both God's goodness and real evil, gives reasons in principle (creaturely rebellion, God's hidden purposes), and points to the cross and the new creation as God's answer.

Key texts

  • Hab 1:2–3: "O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear?... Why do you make me see iniquity?"
  • Job 38:2, 4: "Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge?... Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?"
  • Acts 4:27–28: Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and Israel gathered against Jesus "to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. The logical problem: an all-good God would prevent evil if he could; an all-powerful God could; evil exists; so no such God exists.
  2. The evidential problem (William Rowe): even if God could have reasons for some evil, the sheer amount of apparently pointless suffering (a fawn burning slowly in a forest fire) makes God's existence unlikely.
  3. Free will doesn't explain natural evil: earthquakes, cancer, and childhood leukemia aren't anyone's choice.
  4. "Mysterious reasons" is a dodge. Any belief can be protected by saying "God has reasons."

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The objection claims that evil is objectively bad, something that really ought not to be.
  • P2. On atheism there is no grounding for objective good and evil (1B, the moral argument; 1A).
  • P3. On Christianity, evil is real and objectively wrong, and Scripture gives reasons a good God may permit it: creaturely rebellion (Gen 3; Rom 5:12), purposes beyond our sight (Gen 50:20; Job 38–41), and the redemption of all things (Rom 8:18–23).
  • C. The existence of evil doesn't disprove God; it presupposes a moral order that only God grounds, and Christianity explains evil better than atheism does.

Evidence for each premise

The logical version is generally judged answered. Alvin Plantinga's free will defense (God, Freedom, and Evil, 1974) showed there is no formal contradiction between God and evil if God has a morally sufficient reason, such as the value of free creatures. Many atheist philosophers now press only the evidential version (e.g., William Rowe's own move to it).

Our limited vantage point is a real factor. We would expect a God who governs all history to have reasons we can't trace, as Joseph couldn't in prison (Gen 50:20) and Job couldn't in the ash heap (Job 38–42). This isn't a dodge if we have independent reasons to trust God's goodness: the cross and resurrection (Rom 5:8; 1C).

Natural evil. Scripture ties the creation's "bondage to corruption" to the fall and promises its liberation (Rom 8:20–22). Natural evil is also the setting in which courage, compassion, and sacrifice exist at all.

The cross is God's answer. God didn't stay distant from suffering. The worst evil ever done, the murder of the innocent Son, was the means of the greatest good, the world's redemption (Acts 2:23; Acts 4:27–28). If God could bring that good out of that evil, he can be trusted with ours.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: horrendous suffering. "Tell that to a parent whose child died of cancer. No reason could justify that."

Answer: First, don't argue; grieve with them (Rom 12:15; John 11:35). Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb even though he was about to raise him. Then, gently: Christianity doesn't say the suffering is good; it says God will defeat it and wipe away every tear (Rev 21:4). Atheism says the child's death was the meaningless outcome of physics, and no one will ever make it right. The question "how could this be allowed?" is a protest that assumes the world should be just, which is a Christian expectation.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Free will doesn't explain cancer and earthquakes."

  • Close (R1): Scripture ties creation's brokenness to the fall (Rom 8:20–22), and God promises its renewal. Free will was never the whole Christian answer.
  • Their comeback: "Then God is responsible for a broken world."
  • Close (R2): He has taken responsibility for its rescue at the cost of his Son (Rom 8:32). The question is whether he can be trusted, and the cross is the evidence.

2. "God's 'hidden reasons' is unfalsifiable."

  • Close (R1): It would be, if we had no other evidence about God. But we do: the case for God (1A, 1B) and the resurrection (1C).
  • Their comeback: "Then the evidence for God must outweigh the evidence against."
  • Close (R2): Yes, and that's the right way to weigh it. Evil counts as a question, not a refutation.

3. "You're just assuming objective morality."

  • Close (R1): So is the objection. If evil is only my dislike, there is no problem of evil, just things we don't like.
  • Their comeback: "I'm using your standards against you (internal critique)."
  • Close (R2): Fine, and internally Christianity teaches that God permits evil for purposes he will vindicate (Gen 50:20; Rom 8:28). No contradiction there.

Boomerang check

"Christians also suffer and pray unanswered prayers." Yes. Scripture never promises otherwise (John 16:33; 2 Cor 12:7–9). The Christian claim isn't that believers escape suffering, but that it isn't the end and isn't meaningless.

Strength rating

MODERATE. The logical problem is widely regarded as answered, and the moral-grounding point is strong. The evidential problem remains a real philosophical debate, and its emotional force is great. Lead with compassion and the cross, not with a syllogism.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
The grieving Not looking for arguments Listen, weep, pray; save the logic for later.
Philosophy-minded atheists Know Rowe and Plantinga Use the moral-grounding point and the evidential framing.
Ex-Christians Often left after personal tragedy Acknowledge the hurt; show the psalms of lament (Ps 13; Ps 88).

Trap questions

  1. "When you call this suffering evil, do you mean it's really wrong, or that you don't like it?"
  2. "If there's no God, who will ever make this right?"
  3. "Joseph's brothers meant evil. Could God have had a purpose they couldn't see?" (Gen 50:20)

30-second version

"Calling something evil means it really ought not to be, and that needs a standard above us. Christianity takes evil seriously: it came through our rebellion, God works even through it (Gen 50:20), and he entered our suffering on the cross. One day he'll wipe away every tear (Rev 21:4). Atheism can't promise anyone that."

2-minute version

"This is the hardest question there is, and the Bible doesn't avoid it. Whole psalms ask God, 'How long?'

Here's how I see it. When we call something evil, we mean it's really wrong, not just unpleasant. But if there's no God, there's no real standard of good and evil, just nature doing what it does. So the problem of evil actually assumes a moral order.

Christianity says evil is real, it came through our rebellion, and God hasn't stayed far away from it. Joseph was sold into slavery, and years later said, 'You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.' The worst thing ever done, the murder of Jesus, became the way God saved the world. And the story ends with God wiping away every tear. I don't know why God allows each particular sorrow, but I know he can be trusted, because of the cross."

Further reading

  • Alvin Plantinga, God, Freedom, and Evil (Harper & Row, 1974; Eerdmans reprint, 1977)
  • Timothy Keller, Walking with God through Pain and Suffering (Dutton, 2013)
  • D. A. Carson, How Long, O Lord? (Baker, 2nd ed. 2006)
  • John MacArthur, The Power of Suffering (Victor, 1995)
  • Other side: William Rowe, "The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism," American Philosophical Quarterly 16 (1979)
  • Videos on this topic: Grace to You, "Why Does God Allow So Much Suffering?"
Argument1EMODERATE

Animal Suffering

Christians agree on the scriptural principles but disagree on the age of the earth; the question keeps its emotional force

Name + thesis

Animal suffering. "Millions of years of predation, parasites, and pain before humans existed. A good God wouldn't design that." Scripture says God cares for animals, governs even predation, and promises to liberate the whole creation from its bondage. Christians differ on whether animal death began at the fall or before humans, but both views have scriptural reasons, and atheism has no standard by which nature "red in tooth and claw" is wrong.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "Not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father" (Matt 10:29); "your heavenly Father feeds them" (Matt 6:26).
  • "The young lions roar for their prey, seeking their food from God" (Ps 104:21); God provides prey for the lion and food for the raven (Job 38:39–41).
  • "The creation was subjected to futility... the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption" (Rom 8:20–21).
  • "The wolf shall dwell with the lamb... they shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain" (Isa 11:6–9).
  • God cares about animals in judgment and mercy: "and also much cattle" (Jonah 4:11); "Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his beast" (Prov 12:10).
  • Verdict: Animals matter to God; he sustains them, even the predators; and their present condition is not the final word.

Key texts

  • Gen 1:30: "to every beast of the earth... I have given every green plant for food."
  • Rom 8:22: "the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now."
  • Darwin to Asa Gray, 22 May 1860: he could not persuade himself that a beneficent and omnipotent God would have designedly created the Ichneumonidae (parasitic wasps) to feed within the living bodies of caterpillars.

Their best case (steelman)

  1. The scale is enormous. Predation, disease, and parasitism have existed for hundreds of millions of years, long before any human sin.
  2. Animals can't learn or grow from suffering, so soul-making theodicies don't apply, and they have no free will to misuse.
