  3. The design is cruel: parasitic wasps, cats playing with mice, starvation built into population dynamics.
  4. Blaming the fall is unjust: why should animals suffer for human sin?

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Scripture teaches that God cares for animals and sustains them, predators included (Matt 10:29; Ps 104:21; Job 38:39–41).
  • P2. Scripture teaches that creation is now "subjected to futility" and will be liberated (Rom 8:20–22; Isa 11:6–9).
  • P3. The objection assumes animal suffering is objectively bad, a judgment atheism can't ground (1B).
  • C. Animal suffering is a real mystery but not a disproof of God; Christianity explains why it grieves us and promises its end, while atheism can only call it nature.

Evidence for each premise

Two scriptural views, one hope. Many Christians (young-earth) hold that animal death entered with the fall: the first creatures were given plants for food (Gen 1:30), and creation was subjected to futility because of human sin (Rom 8:20; Gen 3:17). Others (old-earth) note that Scripture presents predation as part of God's provision (Ps 104:21; Job 38:39–41; Job 39:29–30) and that Rom 5:12 speaks of human death. Both agree on God's care, his providence, and the coming liberation of creation (Rom 8:21). Know both views; you needn't settle the age of the earth to answer the objection.

God answers Job with animals. When Job demands an explanation for suffering, God points him to lions, ravens, mountain goats, the ostrich, the hawk, and the eagle feeding its young on blood (Job 38:39–39:30). The point: God governs a wild world whose purposes exceed our understanding, and he is good and wise in it.

Pain in animals isn't identical to human suffering. Some Christian philosophers argue that many animals lack the self-awareness that makes pain into suffering over time (Michael Murray, Nature Red in Tooth and Claw, Oxford, 2008). Use this carefully; it reduces the problem without removing it.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: millions of years before humans. "On the scientific timeline, animals suffered for ages before any human sinned. The fall can't explain it."

Answer: That's a challenge only to one view (animal death from the fall). On the other view, God created a world where predation serves his purposes (Ps 104:21–28) while creation as a whole awaits liberation (Rom 8:21). Either way, Scripture's answer is not that animal suffering is good, but that God governs it and will end it (Isa 11:6–9). And the atheist still needs to say why it's wrong, rather than just how evolution works.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Animals can't benefit from suffering."

  • Close (R1): Their suffering may serve purposes in the whole creation we don't see (Job 38–39), and God promises the creation's liberation (Rom 8:21).
  • Their comeback: "That's an assertion."
  • Close (R2): It's a scriptural claim backed by reasons to trust God (the resurrection, 1C). The atheist alternative is that suffering has no purpose and no end.

2. "Why should animals suffer for human sin?"

  • Close (R1): Scripture says creation was subjected "in hope" (Rom 8:20), and its renewal is bound up with ours (Rom 8:21).
  • Their comeback: "That's still unfair to animals."
  • Close (R2): Fairness is a moral category. On atheism, there's no unfairness in nature, just nature. Your sense that it's unfair fits a world made by a just God.

3. "Parasitic wasps prove there's no designer."

  • Close (R1): Darwin's objection was moral, not scientific: he couldn't believe a good God would do it. That assumes a moral standard.
  • Their comeback: "It's still evidence against a good designer."
  • Close (R2): It's evidence that the world isn't as it should be, which Scripture says (Rom 8:22). It doesn't show God isn't good, any more than a hospital shows doctors want disease.

Boomerang check

"Christians eat animals and kill pests." God permits eating animals (Gen 9:3) and still requires care for them (Prov 12:10; Deut 25:4). Responsible use isn't cruelty.

Strength rating

MODERATE. Scripture gives clear principles (God's care, providence, and promised liberation), and the moral-grounding point is strong. But Christians disagree on the timeline, and the question keeps real emotional force. Don't claim to have dissolved it.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Animal lovers Feel the objection deeply Begin with God's care: Matt 10:29; Jonah 4:11.
Science-minded atheists Assume Christians must deny deep time Show both Christian views; focus on the moral question.
Christians troubled by it Worried their faith requires one timeline Reassure them that Rom 8:21 is the shared hope.

Trap questions

  1. "When you say nature is cruel, cruel by what standard?"
  2. "What does God point Job to when Job asks why he's suffering?" (Job 38–39)
  3. "If there's no God, will animal suffering ever be put right?"

30-second version

"Jesus said not one sparrow falls without the Father (Matt 10:29), and Paul says the whole creation is groaning but will be set free (Rom 8:21). I don't know every reason God allows animal suffering, but calling it cruel needs a moral standard, and only God provides one. Atheism can say it happens; it can't say it's wrong or promise it will end."

2-minute version

"I feel this one too. Watching an animal suffer is awful, and the Bible doesn't call it trivial. Jesus said not even a sparrow falls without the Father's knowledge.

Christians answer the timeline question in different ways. Some think animal death came after the fall; others think predation has always been part of God's provision, as Psalm 104 says the lions seek their food from God. But all agree on what Paul says in Romans 8: the creation is groaning now, and it will be set free. Isaiah pictures the wolf and the lamb living together.

Here's what strikes me: when we call nature cruel, we're making a moral judgment. On atheism, nature isn't cruel; it just is. The fact that it grieves us fits a world made by a good God, and he's promised to heal it."

Further reading

  • Michael J. Murray, Nature Red in Tooth and Claw: Theism and the Problem of Animal Suffering (Oxford, 2008)
  • Christopher Southgate, The Groaning of Creation (Westminster John Knox, 2008)
  • Ronald E. Osborn, Death Before the Fall (IVP Academic, 2014)
  • Videos on this topic: Wise Disciple, "The Animal Suffering Argument Christians Need to Face"
Argument1EMODERATE

Is Hell Just?

the justice of final judgment is clear in Scripture; its duration and nature are debated among evangelicals

Name + thesis

Hell. "Eternal torment for finite sins is monstrously unjust." Scripture teaches a final judgment that is just, measured by deeds and by the light each person had, and grounded in the infinite worth of the God sinned against. Hell is not God failing to love but people receiving the separation from him they chose, and God himself provided the way out at the cost of his Son.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?" (Gen 18:25).
  • "These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life" (Matt 25:46); "the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord" (2 Thess 1:9).
  • Judgment is "according to what they had done" (Rev 20:12); the servant who knew his master's will receives "a severe beating," the one who didn't, "a light beating" (Luke 12:47–48; Matt 11:22–24).
  • "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked" (Ezek 33:11); God is "not wishing that any should perish" (2 Pet 3:9).
  • "The light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light" (John 3:19).
  • Verdict: Scripture teaches real, final, just judgment, with degrees, and God's desire that people be saved.

Key texts

  • Mark 9:47–48: "...to be thrown into hell, 'where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.'"
  • Rom 2:5–8: "God's righteous judgment... He will render to each one according to his works."
  • Rev 22:11: "Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. Infinite punishment for finite crimes is disproportionate. No human sin, committed in a finite life, deserves endless torment.
  2. A loving parent would never torture a child forever. If human parents are better than God, something is wrong.
  3. Many never heard the gospel. Punishing them for not believing is unjust.
  4. Even Christians disagree. Respected evangelicals (John Stott, Edward Fudge) held that the lost are destroyed, not tormented forever (annihilationism).
  5. Fear-based belief is not love. A God who threatens hell manipulates people.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Justice requires that wrongdoing be punished in proportion to its seriousness (Gen 18:25; Rom 2:6).
  • P2. The seriousness of a wrong depends partly on the worth of the one wronged, and sin is against the infinitely worthy God (Ps 51:4).
  • P3. Scripture teaches degrees of punishment by deeds and knowledge (Luke 12:47–48; Matt 11:22–24), and that the lost remain opposed to God (John 3:19; Rev 22:11).
  • C. Final judgment, including hell, is not unjust; and God's provision of salvation through Christ shows that he desires mercy (Ezek 33:11; John 3:16–17).

Evidence for each premise

Seriousness tracks the one offended. Striking a rock, an animal, and a person are different acts with the same motion. David says of his sin against Uriah, "Against you, you only, have I sinned" (Ps 51:4): sin is first an offense against God. If God is infinitely worthy, rebellion against him is no small thing.

Hell has degrees. Jesus says it will be "more bearable" for Tyre and Sodom than for those who saw his miracles and refused him (Matt 11:22–24), and that the servant who didn't know his master's will receives a lighter beating (Luke 12:47–48). Judgment is according to deeds and light (Rom 2:6, 12).

The lost don't want God. John says people "loved the darkness rather than the light" (John 3:19). Revelation pictures the final state as character fixed: "let the evildoer still do evil" (Rev 22:11). C. S. Lewis put it memorably: the doors of hell are locked on the inside (The Problem of Pain, ch. 8).

God paid the cost himself. The same Jesus who taught most about hell went to the cross to bear judgment for sinners (Isa 53:5–6; 1 Pet 3:18). A God who wanted people in hell wouldn't do that.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: duration. "Even granting justice and degrees, eternal conscious torment for one lifetime is disproportionate."

Answer: Scripture uses the same word "eternal" for the punishment and the life (Matt 25:46). Some evangelicals read "eternal destruction" (2 Thess 1:9) as final annihilation; others as unending separation. Either way, the defense of God's justice stands: sin against an infinitely worthy God, continuing rebellion, and degrees of judgment. Be honest that believers debate the nature of hell (rated MODERATE), and keep the focus on what all agree: judgment is real, just, and avoidable through Christ.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Finite sins can't deserve infinite punishment."

  • Close (R1): The seriousness of a wrong isn't measured only by how long it took; a murder takes seconds. It depends on whom it's against (Ps 51:4).
  • Their comeback: "Then everyone's sin is equally infinite, which is unjust."
  • Close (R2): Scripture says no: punishment has degrees according to deeds and knowledge (Luke 12:47–48; Matt 11:22–24).

2. "A loving parent wouldn't do that."

  • Close (R1): A loving parent who is also a judge must uphold justice. And God did what no parent could: gave his own Son to bear the penalty (Rom 8:32).
  • Their comeback: "Then forgive everyone."
  • Close (R2): He offers forgiveness to everyone (2 Pet 3:9; Rev 22:17). He won't force people who love darkness into his presence (John 3:19).

3. "What about those who never heard?"

  • Close (R1): Judgment is according to the light people had (Rom 2:12–16; Luke 12:48). God is the "Judge of all the earth" who will do right (Gen 18:25).
  • Their comeback: "That's convenient."
  • Close (R2): It's what the text says. And you have heard. The question for you is what you'll do with Jesus.

Boomerang check

"Islam and other religions have hell too, so Christianity isn't unique." True. The Christian difference is that God himself bears the judgment for sinners and offers forgiveness as a free gift, not earned by balancing deeds (Rom 6:23; Eph 2:8–9). See 2H.

Strength rating

MODERATE. The justice of final judgment, degrees of punishment, and God's provision of salvation are clearly scriptural. The duration and nature of hell are debated among Bible-believing Christians, and the emotional weight of the question is great.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Ex-Christians traumatized by fear Often heard hell used manipulatively Acknowledge that; lead with God's heart (Ezek 33:11).
Moral-philosophy atheists Press proportionality Use Ps 51:4 and the degrees of punishment.
Muslims Believe in hell; question assurance Turn to 2H.

Trap questions

  1. "Is a crime's seriousness measured only by how long it takes, or also by whom it's against?"
  2. "Did Jesus teach that everyone in hell receives the same punishment?" (Luke 12:47–48)
  3. "If God wanted people in hell, why would he go to the cross?"

30-second version

"Jesus taught that judgment is just and has degrees, by what each person did and knew (Luke 12:47–48). Sin is serious because it's against an infinitely good God (Ps 51:4). But God takes no pleasure in anyone's death (Ezek 33:11), and Jesus bore judgment himself so we don't have to (1 Pet 3:18). The door is open."

2-minute version

"I don't think anyone should talk about hell lightly. Jesus spoke about it with tears in his voice, and then he went to the cross.

Here's how I think about the justice question. How serious a wrong is depends partly on whom it's against. Lying to a stranger and betraying your mother aren't the same. If God is infinitely good, rejecting him is no small thing. But Jesus also taught that judgment has degrees: it will be more bearable for some than for others, depending on what they did and how much they knew.

And hell isn't God dragging unwilling people away from a heaven they long for. John says people loved the darkness rather than the light. Most of all, God himself provided the way out: Jesus bore the judgment for us. God says, 'I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; turn back and live.'"

Further reading

  • Christopher W. Morgan and Robert A. Peterson (eds.), Hell Under Fire (Zondervan, 2004)
  • Preston Sprinkle (ed.), Four Views on Hell (Zondervan, 2nd ed. 2016): includes eternal conscious punishment and annihilationism
  • C. S. Lewis, The Problem of Pain (1940), ch. 8; The Great Divorce (1945)
  • Other side: Bart D. Ehrman, Heaven and Hell (Simon & Schuster, 2020)
  • Videos on this topic: Grace to You, "The Truth About Hell" (Parts 1–2) and "A Voice from Hell" (Luke 16:19–31)
Argument1EMODERATE

"Scholars Say the Gospels Are Anonymous and Late"

traditional authorship is debated; the eyewitness case is good but not consensus

Name + thesis

Authorship and dating. Popular skeptics say "scholars agree" the Gospels were written anonymously, decades later, by people who never knew Jesus. In fact the evidence for the traditional authors is substantial: the titles are uniform in every manuscript, early witnesses name the same four authors, and nothing in the texts requires a late date unless one assumes Jesus couldn't predict the Temple's fall. The core facts about Jesus don't depend on settling every authorship question (1C).

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • Luke investigated "from those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word" (Luke 1:1–4).
  • "He who saw it has borne witness... and he knows that he is telling the truth" (John 19:35; John 21:24).
  • "We did not follow cleverly devised myths... we were eyewitnesses of his majesty" (2 Pet 1:16).
  • Verdict: The Gospels present themselves as grounded in eyewitness testimony.

Key texts

  • Papias (c. 110–130), quoted by Eusebius, Church History 3.39.15–16: Mark, "having become the interpreter of Peter, wrote down accurately whatever he remembered"; "Matthew collected the oracles in the Hebrew language."
  • Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.1.1 (c. 180): names Matthew, Mark (Peter's disciple), Luke (Paul's companion), and John.
  • P75 (c. 175–225): contains the end of Luke followed by the title "Gospel according to John."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. The Gospels never name their authors in the text. The titles were added later.
  2. They were written in Greek by educated authors, while Jesus' disciples were Aramaic-speaking Galilean fishermen, "uneducated" (Acts 4:13).
  3. Mark was written around 70, after the Temple's destruction, because Mark 13 "predicts" it; Matthew and Luke used Mark and are later still.
  4. Papias is late and unreliable, and the authorship tradition grew to give the books authority.
  5. The scholarly consensus (Ehrman and many others) holds that none of the Gospels was written by an eyewitness.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Ancient books' authorship is normally established by manuscript titles and early external testimony.
  • P2. For the Gospels, both are uniform and early: every manuscript with a title bears the same author, and Papias and Irenaeus name the same people.
  • P3. The main argument for late dates (prophecy of the Temple's fall) assumes that prediction is impossible, which is a philosophical assumption, not historical evidence.
  • C. The traditional authorship has strong historical support, and even on later dates the Gospels remain early, eyewitness-based sources.

Evidence for each premise

Uniform titles. No manuscript attributes any Gospel to anyone other than its traditional author; there are no rival attributions. Martin Hengel argued the titles must have been attached early, as soon as several Gospels circulated together (The Four Gospels and the One Gospel of Jesus Christ, Trinity Press, 2000). Simon Gathercole argues the Gospels were never truly anonymous (Journal of Theological Studies 69.2, 2018, pp. 447–476).

Unlikely choices. If later Christians invented authors to gain authority, why choose Mark and Luke, who weren't apostles, instead of Peter or Paul? Fabricated gospels (Peter, Thomas, Judas) chose famous names.

The dating argument. Mark 13's prediction of the Temple's fall is the main reason for dating Mark around 70. That reasoning assumes Jesus couldn't predict it, which is methodological naturalism. Acts ends with Paul alive in Rome around 62 (Acts 28:30–31) and never mentions Paul's death, James's death (62), Nero's persecution (64), or the Temple's fall (70). Several scholars take that to suggest Luke-Acts was finished in the early 60s, which would put Mark earlier still.

Education. "Uneducated" (Acts 4:13) means without formal rabbinic training, not illiterate. Galilee was bilingual, Matthew was a tax collector who worked with records, and authors used secretaries (Rom 16:22; 1 Pet 5:12).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "Even if the names are right, the Gospels are 40–60 years after Jesus."

Answer: Even on mainstream dates, that is well within the lifetime of eyewitnesses, and far closer than most ancient biographies (the earliest surviving biographies of Alexander the Great are some 400 years after him). And the core facts (crucifixion, burial, appearances) are attested by Paul's creed in 1 Cor 15:3–7, dated within a few years of the events (1C).

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "The titles were added later."

  • Close (R1): Then explain why every manuscript carries the same names, with no rivals.
  • Their comeback: "Uniformity came from later standardization."
  • Close (R2): Standardization by whom? The Gospels circulated widely across the empire before any central authority. And standardizers wanting authority would pick apostles, not Mark and Luke.

2. "Mark was written after 70 because of Mark 13."

  • Close (R1): That assumes Jesus couldn't predict it. Is that a historical conclusion or a philosophical assumption?
  • Their comeback: "Historians can't assume miracles."
  • Close (R2): Then at least admit the late date depends on that assumption. And Acts, Luke's sequel, ends around 62 with no mention of the Temple's fall or Paul's death.

3. "Scholars agree no Gospel was by an eyewitness."

  • Close (R1): Many do, and many don't (Richard Bauckham, Craig Blomberg, Martin Hengel). "Consensus" is a head count, not evidence. What's the evidence?
  • Their comeback: "You're dismissing expertise."
  • Close (R2): I'm asking for the reasons experts give. If the main reason for late dating is "prophecy can't happen," that's philosophy, not history.

Boomerang check

"You trust Papias and Irenaeus, but they're church tradition." We use them as historical witnesses, exactly as historians use Plutarch or Suetonius (1D). They're the earliest external testimony we have, and they agree.

Strength rating

MODERATE. The evidence for traditional authorship is substantial and the late-dating argument rests heavily on an assumption, but authorship is genuinely debated among scholars. The resurrection case doesn't depend on winning this debate.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Online skeptics (YouTube, TikTok) Repeat "scholars agree" Ask for the reasons behind the consensus.
Ehrman readers Know the arguments well Use Hengel, Bauckham, and the Acts ending.
Christians shaken by a video Feel the ground has moved Show 1 Cor 15:3–7: the core is early regardless.

Trap questions

  1. "Is there a single manuscript that names a different author for any Gospel?"
  2. "Why would someone faking authority choose Mark and Luke instead of Peter and Paul?"
  3. "Is dating Mark after 70 a historical finding, or does it assume Jesus couldn't predict the future?"

30-second version

"Every manuscript with a title names the same four authors, with no rivals, and the earliest writers (Papias, Irenaeus) agree. Forgers would have chosen Peter or Paul, not Mark and Luke. The main reason for late dates is the assumption that Jesus couldn't predict the Temple's fall. And Paul's creed in 1 Corinthians 15 dates the core facts to within a few years anyway."

2-minute version

"I hear 'scholars agree the Gospels are anonymous' a lot, so I looked into it. Here's what surprised me.

First, every manuscript that has a title names the same author: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John. There are no rival attributions. Second, the earliest writers who talk about it, Papias around 110 to 130 and Irenaeus around 180, name the same people, and Papias says Mark got his material from Peter. Third, if someone were inventing authors for prestige, why pick Mark and Luke, who weren't even apostles?

The main reason for dating Mark after 70 is that Jesus predicts the Temple's destruction, which assumes he couldn't. Meanwhile Acts ends with Paul still alive around 62. And even if you take the later dates, Paul quotes a creed about Jesus' death and resurrection that goes back to within a few years of the events. The case doesn't rest on one scholarly debate."

Further reading

  • Richard Bauckham, Jesus and the Eyewitnesses (Eerdmans, 2nd ed. 2017)
  • Craig L. Blomberg, The Historical Reliability of the Gospels (IVP, 2nd ed. 2007)
  • Peter J. Williams, Can We Trust the Gospels? (Crossway, 2018)
  • The MacArthur Study Bible: its introductions to the four Gospels defend the traditional authors and dates
  • Other side: Bart D. Ehrman, Jesus, Interrupted (HarperOne, 2009)
  • Videos on this topic: Testify, "This Terrible Atheist Meme About the Gospels Must Stop"; Wes Huff, "Can the Gospels survive historical scrutiny?"; Kyrillos Apologetics, "Undeniable PROOF Luke Was Written In the EARLY 50s AD" (treat its early dating as a minority view)
Defense1E

"The scholarly consensus says..."

The objection (best form)

"Bible scholars agree that Moses didn't write the Torah, the Gospels are anonymous, Paul didn't write half his letters, and Israel's God began as one god in a Canaanite pantheon. Online scholars repeat this daily. Who are you to disagree with the experts?"

Answer

  • Ask what the consensus is based on. A consensus is only as good as its reasons. Many conclusions in biblical studies rest on methodological naturalism: excluding prophecy and miracle in advance. Then the "consensus" can't count against miracles; it assumed them away.
  • Check the scope. "Scholars" often means scholars in secular departments. Many credentialed scholars (Richard Bauckham, Craig Blomberg, Daniel Wallace, Michael Kruger, Peter Williams) disagree, with peer-reviewed work. A consensus within one school isn't a consensus of the field.
  • Consensus changes. In the 19th century, the influential Tübingen school of F. C. Baur dated John's Gospel to around AD 160–170. The publication in 1935 of P52, a fragment of John usually dated to the first half of the 2nd century, made that impossible.
  • Weigh the arguments, not the credentials. Experts deserve a hearing, and Christians shouldn't sneer at scholarship. But "scholars say" is where the conversation starts, not where it ends.

30-second version

"I respect scholars, so let's look at their reasons. If a conclusion depends on assuming miracles and prophecy can't happen, it can't be used as evidence that they didn't. Plenty of credentialed scholars disagree with that consensus. What's the strongest piece of evidence for the claim?"

Defense1E

"The Pastoral Epistles (1–2 Timothy, Titus) are forgeries."

The objection (best form)

"Most critical scholars think Paul didn't write 1–2 Timothy and Titus. They differ in vocabulary and assume later church structures. So the Bible contains forgeries."

Answer

  • It's genuinely debated. Many critical scholars doubt Pauline authorship, but serious scholars defend it, including Luke Timothy Johnson, a Catholic New Testament scholar, in the Anchor Bible commentary (The First and Second Letters to Timothy, 2001).
  • Vocabulary shifts have explanations: different subjects (church order, not justification), Paul's age, and the use of a secretary (compare Rom 16:22).
  • The personal details are hard to explain as forgery: a forger has no reason to write "bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, also the books, and above all the parchments" (2 Tim 4:13), or to name obscure people like Onesiphorus (2 Tim 1:16; 2 Tim 4:19).
  • Nothing central depends on them. The gospel, the resurrection, and justification by faith are taught in Paul's undisputed letters (Romans, Galatians, 1 Corinthians).

30-second version

"That's debated, not settled. Luke Timothy Johnson, a major Catholic scholar, argues Paul wrote them. A forger wouldn't bother asking for a cloak left at Troas (2 Tim 4:13). And nothing central depends on them: the gospel is in Romans, Galatians, and 1 Corinthians, which everyone agrees Paul wrote."

Defense1E

"Jesus was wrong: the mustard seed isn't the smallest seed."

The objection (best form)

"Jesus said the mustard seed is 'the smallest of all the seeds on earth' (Mark 4:31). Orchid seeds are smaller. So Jesus made a factual error."

Answer

  • Read the setting. Jesus speaks of a seed "sown on the ground" that grows into the largest of garden plants (Mark 4:31–32; Matt 13:31–32: "larger than all the garden plants"). He's comparing seeds Galilean farmers sowed, not cataloguing world botany.
  • The mustard seed was proverbial for smallness in Jesus' world; Jesus uses it the same way elsewhere ("faith like a grain of mustard seed," Matt 17:20), and later Jewish writings use it as a byword for a tiny amount (e.g., Mishnah Niddah 5.2, "even the size of a mustard seed").
  • The point is the contrast: the smallest seed a farmer plants becomes a plant birds nest in. That's what Jesus says the kingdom is like.
  • Ordinary language isn't error. We say "the sun rises" without denying astronomy. Scripture's truthfulness is judged by what it means to assert.

30-second version

"Jesus was talking about seeds a Galilean farmer sowed in his field, and among those the mustard seed was the proverbial smallest, growing into the biggest garden plant (Matt 13:32). He wasn't writing a botany textbook any more than we are when we say 'the sun rises.' The point is that the kingdom starts tiny and grows huge."

Defense1E

"Jesus said he would return within his own generation, and he didn't."

The objection (best form)

"Jesus said, 'Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place' (Matt 24:34), and 'there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God after it has come with power' (Mark 9:1). Bertrand Russell put it bluntly: 'He certainly thought that His second coming would occur in clouds of glory before the death of all the people who were living at that time' (Why I Am Not a Christian, 1927). He was wrong."

Answer

  • Mark 9:1 is fulfilled six days later. The very next verses tell how Peter, James, and John saw Jesus transfigured in glory (Mark 9:2–8). Only "some standing here" saw it, and Peter later wrote of that mountain: "we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty" (2 Pet 1:16–18).
  • In Matthew 24, "all these things" begins with the temple. Jesus predicts that "there will not be left here one stone upon another" (Matt 24:2), and the disciples ask, "When will these things be?" (Matt 24:3). Rome destroyed the temple in AD 70, within that generation, as Josephus records (Jewish War 6).
  • The same speech refuses to give a date. Two verses later Jesus says, "But concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only" (Matt 24:36). Someone who says he doesn't know the date hasn't set one.
  • Christians read these verses in more than one way, but each main reading fits the history. See also 2B-7 and, on date-setters, 3O.

30-second version

"Read the next verses. Six days after Mark 9:1, three disciples saw Jesus in his glory, and Peter says they were eyewitnesses of his power and coming (2 Pet 1:16–18). In Matthew 24, 'all these things' starts with the temple's destruction, which happened in AD 70, within that generation. And two verses later Jesus says no one knows the day or hour (Matt 24:36). He didn't set a date."

1F

Is the God of the Old Testament Evil?

55 cards3 moderate

New terms

Herem: Hebrew for "the ban": something handed over to God irrevocably, often by destruction (Deut 7:2; Josh 6:17).

Ancient Near East (ANE): The world of the Old Testament: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Canaan, and their neighbors.

Hyperbole: Deliberate exaggeration for effect. Ancient war reports used it routinely ("left none remaining").

Accommodation: God regulating a practice of a fallen world (divorce, slavery, polygamy) without approving it (Matt 19:8).

Judicial hardening: God's judgment of handing people over to the course they have already chosen (Rom 1:24).

Imprecatory psalm: A psalm that asks God to judge the wicked, such as Psalms 109 and 137.

Covenant curses: The warnings in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 of what will follow if Israel breaks its covenant with God: defeat, siege, and exile.

Levirate marriage: The duty of a dead man's brother to marry the widow and raise an heir in the dead man's name (Deut 25:5–10).

Marcionism: The second-century heresy of Marcion, who taught that the God of the Old Testament is a different and lesser being than the Father of Jesus.

The verses critics quote to argue that Yahweh, the God of the Old Testament, is evil: the flood, the conquest of Canaan, slavery, the deaths of children, harsh laws, and "I create evil." Most of them fall to context. A few stay hard, and the cards say which. Learn the framework card first, because its seven moves answer most of the rest. The short Defense entries take one verse each and end with how firm the answer is. Quotes are short phrases in ESV wording unless marked. Related: the problem of evil (1E) and the Old Testament warfare boomerang in 2I.

Argument1FMODERATE

Is Yahweh Evil? A Seven-Move Framework for the Old Testament

strong as a way to sort the verses; the deaths of children and the conquest rest on a premise skeptics reject

Name + thesis

Is Yahweh evil? Critics quote the flood, the conquest of Canaan, the slave laws, and dozens of single verses to argue that the God of the Old Testament is a moral monster. Seven moves answer most of them: ask what kind of critique it is, separate what the Bible describes from what it approves, separate what the law regulates from what God calls good, read the genre, remember that the giver of life has rights over life, notice that judgment came slowly and fell on Israel too, and read the whole portrait up to the cross. Most of the verses fall to context. A few stay hard, and an honest answer says so.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • God's description of himself: "merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love," who "will by no means clear the guilty" (Exod 34:6–7).
  • "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live" (Ezek 33:11).
  • "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?" (Gen 18:25).
  • "The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away" (Job 1:21); "I kill and I make alive" (Deut 32:39).
  • God put Christ forward "so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Rom 3:25–26).
  • Verdict: Scripture presents one God in both Testaments, patient and just, who judges evil and bears judgment himself at the cross.

Key texts

  • Matt 19:8: "Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so." Jesus says some laws regulate sin without approving it.
  • Judg 21:25: "Everyone did what was right in his own eyes." The narrator's verdict on the worst stories in Judges.
  • Gen 15:16: The conquest waits four generations because "the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete."
  • Lev 18:28: Israel is warned the land will "vomit you out" too, "as it vomited out the nation that was before you."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. The catalogue. Richard Dawkins calls the God of the Old Testament "arguably the most unpleasant character in all fiction" (The God Delusion, 2006, ch. 2), and Dan Barker's God: The Most Unpleasant Character in All Fiction (2016) lists the verses.
  2. It is an internal critique. "I don't need my own moral theory. Your Bible says God is good and just (Ps 145:9; Deut 32:4), then shows him ordering infants killed (1 Sam 15:3). That breaks your own rule (Deut 24:16)."
  3. Context is special pleading. "Every 'read it in context' makes the text mean less than it says. Deut 20:16 says to leave alive nothing that breathes."
  4. You would not accept this from anyone else. "If a man today said God told him to kill a town, you would call him deluded. Why believe it of ancient Israel?" (Wes Morriston; Randal Rauser.)

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. An external critique (God breaks the critic's own standard) needs a standard that binds every culture and century, and atheism has no ground for one (1A; the moral argument in 1B).
  • P2. An internal critique must use all the Bible's premises: God made and owns every life, judges with full knowledge, and death is not the end (Deut 32:39; Job 1:21; Gen 18:25).
  • P3. Read with the seven moves, most of the quoted verses are a narrative of human sin, a regulation of an existing evil, a prayer, a prediction, or a covenant warning. They are not commands or approvals.
  • P4. Where God does take life in judgment, the texts give the reason, show long patience, and hold Israel to the same standard (Gen 15:16; Lev 18:28; Ezek 33:11).
  • C. The Old Testament does not show an evil God. It shows the same God as the New: patient, just, and finally bearing judgment himself (Rom 3:25–26).

Evidence for each premise

Move 1: which critique is it? (P1, P2) If the critic appeals to his own moral standard, ask what makes it binding on an ancient Israelite, or on God. If he says the Bible contradicts itself, grant that this is a fair challenge and that "you have no standard" does not answer it. Then hold him to the Bible's whole picture of God.

Move 2: described is not approved. (P3) Lot offering his daughters (Gen 19:8), Jephthah's vow (Judg 11:30–40), and the Levite's concubine (Judg 19:22–30) are told as failures. Judges ends with its own verdict (Judg 21:25).

Move 3: regulated is not ideal. (P3) Case law often limits an evil that already exists. Jesus says so of divorce (Matt 19:8). The ideal is in creation (Gen 1:27; Gen 2:24) and in the direction the law moves.

Move 4: read the genre. (P3) War reports in the ancient Near East used stock exaggeration (compare Josh 10:40 with Josh 13:1). Psalms record what people say to God (Ps 137:9). Covenant curses warn (Deut 28:53). A prophecy of what an invader will do is not approval of it (compare Hos 13:16 with Amos 1:13).

Move 5: God has rights over life that people do not. (P2, P4) A human who kills takes what is not his. God takes back what he gave (Job 1:21), and every person already lives under a sentence of death (Gen 2:17; Rom 6:23). This is the premise most critics reject, so state it openly.

Move 6: judgment came slowly and fell on Israel too. (P4) God waited four centuries on the Amorites (Gen 15:16), sent Jonah to Nineveh (Jonah 4:11), and spared Rahab (Josh 6:25). Israel was warned of the same treatment (Lev 18:28) and received it from Assyria in 722 BC and Babylon in 586 BC.

Move 7: read the whole portrait. (C) God's self-description in Exod 34:6–7 is repeated across the Old Testament (Num 14:18; Neh 9:17; Ps 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2). The love commands Jesus quotes come from the Torah (Deut 6:5; Lev 19:18; Lev 19:34).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Weakest premise: P2, at the deaths of children. In the flood, at Sodom, in Egypt, and in Canaan, children died who had done nothing. Context does not remove that. The only answer is Move 5: the giver of life may take it, he alone judges with full knowledge, and death is not the end for them (2 Sam 12:23). A skeptic who rejects that premise will not be persuaded, and you should say so instead of pretending the difficulty is gone.

Hardest objection (Morriston, Rauser): "You would reject a modern claim that God ordered a killing as contrary to his character. So why accept the ancient one?" Answer: Israel's commission sat inside a public, one-time stage of the Bible's history, marked by the exodus and Sinai, and the same Scripture closes the door on repeats (Heb 1:1–2; John 18:36). A private modern voice has none of that. This reply is reasonable. It will not compel an outsider.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "You're dodging. I'm using your Bible against you."

  • Close (R1): Fair. Then we use all of it: the God who gives life, knows every heart, and raises the dead.
  • Their comeback: "That lets God do anything."
  • Close (R2): No. His commands come from a character that does not change (Mal 3:6). The claim is narrow: life is his to give and take, and he judges justly (Gen 18:25).

2. "Context is just an excuse."

  • Close (R1): Context is how we read everything. Ps 137:9 is a victim's prayer, and Hos 13:16 predicts what Assyria will do. Neither is a command.
  • Their comeback: "But Deut 20:16 is a command."
  • Close (R2): Yes, and I won't soften it: see the conquest card below. Context sorts the easy cases from the hard ones.

3. "A loving God would never judge like that."

  • Close (R1): A God who never judged child sacrifice, the enslaving of Israel, or Assyria's cruelty would not be more loving. He would be indifferent.
  • Their comeback: "He could judge without killing."
  • Close (R2): Every death is in his hands either way (Deut 32:39). The question is whether he is just, and the Bible's answer is that he waited centuries, warned first, and took the judgment on himself at the cross (Rom 3:25–26).

4. "That's the Old Testament. Jesus is different."

  • Close (R1): Jesus says he came to fulfill the Law and the Prophets, not to abolish them (Matt 5:17–18), and he treats the flood and Sodom as real judgments (Luke 17:26–29).
  • Their comeback: "Jesus taught love of enemies."
  • Close (R2): He also warned of judgment more than anyone in the Bible (Matt 25:41; Matt 25:46). Splitting the Bible's God in two is the old heresy of Marcion.

Boomerang check

"If 'God commanded it' excuses Canaan, it excuses jihad." A Muslim, or an atheist comparing the two, can turn Move 5 around. Answer: Apply one standard. Read Qur'an 9:5 and 9:29 with the same care for context, genre, and occasion that you ask for the conquest. Then argue the difference from the sources: the conquest commands covered one land and one generation and are no rule for the church (John 18:36; 2 Cor 10:4). Whether the Qur'an's war verses are limited in the same way is debated among Muslims themselves. See 2I and 2K.

"You say Allah is 'the best of schemers' (Qur'an 3:54). Your God sends lying spirits." The two cases are closer than most Christian debaters admit: both are presented as God's answer to people who had already rejected the truth. Use 2B-6 with that in mind, and see the lying-spirit entry below.

Strength rating

MODERATE. As a way to sort the objections it is strong, and most single-verse charges fall to it. It does not make the hard cases easy: the deaths of children and the conquest rest on Move 5, which a skeptic need not grant. Never use Move 1 ("you have no standard") as your whole answer.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Atheists and skeptics The main users of this argument; they expect dodging Open with Move 1 in one sentence, then go to the text. Concede the hard parts.
Progressive or "red-letter" Christians Tempted to keep Jesus and drop the Old Testament Show Jesus' own use of the Old Testament (escape route 4).
Muslims Do not call the God of Moses evil; the Qur'an retells the flood, Lot's city, and Pharaoh's drowning as just judgments (Qur'an 11:25–48; 11:77–83; 7:133–136) Agree on that ground. Expect these passages as a "your Bible is worse" reply (2K).
Fellow Christians Often shaken by a verse they have never read Read the passage with them before answering.

Trap questions

  1. "When you call that evil, do you mean it breaks a rule that binds everyone, everywhere? Where does that rule come from?"
  2. "Are you saying the Bible contradicts itself, or that it contradicts you? If the first, may I use the rest of what it says about God?"
  3. "If God gave every life, does he have any right over it that I don't have?"
  4. "Would a God who never judged anything be better? What would you say to him about the victims?"

30-second version

"Three things. First, most of these verses are misread: a prayer, a prediction, or a regulation gets quoted as if it were a command. Second, where God does judge, the text says why, shows long patience, and holds Israel to the same standard. Third, if God gave life, he has rights over it that we don't. You may reject that, but then we disagree about whether God exists, not about one verse."

2-minute version

"I want to take this seriously, because some of these passages are hard.

Start with what kind of objection it is. If you mean God breaks your moral standard, I'd ask where a standard that binds every culture comes from without God. If you mean the Bible contradicts itself, that's fair. But then we use everything it says about God: he made every life, he knows every heart, and death isn't the end.

Second, many of the famous verses aren't what they look like. Psalm 137 is a refugee's prayer, not a command. Hosea 13 predicts what Assyria will do, and God condemns that same act in Amos 1. 'I create evil' in Isaiah 45 means calamity, which is how modern translations put it. The slave laws never tell anyone to take a slave. They make kidnapping a capital crime and free a slave whose master injures him.

Third, the judgments. God waits four hundred years on the Canaanites. He spares Rahab, who turns to him. He warns Israel it will get the same treatment, and it does. That still leaves the fact that God took lives, some of them young. So here is the bottom line: if God gives life, taking it is his right in a way it could never be mine, and he is the one judge who knows exactly what he is doing.

Last, look at the whole picture. This God calls himself slow to anger and says he takes no pleasure in anyone's death. Christians believe he finally took the judgment on himself at the cross. A God who never judged evil wouldn't be more good. He'd be indifferent."

Further reading

  • Paul Copan, Is God a Moral Monster? (Baker, 2011): the most accessible defense; critics say it overstates in places
  • Christopher J. H. Wright, The God I Don't Understand (Zondervan, 2008)
  • David Lamb, God Behaving Badly (IVP, 2011): beginner level
  • William Webb and Gordon Oeste, Bloody, Brutal, and Barbaric? (IVP Academic, 2019): concedes more than Copan does
  • Other side: Richard Dawkins, The God Delusion (2006), chs. 2 and 7; Dan Barker, God: The Most Unpleasant Character in All Fiction (2016)
  • Other side: Wes Morriston, "Did God Command Genocide? A Challenge to the Biblical Inerrantist," Philosophia Christi 11 (2009)
  • Christians who reject the traditional defense: Eric Seibert, Disturbing Divine Behavior (Fortress, 2009); Randal Rauser, Jesus Loved Canaanites (2021)
Argument1FMODERATE

The Conquest of Canaan: Was It Genocide?

judgment and not ethnic cleansing is clear in the text; that some children died rests on God's right over life

Name + thesis

The conquest of Canaan. Critics call Deut 20:16–17 and Joshua's battles a genocide ordered by God. The texts present something else: a one-time judgment on a culture's sins after four centuries of patience, described in the stock exaggeration of ancient war reports, with the same sentence threatened against Israel and mercy for Canaanites who turned. That answers the charge of genocide. It does not remove the fact that God ordered lives taken, and the last step of the answer is his right over life.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "The iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete" (Gen 15:16): the conquest waits four generations.
  • "Not because of your righteousness... but because of the wickedness of these nations" (Deut 9:5).
  • "They even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods" (Deut 12:31).
  • Israel is warned of the same end: "lest the land vomit you out" (Lev 18:28).
  • Rahab the Canaanite is spared with her whole family (Josh 6:25).
  • Verdict: Scripture presents the conquest as God's judicial act against sin, limited to one land and time, and never as a pattern for his people to imitate.

Key texts

  • Deut 20:16–17: In the cities of Canaan "you shall save alive nothing that breathes, but you shall devote them to complete destruction."
  • Josh 6:21: At Jericho they devoted all in the city to destruction, "both men and women, young and old."
  • Josh 10:40: Joshua "left none remaining, but devoted to destruction all that breathed."
  • Josh 13:1: Yet "there remains yet very much land to possess."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. It is law, not battle poetry. Deut 20:16–17 is an instruction given in advance, so "war rhetoric" cannot explain it away (Thom Stark).
  2. It names peoples. The targets are listed nation by nation (Deut 7:1), which is what genocide means.
  3. Children had done nothing. Whatever the adults did, "young and old" (Josh 6:21) includes infants.
  4. You would never accept this today. A modern commander who said God ordered it would be judged insane or evil (Wes Morriston).

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The stated reason for the conquest is sin after long patience, not ethnicity (Gen 15:16; Lev 18:24–25; Deut 9:4–6).
  • P2. The same sentence falls on Israelites, and Canaanites who turn are spared (Deut 13:12–18; Josh 7:24–26; Josh 6:25; Josh 9:15).
  • P3. The totals are the conventional exaggeration of ancient war reports, and the main command is to drive out (compare Josh 10:40 with Josh 13:1; Exod 23:28–30).
  • P4. It was a single event in one land, not a standing rule (Deut 20:10–15), and it gives the church no warrant (John 18:36).
  • P5. God, the giver of life, may take life in judgment (Deut 32:39).
  • C. The conquest was a limited divine judgment. It was not genocide, and it was not evil.

Evidence for each premise

P1: judgment, not ethnic hatred. God tells Abraham the conquest must wait four generations because the Amorites' sin "is not yet complete" (Gen 15:16). The sins named include child sacrifice, and they are the stated reason the land "vomited out its inhabitants" (Lev 18:21; Lev 18:24–25; Deut 12:31). Israel is told three times that it is not about their own goodness (Deut 9:4–6).

P2: one standard. An Israelite town that turns to idols is put under the same ban, herem (Deut 13:12–18). Achan the Israelite is treated as a Canaanite (Josh 7:24–26). Rahab the Canaanite is treated as an Israelite (Josh 6:25), and the Gibeonites live (Josh 9:15). Ethnic cleansing does not work like that.

P3: the language of ancient war. Joshua "left none remaining" (Josh 10:40), yet the same book says much land remained (Josh 13:1), Caleb later drives the Anakim from Hebron (Josh 15:13–14), and Judges opens with Canaanites still living in the land (Judg 1:27–33). Deut 7:2 orders total destruction, and the next verse forbids marrying the survivors (Deut 7:3). Egypt's Merneptah Stele (about 1208 BC) boasts that Israel's "seed is not." K. Lawson Younger's Ancient Conquest Accounts (1990) documents the convention. The dominant verb is "drive out," little by little (Exod 23:28–30; Deut 7:22).

P4: once, in one place. Cities outside Canaan are offered peace first (Deut 20:10–15). No later king is told to repeat the conquest, and the New Testament gives the church no sword (John 18:36; 2 Cor 10:4).

P5: God's right. See the framework card above, Move 5.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Weakest premise: P3 does less than its fans claim. Hyperbole lowers the numbers. It does not change the kind of act. Deut 20:16–17 is an instruction, not a victory report, and some children almost certainly died. Do not say "no women or children were killed."

Answer: At that point the honest reply is P5. God holds a right over life that soldiers and critics do not, he acted as judge after centuries of patience, and death was not the end for those children (2 Sam 12:23). A critic who rejects that premise will not be persuaded, and you should say so.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "So anything God commands becomes good?"

  • Close (R1): No. His commands come from his character, which does not change (Mal 3:6). The claim is narrower: taking life is his right, and he delegated it once, publicly.
  • Their comeback: "That is still 'good is whatever God says.'"
  • Close (R2): The Euthyphro question is answered in 1B: good is neither above God nor arbitrary; it is what he is. A judge who carries out a just sentence is not a murderer.

2. "Every holy warrior says God told him."

  • Close (R1): Sincerity is not the test. Israel's commission came with the exodus, Sinai, and forty years of public signs, and it expired with that generation.
  • Their comeback: "Convenient that it can't be checked now."
  • Close (R2): It is the opposite of convenient: no Christian can ever claim it. Revelation of that kind reached its goal in Christ (Heb 1:1–2), and his kingdom does not advance by the sword (John 18:36).

3. "Why kill the children?"

  • Close (R1): Scripture does not give a full answer. It gives the judge's character: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?" (Gen 18:25).
  • Their comeback: "That is no answer."
  • Close (R2): It is the answer Abraham got, and Job. I trust it because of what this judge did next: he gave his own Son (Rom 8:32). If there is no God, those deaths, like every death, mean nothing and are never put right.

4. "It's all hyperbole, so nobody really died." (said by Christians)

  • Close (R1): That overclaims. Jericho and Ai fell, and people died.
  • Their comeback: "Then hyperbole changes nothing."
  • Close (R2): It changes the scale and the charge. A campaign of expulsion and judgment that leaves survivors and takes in converts is not the extermination of a race.

Boomerang check

"Then you cannot criticize jihad or the Banu Qurayza executions." A Muslim will cite the conquest and 1 Sam 15:3 the moment you raise Qur'an 9:5 or 9:29. Answer: Grant the comparison and apply one standard. The conquest was confined to one land and one generation and is not a command to the church. Whether the Qur'an's war verses are confined in the same way is a real debate among Muslims; argue it from their sources, as 2I does, and not by assertion. The Banu Qurayza judgment is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari 3043 and 4121 and Sahih Muslim 1768, in the two collections Sunni scholars grade sahih (VERIFY the three numbers on sunnah.com).

Strength rating

MODERATE. "Judgment, not ethnic cleansing" is strong on the texts. "The totals are hyperbole" is strong that hyperbole is present and moderate on how far it reaches. The deaths of children rest on P5. "No non-combatants died" is weak: drop it.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Atheists and skeptics Their strongest single example Concede the hard part early, then ask them to state their standard.
Muslims Used as "the Bible is worse" One standard for both books, then the limits in Deut 20:10–18 (2I).
Christians troubled by it Fear the text makes God cruel Walk through Gen 15:16, Rahab, and Lev 18:28 before the philosophy.

Trap questions

  1. "Should a just judge ever stop a culture that burns its children? How long should he wait first? The text says four hundred years."
  2. "If this was ethnic cleansing, why was Rahab spared and Achan executed?"
  3. "Joshua says none were left, and Judges says they were still there. How do you read that?"
  4. "If there is no God, on what ground was the conquest wrong, and not just ancient?"

30-second version

"The Bible doesn't present Canaan as killing a race. God waits four hundred years, names the sins, including burning children, and warns Israel it will get the same treatment, which it later does. Rahab the Canaanite is spared; Achan the Israelite is not. 'Left none remaining' is the war language of the day: the same book says plenty remained. People did die, and I won't pretend otherwise. But the judge of all the earth has a right over life that I don't."

2-minute version

"This is the hardest one, so I won't dodge it.

First, the reason the text gives is not race. In Genesis 15 God tells Abraham his family must wait four generations because the Amorites' sin is not yet full. Leviticus 18 lists what that sin was, including burning children as offerings, and then warns Israel: do the same and the land will vomit you out too. It did, through Assyria and Babylon.

Second, look at who lives and who dies. Rahab, a Canaanite, is spared with her family. The Gibeonites are spared. Achan, an Israelite, is executed. That is a judgment on what people did, with a door left open.

Third, the totals. Joshua says he left nothing breathing. The same book then says much land remained, and Judges begins with Canaanites still there. That is how ancient kings wrote up campaigns, so the scale was smaller than it sounds.

But some people, including children, did die at God's command, and no amount of context removes that. My answer is that God gives every life and has the right to take it, that he waited centuries first, and that this same God later took judgment on himself at the cross. If you reject God, I understand why that doesn't satisfy you. But then I'd ask what standard makes it wrong."

Further reading

  • Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan, Did God Really Command Genocide? (Baker, 2014)
  • Christopher J. H. Wright, The God I Don't Understand (Zondervan, 2008)
  • William Webb and Gordon Oeste, Bloody, Brutal, and Barbaric? (IVP Academic, 2019)
  • John H. Walton and J. Harvey Walton, The Lost World of the Israelite Conquest (IVP Academic, 2017)
  • Academic: K. Lawson Younger Jr., Ancient Conquest Accounts (JSOT Press, 1990)
  • Other side: Wes Morriston, "Did God Command Genocide? A Challenge to the Biblical Inerrantist," Philosophia Christi 11 (2009); Thom Stark, The Human Faces of God (Wipf and Stock, 2011)
Argument1FMODERATE

Slavery in Ancient Israel's Law

the kidnapping ban and the protections are clear; Lev 25:44–46 and "why not abolish it?" stay hard

Name + thesis

"The Bible endorses slavery." The law of Moses never commands anyone to take a slave. It makes kidnapping a person for sale a capital crime, frees Hebrew debt-servants in the seventh year, frees any slave whose master maims him, and grounds all of it in "you were a slave in Egypt." But it does permit holding foreign slaves for life (Lev 25:44–46), so "it was just a job" is false. The honest claim is that God regulated a universal institution and set it on a path the New Testament continues.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "Whoever steals a man and sells him, and anyone found in possession of him, shall be put to death" (Exod 21:16).
  • "Did not he who made me in the womb make him?" (Job 31:15).
  • "You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you" (Deut 15:15).
  • "Enslavers" are listed among the lawless, with murderers (1 Tim 1:9–10).
  • Paul sends Onesimus home "no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother" (Philemon 16).
  • Verdict: Scripture regulates slavery as a fact of a fallen world, forbids its worst forms outright, and lays down the truths (one Maker, one image, one redemption) that undo it.

Key texts

  • Lev 25:44–46: "You may buy male and female slaves from among the nations that are around you... You may bequeath them to your sons after you to inherit as a possession forever."
  • Exod 21:20–21: A master who beats a slave to death "shall be avenged. But if the slave survives a day or two, he is not to be avenged, for the slave is his money."
  • Exod 21:26–27: A master who destroys a slave's eye or tooth "shall let the slave go free."
  • Deut 23:15–16: "You shall not give up to his master a slave who has escaped from his master to you."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. God could have banned it. He banned shellfish and mixed fabrics. He never says "you shall not own people" (Joshua Bowen, Did the Old Testament Endorse Slavery?, 2020).
  2. Lev 25:44–46 is chattel slavery. Foreigners can be bought, kept for life, and inherited. The kinder terms of Lev 25:39–43 are for Israelites only.
  3. Exod 21:20–21 permits brutal beating. The master is punished only if the slave dies at once.
  4. History proves the reading. American slaveholders quoted these verses, and for centuries most of the church did not object (Hector Avalos, Slavery, Abolitionism, and the Ethics of Biblical Scholarship, 2011).

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The law never commands slavery; it regulates an institution every ancient society had (compare Matt 19:8 on divorce).
  • P2. It forbids the root of the slave trade, kidnapping, on pain of death (Exod 21:16; Deut 24:7).
  • P3. It gives slaves protections unknown in neighboring codes: rest, legal standing against injury and killing, and refuge (Exod 20:10; Exod 21:20; Exod 21:26–27; Deut 23:15–16).
  • P4. Its foundation is that master and slave share one Maker and that Israel were slaves whom God set free (Job 31:13–15; Deut 15:15), and the New Testament builds on that foundation (Philemon 16; 1 Tim 1:9–10).
  • C. The Old Testament does not endorse slavery as good. It restrains it and plants the principles that end it.

Evidence for each premise

P1. The slave laws are case law ("when a man...", "if you buy..."), the form used for regulating what already exists. The ideal is stated elsewhere: every person bears God's image (Gen 1:27).

P2. "Whoever steals a man and sells him" dies (Exod 21:16), and Deut 24:7 repeats it for Israelites. A trade built on capturing people, like the Atlantic trade, would be a capital crime under this law. Paul's word "enslavers" (1 Tim 1:10) carries the same ban into the New Testament.

P3. Slaves rest on the Sabbath "as well as you" (Deut 5:14). A master who kills a slave is punished, and one who maims a slave loses him (Exod 21:20; Exod 21:26–27). Runaways are not handed back (Deut 23:15–16); the Code of Hammurabi sets death for harboring one (laws 15–16). Hebrew debt-servants, men and women, go free in the seventh year with generous provisions (Exod 21:2; Deut 15:12–14). A foreign slave could be circumcised and eat the Passover (Exod 12:44).

P4. Job grounds his slaves' rights in creation (Job 31:13–15). The motive "you were a slave in Egypt" recurs across the law (Deut 15:15; Deut 24:18). Gregory of Nyssa attacked slave-owning itself from Gen 1:27 in the late fourth century (Homilies on Ecclesiastes 4), and Christian abolitionists later argued from the same texts.

The foreigner was not outside the law's care. Israel must love the sojourner "as yourself" (Lev 19:34), and a foreigner in Israel could grow rich and take on an Israelite debtor (Lev 25:47), so the system was not racial.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Weakest premise: P1 cannot fully explain Lev 25:44–46. Lifelong, inheritable foreign slaves are permitted. The protections in P3 apply to them, but the permission is real.

Hardest objection: "Why didn't God just ban it?" There is no knock-down answer. The best one: God gave law to a real ancient society, where the alternative for a debtor or a war captive was often starvation or death, and the law begins a movement it does not finish, as Jesus says of divorce (Matt 19:8). Critics reply that God banned idolatry outright, however entrenched it was. Concede the force of that, then return to what the law did forbid.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "'The slave is his money' (Exod 21:21). You can beat him nearly to death."

  • Close (R1): The verse sits among injury laws. When free men fight and the victim recovers, the attacker pays only for lost time (Exod 21:18–19). A master already bears that loss himself, which is what "his money" means.
  • Their comeback: "So beating is fine if he survives."
  • Close (R2): No. If the slave dies, the master is punished, and the Hebrew verb, naqam, is the word for blood-vengeance (Exod 21:20). If the slave is maimed, he goes free (Exod 21:26–27). Scholars often say no other ancient code punishes a master for killing his own slave (VERIFY in Christopher Wright's Old Testament Ethics for the People of God before quoting).

2. "A man could sell his daughter (Exod 21:7)."

  • Close (R1): Read on. It is a marriage arrangement with enforceable rights: food, clothing, and marital rights, or she leaves free (Exod 21:10–11). She cannot be resold to foreigners (Exod 21:8).
  • Their comeback: "She doesn't go free after six years like the men."
  • Close (R2): Because a wife is not dismissed after six years. Where a woman is a debt-servant and not a wife, Deut 15:12 gives her the same seventh-year release.

3. "Christians used these verses to defend slavery."

  • Close (R1): Some did, sinfully. They had to ignore Exod 21:16, which made their whole trade a capital crime.
  • Their comeback: "The Bible was clear enough for them."
  • Close (R2): It was clear enough for Gregory of Nyssa in the fourth century and for the abolitionists, who argued from Gen 1:27 and Philemon. A book that only blessed slavery would not have produced them (3H).

4. "A freed man's wife and children stay with the master (Exod 21:4)."

  • Close (R1): The wife is still serving her own term, and the man may stay with them (Exod 21:5–6).
  • Their comeback: "That uses his family as leverage."
  • Close (R2): It is a real hardship in the text, and I won't explain it away. It is one of the places where the law restrains an institution it does not yet end.

Boomerang check

"Then you can't criticize slavery in Islam." The same honesty is owed both ways. The Bible regulates slavery, forbids kidnapping, and ends with "a beloved brother" (Philemon 16). If you raise slavery or concubinage in Islamic sources, expect Lev 25:44–46 and Deut 21:10–14 in reply (2K, "the Bible says worse"), and do not claim the Old Testament had no real slavery.

Strength rating

MODERATE. The kidnapping ban, the protections, and the ground in creation are strong. That the law's direction is toward freedom is moderate: true, but argued from a trajectory. "Old Testament slavery was only indentured service" is weak as a blanket claim. It is true of Hebrew debt-servants and false of Lev 25:44–46.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Atheists and skeptics Often know Lev 25:44–46 and Exod 21:20–21 by heart Quote those verses yourself, first.
Hebrew Israelites and others hurt by slavery's history Deeply personal Acknowledge the history; lead with Exod 21:16 and Gen 1:27 (3M).
Muslims Raised as a "you too" reply One standard for both books (2K).
Fellow Christians May have been told "it was just employment" Correct it gently. The true answer is stronger than the easy one.

Trap questions

  1. "What does Exod 21:16 say should happen to someone who kidnaps a person to sell him?"
  2. "If the Bible simply endorsed slavery, why did the people who ended the slave trade argue from it?"
  3. "On your view, what makes slavery wrong in every century, including the ones where everyone accepted it?"

30-second version

"The law of Moses never tells anyone to take a slave. It makes kidnapping a person to sell him a capital crime, frees debt-servants in the seventh year, frees a slave whose master maims him, and won't send a runaway back. It did permit lifelong foreign slaves, and I won't hide that. But it grounds everything in one Maker and 'you were slaves in Egypt,' and that is the root the abolitionists pulled on."

2-minute version

"Let me say the uncomfortable part first: the Old Testament does not abolish slavery, and Leviticus 25 lets Israel keep foreign slaves for life. Anyone who tells you it was just a job is wrong.

Now look at what the law does. It never commands slavery. It regulates something every ancient nation had, and its rules run against the grain of that world. Kidnap someone to sell him: death, in Exodus 21:16. That alone would have outlawed the Atlantic slave trade. Kill your slave: you are punished. Knock out his tooth: he goes free. A runaway comes to your town: you may not send him back. In the Code of Hammurabi, sheltering a runaway got you killed. Every slave rests on the Sabbath, and the reason given is, 'You were slaves in Egypt.'

Why didn't God ban it outright? I don't have a complete answer. Jesus says Moses allowed divorce because of hard hearts, and that it was not so from the beginning. I think slavery is the same kind of case. What I can show you is the direction: one Maker of master and slave in Job, 'enslavers' condemned in 1 Timothy, and Paul sending a runaway home as 'a beloved brother.' The people who ended the slave trade were reading that."

Further reading

  • Paul Copan, Is God a Moral Monster? (Baker, 2011): accessible; critics say it overstates in places, especially on slavery
  • Christopher J. H. Wright, Old Testament Ethics for the People of God (IVP, 2004)
  • William Webb, Slaves, Women and Homosexuals (IVP, 2001): the "redemptive movement" reading
  • David L. Baker, Tight Fists or Open Hands? Wealth and Poverty in Old Testament Law (Eerdmans, 2009)
  • Martha Roth, Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor (Scholars Press, 2nd ed. 1997): check every Hammurabi law number here
  • Other side: Joshua Bowen, Did the Old Testament Endorse Slavery? (2020); Hector Avalos, Slavery, Abolitionism, and the Ethics of Biblical Scholarship (Sheffield Phoenix, 2011)

Short answers, verse by verse

The entries below take one charge each, in seven groups: judgment and war, children, slavery, women, harsh laws, human sacrifice, and God's character. Each answer ends with the other side's hardest comeback and with how firm the answer is (STRONG, MODERATE, or WEAK), using the handbook's usual rating rule. "Framework, Move 5" and similar notes point to the seven moves in the first card of this section.

Defense1F

"The flood drowned the whole world, babies included."

The objection (best form)

"In Genesis 6–8 God kills nearly every human being and animal on earth, infants included, because he regrets making them. That is the largest mass killing in any book."

Answer

  • The reason given is violence. "Every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Gen 6:5), and "the earth was filled with violence" (Gen 6:11).
  • God is grieved, not gleeful. "It grieved him to his heart" (Gen 6:6).
  • There was warning and a way out. Noah was "a herald of righteousness" while the ark was being built (2 Pet 2:5; 1 Pet 3:20).
  • God binds himself never to repeat it (Gen 9:11), and Jesus treats it as a real judgment and a warning (Luke 17:26–27).
  • Their hardest comeback: infants and animals had done nothing. Only God's right over the life he gives answers that (Job 1:21; framework, Move 5).
  • How firm: MODERATE. Clear on the reason and the warning; the deaths of children rest on Move 5.

30-second version

"Genesis says why: human life had become violence from end to end, and it grieved God to his heart. He warned through Noah for years, saved those who listened, and then swore never to do it again. The children are the hard part, and I won't pretend otherwise. But the one who gives every life is the only one with the right to take it, and he is the judge who knows what he is doing."

Defense1F

"Sodom and Gomorrah were burned, children and all."

The objection (best form)

"God rained fire on two whole cities (Gen 19:24–25). Collective punishment of every man, woman, and child is evil."

Answer

  • God invited a challenge first. Abraham bargains him down, and God agrees to spare the whole city for ten righteous people (Gen 18:32). Ten are not found.
  • The one family that will leave is led out by the hand (Gen 19:16).
  • The sins are named: "pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy," and "an abomination" (Ezek 16:49–50). The men of the city try to gang-rape Lot's guests (Gen 19:4–5).
  • Abraham's question is the Bible's own: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?" (Gen 18:25).
  • Their hardest comeback: the city's children. Framework, Move 5.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"Before Sodom falls, God lets Abraham argue with him, and agrees to spare the whole city for ten decent people. There weren't ten. The one family that would leave was led out by the hand. Ezekiel names the city's sins: pride, luxury, and ignoring the poor, along with the violence in Genesis 19. That is a judge who looks for a reason to spare."

Defense1F

"Saul was ordered to kill the Amalekite women, children, and infants."

The objection (best form)

"1 Sam 15:3: 'Do not spare them, but kill both man and woman, child and infant.' That is a command to murder babies, given in God's name."

Answer

  • The history. Amalek attacked Israel's exhausted stragglers at the exodus (Deut 25:17–18) and raided Israel for centuries afterward (Judg 6:3–5; 1 Sam 14:48). This is the end of a long war, not an unprovoked attack.
  • It is targeted. The Kenites living among them are warned to leave first (1 Sam 15:6).
  • The language is conventional. Saul "devoted to destruction all the people" (1 Sam 15:8), yet Amalekites are raiding again a few chapters later (1 Sam 27:8; 1 Sam 30:1).
  • Do not minimize it. Christians should feel the weight of this verse (2I makes the same point).
  • Their hardest comeback: "child and infant" is specific. Hyperbole softens it but does not erase it; the final answer is God's right as judge (Deut 32:39).
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"Amalek had attacked Israel's weakest at the exodus and kept raiding for centuries. The order comes at the end of that war, and neighbors living among them were warned out first. 'All the people' is war language: the same book has Amalekites raiding again a few chapters later. I still feel the weight of 'child and infant.' My answer is that the judge of all the earth has rights over life that no soldier has."

Defense1F

"Moses told the soldiers to kill the boys and keep the virgin girls for themselves."

The objection (best form)

"Num 31:17–18: 'Kill every male among the little ones... but all the young girls who have not known man by lying with him keep alive for yourselves.' That is child murder and sex slavery."

Answer

  • The cause. At Baal Peor, Midianite women were used, on Balaam's advice, to draw Israel into idolatry, and 24,000 died (Num 25:1–9; Num 31:16). The war answers that attack.
  • "For yourselves" is not a license for rape. The text says nothing of sex. The law's only provision for sex with a captive is marriage after a month of mourning, with a wife's standing and her freedom if he ends it (Deut 21:10–14).
  • The action was limited. Midian survives as a people and oppresses Israel later (Judg 6:1–6).
  • Their hardest comeback: the boys died, and the girls had no real choice. This is one of the hardest passages in the Bible. Do not pretend otherwise.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"This comes after Baal Peor, where Midian used its women to pull Israel into idolatry and thousands died. 'Keep them alive for yourselves' means as members of the household. The law's only path to a captive woman was marriage, after a month of mourning, with a wife's rights. I won't dress it up: the boys died, and it is one of the hardest passages there is. But it is war and judgment, not a sex trade."

Defense1F

"Pharaoh was hardened and then punished for it."

The objection (best form)

"God says, 'I will harden his heart' (Exod 4:21), and then destroys Egypt because Pharaoh won't let Israel go. Pharaoh had no choice."

Answer

  • Pharaoh hardens his own heart first (Exod 8:15; Exod 8:32). He had already enslaved Israel and ordered their baby boys drowned (Exod 1:22).
  • The first plain statement that the LORD hardened him comes after six plagues (Exod 9:12). The verb there, hazaq, means "strengthen": God firms up a resolve Pharaoh already had.
  • This is judicial hardening: God hands a man over to what he has chosen, as in Rom 1:24.
  • Both are true. The text says Pharaoh hardened his heart and that God did. Neither cancels the other.
  • Their hardest comeback: Exod 4:21 announces the hardening in advance, and Paul stresses God's freedom (Rom 9:17–18). Reformed readers accept that fully and still hold Pharaoh responsible, as Joseph's brothers were (Gen 50:20).
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"Read the order. Pharaoh enslaves Israel, drowns their sons, and hardens his own heart again and again. Only after six plagues does it say the LORD hardened him, and the word means 'strengthened': God gave him over to the course he had chosen. Scripture says both things, that Pharaoh did it and that God did it, and it holds Pharaoh responsible."

Defense1F

"Every firstborn child in Egypt was killed."

The objection (best form)

"Exod 12:29: God struck down every firstborn, 'from the firstborn of Pharaoh... to the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon.' Children died for one man's stubbornness."

Answer

  • It answers a crime. Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew baby boy thrown into the Nile (Exod 1:22). God had warned him at the start: "Israel is my firstborn son... If you refuse to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son" (Exod 4:22–23).
  • It came last, after nine warnings, and Egyptians who heeded an earlier warning were spared (Exod 9:20).
  • The door was open. A "mixed multitude" left Egypt with Israel (Exod 12:38).
  • Their hardest comeback: the firstborn of the slave girl and of the prisoner had no say in Pharaoh's policy (Exod 11:5; Exod 12:29). Corporate judgment and God's right over life are the only answers.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"Egypt had been drowning Hebrew baby boys. God warned Pharaoh at the start that his own firstborn was at stake, sent nine plagues first, and spared Egyptians who listened. The tenth mirrors the crime. The hard part is the children of people who had no power, and I can only say that nations stand and fall together, and that the giver of life is the judge of it."

Defense1F

"Deuteronomy 20 tells Israel to enslave or slaughter every city that resists."

The objection (best form)

"Deut 20:10–15: offer a city peace, and if it accepts, its people do forced labor; if not, kill the men and take the women and children as plunder. That is conquest and enslavement by divine order."

Answer

  • It limits war in a world that did not. Peace must be offered first (Deut 20:10). Fruit trees may not be cut down for siege works (Deut 20:19–20). Wide exemptions send soldiers home (Deut 20:5–8).
  • "Forced labor" is vassal service, the normal ancient terms of surrender, not chattel slavery.
  • Captive women had legal protection (Deut 21:10–14).
  • It is Israel's law of war, not the church's. Christ's kingdom is not spread by the sword (John 18:36).
  • Their hardest comeback: it is still conquest with captives. True: this regulates ancient warfare and is not the ideal (Isa 2:4; framework, Move 3).
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"Deuteronomy 20 is a law that restrains war: offer peace first, don't destroy the fruit trees, send home anyone newly engaged or afraid. Surrender meant tribute labor, the standard terms in that world. It is ancient warfare with limits on it, given to one nation for one era, and the prophets look ahead to the day swords become plowshares."

Defense1F

"Bears mauled 42 children for calling Elisha bald."

The objection (best form)

"2 Kgs 2:23–24: some small boys mock Elisha, 'Go up, you baldhead!' He curses them in God's name, and two she-bears tear forty-two of them. God kills children over a joke."

Answer

  • The place. Bethel was the seat of the golden-calf shrine (1 Kgs 12:28–29). This is a town's contempt for the LORD's prophet, not playground teasing.
  • "Go up" most likely mocks Elijah's ascension just before (2 Kgs 2:11): vanish like your master.
  • Forty-two struck means a large mob.
  • The verb means "tore" or "mauled." The text does not say they died.
  • Wild animals were a stated covenant curse on a nation that rejected God (Lev 26:22).
  • Their hardest comeback: the Hebrew ne'arim qetannim can mean young men (Solomon uses it of himself as king, 1 Kgs 3:7) but also small boys (2 Kgs 5:14). Their age is uncertain, and a mauling for mockery still looks severe. Do not say "they were a gang of adult thugs" as if it were certain.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"This happens at Bethel, the center of calf worship, right after Elijah was taken up. A crowd comes out to jeer the new prophet: 'Go up, baldhead,' meaning vanish like Elijah did. At least forty-two of them. The word may mean youths or young boys; we can't be sure. The text says the bears mauled them, not that they died. It is a covenant judgment on a town's contempt for God, and it is still a severe one."

Defense1F
