"Psalm 137:9 blesses smashing babies against rocks."

The objection (best form)

"Ps 137:9 blesses the one 'who takes your little ones and dashes them against the rock.' Your holy book celebrates killing infants."

Answer

  • Who is speaking? An exile who survived Babylon's sack of Jerusalem in 586 BC (Ps 137:1). It is a prayer of grief and rage, human speech addressed to God. It is not God's command to anyone.
  • He asks that Babylon be repaid "with what you have done to us" (Ps 137:8), which is what the prophets had already announced (Isa 13:16; Jer 51:56).
  • It hands vengeance to God instead of taking it, which is what Scripture requires (Deut 32:35; Rom 12:19).
  • The Bible records such prayers honestly, as it records Job's complaints. An imprecatory psalm shows what a victim may bring to God; it does not make every wish in it a rule.
  • Their hardest comeback: "It is still in your Bible." Yes, and it tells victims of atrocity that they may bring even this to God.
  • How firm: STRONG.

30-second version

"Look at who is talking. Psalm 137 is a refugee whose city was burned by Babylon, asking that Babylon be repaid for what it did. He isn't told to do anything, and he doesn't. He pours out his rage to God and leaves the repayment with him. The Bible records that prayer honestly. It is a victim's cry, not a command."

Defense1F

"Infants dashed to pieces and pregnant women ripped open (Hosea 13:16)."

The objection (best form)

"Hos 13:16: 'their little ones shall be dashed in pieces, and their pregnant women ripped open.' Isa 13:16 says the same of Babylon. God orders atrocities."

Answer

  • These are predictions, not orders. Hosea foretells what Assyria will do to Samaria, which fell in 722 BC. Isaiah foretells what the Medes will do to Babylon (Isa 13:17). No Israelite is told to do anything.
  • God condemns the act itself. He judges Ammon "because they have ripped open pregnant women in Gilead" (Amos 1:13).
  • God judges the instrument too. Assyria is "the rod of my anger" and is then punished for its arrogance (Isa 10:5; Isa 10:12).
  • Their hardest comeback: God still "stirs up" the invaders (Isa 13:17). Using a wicked nation as an instrument is not approving what it does (Hab 1:13; Gen 50:20). That is the wider problem of evil (1E).
  • How firm: STRONG that these are not commands; MODERATE on the question of God's sovereignty behind them.

30-second version

"Those verses are warnings of what invading armies will do, Assyria to Samaria and the Medes to Babylon. Nobody is commanded to do it. In Amos 1 God condemns Ammon for exactly that crime, and in Isaiah 10 he punishes Assyria after using it. Predicting an atrocity is not ordering one."

Defense1F

"Children are punished for their parents' wrongdoing (Exodus 20:5)."

The objection (best form)

"Exod 20:5: God visits 'the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and the fourth generation.' Punishing children for what their parents did is unjust."

Answer

  • Read the next words: "of those who hate me." The pattern runs on in children who continue their fathers' hatred.
  • Courts may not do it. Children shall not "be put to death because of their fathers" (Deut 24:16), a rule King Amaziah applied (2 Kgs 14:6).
  • Ezekiel states the principle: "The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father" (Ezek 18:20).
  • Three or four generations is one household under one roof: sin's consequences spread through a family.
  • The contrast is the point: iniquity to three or four generations, steadfast love "to thousands" (Exod 20:6).
  • Their hardest comeback: in a few stories a child does suffer for a parent's sin (2 Sam 12:14). See the next entry.
  • How firm: STRONG.

30-second version

"Finish the sentence: 'to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me.' It describes a family that keeps going the same way, three or four generations under one roof. The law forbids courts to punish a child for a parent, and Ezekiel 18 says each person answers for his own sin. And the next line says God's love runs to thousands of generations."

Defense1F

"David's baby was killed to punish David."

The objection (best form)

"2 Sam 12:14–18: because of David's adultery and murder, 'the child who is born to you shall die,' and God strikes the baby with sickness. An innocent infant dies for his father's crime."

Answer

  • God, not a court, takes this life, and the giver of life has that right (Job 1:21; Deut 32:39).
  • The sentence David deserved was his own death, and it is lifted: "The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die" (2 Sam 12:13).
  • David expects to see the child again: "I shall go to him, but he will not return to me" (2 Sam 12:23).
  • The consequences fall across David's whole house (2 Sam 12:10–12). Sin in a king is never private.
  • Their hardest comeback: the child bears the cost. There is no tidy answer. The Bible's final word on an innocent son dying for the guilty is the cross (Isa 53:5).
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"David had taken a man's wife and had him killed, and the penalty he deserved was his own death. God spares him, but the child dies. I don't have a neat explanation. I notice two things: David believed he would see his son again, and the Bible's story ends with God giving his own innocent Son for the guilty. Every life is God's to give and to take."

Defense1F

"Achan's and Korah's families died with them."

The objection (best form)

"Achan steals, and his sons and daughters are stoned and burned with him (Josh 7:24–25). Korah rebels, and the ground swallows the rebels' wives and little ones (Num 16:27–33). That is collective punishment."

Answer

  • Achan. The loot was buried inside the family tent (Josh 7:21), which suggests the household knew. The law already forbade executing children for a father's crime (Deut 24:16), so Israel's judges were not free to kill the innocent.
  • Korah. Everyone was told to move away from the rebels' tents first (Num 16:26), and "the sons of Korah did not die" (Num 26:11). Their descendants wrote psalms (see the titles of Psalms 42 and 84).
  • Both come at founding moments, when the whole people's survival hung on the covenant.
  • Their hardest comeback: the household's complicity is an inference that the text does not state, and Dathan and Abiram's "little ones" are named (Num 16:27).
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"With Achan, the stolen goods were buried under the family's own tent, so this was no secret from his household, and Israel's law forbade executing children for a father's crime. With Korah, everyone was warned to step away first, and the text says Korah's sons did not die. Their family later wrote psalms. These are judgments at Israel's founding, with a way out given."

Defense1F

"Parents will be made to eat their own children (Leviticus 26:29)."

The objection (best form)

"Lev 26:29: 'You shall eat the flesh of your sons.' Jer 19:9: 'I will make them eat the flesh of their sons and their daughters.' God threatens cannibalism."

Answer

  • These are covenant curses: warnings of what siege and famine will bring if Israel abandons God (Lev 26:14–16; Deut 28:52–53).
  • The act is presented as horror, never commanded or approved. When it happens, the king tears his clothes (2 Kgs 6:28–30), and Lamentations weeps over it (Lam 4:10).
  • "I will make them" is the Bible's way of saying that God will send the siege as judgment (Jer 19:7–9). The enemy besieges; starvation does the rest.
  • The warning came first, for centuries, so that it need never happen (Jer 18:7–8).
  • How firm: STRONG.

30-second version

"Those lines are in the covenant warnings: if Israel abandons God, enemies will besiege their cities, and starvation will drive people to the unthinkable. It is a warning of consequences, described as a horror. When it did happen, the Bible mourns it. A warning sign on a cliff is not an order to jump."

Defense1F

"You can beat your slave as long as he doesn't die right away (Exodus 21:20–21)."

The objection (best form)

"Exod 21:20–21: if a master beats his slave and the slave 'survives a day or two, he is not to be avenged, for the slave is his money.' God permits beating slaves almost to death."

Answer

  • Read it with the law beside it. When free men fight and the victim recovers, the attacker pays only for his lost time (Exod 21:18–19). A master already bears that loss himself, which is the meaning of "his money."
  • If the slave dies, the master is punished (Exod 21:20). The Hebrew verb, naqam, is the word for blood-vengeance.
  • If the slave is maimed, even by a tooth, he goes free (Exod 21:26–27).
  • The day or two tests intent: a master who meant to kill gains nothing by destroying his own worker.
  • Their hardest comeback: a free victim still gets more protection than a slave. True. See the slavery card above for what the law did and did not do.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"Read three verses together. If a master beats a slave to death, he is punished, and the word is the one for blood-vengeance. If he knocks out so much as a tooth, the slave goes free. Verse 21 covers the case in between: the master pays no fine to himself, because the lost labor is already his loss. It is a limit on masters, not a license."

Defense1F

"A father could sell his daughter as a slave."

The objection (best form)

"Exod 21:7: 'When a man sells his daughter as a slave, she shall not go out as the male slaves do.' God allows fathers to sell girls, and they never go free."

Answer

  • Read the next four verses. The arrangement is a marriage into the buyer's family, to him or to his son (Exod 21:8–9).
  • She has enforceable rights: food, clothing, and marital rights. If he fails in these, "she shall go out for nothing, without payment of money" (Exod 21:10–11).
  • She cannot be resold to foreigners, and if she is given to a son she must be treated "as with a daughter" (Exod 21:8–9).
  • "Not as the male slaves" means she is not dismissed after six years like a hired hand; she has a wife's permanence. Where a woman serves as a debt-servant and not a wife, she goes free in the seventh year (Deut 15:12).
  • Their hardest comeback: her father arranges it, and her consent is not mentioned. That was true of nearly all marriage in the ancient world; the law's work is to protect her within it.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"Keep reading. The next verses show it is a marriage arrangement for a poor family's daughter, and they give her rights a slave never had: food, clothing, and a wife's standing, or she walks free without paying anything. She can't be sold on. It is a law protecting a vulnerable girl inside the marriage customs of that world."

Defense1F

"A rape victim must marry her rapist (Deuteronomy 22:28–29)."

The objection (best form)

"Deut 22:28–29: if a man seizes an unbetrothed virgin and lies with her, he pays her father fifty shekels and 'she shall be his wife... He may not divorce her all his days.' The victim is handed to her attacker for life."

Key texts

  • Deut 22:25–27: The rape law. The man who forces a woman dies; "the young woman has committed no offense."
  • Deut 22:28–29: A man "seizes" (taphas) an unbetrothed virgin "and they are found."
  • Exod 22:16–17: A man who seduces an unbetrothed virgin must pay and marry her, but "if her father utterly refuses to give her to him," he only pays.

Answer

  • The rape law is the paragraph before. There the verb is hazaq, "overpower." The man alone dies, the woman is declared innocent, and the crime is compared to murder (Deut 22:25–27).
  • Verses 28–29 change the wording. They use a different verb and add "they are found," treating the pair together. The word "violated" ('innah) is also used in Deut 22:24 for a case the law treats as consensual. The vocabulary does not settle whether force is meant.
  • The parallel law lets the father refuse (Exod 22:16–17). Read together, the duty binds the man and not the woman: he must provide for life and can never divorce her.
  • The point is that he cannot walk away. After Amnon rapes Tamar, she says that sending her away is the greater wrong (2 Sam 13:16).
  • Their hardest comeback: taphas does mean seize, and several modern translations say "rapes" (VERIFY the wording in your own edition). On that reading the woman's own voice is not recorded; her father decides. Do not claim the passage is "clearly consensual."
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"The rape law is the paragraph just before: the rapist dies and the woman is declared innocent. Verses 28 and 29 use a different word and say 'they are found,' so it may be seduction. Either way, the parallel law in Exodus 22 lets her father refuse the marriage. What the law does is bind the man: he pays, he provides for life, and he can never divorce her. In that world it stopped him from ruining her and walking away."

Defense1F

"Israelite soldiers could take captive women as wives."

The objection (best form)

"Deut 21:10–14: a soldier who sees a beautiful captive may take her home and make her his wife. That is legalized wartime rape."

Answer

  • It forbids what armies normally did. There is no sex on the battlefield: she is brought home and given a full month to mourn her parents (Deut 21:12–13).
  • Then comes marriage, with a wife's standing, not concubinage or slavery.
  • If he ends it, she goes free. "You shall not sell her for money, nor shall you treat her as a slave" (Deut 21:14).
  • Compare the alternative. In ancient war, captive women were raped, enslaved, or killed with no law at all.
  • Their hardest comeback: her consent is never mentioned. True. The law restrains a soldier's power; it does not make the situation just by modern standards (framework, Move 3).
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"In ancient warfare, captured women had no protection at all. This law says a soldier may not touch her on the battlefield. He must bring her home, give her a month to grieve, and then marry her as a full wife. If he changes his mind she leaves free and can never be sold. It doesn't make war good. It puts a fence around a soldier's power."

Defense1F

"Numbers 5 prescribes an abortion."

The objection (best form)

"In Num 5:11–31 a jealous husband takes his wife to the priest, who makes her drink a potion that causes a miscarriage if she was unfaithful. God prescribes abortion, and a trial by ordeal for women only."

Answer

  • The Hebrew does not mention pregnancy or miscarriage. It speaks of her belly (beten) swelling and her thigh (yarek) wasting (Num 5:27). The NIV's "miscarry" is an interpretation; the ESV has "her womb shall swell, and her thigh shall fall away."
  • The innocent wife "shall be free and shall conceive children" (Num 5:28). The curse is barrenness, the opposite of that blessing.
  • The drink is holy water with dust from the floor (Num 5:17). It is harmless unless God acts, so the default verdict is acquittal.
  • It protects the wife. The case is taken out of a jealous husband's hands and placed before God. In the Code of Hammurabi an accused wife must throw herself into the river (law 132).
  • Their hardest comeback: there is no matching rite for a suspected husband. True.
  • How firm: STRONG that it is not abortion; MODERATE on fairness.

30-second version

"The Hebrew says nothing about a pregnancy. It says her belly will swell and her thigh waste away, and that an innocent wife will go on to have children, so the curse is barrenness. The drink is water and dust: it does nothing unless God acts, which means a suspicious husband has to leave the verdict to God and not to his fists. Babylon's law threw the wife in the river."

Defense1F

"The law treats women as worth less than men."

The objection (best form)

"A mother is unclean twice as long after bearing a girl (Lev 12:2–5), and a woman's vow value is thirty shekels to a man's fifty (Lev 27:3–4). The law says females are worth less."

Answer

  • Ritual uncleanness is not sin, and it is not worth. It also follows ordinary bodily events for men (Lev 15:16). The offering after a birth is identical for a son or a daughter (Lev 12:6).
  • The text gives no reason for the longer period, and you should not invent one.
  • The vow values track labor in a farming economy. They also fall for the old and for small children (Lev 27:5–7). They price work, not persons.
  • Worth is settled at creation: "male and female he created them," both in God's image (Gen 1:27), and the law commands honor for mother and father alike (Exod 20:12; Lev 19:3).
  • Their hardest comeback: "no reason given" is not an explanation for Lev 12.
  • How firm: MODERATE on Leviticus 12; STRONG on Leviticus 27.

30-second version

"Being ritually unclean wasn't a sin or a rating of your worth: men became unclean from normal bodily things too, and the offering for a baby girl is exactly the same as for a boy. The shekel table in Leviticus 27 prices farm labor, which is why it also drops for the elderly and for children. The Bible states human worth in Genesis 1: male and female, both in God's image."

Defense1F

"Polygamy has divine approval."

The objection (best form)

"Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon had many wives, the law regulates it (Exod 21:10; Deut 21:15–17), and God says he gave David Saul's wives (2 Sam 12:8). The Bible's God endorses polygamy."

Answer

  • It is never commanded, and the pattern is set at creation: one man, one woman, "one flesh" (Gen 2:24), which Jesus makes the standard (Matt 19:4–6).
  • Kings are told not to multiply wives (Deut 17:17). Solomon's wives turn his heart away (1 Kgs 11:3–4).
  • Every polygamous home in the narratives is miserable: Sarah and Hagar (Gen 16:4–6), Leah and Rachel (Gen 30:1), Hannah and Peninnah (1 Sam 1:6–7).
  • The laws protect the less-loved wife and her son (Deut 21:15–17). That is regulation, not approval (framework, Move 3).
  • Their hardest comeback: 2 Sam 12:8. It describes the transfer of Saul's royal house to David, the sign of kingship. It is not praise of polygamy.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"The Bible reports polygamy and never recommends it. The pattern is Genesis 2, one man and one woman, and Jesus goes back to it. Kings are told not to multiply wives, and every story of a man with several wives is a story of jealousy and grief. The laws about it protect the wife who is loved less. Reporting and regulating are not approving."

Defense1F

"David's wives were handed over to be raped (2 Samuel 12:11)."

The objection (best form)

"2 Sam 12:11: 'I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor.' God arranges the rape of innocent women to punish David."

Answer

  • It is a sentence announced, and a guilty man carries it out. Absalom does it on Ahithophel's advice, to seize the throne (2 Sam 16:21–22), and both die under judgment (2 Sam 17:23; 2 Sam 18:14–15).
  • Scripture often says God "does" what he hands sinners over to do, while holding the doers guilty. Assyria is God's rod and is then punished (Isa 10:5; Isa 10:12). Joseph's brothers "meant evil" (Gen 50:20).
  • The punishment mirrors David's crime: he took a man's wife in secret, and his own house is violated in public (2 Sam 12:12).
  • Their hardest comeback: the women are innocent and bear the cost. That is a real difficulty, the same one as every case where the sins of the powerful fall on the weak.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"God is announcing what David's sin will bring on his house, and it happens through Absalom, who chose it freely to grab the throne and died for his rebellion. The Bible often speaks of God 'doing' what he hands people over to, while holding them fully guilty, as with Joseph's brothers. The women suffer for men's sins, and Scripture does not call that good."

Defense1F

"Lot offered his daughters to a mob and is still called righteous."

The objection (best form)

"In Gen 19:8 Lot offers his virgin daughters to a mob to protect his guests. In Judges 19 a Levite hands over his concubine to be raped to death. Yet 2 Pet 2:7 calls Lot 'righteous.' The Bible treats women as disposable."

Answer

  • Described is not approved (framework, Move 2). Neither act is commanded or praised.
  • Genesis shows Lot's compromise: he chose Sodom (Gen 13:10–13), lingers when told to flee (Gen 19:16), and ends in a cave in disgrace (Gen 19:30–36).
  • Judges presents Gibeah as the pit of a lawless age. "Such a thing has never happened or been seen" (Judg 19:30), and the book's refrain is its verdict (Judg 21:25).
  • "Righteous Lot" (2 Pet 2:7–8) means righteous by faith and by contrast with Sodom, "tormenting his righteous soul" over what he saw. Scripture calls flawed people righteous on those terms, David included.
  • How firm: STRONG.

30-second version

"The Bible reports those acts; it doesn't approve them. Genesis shows Lot as a compromised man who chose Sodom and barely got out. Judges tells the Gibeah story as the lowest point of an age when 'everyone did what was right in his own eyes.' Peter calls Lot righteous the way Scripture calls any sinner righteous: by faith, not because of that night."

Defense1F

"The law says to cut off a woman's hand."

The objection (best form)

"Deut 25:11–12: if a wife grabs the genitals of a man who is fighting her husband, 'you shall cut off her hand. Your eye shall have no pity.' That is barbaric mutilation."

Answer

  • It is the only mutilation penalty in the whole law. Neighboring codes are full of them; the Middle Assyrian Laws order ears, noses, and fingers cut off.
  • The offense is an attack on a man's ability to father children, in a law code that guards family lines.
  • Later Jewish interpreters read it as a fine, not an amputation (VERIFY the rabbinic reference before citing).
  • A minority of scholars read the Hebrew as a shaming penalty and not amputation (Jerome Walsh, Journal of Semitic Studies, 2004; VERIFY). Do not rely on it.
  • Their hardest comeback: a hand for a grab is still harsh. It is the law of one ancient nation (framework, Move 3), not a rule for the church.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"That is the one and only mutilation penalty in the law of Moses, where other ancient codes had dozens. It protects a man's ability to have children, which mattered enormously in that society. It belongs to ancient Israel's civil code, and no Christian thinks it is a rule for today."

Defense1F

"Women were cursed to be ruled by men (Genesis 3:16)."

The objection (best form)

"Gen 3:16: 'he shall rule over you.' God decrees male domination as a punishment on all women."

Answer

  • It stands among the results of the fall, beside thorns, sweat, and death (Gen 3:17–19). It describes a broken world; it does not command one.
  • Nobody thinks using a plow defies God. Easing the curse on the ground is good, and so is healing the strife between husband and wife.
  • Before the fall, man and woman bear God's image together and receive the same commission (Gen 1:27–28).
  • The gospel's pattern for a husband is the reverse of domination: "love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (Eph 5:25).
  • Their hardest comeback: Christians disagree about how a husband's headship (Eph 5:22–33) relates to this verse. They agree that harsh rule is the curse, not the design.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"That line is in the list of what sin broke, next to thorns and death. It describes the war between the sexes; it doesn't order it. Before the fall, man and woman bear God's image together. And when the New Testament tells husbands what to do, it says to love their wives the way Christ did, by giving himself up."

Defense1F

"Ezekiel 16 and 23 threaten women with stripping and sexual humiliation."

The objection (best form)

"In Ezekiel 16 and 23, Jer 13:22–26, and Nah 3:5, God says he will lift women's skirts, expose them, and hand them over to be abused. God speaks like an abusive husband."

Answer

  • The "woman" is a city or nation: Jerusalem, Samaria, Nineveh. These are extended pictures of the covenant as a marriage and of idolatry as adultery (Ezek 16:8; Ezek 16:15).
  • The images describe what conquering armies did to cities: stripped, plundered, exposed. The prophets use the shock of it as a warning (Ezek 16:37–39).
  • They are not instructions about women. The law these prophets preach punishes rape with death (Deut 22:25–27).
  • The marriage picture ends in restoration: "I will establish my covenant with you" (Ezek 16:62–63); "I will betroth you to me forever" (Hos 2:19).
  • Their hardest comeback: the metaphor still pictures judgment as a husband's violence, and feminist scholars press this. It is fair to say the language is meant to disturb.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"In those chapters the woman is a city: Jerusalem, Samaria, or Nineveh. The prophets picture God's covenant as a marriage and idolatry as adultery, and they describe in shocking terms what invading armies will do to the city. It is a warning in the harshest language they had, not a rule for treating women, and the picture ends with God taking his people back."

Defense1F

"Rebellious children are to be stoned (Deuteronomy 21:18–21)."

The objection (best form)

"Deut 21:18–21: parents take a stubborn and rebellious child to the elders, and 'all the men of the city shall stone him to death.' The Bible commands killing disobedient kids."

Answer

  • He is not a child. The charge is "he is a glutton and a drunkard" (Deut 21:20): a grown son whose life is wrecking the family.
  • Parents cannot act alone. A Roman father could kill his own child; an Israelite father could not. Both parents must agree and bring him to the elders for a public hearing (Deut 21:19–20).
  • There is no record of it ever being carried out. One Talmudic tradition says no such case ever happened (b. Sanhedrin 71a), though another rabbi there disagrees.
  • The law's effect was to take the power of death out of the household and put it under public justice.
  • Their hardest comeback: it still stands in the text as God's law for Israel. Yes: it shows how seriously God takes the destruction of a family (Exod 20:12), within one nation's civil code (framework, Move 3).
  • How firm: STRONG that it is not about children.

30-second version

"It isn't about children. The son in that law is 'a glutton and a drunkard,' an adult wrecking his family. In Rome a father could kill his own child. This law takes that power away: both parents have to agree and bring the case to the town's elders for a public hearing. There is no record in the Bible of it ever being done."

Defense1F

"A man was executed for gathering sticks on the Sabbath."

The objection (best form)

"Num 15:32–36: a man is found gathering sticks on the Sabbath, and God tells Moses, 'The man shall be put to death.' The whole camp stones him. That is death for picking up firewood."

Answer

  • Read what comes just before. The law has just separated unintentional sin, which is forgiven, from sin "with a high hand," which "reviles the LORD" (Num 15:27–31). The story is the example.
  • The Sabbath was the sign of the covenant Israel had sworn at Sinai (Exod 31:13–14). This is open defiance of it in front of the whole camp.
  • They did not rush. They held him in custody until God answered (Num 15:34).
  • It belongs to Israel under Moses. For the church the Sabbath is not a matter of civil penalty at all (Col 2:16–17).
  • Their hardest comeback: the penalty still looks out of proportion. The answer rests on how serious defiance of God is, which a skeptic will not grant.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"The story comes right after a law separating accidental sin, which is forgiven, from sin 'with a high hand,' meaning open defiance. The Sabbath was the sign of the covenant the whole nation had sworn. This man is the example of throwing it off in public. It is severe, it belongs to Israel's founding years, and Paul says no one is to judge Christians over Sabbaths."

Defense1F

"Death for adultery, homosexuality, blasphemy, and witchcraft."

The objection (best form)

"Lev 20:10 and 20:13, Lev 24:16, Exod 22:18, and Deuteronomy 13: death for adulterers, for men who lie with men, for blasphemers, for sorceresses, and for anyone who leads others from the faith. A good God would not write that code."

Answer

  • It was the civil law of one covenant nation, with God as its king. Paul quotes Deuteronomy's formula, "Purge the evil person from among you," and applies it to the church as excommunication, not execution (1 Cor 5:13).
  • Conviction was hard. Two or three eyewitnesses were required (Deut 17:6; Deut 19:15), the witnesses had to throw the first stones (Deut 17:7), and a false witness received the penalty he sought (Deut 19:16–19).
  • It was milder than its neighbors where they were harshest. There was no death penalty for theft of property, which the Code of Hammurabi imposed (laws 6–8 and 21–22). No child could be killed for a parent's crime (Deut 24:16). There was one law for native and foreigner (Lev 24:22).
  • The list shows what the law held sacred: God's exclusive claim, human life, and the family.
  • Penalties may have been maximums. Ransom is forbidden for murder (Num 35:31), which may imply it was possible in other cases. This is an inference.
  • Their hardest comeback: "Was it ever just?" The Christian answer is yes, for that nation under that covenant. Christians keep the moral teaching and not the civil penalty.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"Those were the criminal laws of ancient Israel, a nation with God as its king. Conviction needed two or three eyewitnesses, and a false accuser got the penalty himself. The list tells you what that covenant treated as sacred: God, life, and marriage. It was never the church's law. When Paul quotes the same formula in 1 Corinthians 5, the penalty is to put the person out of the church, not to death."

Defense1F

"Uzzah was struck dead for trying to keep the ark from falling."

The objection (best form)

"2 Sam 6:6–7: the oxen stumble, Uzzah puts out his hand to steady the ark, and 'God struck him down there because of his error.' He dies for a reflex. The same God burns Nadab and Abihu over incense (Lev 10:1–2)."

Answer

  • The ark should never have been on a cart. It was to be carried on poles by Levites, who must not touch it "lest they die" (Num 4:15; Exod 25:14). David admits the fault: "we did not seek him according to the rule" (1 Chr 15:13).
  • The cart was the Philistines' method (1 Sam 6:7). Israel was handling the sign of God's presence like a pagan trophy.
  • Nadab and Abihu were priests at the very start of the priesthood who offered "unauthorized fire" that God "had not commanded them" (Lev 10:1). A warning against serving drunk follows at once (Lev 10:9).
  • Both come at founding moments and teach one thing: God is holy and is approached on his terms (Lev 10:3).
  • Their hardest comeback: Uzzah meant well. The text's answer is that the fault began with ignoring God's instructions for the ark, not with the stumble.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"The ark was never supposed to be on a cart. God had said it must be carried on poles and not touched, on pain of death. David copied the Philistines' method and later admitted it was his fault. Uzzah's death taught Israel that God's holiness is real and is not handled casually. It is a hard lesson at a founding moment, like Ananias and Sapphira in Acts 5."

Defense1F

"David was incited to take a census, and 70,000 died for it."

The objection (best form)

"2 Sam 24:1 says God 'incited David' to number Israel. Then God sends a plague that kills seventy thousand (2 Sam 24:15). And 1 Chr 21:1 says it was Satan. God sets a trap and punishes the victims."

Answer

  • The story begins with Israel already under God's anger: "Again the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel" (2 Sam 24:1). The people are not bystanders.
  • Two agents, one event. Chronicles names Satan as the one who incites (1 Chr 21:1). God permits and Satan acts, as in Job 1:12. Hebrew narrative often credits God with what he permits.
  • David is warned and overrules the warning (2 Sam 24:3–4), then confesses, "I have sinned greatly" (2 Sam 24:10).
  • David chooses the penalty, and chooses to fall into God's hand, "for his mercy is great" (2 Sam 24:14). God stops the plague short (2 Sam 24:16).
  • Their hardest comeback: it looks like entrapment, and the text never says what Israel's sin was.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"The chapter opens by saying God was already angry with Israel, so the people aren't innocent bystanders. Chronicles tells us Satan did the inciting: God allowed it, as in Job. David's own general warned him, he did it anyway, and he admitted his guilt. He then chose to fall into God's hands because God is merciful, and God cut the plague short."

Defense1F

"Israel was slaughtered by the thousand in the wilderness."

The objection (best form)

"Three thousand killed after the golden calf (Exod 32:28), 14,700 after Korah's revolt (Num 16:49), 24,000 at Baal Peor (Num 25:9), plus fire, plague, and snakes. This God kills his own followers by the thousand."

Answer

  • It proves he has no favorites. In the Torah, Israel is judged more often and more severely than any other nation. "You only have I known... therefore I will punish you" (Amos 3:2).
  • Each case is a revolt against the covenant they had just sworn (Exod 24:7), usually with idolatry, and usually after a warning.
  • Intercession works. Moses pleads and God relents (Exod 32:11–14). Aaron stands "between the dead and the living," and the plague stops (Num 16:48).
  • Paul says these things were written "for our instruction" (1 Cor 10:11): judgment begins with God's own house (1 Pet 4:17).
  • How firm: STRONG as evidence that God shows no partiality.

30-second version

"Notice who is being judged: Israel. The God accused of ethnic favoritism judges his own people more often than anyone else in those books, each time after they broke a covenant they had just sworn. And each time someone steps in to plead, Moses or Aaron, he relents. That is the opposite of a tribal god protecting his own."

Defense1F

"Elijah slaughtered 450 prophets of Baal."

The objection (best form)

"1 Kgs 18:40: after the contest on Mount Carmel, Elijah has the prophets of Baal seized and kills them all. That is a religious massacre done in God's name."

Answer

  • Leading Israel into idolatry was a capital crime under Israel's own law (Deut 13:1–5). Elijah acts as that law's officer.
  • These were not harmless clergy. They were the court prophets of Jezebel (1 Kgs 18:19), who had been killing the LORD's prophets (1 Kgs 18:4; 1 Kgs 18:13). Baal worship later included burning children (Jer 19:5).
  • The contest came first, in public, with every chance to back down (1 Kgs 18:21–39).
  • Jesus refuses to let his disciples repeat Elijah. When they ask to call down fire on a village, he rebukes them (Luke 9:54–55).
  • Their hardest comeback: it is still killing over religion. It belongs to Israel's civil covenant, which the church does not inherit (John 18:36).
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"Those prophets served Queen Jezebel, who had been murdering the LORD's prophets, and under Israel's law leading the nation into idol worship was a capital crime. Elijah gave them a public test first. But notice what Jesus does when his disciples want to copy Elijah and call down fire: he rebukes them. That was Israel's civil law, and the church has none like it."

Defense1F

"An attempt to kill Moses (Exodus 4:24)."

The objection (best form)

"Exod 4:24: on the way back to Egypt God meets Moses and 'sought to put him to death.' God sends Moses on a mission and then tries to kill him."

Answer

  • The issue is circumcision. Zipporah circumcises their son, and "so he let him alone" (Exod 4:25–26).
  • Circumcision was the sign of the covenant, and the uncircumcised male "shall be cut off from his people" (Gen 17:14). The man sent to lead the covenant people had neglected it in his own house.
  • It follows God's warning about Pharaoh's firstborn (Exod 4:22–23): the covenant's terms apply to Moses' family first.
  • The Hebrew is obscure. It is not even certain whether "him" is Moses or his son.
  • Their hardest comeback: an obscure text makes a weak objection and a weak answer. Say so.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"That is one of the most obscure passages in the Bible, and even who 'him' refers to is unclear. What is clear is the cause: Moses had not circumcised his son, the sign of the covenant he was about to represent, and the moment it is done the danger ends. The lesson is that the messenger is not exempt from the message."

Defense1F

"Onan was killed for using birth control."

The objection (best form)

"Gen 38:9–10: Onan 'would waste the semen on the ground,' and because this 'was wicked,' God 'put him to death.' God executes a man over contraception."

Answer

  • The sin is fraud against a widow. Onan's duty was levirate marriage: to give his dead brother's widow, Tamar, a son who would carry the brother's name and inheritance (Gen 38:8; Deut 25:5–6).
  • His motive is stated: "Onan knew that the offspring would not be his" (Gen 38:9). An heir for his brother would shrink his own share.
  • He took the benefit and refused the duty, repeatedly, leaving Tamar with no son and no security.
  • The law later let a man decline this duty at the cost of public shame only (Deut 25:7–10), which shows the sin was the deceit and cruelty, not the method.
  • Their hardest comeback: death still seems severe. Framework, Move 5.
  • How firm: STRONG that it is not about contraception.

30-second version

"Onan's duty was to give his dead brother's widow a son, who would inherit in the brother's name. The text gives his motive: he knew the child wouldn't count as his. So he used Tamar and made sure she got nothing, again and again. His sin was defrauding a widow and his dead brother, not birth control."

Defense1F

"Genesis 22: a father is asked to offer up his own child."

The objection (best form)

"In Gen 22:2 God tells Abraham, 'Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love... and offer him there as a burnt offering.' A God who asks for a child sacrifice, even as a test, is evil, and a father who obeys is worse."

Answer

  • The reader is told at the start that it is a test (Gen 22:1), and God stops it: "Do not lay your hand on the boy" (Gen 22:12).
  • Abraham expects to come back with Isaac. He tells his servants, "I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you" (Gen 22:5), and tells Isaac, "God will provide for himself the lamb" (Gen 22:8).
  • He had a promise that needed Isaac alive (Gen 21:12), so "he considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead" (Heb 11:19).
  • In a world where gods took children, this is the story where God refuses one and supplies a substitute (Gen 22:13). The law then forbids child sacrifice outright (Deut 12:31; Lev 18:21).
  • Their hardest comeback: a good God would not ask, even as a test. Reply: nothing is taken, and what the test reveals is the kind of God he is. Christians add that the Father later gave what he spared Abraham from giving (Rom 8:32).
  • How firm: STRONG.

30-second version

"Genesis tells you in the first line that it is a test, and God stops it before any harm is done. Abraham told his servants, 'We will come back to you,' because God had promised him descendants through Isaac. Every god around him took children. This is the story where God says no and provides a ram, and his law then bans child sacrifice. Christians see in it the Father who did not spare his own Son."

Defense1F

"Jephthah's vow and his daughter (Judges 11)."

The objection (best form)

"Judg 11:30–39: Jephthah vows to offer as a burnt offering whatever comes out of his house, his daughter comes out, and he 'did with her according to his vow.' God accepts a human sacrifice."

Answer

  • God never asks for the vow, never speaks in the story, and never approves it. Described is not approved (framework, Move 2).
  • Jephthah thinks like his pagan neighbors. He speaks of the god Chemosh giving land (Judg 11:24). Judges is a record of what happens when "everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (Judg 21:25).
  • The law forbade it and offered a way out. Human sacrifice is an abomination (Deut 12:31), a rash vow could be confessed (Lev 5:4–6), and a vowed person was redeemed for silver (Lev 27:1–8).
  • A minority view holds that she was given to lifelong virginity, since she mourns her virginity and "had never known a man" (Judg 11:37–39). Most scholars think he killed her. The answer does not depend on it.
  • Their hardest comeback: the Spirit came on Jephthah (Judg 11:29), and Heb 11:32 names him. The Spirit empowered him for battle, as with Samson, and Hebrews 11 commends faith, not every deed.
  • How firm: STRONG that God did not command or approve it.

30-second version

"God never asks for that vow and never says a word in the story. Jephthah is a half-pagan warlord in the book of Judges, which exists to show what Israel became when everyone did what was right in his own eyes. God's law called human sacrifice an abomination and gave a way to undo a rash vow. The Bible reports his vow as a tragedy, not a model."

Defense1F

"Exodus 22:29 claims every firstborn."

The objection (best form)

"Exod 22:29: 'The firstborn of your sons you shall give to me.' And in Ezek 20:25–26 God admits, 'I gave them statutes that were not good... in their offering up all their firstborn.' So child sacrifice was required at first."

Answer

  • "Give" means dedicate, then redeem. "All the firstborn of your sons you shall redeem" (Exod 34:20; Exod 13:13). The Levites serve in the firstborn's place (Num 3:12–13), and each firstborn is bought back for five shekels (Num 18:15–16).
  • God says he never commanded child sacrifice: "which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind" (Jer 7:31).
  • Ezek 20:25–26 is judgment by handing over. God gave rebels up to the pagan statutes they preferred, as in Ps 81:11–12 and Rom 1:24. The same chapter calls child sacrifice defilement (Ezek 20:31) and tells them, "Go serve every one of you his idols" (Ezek 20:39).
  • Their hardest comeback: some scholars, such as Jon Levenson, think Ezekiel means Exod 22:29 literally. Against that, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, and the Torah all deny that God ever commanded it.
  • How firm: STRONG on Exod 22:29; MODERATE on Ezek 20:25–26.

30-second version

"In Exodus, 'give me your firstborn' is followed by 'you shall redeem every firstborn son': they were dedicated and bought back, and the Levites served in their place. In Ezekiel 20 God is saying he handed rebels over to the pagan practices they wanted, and the same chapter calls child sacrifice defilement. Jeremiah quotes God directly: it never entered his mind."

Defense1F

"Leviticus 27:29 and people 'devoted to destruction.'"

The objection (best form)

"Lev 27:29: 'No one devoted, who is to be devoted for destruction from mankind, shall be ransomed; he shall surely be put to death.' People could be vowed to God and killed."

Answer

  • "Devoted" here is herem, the judicial ban, not a private vow. It is the sentence on convicted idolaters (Exod 22:20) and on an apostate city (Deut 13:12–15).
  • The verse closes a loophole: someone under that sentence cannot be bought off with money. It is a rule against bribery in capital cases, like Num 35:31.
  • Ordinary vows of persons were always redeemed for silver, in the same chapter (Lev 27:1–8).
  • Human sacrifice is forbidden in the same book (Lev 18:21; Lev 20:2–5).
  • How firm: STRONG.

30-second version

"That verse is about people under a court's sentence of destruction, such as convicted idolaters, and it says they can't buy their way out. It is not a way to vow a person to death. The same chapter says a person vowed to God is redeemed with silver, and the same book bans human sacrifice twice."

Defense1F

"Seven of Saul's descendants were hanged to end a famine."

The objection (best form)

"2 Sam 21:1–14: a famine comes because Saul killed Gibeonites. David hands over seven of Saul's sons and grandsons to be hanged, and then the famine ends. God accepts human sacrifice and punishes children for a grandfather's crime."

Answer

  • God names the cause, not the remedy. He says the famine is for Saul's massacre of the Gibeonites, which broke an oath sworn in God's name (2 Sam 21:1–2; Josh 9:15).
  • The Gibeonites propose the hangings, and David agrees (2 Sam 21:4–6). God does not command it.
  • The text ties God's answer to the burial. After Rizpah's vigil moves David to bury the dead with honor, "after that God responded to the plea for the land" (2 Sam 21:10–14).
  • The guilt is laid "on Saul and on his house" (2 Sam 21:1), which may mean his family took part.
  • Their hardest comeback: it sits uneasily with Deut 24:16, and the narrator does not condemn David. That is a real tension.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"Read who says what. God tells David the famine is because Saul massacred the Gibeonites, breaking an oath sworn in God's name. The demand for seven men comes from the Gibeonites, not from God. And the text says God answered prayer for the land after the dead were given an honorable burial. It is a story about blood-guilt and a broken oath, told without approval of every step."

Defense1F

"'I create evil' (Isaiah 45:7)."

The objection (best form)

"Isa 45:7 in the King James Version: 'I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil.' God admits he is the author of evil."

Answer

  • The Hebrew word ra' has a range. It can mean moral evil, and it can mean disaster, harm, or hardship.
  • The parallel decides it. Its opposite here is shalom, peace or well-being, not righteousness. So it means calamity: "I make well-being and create calamity" (ESV); "I bring prosperity and create disaster" (NIV).
  • The setting is God's rule over nations. He is addressing Cyrus, whom he raises up to topple Babylon (Isa 45:1).
  • The same sense appears elsewhere: "Does disaster come to a city, unless the LORD has done it?" (Amos 3:6; Lam 3:38).
  • Scripture denies that God does moral evil: "just and upright is he" (Deut 32:4; Jas 1:13).
  • Their hardest comeback: if God ordains everything, moral evil is in his plan too. That is the general problem of evil (1E): God ordains that evil be, for good, without doing evil (Gen 50:20; Acts 2:23).
  • How firm: STRONG.

30-second version

"That is the King James wording of a Hebrew word that also means disaster. Look at the pairs: light and darkness, peace and its opposite. The opposite of peace is calamity, which is how modern translations put it. God is telling Cyrus that he rules the rise and fall of empires. The Bible is clear elsewhere that God does no moral wrong."

Defense1F

"Lying spirits are sent to deceive (1 Kings 22)."

The objection (best form)

"1 Kgs 22:23: God 'has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets.' In Ezek 14:9 God says he has 'deceived that prophet.' Jeremiah says, 'You have deceived me' (Jer 20:7). A God who deceives cannot be trusted."

Answer

  • Ahab had chosen the lie already. He kept four hundred prophets who told him what he liked and hated the one who told the truth (1 Kgs 22:6–8).
  • God discloses the whole plan to Ahab's face before the battle, through Micaiah (1 Kgs 22:19–23). A deceiver does not announce the deception. Ahab goes anyway.
  • This is judgment by handing over: people who refuse the truth are given the lie they prefer (Ezek 14:4–9; 2 Thess 2:10–11).
  • Jer 20:7 is Jeremiah's own cry of anguish. The verb patah also means persuade or entice. A prophet's complaint is not a doctrine about God.
  • Scripture's teaching is plain: "God is not man, that he should lie" (Num 23:19; Titus 1:2).
  • Their hardest comeback: God still commissions the spirit. Yes: as a judge passing sentence on a man who demanded lies.
  • Boomerang: if you press Qur'an 3:54 ("the best of schemers") against Islam, expect this passage in return (2B-6).
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"Ahab had surrounded himself with four hundred prophets who said what he wanted and hated the one honest one. So God gives him what he chose, and then has Micaiah tell Ahab the entire plan to his face before the battle. Someone who tells you he is letting you be lied to is not deceiving you. Ahab picked the lie anyway. It is a judgment on a man who refused the truth."

Defense1F

"An evil spirit was sent to torment Saul."

The objection (best form)

"1 Sam 16:14: God's Spirit leaves Saul, and 'a harmful spirit' from God torments him. The King James says 'an evil spirit.' God sends demons on people."

Answer

  • The word is ra' again: harmful, distressing, troubling. The ESV has "a harmful spirit."
  • It is judgment after rebellion. Saul had twice defied God's direct command and been told the kingdom was torn from him (1 Sam 13:13–14; 1 Sam 15:22–28).
  • God withdraws his Spirit and hands Saul over to the misery he had chosen. Whatever the spirit is, it goes only where God permits (Job 1:12).
  • Mercy is still within reach. David's music relieves him (1 Sam 16:23), and Saul's response is to try to kill David (1 Sam 18:10–11).
  • Their hardest comeback: God is still the sender. It is the same judicial handing-over as with Ahab (1 Kgs 22:22).
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"The Hebrew word means harmful or distressing, which is how modern translations put it. It comes after Saul twice defied God and lost the kingdom. God's Spirit leaves him, and he is given over to torment as a judgment. Even then God sends relief through David's music, and Saul answers by throwing a spear at him."

Defense1F

"Jealousy is a vice (Exodus 20:5; 34:14)."

The objection (best form)

"In Exod 20:5 God calls himself 'a jealous God.' Exod 34:14 says his very name is Jealous. Jealousy is a petty, insecure vice. Why worship a being who has it?"

Answer

  • The word is covenant jealousy. Qanna' is used only of God, and the picture is a marriage: the right of a husband or wife to the other's faithfulness.
  • Jealousy is not envy. Envy wants what belongs to someone else. Jealousy guards what is rightly one's own. A husband indifferent to his wife's adultery does not love her more.
  • The rivals were not harmless. The gods Israel ran to demanded their children: "They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to the demons" (Ps 106:37–38).
  • God's jealousy is for his people's good: he will not share them with what destroys them (Deut 4:24; Deut 6:14–15).
  • How firm: STRONG.

30-second version

"It is the jealousy of a marriage, not envy. Envy wants what isn't yours. This is a husband who won't shrug when his wife is being taken by someone who will destroy her. And the rivals were gods that demanded people's children. A God who didn't care whether we gave ourselves to that would not be more loving."

Defense1F

"Divine regret means divine mistakes (Genesis 6:6)."

The objection (best form)

"Gen 6:6 says God 'regretted that he had made man.' 1 Sam 15:11: 'I regret that I have made Saul king.' A God who regrets is not all-knowing, and a God who changes his mind is not trustworthy."

Answer

  • One chapter uses the word both ways. God "regrets" making Saul king (1 Sam 15:11), and Samuel says God "will not lie or have regret, for he is not a man" (1 Sam 15:29). The writer is not contradicting himself eighteen verses apart.
  • The verb naham means to grieve or to relent. Of God it describes real sorrow over sin (Gen 6:6 adds, "it grieved him to his heart"), not surprise.
  • Relenting when people repent is God's stated policy, announced in advance (Jer 18:7–10; Jonah 3:10; Jonah 4:2).
  • Scripture speaks of God in human terms so that we can know him. It also says he declares "the end from the beginning" (Isa 46:9–10).
  • How firm: STRONG.

30-second version

"The same chapter that says God regretted making Saul king also says God does not regret like a man. So the writer plainly means two different things. The word means to grieve, or to relent. God is truly grieved by sin, and he tells us ahead of time that he will relent when people turn. That is consistency, not a mistake."

Defense1F

"The serpent was right in Eden."

The objection (best form)

"God said, 'In the day that you eat of it you shall surely die' (Gen 2:17). The serpent said, 'You will not surely die' (Gen 3:4). They ate, and Adam lived 930 years (Gen 5:5). The serpent was right."

Answer

  • "In the day" is a Hebrew idiom for "when." The same phrase is used of the whole creation week (Gen 2:4).
  • "You shall surely die" is the form of a death sentence. Solomon tells Shimei, "On the day you go out... you shall die" (1 Kgs 2:37), and Shimei is executed later, after a journey and a hearing (1 Kgs 2:39–46).
  • Death began that day. They were cut off from God's presence and from the tree of life (Gen 3:22–24), and the sentence was pronounced: "to dust you shall return" (Gen 3:19).
  • The serpent's half-truth is the model of a lie. Their eyes were opened (Gen 3:7), to shame. Jesus calls him "a liar and the father of lies" (John 8:44).
  • How firm: STRONG.

30-second version

"'In the day you eat' is the Hebrew way of saying 'when you eat,' and 'you shall surely die' is how a death sentence was worded. Solomon uses the same formula for a man who was executed later, not that afternoon. That day Adam and Eve were sentenced and cut off from God and from the tree of life, and they did die. The serpent's promise was the lie."

Defense1F

"Satan was allowed to kill Job's children to win a bet."

The objection (best form)

"In Job 1–2 God points Job out to Satan, lets Satan kill his ten children and his servants and ruin his health, all to prove a point. Then he 'replaces' the children. God gambles with human lives."

Answer

  • The question is not a wager for sport. Satan's charge is that no one loves God for his own sake: "Does Job fear God for no reason?" (Job 1:9). If that is true, all faith is a bribe.
  • Satan does the harm, inside limits God sets (Job 1:12; Job 2:6).
  • The book exists to destroy the idea that suffering proves guilt. The friends who say so are rebuked: "you have not spoken of me what is right" (Job 42:7).
  • God never tells Job about the scene in heaven. He shows Job the limits of his sight (Job 38:4), and Job is satisfied by meeting God, not by an explanation (Job 42:5–6).
  • Their hardest comeback: the children and servants still die, and children are not replaceable. Job's own answer is hope beyond death: "I know that my Redeemer lives" (Job 19:25–27).
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"It isn't a bet for amusement. Satan's accusation is that nobody loves God except for what they get, and Job's suffering answers it for every believer since. Satan does the harm, within limits. The book's whole point is that suffering does not prove guilt, and the friends who say it does are rebuked. The dead are not forgotten: Job himself says, 'I know that my Redeemer lives.'"

Defense1F

"Delight in bringing ruin (Deuteronomy 28:63)."

The objection (best form)

"Deut 28:63 says God 'will take delight in bringing ruin upon you and destroying you.' God enjoys ruining people."

Answer

  • It is the climax of the covenant curses, written in deliberate symmetry: as he delighted to do good, so he will judge. The point is certainty, not appetite.
  • Scripture says directly what God feels about judgment: "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked" (Ezek 33:11); "he does not afflict from his heart" (Lam 3:33).
  • His heart is shown in Hosea: "How can I give you up, O Ephraim?... My heart recoils within me" (Hos 11:8).
  • To approve of justice is not to enjoy pain. A good judge is glad when justice is done and takes no pleasure in the prisoner's suffering.
  • The same speech promises restoration when Israel returns (Deut 30:1–3).
  • Their hardest comeback: the verse does say "delight." Let the plain statements of Ezekiel and Lamentations interpret the rhetorical one.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"That line closes a long list of covenant warnings and is built as a mirror: as surely as God blessed, so surely he will judge. When the Bible speaks plainly about how God feels, it says he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and does not afflict from his heart. Two chapters later he promises to bring them back."

Defense1F

"Yahweh is a tribal deity who plays favorites."

The objection (best form)

"Yahweh chooses one nation, gives them other people's land, and bars Ammonites and Moabites from his assembly (Deut 23:3). That is a tribal war god, not the God of all humanity."

Answer

  • Israel is chosen for the nations, not against them: "in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed" (Gen 12:3).
  • Not for merit: "It was not because you were more in number... but it is because the LORD loves you" (Deut 7:7–8), and "not because of your righteousness" (Deut 9:5).
  • Chosen means held to a stricter standard: "You only have I known... therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities" (Amos 3:2).
  • Outsiders are welcomed throughout: Rahab of Jericho, Ruth the Moabite, Naaman the Syrian (2 Kgs 5:15), the city of Nineveh (Jonah 4:11). Foreigners and eunuchs are promised a place in God's house (Isa 56:3–7).
  • The goal is stated: "Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance" (Isa 19:25).
  • How firm: STRONG.

30-second version

"God chooses Abraham in order to bless every family on earth, and tells Israel it wasn't because they were better. Being chosen meant being judged more strictly. All through the Old Testament outsiders come in: Rahab, Ruth, Naaman, the whole city of Nineveh. Isaiah even looks ahead to God calling Egypt 'my people.' That is not a tribal god."

Defense1F

"The curse of Ham: Black people were cursed to be slaves."

The objection (best form)

"In Gen 9:25 Ham's descendants are cursed to be slaves. Christians used this to say that God made Africans a slave race."

Answer

  • Noah speaks the curse, not God, and the text never says God endorsed it.
  • It falls on Canaan, not on Ham and not on Ham's other sons: "Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be" (Gen 9:25). Canaan's descendants lived in Palestine, not Africa (Gen 10:15–19).
  • It says nothing about skin color.
  • The racial reading was invented much later to defend the slave trade, against the Bible's teaching that God "made from one man every nation of mankind" (Acts 17:26).
  • Their hardest comeback: "Christians did use it." Yes, sinfully, and other Christians refuted them from the same Bible (3M).
  • How firm: STRONG.

30-second version

"Read the verse: Noah, not God, speaks the curse, and it lands on Canaan, not on Ham. Canaan's descendants lived in Palestine. Nothing in the passage mentions Africa or skin color. Slave traders invented that reading centuries later, and it contradicts Acts 17: God made every nation from one man."

Defense1F

"The disabled are barred from the altar (Leviticus 21)."

The objection (best form)

"Lev 21:17–23: no descendant of Aaron who is blind, lame, or has any defect may approach the altar. God bars the disabled from his presence."

Answer

  • The rule covers one office: priests serving at the altar. It does not cover worshipers or the disabled in general.
  • The priest with a defect still eats the holiest food: "He may eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy and of the holy things" (Lev 21:22). He keeps his place and his living.
  • It is symbolism, like the unblemished animal (Lev 22:19–21). The altar pictured a wholeness that pointed ahead to the perfect priest and offering (Heb 7:26–27).
  • The same law protects the disabled: "You shall not curse the deaf or put a stumbling block before the blind" (Lev 19:14).
  • The promise runs the other way. Eunuchs receive "a name better than sons and daughters" (Isa 56:4–5), and Jesus tells hosts to invite "the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind" (Luke 14:13).
  • Their hardest comeback: symbolic exclusion still excludes. True for that office, in that covenant.
  • How firm: MODERATE.

30-second version

"That rule is only about priests serving at the altar. A priest with a disability kept his position and ate the same holy food. The altar was a picture of perfection that pointed forward to Christ, like the rule that sacrificial animals be unblemished. The same book forbids mistreating the deaf and the blind, and Jesus says to invite them to the feast."

Defense1F

"Old Testament wrath, New Testament love: two different deities."

The objection (best form)

"The Old Testament God is wrathful and violent. Jesus teaches love and forgiveness. They are different gods, or Christians should drop the Old Testament and just follow Jesus."

Answer

  • Jesus disagrees. "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets" (Matt 5:17). He treats the flood and Sodom as real judgments (Luke 17:26–29) and calls the God of Israel his Father (John 8:54).
  • Jesus' love commands are quotations from the Torah: love God (Deut 6:5), love your neighbor (Lev 19:18), love the foreigner "as yourself" (Lev 19:34).
  • The Old Testament is full of mercy. Its most repeated description of God is "merciful and gracious, slow to anger" (Exod 34:6; Ps 103:8; Jonah 4:2).
  • The New Testament is full of judgment. Jesus warns of hell more than anyone in Scripture (Matt 25:41; Matt 25:46), and Revelation shows him as judge (Rev 19:11–15).
  • This split is an old heresy, Marcionism. Marcion taught it in the second century, and the church rejected it.
  • How firm: STRONG.

30-second version

"Jesus didn't think so. He said he came to fulfill the Law and the Prophets, he called the God of Israel his Father, and when he taught 'love your neighbor' he was quoting Leviticus. The Old Testament's favorite description of God is 'merciful and gracious, slow to anger,' and the New Testament has Jesus warning about judgment more than anyone. It is one God and one story."

Popular answers to drop

These answers are common in sermons and online, and each one loses more than it wins, because an informed opponent has the counter-text ready.

Popular answer Why it fails Say this
"No women or children died in Canaan. It is all hyperbole." Deut 20:16–17 is an instruction, and Josh 6:21 names them. Hyperbole is real and limits the scale. Some died, and God had the right.
"Old Testament slavery was just a job." Lev 25:44–46 allows lifelong, inheritable foreign slaves. Debt service for Hebrews; regulated, protected servitude for foreigners; kidnapping a capital crime.
"The 42 were a gang of adult thugs." The Hebrew phrase can mean small boys (2 Kgs 5:14). Their age is uncertain. The setting and the size of the mob matter more.
"Deut 22:28–29 is clearly consensual." The verb means seize, and major translations say rape. Either way the duty falls on the man, and the father can refuse (Exod 22:17).
"You're an atheist, so you can't call anything evil." (as the whole answer) It ignores the internal critique. Use it to frame the discussion, then open the text.
"That's the Old Testament. We follow Jesus." Jesus affirms the Old Testament (Matt 5:17–18). This is Marcionism. Same God, same character, a different covenant administration.
"Archaeology proves the Canaanites were the worst people ever." The clearest evidence of child sacrifice comes from later Phoenician sites such as Carthage; for Bronze Age Canaan it is debated (VERIFY before citing any excavation). "The text gives this as the reason" (Lev 18:24–25; Deut 12:31).
"God didn't command it. Moses or Samuel did." 1 Sam 15:2 opens with "Thus says the LORD." This answer costs you the authority of Scripture. Own the text and defend it.

Part 2

Islam

2A

The Islamic Dilemma

1 card1 strong

New terms

Tawrat / Injil: The Qur'an's names for the Torah and the Gospel.

Ahl al-Kitab: "People of the Book/Scripture": Jews and Christians.

Tahrif: "Distortion" or corruption of scripture.

Tahrif al-nass: Corruption of the text itself (the words were changed).

Tahrif al-ma'na: Corruption of the meaning (twisted interpretation, text intact).

Tafsir: Qur'anic commentary.

Hadith: A report of Muhammad's words or deeds, passed down through a chain of narrators.

Isnad: The chain of narrators attached to a hadith.

Sahih: "Sound": the top grade of hadith.

Hasan: "Good": an acceptable hadith grade, a step below sahih.

Da'if: "Weak": a hadith grade not reliable enough to base doctrine on.

Mu'allaq: "Suspended": a report quoted without its full chain (Bukhari often does this in chapter headings). Not the same as a fully connected sahih hadith.

Qira'a (pl. qira'at): One of the recognized canonical "readings" of the Qur'an.

Muhaymin: "Guardian / watcher / witness" (5:48).

Argument2ASTRONG

The Islamic Dilemma

core form P1 + P3 + P4; MODERATE if you lean on P2

Name + thesis

The Qur'an tells the Jews and Christians of Muhammad's day to judge by the Torah and Gospel they possessed. Those books are substantially the Bible we have today, and they contradict the Qur'an about Jesus. So either the Bible is reliable and the Qur'an is wrong, or the Bible is unreliable and the Qur'an was wrong to affirm it.

Key texts

The Qur'an on the scriptures "they have":

  • 5:43: "But how is it that they come to you for judgment while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah?" (wa 'indahumu t-tawratu fiha hukmu llah: "and with them is the Torah, in it is Allah's judgment")
  • 5:46–47: "...We gave him [Jesus] the Gospel, in which was guidance and light... And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein (wa-l-yahkum ahlu l-injili bima anzala llahu fihi)."
  • 5:68: "Say, 'O People of the Scripture, you are [standing] on nothing until you uphold the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been revealed to you from your Lord.'"
  • 7:157: "...the unlettered prophet, whom they find written in what they have of the Torah and the Gospel" (yajidunahu maktuban 'indahum)
  • 10:94: "So if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to you, then ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you."
  • 3:3: "He has sent down upon you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it (musaddiqan lima bayna yadayhi). And He revealed the Torah and the Gospel."

The Qur'an on God's words:

  • 6:115: "None can alter His words (la mubaddila li-kalimatihi)." (Also 6:34, 10:64, 18:27.)

The Qur'an on Jesus:

  • 4:157: "They did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but it was made to appear so to them (wa lakin shubbiha lahum)."
  • 5:72: "They have certainly disbelieved who say, 'Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary.'"

The Bible on Jesus:

  • 1 Cor 15:3–4: "Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures... he was buried... he was raised on the third day."
  • John 20:28: Thomas to the risen Jesus: "My Lord and my God!"

Their best case (steelman)

A capable Muslim scholar-debater (in the line of Ibn Hazm, Shabir Ally, or a well-read Salafi) would argue:

  1. "Torah" and "Injil" mean the original revelations, not your Bible. The Injil was given to Jesus (5:46). The four Gospels were written about him by others decades later. When the Qur'an affirms the Injil, it is affirming what God gave Jesus, not Matthew through John.
  2. The Qur'an itself says they corrupted their scripture. They "distort words from their places" (5:13; 4:46), "write the scripture with their own hands, then say, 'This is from Allah'" (2:79), and "twist their tongues with the Book" (3:78).
  3. The Qur'an is the muhaymin (guardian/judge) over earlier scripture (5:48). It confirms what is true in them and corrects what is false. "Confirming" never meant certifying every word.
  4. God never promised to preserve the Torah; He promised to preserve the Qur'an. The rabbis were "entrusted with preserving" the Torah (5:44, bima-stuhfizu), and they failed. But of the Qur'an God says, "We will be its guardian" (15:9). The "no one can change His words" verses (6:34, 10:64) are about God's decrees and promises, not manuscripts.
  5. Modern scholarship agrees the Bible changed. Critical scholars say the Gospels are anonymous, late, and contain additions (Mark 16:9–20, John 7:53–8:11). That is exactly what the Qur'an predicted.

Premises → conclusion

Red-team fix: the argument is built so that it does not depend on P2. P2 is disputed (see below), so it is used only as reinforcement.

  • P1. The Qur'an treats the Torah and Gospel possessed by Jews and Christians in Muhammad's day as containing God's revelation, sufficient to judge by (5:43, 5:47, 5:68, 7:157, 10:94).
  • P2 (reinforcing, not load-bearing). The Qur'an says God's words cannot be changed (6:115; 18:27).
  • P3. The Torah and Gospel of the 7th century are substantially the same as the Bible today.
  • P4. Today's Bible clearly teaches Jesus' crucifixion, death, resurrection, and deity, which the Qur'an denies (4:157; 5:72).
  • C1. So the Bible the Qur'an told Christians to judge by contradicted the Qur'an on its central claim about Jesus. (P1, P3, P4)
  • C2. If that Bible was reliable, the Qur'an is wrong about Jesus. If it was unreliable, the Qur'an was wrong to tell Christians to judge by it (and, with P2, wrong that God's words cannot be changed).
  • C. Either way, the Qur'an contains a serious error, so it is not the word of an all-knowing God.

Evidence for each premise

P1 (the Qur'an affirms the scriptures in their hands).

  • Present tense, present possession. 5:43 says "with them is the Torah"; 7:157 says "written with them"; 5:68 is a command with qul ("Say!") addressed to contemporaries: "you stand on nothing until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel." You cannot uphold a book you do not have.
  • The Medina stoning case. Some Jews brought an adultery case to Muhammad. He asked what the Torah says. A Torah was brought, one man covered the stoning verse with his hand, and the convert Abdullah ibn Salam exposed it. Muhammad then ruled by what the Torah said. Sahih al-Bukhari 3635 (in-book 61/139), narrated by Ibn Umar; parallel in Sahih Muslim 1699a (in-book 29/40), narrated by Ibn Umar. What it shows: the Torah in 7th-century Medina contained the correct ruling. The Jews hid the text; they had not changed it.
  • 10:94 tells Muhammad to check his revelation against those who read the earlier scripture. The scripture in their hands is treated as a reliable check, not as something needing correction.
  • The accusation and the affirmation are two verses apart. 5:41 accuses some Jews: "they distort words beyond their [proper] places" (yuharrifuna l-kalima min ba'di mawadi'ihi). Two verses later, 5:43 says of the same people: "they have the Torah, in which is Allah's judgment." Ibn Kathir calls it "the correct opinion" that 5:41 was revealed about the two Jews who committed adultery, which is the Medina stoning case above. He also reports a second occasion: a blood-money dispute between Banu al-Nadir and Banu Qurayza, which he ties to 5:42 onward. He concludes that both may lie behind the passage. Either way, the very passage that accuses them of distortion also affirms that the Torah in their hands contains God's judgment.

P2 (God's words unchangeable). 6:115 and 18:27 say there is "no changer of His words," and 18:27 sits in the context of "the Book of your Lord." But see the hardest objection: 6:34 and 10:64 are about God's promises and decrees.

P3 (the 7th-century Bible = our Bible). Muhammad lived c. 570–632.

Witness Date What survives Before Muhammad's birth (c. 570)
Dead Sea Scrolls c. 250 BC – AD 68 (Great Isaiah Scroll, 1QIsaᵃ, c. 125 BC) Old Testament only; they predate Jesus ~500–800 years
P66, P75 c. 175–225 (Brent Nongbri argues it may be as late as the 4th c.) P66: much of John, fragmentary toward the end; P75: fragmentary portions of Luke and John ~350–400 years (possibly less)
Codex Vaticanus c. 300–350 Greek OT and NT, but it lacks most of Genesis (Gen 1:1–46:28), part of the Psalms, and the NT from Heb 9:14 on (1–2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon, Revelation). All four Gospels are present. ~220–270 years
Codex Sinaiticus c. 330–360 the entire New Testament (the oldest complete NT), but much of the OT is lost ~210–240 years
Codex Alexandrinus 5th c. most of both testaments; gaps include Matt 1:1–25:6 ~70–170 years
Syriac Peshitta (Church of the East, Syriac Orthodox) 5th c. Gospels complete; the NT lacks 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude, and Revelation ~70–170 years

Scope of the claim. Every New Testament witness in this table that preserves the Gospel passion narratives (Vaticanus, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and the Peshitta) contains the crucifixion. The Dead Sea Scrolls predate Jesus and are cited only for the stability of the Old Testament text. The early papyri are fragmentary and are cited for textual stability, not as complete witnesses. Every Christian community near Arabia in the 7th century also affirmed the crucifixion: Byzantine (Melkite), Syriac Orthodox, Church of the East, Coptic, and Ethiopian/Abyssinian. The Abyssinian church is the one whose king sheltered the first Muslim emigrants.

P4 (the contradiction). The crucifixion appears in all four Gospels (Mark 15; Matt 27; Luke 23; John 19), in Paul's letters (1 Cor 15:3–4, an early creed most scholars date to within a few years of the events), and in non-Christian sources (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). Jesus' deity: John 1:1, 20:28; Mark 14:61–64. None of this depends on any disputed textual variant.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Weakest premise: P2 in its strong form. The contexts of 6:34 and 10:64 are about God's promises and decrees, and 5:44 says the rabbis were entrusted with preserving the Torah, while 15:9 says God Himself guards the Qur'an. A well-read Muslim will press this, and he has a point. That is why the card does not rest on P2.

Hardest surviving objection (against P1):

"The Qur'an's affirmation means: act on whatever true revelation remains in your books, and it will lead you to Muhammad. It is not a certificate for every word in every copy. 'Confirming what is before it' means confirming the truth in it."

Why it survives: it is a coherent reading, and no single verse refutes it outright. Why it is still in trouble: (a) 5:43 rebukes the Jews for coming to Muhammad when the Torah with them already contains God's judgment, a rebuke that only works if their Torah is reliable on the matter in dispute. (b) The Qur'an never warns Christians that their Gospel is wrong about the cross; it tells them to judge by it (5:47). (c) Even on a "true remnant" view, the crucifixion is the least plausible candidate for corruption, since it is in every Gospel, every manuscript, Paul's letters, and pagan sources. So the remnant would still include the cross.

Honest bottom line: this is a strong cumulative case, not a one-verse knockout. Present it that way.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "It was corrupted in text" (tahrif al-nass), not just meaning.

  • Close (Round 1): Look at what the tahrif verses actually describe. 3:78 is about twisting tongues (oral recitation): "so you think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book." That only works if the real Book is still there to compare against. 4:46 is wordplay (ra'ina). Most tellingly, 5:41 ("they distort words beyond their places") is followed two verses later by 5:43 ("they have the Torah, in which is Allah's judgment"), and Ibn Kathir ties 5:41 to the Medina stoning case, where the text was hidden, not changed. One strand of early Muslim interpretation read these verses as corruption of meaning. That strand appears in a chapter heading of Bukhari's Book of Tawhid (Book 97, chapter 55, on "Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a preserved tablet," 85:21–22, just before no. 7553). It glosses yuharrifun ("they distort") as yuzilun ("they remove") and adds: "no one removes a word of any of the books of Allah, but they distort it by interpreting it wrongly." Attribution is disputed. The gloss yuzilun is attributed to Ibn Abbas without a connected chain (it is mu'allaq). On the second sentence, Ibn Hajar says the wording "is nearly explicit" that it is al-Bukhari's own comment, added after Ibn Abbas's gloss, though it could be the rest of Ibn Abbas's words. He also quotes his teacher Ibn al-Mulaqqin: this is one of the two views on the verse, and the one al-Bukhari chose (Fath al-Bari, Kitab al-Tawhid, ch. 55). Ibn al-Qayyim likewise quotes it as Bukhari's own. Either way it is useful: if it is Bukhari's, then the compiler of the most trusted hadith collection (d. 870) held that the scriptures' wording was not removed. (Full treatment in 2B-2.)
  • Their comeback A: "2:79 is textual: they write the scripture with their own hands."
  • Close (Round 2A): 2:79 describes some people producing a writing and passing it off as from God. It does not say every Torah scroll across the world was replaced. And Surah 2 itself, 38 verses earlier, tells the Jews to believe in the Qur'an "confirming that which is with you" (2:41). The Medina stoning case shows the Torah there still contained the true ruling.
  • Their comeback B (the strongest one, so be ready for it): "Your own Ibn Abbas taught textual corruption. In Sahih al-Bukhari 2685 (Book of Witnesses), repeated at 7363 (Book of Holding Fast) and 7523 (Book of Tawhid), with a sound chain to Ibn Abbas, he says: 'O Muslims, how can you ask the People of the Book, when your Book, revealed to your Prophet, is the newest news from Allah, which you read pure and undistorted? Allah has told you that the People of the Book changed what Allah wrote and altered it with their hands (baddalu... wa ghayyaruhu bi-aydihim), and said, "This is from Allah," to buy a small price with it.'" (Verified: Sahih al-Bukhari 2685 (in-book 52/46), a statement of Ibn Abbas (mawquf); Sahih al-Bukhari 7363 (in-book 96/90), the same Ibn Abbas statement; Sahih al-Bukhari 7523 (Book of Tawhid), a third occurrence.)
  • Close (Round 2B): Concede that the report is authentic. It is Ibn Abbas's real view, and it is textual. Then give four answers: 1. It is mawquf (it stops at a Companion). This is Ibn Abbas's own judgment, not a saying of Muhammad. It carries a Companion's authority, not prophetic authority. 2. It is his reading of 2:79, not independent evidence. He says, "Allah has told you...," and the closing words ("to buy a small price with it") quote 2:79. So it adds no new information about what happened to the manuscripts. It simply restates how he understood the verse. 3. It says nothing about scope or timing. It does not say every copy everywhere was altered, or when. The setting is pastoral: it discourages Muslims from consulting Jews and Christians, decades after Muhammad. Ibn Abbas died c. 687. 4. It walks straight into the timing trap (2B-1). If he means the Bible of his day was textually changed, that Bible matches manuscripts from centuries before Muhammad, the same scripture the Qur'an affirmed as "with them" (5:43; 7:157). So the alteration, if any, came before the Qur'an affirmed those books.
  • Note on 5:47: Hamza and al-A'mash read wa-li-yahkuma ("so that [they] might judge"), which makes the verse say why the Injil was given (al-Qurtubi on 5:47).
