Some use this to place the verse in Jesus' time. But al-Tabari calls both readings well known and close in meaning, and says a reader who uses either is correct (al-Tabari on 5:47). The Dilemma does not depend on 5:47; see escape route 3 in 2B-1.
  • Honest takeaway: early Muslims were not united on meaning-only corruption. Say "some early Muslims, possibly including Bukhari, held that the text was intact," never "early Muslims taught..."

2. "The Injil was a lost book given to Jesus."

  • Close (Round 1): The Qur'an never says the Injil was lost. It calls Christians "the People of the Gospel" (ahl al-injil, 5:47) and says they find Muhammad written in the Gospel "with them" (7:157). You cannot find something written in a book you don't have.
  • Their comeback: "They had a corrupted version, not the real Injil."
  • Close (Round 2): Then 7:157 says Muhammad is written in the corrupted version, and 5:47 commands Christians to judge by a corrupted book. The Qur'an never distinguishes "the real Injil" from "your Injil"; that distinction is brought in from outside the text. (Full treatment in 2B-5.)

3. "The Qur'an is muhaymin, the judge over earlier scripture (5:48)."

  • Close (Round 1): Read the full verse: "confirming (musaddiqan) that which preceded it of the Scripture, and as a guardian (muhayminan) over it." A guardian protects what is in its care. Al-Tabari's reports from Ibn Abbas gloss muhaymin as "witness" (shahid) and "entrusted with it" (mu'taman 'alayhi), and al-Tabari sums up the meaning: the Qur'an confirms the earlier books, testifies that they are true and from God, and guards them (al-Tabari on 5:48). Be ready: one report from Ibn Abbas there adds "judging the books before it," which is the comeback below.
  • Their comeback: "Guardian means it overrides whatever disagrees with it."
  • Close (Round 2): Then "confirming" in the same verse means nothing. And a judge can correct an interpretation, but the crucifixion is not an interpretation. It is the plain narrative of every Gospel. Overriding that is not guarding the Gospel; it is replacing it.

4. "Only the parts that agree with the Qur'an are true."

  • Close (Round 1): Then the Qur'an's command to "judge by the Gospel" adds nothing, because you would really be judging by the Qur'an. The test becomes circular: the Bible is true where it agrees with the Qur'an, and the Qur'an is confirmed by the true parts of the Bible.
  • Their comeback: "Yes, the Qur'an is the criterion (furqan). That's not circular, that's its role."
  • Close (Round 2): But 10:94 runs the check the other way: Muhammad, if in doubt, should ask those who read the earlier scripture. The Qur'an treats their scripture as a check on revelation, not the reverse.

5. "P2 means God's decrees, not scripture" (+ 5:44 and 15:9).

  • Close (Round 1): Partly concede, which builds trust. "Fair point on 6:34 and 10:64. The argument doesn't need P2. It stands on P1, P3, and P4."
  • Their comeback: "Right, so the Torah wasn't protected, and the rabbis failed (5:44)."
  • Close (Round 2): 5:44 praises the rabbis who judged by the Torah: "they were witnesses to it." It does not predict their failure. And this raises the timing question: when did they fail? If before the 7th century, the Qur'an told Christians to judge by already-corrupt books. If after, the manuscripts from centuries before Muhammad (P3) show no change on the crucifixion. (Full treatment in 2B-1.)

Boomerang check

Counter A: "Your own Bible has corruptions: Mark 16:9–20, John 7:53–8:11, 1 John 5:7."

  • Answer: We know about these because the manuscript tradition preserved the earlier readings. Modern Bibles bracket or footnote them. No doctrine depends on them. More importantly for the Dilemma, these variants already existed before Muhammad: Sinaiticus and Vaticanus lack Mark 16:9–20 and John 7:53–8:11, and the Comma Johanneum (1 John 5:7) is absent from the early Greek manuscripts. They do not show a change after the Qur'an affirmed the Bible, and none of them touches the crucifixion.

Counter B: "The New Testament also 'affirms' the Old Testament while overriding it (food laws, sacrifices). Isn't that your muhaymin?"

  • Answer: Jesus affirms the Old Testament text without reservation (Matt 5:17–18; John 10:35, "Scripture cannot be broken"). The New Testament claims fulfillment, not that the earlier text was falsified. Its dispute with Judaism is over interpretation, which is exactly the position early Muslims took toward the Bible (tahrif al-ma'na). If the Muslim adopts that position, the Dilemma comes back, because the crucifixion is text, not interpretation.

Counter C: "Critical scholars (Bart Ehrman) say the Gospels were changed."

  • Answer: Even Ehrman dates the Gospels' substantial form centuries before Muhammad. And Ehrman considers the crucifixion one of the most certain facts about Jesus. Using him as a witness for corruption makes him a witness against 4:157.

Counter D: "Basilides (2nd century) taught someone else was crucified."

  • Answer: Basilides is known only through Irenaeus (Against Heresies 1.24.4), was a Gnostic who also denied Jesus' real humanity, and was not "the People of the Gospel" in 7th-century Arabia. (Full treatment in 2B-14.)

No double standard: we claim the Bible was transmitted substantially, not without any variants. That is exactly the standard we will apply to the Qur'an in 2F.

Strength rating

Why: P1 rests on clear, present-tense Qur'anic texts (5:43, 5:47, 5:68, 7:157), reinforced by a sahih hadith (the Medina stoning case). P3 rests on manuscript dates no serious scholar disputes. P4 is simply what the texts say. The standard Muslim replies all have clear answers. The one coherent reply ("affirm the true remnant") remains open, but it is strained, and the crucifixion is the hardest thing to place outside the "remnant." P2 depends on a disputed reading of context, so it is demoted to reinforcement.

Trap questions

  1. "In 5:47 the Qur'an says, 'Let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah revealed in it.' Which Gospel were the Christians of Muhammad's day supposed to use?"
  2. "7:157 says they find Muhammad 'written with them' in the Torah and Gospel. How can someone find something written in a book they don't have?"
  3. "If the Bible was changed, when was it changed: before Muhammad or after? And which manuscript from before that change has no crucifixion?"
  4. "5:41 accuses some Jews of distorting words, and two verses later 5:43 says they 'have the Torah, in which is Allah's judgment.' If their Torah was corrupted, why does the Qur'an say God's judgment is in it?"

30-second version

"The Qur'an tells Christians in Muhammad's day, 'Let the People of the Gospel judge by what God revealed in it' (5:47). We have Bible manuscripts from more than 200 years before Muhammad's birth, including Codex Sinaiticus, which contains the entire New Testament, and their Gospels teach that Jesus was crucified and is Lord. So either that Gospel was reliable, and the Qur'an is wrong to deny the cross, or it wasn't, and the Qur'an was wrong to tell Christians to trust it. Either way, there's a problem. How do you see it?"

2-minute version

"I want to ask about something that actually comes from the Qur'an itself. The Qur'an speaks very highly of the Torah and the Gospel. It doesn't just say they were revealed. It speaks to Jews and Christians living at Muhammad's time about the scriptures they had. In 5:43 it says the Jews 'have the Torah, in which is the judgment of God.' In 5:47 it says, 'Let the People of the Gospel judge by what God revealed in it.' In 7:157 it says they find Muhammad 'written with them' in the Torah and Gospel. In 10:94 it even tells Muhammad, if he's in doubt, to ask those who read the scripture before him.

Now, we know what those scriptures said, because we have them from centuries before Muhammad: the Dead Sea Scrolls for the Old Testament, and great manuscripts like Codex Sinaiticus, which has the whole New Testament, and Codex Vaticanus, which has all four Gospels, from more than 200 years before Muhammad's birth. Their text is essentially the Bible I'm holding. And the Gospels in them teach that Jesus was crucified, died, rose again, and is Lord and God.

So here's my question. If the Gospel in Christians' hands was trustworthy, as the Qur'an says, then the Qur'an is wrong to deny the crucifixion in 4:157. If it wasn't trustworthy, then the Qur'an was wrong to tell Christians to judge by it. And the Qur'an never once warns Christians that their Gospel is wrong about the cross; it tells them to follow it.

I'm not trying to score a point. I'm asking because this matters: if the Gospel is true, then God has done something wonderful for us in Jesus, and I'd love to show you what it says."

2B-1

The Timing Trap

1 card1 strong

New terms

Mawquf: A report that stops at a Companion of Muhammad: the Companion's view, not the Prophet's.

Fideism: Holding a belief as immune to evidence.

Miaphysite: The churches (Coptic, Syriac Orthodox, Ethiopian, Armenian) that rejected the Council of Chalcedon (451).

Church of the East: The Syriac-speaking church of the Persian Empire.

Anathematize: To formally condemn as heretical.

Argument2B-1STRONG

The Timing Trap

Name + thesis

Ask when the Bible was corrupted. If the corruption came before Muhammad, the Qur'an pointed Jews and Christians to already-corrupt books as God's guidance. If it came after, that is ruled out by manuscripts and translations older than Muhammad. No window remains in which the corruption could have happened without the Qur'an being wrong.

Key texts

The Qur'an addresses the scripture in their hands, in Muhammad's day:

  • 5:43: "How is it that they come to you for judgment while they have the Torah (wa 'indahumu t-tawratu), in which is the judgment of Allah?"
  • 2:41: "Believe in what I have sent down, confirming that which is with you (musaddiqan lima ma'akum)." (Also 4:47.)
  • 5:68: "Say (qul): 'O People of the Scripture, you stand on nothing until you uphold the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been revealed to you from your Lord.'"
  • 7:157: "...whom they find written with them (yajidunahu maktuban 'indahum) in the Torah and the Gospel."
  • 10:94: "If you are in doubt about what We have revealed to you, ask those who are reading (yaqra'una) the Scripture before you."
  • 5:47: "Let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein. Whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, it is they who are the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqun)."

What the Qur'an denies:

  • 4:157: "...their saying, 'We killed the Messiah'... They did not kill him, nor crucify him."
  • 5:72: "They have certainly disbelieved who say, 'Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary.'"

What the pre-Islamic Gospels say:

  • Mark 15:24: "And they crucified him."
  • 1 Cor 15:3–4: "Christ died for our sins... he was buried... he was raised on the third day."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. Ibn Hazm's position: it happened before Muhammad. Ibn Hazm (d. 1064) argued that the Torah was rewritten after the Babylonian exile (he points to Ezra) and that the Gospels are human biographies, not the Injil given to Jesus (al-Fasl fi al-Milal; see Camilla Adang, Muslim Writers on Judaism and the Hebrew Bible, Brill, 1996, on Ezra; and Theodore Pulcini, Exegesis as Polemical Discourse: Ibn Hazm on Jewish and Christian Scriptures, Scholars Press, 1998, on his view that the four Gospels were written by men and the revealed Injil was lost). On this view, when the Qur'an speaks of the Torah and Injil "with them," it means the remnant of real revelation God left in their books as a proof against them, such as the stoning verse (Sahih al-Bukhari 3635 (in-book 61/139), narrated by Ibn Umar) and passages pointing to Muhammad.
  2. A grammatical restriction. 5:47 says "judge by what Allah revealed in it." The relative clause limits the command to the parts God actually revealed, not everything in the book.
  3. Corruption was ongoing, not a single event. The Qur'an describes tampering in Muhammad's own day (2:79; 5:41). Ibn Abbas, with a sound chain in Bukhari 2685/7363/7523, says they "changed with their hands what Allah wrote."
  4. Revelation outranks history. The Qur'an is God's final word. Manuscript dating is human reconstruction, and the great codices are 300 years after Jesus, which leaves room for early scribal change (Bart Ehrman is often quoted here).
  5. 5:47 may be about Jesus' time. Hamza and al-A'mash read wa-li-yahkuma ("so that [they] might judge"), describing why the Injil was given, not a command to Muhammad's contemporaries (al-Qurtubi on 5:47).

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. If the Bible's teaching on Jesus' crucifixion and deity is a corruption, it entered the text either before Muhammad's mission began (c. 610) or after.
  • P2. It did not enter after. Manuscripts and translations from before 610, in many languages and regions and from rival churches, already contain it.
  • P3. So if it is a corruption, it was already present in the Torah and Gospel that Jews and Christians had when the Qur'an was revealed.
  • P4. The Qur'an affirms those books. It says they are "with them," that God's judgment is "in" them, and that Muhammad is "written" in them. It commands their people to uphold and judge by them, and it appeals to their readers as a check (5:43–47, 5:68, 7:157, 10:94, 2:41, 4:47). It never once warns that the Gospel's text is wrong about the crucifixion.
  • C. Therefore, either the Bible's teaching on Jesus is not a corruption, and the Qur'an is wrong to deny it; or the Qur'an affirmed books that were already corrupt on the central point without warning. Either way, the Qur'an errs.

Why this card is so useful: you don't have to win the debate about the 1st century to win this one. Even if a Muslim argues that changes crept in between AD 30 and 300, that is before Muhammad, and it lands him on the first horn.

Evidence for each premise

P1 is a simple logical division of the possibilities: any change happened either before a given date or after it.

P2: the pre-Islamic record.

Witness Date Language / region Community What it shows
Dead Sea Scrolls c. 250 BC – AD 68 Hebrew/Aramaic; Judea Jewish OT text substantially stable (the Great Isaiah Scroll includes Isa 53)
Septuagint Torah 3rd c. BC; rest by c. 1st c. BC Greek; Alexandria Jewish, then Christian Independent OT witness
Paul, 1 Corinthians c. AD 53–55 Greek Earliest church 15:3–7 is an earlier creed: Christ died, was buried, and was raised
Tatian's Diatessaron c. 170 Syriac/Greek Used in Syriac churches into the 5th c. A harmony of the four Gospels, passion included
Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.11.8 c. 180 Greek; Gaul Western church Four Gospels, "neither more nor fewer"
P75 c. 175–225 (Brent Nongbri argues it may be as late as the 4th c.) Greek; Egypt — Its text of Luke and John is remarkably close to Vaticanus, a sign of stable copying
Sahidic Coptic versions 3rd–4th c. Coptic; Egypt Coptic Independent translation
Codex Vaticanus, Codex Sinaiticus 4th c. Greek Imperial church All four Gospels with passion narratives; Sinaiticus has the whole NT
Latin Vulgate (Jerome) c. 382–405 Latin; West Latin church Independent translation
Old Syriac (Sinaitic and Curetonian manuscripts) 4th–5th c. manuscripts Syriac Syriac churches The language of Christianity nearest to Arabia
Peshitta 5th c. Syriac Church of the East and Syriac Orthodox Gospels complete
Armenian version 5th c. Armenian Armenian church Independent translation
Garima Gospels (Ge'ez) radiocarbon c. 390–570 and c. 530–660 (which codex carries which date is disputed) Ge'ez; Ethiopia Ethiopian church Gospels of the church whose king sheltered the first Muslim emigrants
— c. 610 — — Muhammad's mission begins

The rival-churches point (this makes P2 STRONG, not just probable). After the Councils of Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451), Christianity split into communities that anathematized each other:

Bloc Churches Empire
Chalcedonian Byzantine (Melkite), Latin Byzantine / Western kingdoms
Miaphysite Coptic, Syriac Orthodox, Ethiopian, Armenian Byzantine provinces, Aksum, Armenia
Church of the East Syriac-speaking church of Persia Sasanian Persia, Rome's rival

All three blocs used the same four Gospels with the same passion narratives. A change after 451 would have required churches that condemned one another, living in rival empires, to agree on the same alteration with no one objecting. Meanwhile the Jews, who were opponents of both, kept the Hebrew Torah independently. And after 632, much of this world came under Muslim rule, where Muslims could compare copies themselves.

P3 follows from P1 and P2.

P4: the affirmations. See the key texts. Note the tenses and possessives: 'indahum ("with them," 5:43, 7:157), ma'akum ("with you," 2:41, 4:47), yaqra'una ("they are reading," 10:94), and the command qul ("Say!," 5:68). All of these address people in Muhammad's own day about books they were holding.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Weakest premise: P4, which depends on interpretation. P2 is the strongest premise; no serious scholar disputes those dates.

Hardest surviving objection (two parts):

"(a) The Qur'an affirms only what God revealed in their books, the true remnant (the grammatical restriction in 5:47, and Ibn Hazm's view). (b) And the Qur'an does warn them: 4:171 ('Do not say "Three"'), 5:72–73, 9:30. So the Qur'an did not stay silent about their errors."

Answer:

  • On (b): Every one of those verses condemns what Christians say (qalu, "they said"; la taqulu, "do not say"). Even 4:157 is about "their saying." The Qur'an consistently treats the error as the people's, never the scripture's. It never says "your Injil wrongly teaches the cross." This diagnosis (the scripture is sound, the people misread it) is exactly corruption of meaning. And it is falsified by the evidence, because the crucifixion and Jesus' deity are in the pre-Islamic text, not just in Christian talk.
  • On (a): Any non-circular way of identifying "the remnant" (the earliest sources, multiple attestation, agreement across rival churches) puts the crucifixion inside the remnant. It is in all four Gospels, Paul, the early creed, and Tacitus. The only test that removes it is "whatever disagrees with the Qur'an," which assumes what the Muslim is trying to prove.

Honest status: (a) is still a coherent position. It survives as a possible reading but becomes costly. Present the card as forcing a choice, not as a mathematical proof.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "It happened before: Paul, Constantine, and Nicaea corrupted it."

  • Close (R1): Then you've taken the first horn. The Qur'an came about 300 years after Nicaea (325) and told Christians to judge by the post-Nicene Gospel (5:47). Also, Nicaea did not set the canon: the four Gospels were recognized by c. 180 (Irenaeus 3.11.8; Tatian's Diatessaron). On Paul, see 2B-8.
  • Their comeback: "The Qur'an knew they were corrupt. That's why it came as muhaymin (5:48), to correct them."
  • Close (R2): A corrector does not command people to judge by the text it is correcting, then call those who don't "defiantly disobedient" (5:47). And it never identifies the cross as an insertion into the text. 4:157 attributes the crucifixion claim to "their saying."

2. "Corruption was ongoing: before, during, and after (2:79; 5:41; Bukhari 2685)."

  • Close (R1): Local tampering by "a party" of people (fariq, 2:75; 3:78) is not the question. The question is what the manuscripts say. The relevant content was fixed before 610 and is unchanged since. The Medina stoning case (Bukhari 3635) shows that even the tampering during Muhammad's lifetime was hiding the text with a hand, not changing it.
  • Their comeback: "Fine. Then the decisive corruption was before, and the Qur'an exposed it."
  • Close (R2): Exposed it where? Show the verse that says the Gospel's crucifixion account is a scribal insertion. Ibn Abbas (2685) is a Companion's mawquf reading of 2:79, not a revelation, and it names no time, no scope, and no passage.

3. "5:47 is about Jesus' time (the Hamza reading)."

  • Close (R1): Grant it for 5:47, though al-Tabari says both readings are well known, close in meaning, and both correct. The trap doesn't need that verse. 5:43 is about Jews coming to Muhammad who "have the Torah." 5:68 is a present command (qul). 7:157 is present tense ("they find him written with them"). 2:41 and 4:47 say "confirming what is with you." 10:94 speaks of those "reading" the scripture now.
  • Their comeback: "'With you' just means the remnant you still have."
  • Close (R2): That is the remnant escape, and the cross is in the remnant on every non-circular test (see the hardest objection). A book "with you" is the book you are holding.

4. "History cannot judge revelation" (fideism).

  • Close (R1): The Qur'an itself invites the historical check. 10:94 says "ask those reading the Scripture before you," and 16:43 says "ask the people of the reminder (ahl al-dhikr) if you do not know." Al-Tabari identifies ahl al-dhikr as "those who have read the books before them: the Torah and the Injil," and says the interpreters agree; Ibn Kathir also takes them as the people of the earlier scriptures (both on 16:43). Refusing the check makes the Qur'an's own test unusable.
  • Their comeback: "We accept historical method generally, but revelation has the final word."
  • Close (R2): Then you cannot use historical arguments for the Qur'an either: the Birmingham manuscript, the Sana'a codex, or tawatur (mass transmission). Those are exactly the same kind of evidence. If manuscripts count for your book, they count for ours. That's one standard (see 2F).

5. "The Christians of Arabia had different Gospels."

  • Close (R1): There is no evidence that any 7th-century Christian community used a Gospel that denies the crucifixion. The Gospel of Barnabas survives first in a late-16th-century Italian manuscript (its origin is late medieval or early modern), so it is after Muhammad and falls on the second horn. Early reports of crucifixion-denial are Gnostic: Basilides (reported by Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.24.4) and the Second Treatise of the Great Seth (Nag Hammadi). They come with doctrines the Qur'an would reject, such as an inferior Creator and a Jesus without a real body.
  • Their comeback: "Academic scholars think Jewish-Christian groups influenced the Qur'an." (For example, Patricia Crone, "Jewish Christianity and the Qur'an," in two parts, Journal of Near Eastern Studies 74.2 (2015) and 75.1 (2016).)
  • Close (R2): That is a debated hypothesis about influences. It produces no crucifixion-denying Gospel. And 5:47 addresses "the People of the Gospel" as a whole, not a hidden sect. The Christians the early Muslims actually met, in Abyssinia, Najran, and Syria, used the four Gospels.

Boomerang check

A. "Apply the timing trap to the Qur'an. You claim the Qur'an changed (2F): before or after Uthman?"

  • Answer: The trap works against Bible-corruption because the Qur'an affirms an existing book at a datable moment. The New Testament does not affirm the Qur'an, so there is no parallel trap. The fair parallel is Jesus affirming the Old Testament of his day (Matt 5:17–18; Luke 24:44; John 10:35), and Christians pass that test: the Dead Sea Scrolls show the Old Testament of Jesus' day was substantially ours. Honest caveat: the Scrolls also show textual variety in some books. For example, a shorter form of Jeremiah close to the Septuagint (4QJerᵇ; see Emanuel Tov). Jesus affirmed Scripture as substantially transmitted, not one manuscript family.

B. "Then the Qur'an could also affirm the Bible 'as substantially transmitted' while rejecting some parts."

  • Answer: Yes, for genuine variants. But what the Qur'an rejects (the crucifixion and Jesus' deity) is not a variant. It appears in every textual family and every church's Bible before Muhammad. "Substantially transmitted" includes the cross.

C. "Jesus accused the Pharisees of corrupting God's word (Mark 7:13)."

  • Answer: This parallel helps us. Jesus condemned their traditions while affirming the text: "The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat, so do and observe whatever they tell you" (Matt 23:2–3). Accusing people of misuse while affirming their text is corruption of meaning, which is the same pattern as Qur'an 5:41–43.

Strength rating

  • P2 rests on manuscript and translation dates that no serious scholar disputes, reinforced by the rival-churches point.
  • P4 rests on clear, present-tense Qur'anic texts.
  • The argument works even if the Muslim wins the 1st-century debate, which removes his usual best move.
  • The hardest reply (the "remnant") survives only by using a test for the remnant that assumes the Qur'an is true.

Cultural / nominal Have never been asked "when?" One question, then the timeline. Show a photo of Codex Sinaiticus (it is digitized online).

Trap questions

  1. "When do you think the Bible was changed: before Muhammad, during his life, or after?"
  2. "If before: why would the Qur'an tell Christians to judge by their Gospel (5:47), and say it's 'with them' (7:157), without once warning them that its text is wrong about the cross?"
  3. "If after: can you show me any manuscript from before Muhammad that leaves out the crucifixion?"
  4. "In Muhammad's day, Christians in the Byzantine Empire, Persia, Egypt, and Ethiopia, in churches that condemned each other as heretics, all used the same four Gospels. Who could have changed all of them, and why didn't any rival notice?"

30-second version

"Can I ask a simple question? When was the Bible changed? If it was after Muhammad, we have manuscripts from centuries before him, like Codex Sinaiticus, with the same Gospels and the same crucifixion. If it was before him, then the Qur'an told Christians to judge by already-corrupt books (5:47) and never warned them about the cross. Which do you think it was?"

2-minute version

"Muslims often tell me the Bible was corrupted, and I take that seriously. So I want to ask the most basic historical question: when?

There are only two options: before Muhammad or after. Let's try 'after' first. We have Gospel manuscripts in Greek from more than 200 years before Muhammad's birth. Codex Sinaiticus contains the whole New Testament. We also have translations in Syriac, Coptic, Latin, Armenian, and Ethiopic. These belonged to churches in different empires that were so divided they condemned each other as heretics, yet they all had the same four Gospels and the same account of Jesus' crucifixion. Nobody could have changed all of those after Muhammad without the others noticing.

So it would have to be 'before.' But then look at what the Qur'an says to the Christians and Jews of Muhammad's own day. It says they 'have the Torah, in which is the judgment of God' (5:43). It says Muhammad is 'written with them' in the Torah and Gospel (7:157). It tells Christians to 'judge by what God revealed' in the Gospel (5:47). If those books were already corrupted on the most important question of all, whether Jesus died on the cross, why does the Qur'an point people to them and never warn them?

Either the Gospel is trustworthy, as the Qur'an says, and then the cross really happened. Or it isn't, and then the Qur'an was wrong to send people to it. I'd honestly like to know how you put that together. And if the Gospel is trustworthy, there's a message in it I'd love to show you."

2B-2

Early Muslims on Corruption of Meaning

1 card1 moderate

New terms

Mawsul: "Connected": a report with an unbroken chain of narrators.

Revised after the Ibn Abbas finding (Bukhari 2685). This section no longer claims that "early Muslims taught corruption of meaning, not text." The honest claim is narrower and still useful.

Argument2B-2MODERATE

A Meaning-Corruption Strand in Early Islam

downgraded: early views were mixed

Name + thesis

Islamic tradition never had one view of tahrif. A significant strand of respected scholars read the Qur'an's accusations as concealment, oral twisting, and false interpretation, not wholesale rewriting of the text. The systematic claim that the Torah and Gospel texts are thoroughly corrupted was developed most influentially by Ibn Hazm (d. 1064). So the Qur'an does not require a Muslim to believe the Bible's text was changed, and many Muslim scholars didn't.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 3:78: "There is among them a party who twist their tongues with the Book (yalwuna alsinatahum bi-l-kitab) so that you think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book."
  • Qur'an 4:46: "they distort words from their places and say, 'We hear and disobey'... twisting their tongues."
  • Qur'an 2:79: "woe to those who write the book with their own hands, then say, 'This is from Allah.'"
  • Bukhari, Book of Tawhid (unchained chapter-heading material): "yuharrifun: they remove. No one removes a word of any of the books of Allah, but they distort it, interpreting it wrongly." Attribution disputed. (Book 97, chapter 55, just before no. 7553.)
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 2685 (in-book 52/46), a statement of Ibn Abbas (mawquf): Ibn Abbas: "Allah has told you that the People of the Book changed what Allah wrote and altered it with their hands."
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 4485, narrated by Abu Hurayra: "Do not believe the People of the Book, and do not disbelieve them. Say: 'We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us...'"

Their best case (steelman)

A knowledgeable Muslim says: "Your 'strand' is selective. Ibn Abbas, the greatest Companion commentator, says plainly in Sahih al-Bukhari that they changed the text with their hands. 2:79 describes writing, not interpretation. Ibn Hazm didn't invent textual corruption; he documented it, with long lists of contradictions in the Torah and Gospels. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, and modern scholars (Rahmatullah Kairanawi, Izhar al-Haqq, 1864) agree. And even meaning-corruption is corruption: the Qur'an is still the criterion."

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Respected Muslim authorities across the centuries held that the scriptures in Jewish and Christian hands were largely intact in wording, and that the corruption was mainly of meaning, concealment, or oral misrepresentation.
  • P2. If so, the Qur'an's tahrif verses can be read, by Muslims' own scholars, without requiring textual corruption.
  • P3. On the meaning-corruption view, the text of the Bible stands, and so does what it says about the crucifixion and Jesus' deity (2A, P4).
  • C. A Muslim cannot treat "the Bible's text was changed" as the Islamic position. If he adopts the meaning-only view, the Dilemma returns in full; if he adopts the textual view, he faces the timing trap (2B-1).

Evidence for each premise

Scholar Date Position (summary) Status
Book of Tawhid gloss in Bukhari compiled c. 846 "No one removes a word of the books of Allah; they distort it by interpretation" Attribution disputed: Ibn Abbas (unchained) or Bukhari's own comment. Ibn Hajar: the wording "is nearly explicit" that it is Bukhari's, though it may be Ibn Abbas's (Fath al-Bari, Kitab al-Tawhid, ch. 55); Ibn al-Qayyim also quotes it as Bukhari's
Ibn Abbas, Bukhari 2685/7363/7523 d. c. 687 They "changed with their hands" Sahih chain to Ibn Abbas; mawquf (his view, restating 2:79)
Early commentators (Muqatil ibn Sulayman, d. 767; al-Tabari, d. 923) 8th–10th c. Mostly concealment of Muhammad's description, misrepresentation, and specific acts by Medinan Jews, rarely global textual change Gordon Nickel, Narratives of Tampering (Brill, 2011), whose study of Muqatil and al-Tabari finds the early commentators more interested in stories of deception and obstinacy than in textual corruption
Fakhr al-Din al-Razi d. 1209 Reports the jurist al-Qadi's view that the wording reading of 2:75 is the better one, and that a scripture can't be altered once it is mass-transmitted like the Qur'an, but could be before then (Mafatih al-Ghayb on 2:75) Influential Ash'ari; leans textual here

  • Bukhari 4485 ("neither believe nor disbelieve them") reflects caution, not a judgment that their scripture is wholesale forgery.
  • The Qur'an's own language about the scripture "with them" (2A) fits the meaning-corruption reading better than the textual one.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: Ibn Abbas (Bukhari 2685) is earlier and weightier than anyone in the meaning-only strand. Answer: Concede it. Then: (1) it is mawquf, his reading of 2:79, not prophetic; (2) it names no scope or timing; (3) on any textual view, the timing trap applies (2B-1); (4) the purpose of this card is modest: to show that Islam's own scholars did not agree, so the Muslim cannot simply assert textual corruption as settled Islamic teaching.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Even meaning-corruption means the Bible can't be trusted."

  • Close (R1): Meaning-corruption means people misinterpret a sound text. Then we can read the sound text together. What does Mark 15 say happened to Jesus?
  • Their comeback: "You read it through Paul's theology."
  • Close (R2): The crucifixion isn't an interpretation; it's the narrative. You can dispute what the cross means, but if the text is sound, the cross happened, and 4:157 is wrong.

2. "Ibn Hazm proved textual corruption with contradictions."

  • Close (R1): Ibn Hazm's method finds tensions (e.g., genealogies) and treats them as proof of tampering. Applied to the Qur'an, the same method would yield the same verdict (see 2C-3).
  • Their comeback: "The Qur'an has no contradictions" (4:82).
  • Close (R2): Muslims answer apparent Qur'anic contradictions by harmonization. Christians do the same. One standard.

Boomerang check

"Early Christians accused Jews of corrupting the Old Testament too." True: Justin Martyr (c. 160) accused Jewish scribes of removing passages (Dialogue with Trypho 71–73). Answer: This is a fair parallel. Justin's specific charges were evaluated by later Christian scholarship and mostly not accepted, because the manuscript evidence didn't support them. An accusation is not evidence. The same standard applies to Muslim accusations against the Bible.

Strength rating

Why: The meaning-corruption strand is real (Ibn Taymiyya in part, possibly Bukhari), but the earliest Companion statement on record (Ibn Abbas, 2685) is textual. Several attributions still need verification. Use this card to show that Muslim views are mixed, not that early Islam taught meaning-only corruption.

Trap questions

  2. "If the corruption was of meaning, can we read the text together and see what it actually says?"
  3. "Ibn Abbas said they changed it. When? And which manuscript shows the change?"

30-second version

"Muslim scholars have never been unanimous that the Bible's text was changed. Some of your most respected scholars said the corruption was mainly in interpretation, and Ibn Taymiyya held that only a small part was altered. If that's right, let's read the text together."

2-minute version

"I've found something interesting in Islamic history. Muslims today often say the Bible was rewritten. But your own scholars disagreed about that. Ibn Abbas did say the People of the Book changed their scripture with their hands. Others, possibly including al-Bukhari himself, said no one can remove a word of God's books, and the corruption was in how people interpreted them. Ibn Taymiyya, as Ibn Hajar reports, held that only a small part of the books was altered and most remained as it was. The idea that the text was thoroughly corrupted was argued most fully by Ibn Hazm, about 400 years after Muhammad.

So here's my question. If the problem is interpretation, then the text is sound, and we can open it together and read what it says about Jesus. And if the problem is the text, then we have to ask when it was changed, because we have manuscripts from long before Muhammad."

2B-3

Muhammad Honored the Torah of His Day

1 card1 moderate

Argument2B-3MODERATE

Muhammad Honored the Torah of His Day

Abu Dawud 4449 is hasan; the Bukhari 3635 core and Qur'an 3:93 are stronger

Name + thesis

When Jews in Medina brought a case to Muhammad, he asked for their Torah, ruled from it, and, according to one report, placed it on a cushion and said, "I believe in you and in Him who revealed you." The Qur'an also challenges the Jews to "bring the Torah and recite it." Muhammad treated the Torah in 7th-century Jewish hands as God's genuine word.

Key texts

  • Sunan Abi Dawud 4449 (in-book 40/99), narrated by Ibn Umar; graded hasan by al-Albani: Jews invited Muhammad to judge a case. "He sat on a cushion, then removed it and placed the Torah on it, and said, 'I believe in you and in Him who revealed you' (amantu biki wa bi-man anzalaki)".
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 3635 (in-book 61/139), narrated by Ibn Umar: in the stoning case, the Torah was opened; one man covered the stoning verse with his hand; Abdullah ibn Salam had him lift it; the verse was there, and Muhammad ruled by it.
  • Qur'an 3:93: "All food was lawful to the Children of Israel except what Israel had made unlawful to himself before the Torah was revealed. Say: 'Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful' (fa'tu bi-t-tawrati fa-tluha)."
  • Qur'an 5:43: "How is it that they come to you for judgment while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah?"

Their best case (steelman)

(1) The chain of Abu Dawud 4449 is not the strongest. Al-Albani graded it hasan, not sahih, and its chain runs through Hisham ibn Sa'd, a narrator some hadith critics considered weak. (2) Honoring a book is not endorsing every word. Muslims honor the Torah as a scripture originally from God, and handle remnants of revelation respectfully. (3) Muhammad used the Torah against the Jews, to expose them, not to endorse it. 3:93 is a challenge meant to show they couldn't prove their claim from it. (4) The Medina Torah was one copy, not proof about all copies, or about the Gospel.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Muhammad asked for the Torah of 7th-century Medina, consulted it, and ruled by what it said (Bukhari 3635, sahih).
  • P2. The Qur'an directs Muhammad to challenge the Jews to "bring the Torah and recite it" (3:93), and says the Torah they have contains God's judgment (5:43).
  • P3. According to a hasan report, Muhammad honored that Torah physically and affirmed faith in it and its Revealer (Abu Dawud 4449).
  • C. Muhammad and the Qur'an treated the Torah in Jewish hands in the 7th century as a reliable record of God's word. That Torah is substantially the Hebrew text we have (the Masoretic tradition, attested centuries earlier in the Dead Sea Scrolls).

Evidence for each premise

  • Bukhari 3635 (sahih, narrated by Ibn Umar) is the strongest piece: the text contained the true ruling, and the Jews hid it rather than having changed it.
  • 3:93 makes the Torah an arbiter in a dispute. A challenge to "bring the Torah" only works if both sides accept that the Torah's text will settle it.
  • Abu Dawud 4449: graded hasan by al-Albani (sunnah.com). Hasan hadith are accepted as evidence in Sunni law. Present it at that grade.
  • The text itself: the Hebrew Torah of 7th-century Jewish communities belongs to the proto-Masoretic tradition already dominant among the Dead Sea Scrolls (Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed., 2012).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Weakest premise: P3 (hasan, with some chain criticism). Hardest objection: "Honoring is not endorsing." Answer: "I believe in you" is more than respect. And the stronger evidence (3635, 3:93, 5:43) shows Muhammad treated the text as authoritative for judgment, not merely as a venerable relic.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "3:93 was a challenge to expose them."

  • Close (R1): Exactly: a challenge that assumes their own Torah would prove the Qur'an right. If their Torah were corrupt, it could prove nothing.
  • Their comeback: "God knew the remnant on that point was intact."
  • Close (R2): So the Torah was reliable enough to settle disputes when it agreed with the Qur'an. That's the "remnant" view, and it's circular (2A, escape route 4).

2. "That was only the Torah, not the Gospel."

  • Close (R1): Yes, this card is about the Torah. But the Qur'an treats the Torah and the Gospel the same way: "with them" (7:157), to be "upheld" (5:68), "judge by" it (5:43, 5:47).
  • Their comeback: "The Gospel was more corrupted than the Torah."
  • Close (R2): Then the Qur'an should say so. It never distinguishes them, and the Gospel manuscripts are, if anything, earlier and more numerous (2B-1).

Boomerang check

"Christians honor the Old Testament too, but reject its laws." Answer: Christians affirm the OT text as Scripture (2 Tim 3:16) while understanding its ceremonial laws as fulfilled in Christ (Heb 8–10). That's a view about application, not about corruption. The parallel actually helps: affirming a text while disputing its application is exactly what "meaning corruption" is.

Strength rating

Why: Bukhari 3635 is sahih and Qur'an 3:93 and 5:43 are clear, which together make a strong case that Muhammad treated the 7th-century Torah as reliable. The vivid cushion report (Abu Dawud 4449) is hasan, with some chain criticism, so present it at its grade and never lead with it.

30-second version

2-minute version

One man tried to hide a verse with his hand, but it was there, and Muhammad ruled by it. That's in Sahih al-Bukhari. Another report, graded hasan by al-Albani, says Muhammad put the Torah on a cushion and said, 'I believe in you and in the One who revealed you.' And the Qur'an itself says, 'Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful.'

So Muhammad treated the Torah that Jews had in the 7th century as God's genuine word, enough to judge by. We know what that Torah said; we have Hebrew manuscripts going back centuries before him. If it was God's word then, why would it be corrupt now?"

"Written in What They Have": Testing the Prophecies

1 card1 strong

New terms

Paraclete (parakletos): Greek for 'helper, advocate, comforter': Jesus' name for the Holy Spirit in John 14–16.

Ahmad: 'Most praised': the name in Qur'an 61:6 that Muslims identify with Muhammad.

Argument2B-4STRONG

The Prophecy Test (7:157 and 61:6)

each claimed prophecy fails on its own context

Name + thesis

The Qur'an claims Muhammad is "written" in the Torah and Gospel that Jews and Christians have (7:157), and that Jesus announced a messenger "whose name is Ahmad" (61:6). If so, the claim is testable against the Bible. Every proposed text fails when read in context. Either the claim is false, or it applies to a Bible the Muslim says was corrupted, which returns him to the Dilemma.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 7:157: "Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered prophet (al-nabi al-ummi), whom they find written with them (maktuban 'indahum) in the Torah and the Gospel."
  • Qur'an 61:6: "Jesus son of Mary said, 'O Children of Israel, I am the messenger of Allah to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah, and bringing good tidings of a messenger to come after me, whose name is Ahmad.'"
  • Deut 18:15, 18: "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers... I will put my words in his mouth."
  • John 14:16–17, 26: "another Helper (parakletos)... the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you... the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name."

Their best case (steelman)

Muslim scholars and debaters (Ahmed Deedat, What the Bible Says About Muhammad, 1976; Jamal Badawi; Zakir Naik) propose:

  1. Deut 18:18: "from among their brothers" means the Ishmaelites, the brothers of the Israelites. Muhammad, like Moses, was a lawgiver, a statesman, and had a natural birth; Jesus was not "like Moses."
  2. The Paraclete (John 14–16): the original Greek may have been periklytos ("praised one" = Ahmad/Muhammad), later changed to parakletos. Even as "helper," the Paraclete "will guide you into all truth" and "speak whatever he hears" (John 16:13), like a prophet receiving revelation.
  3. Song 5:16: Hebrew machamaddim ("altogether lovely") sounds like "Muhammad."
  4. Isa 42: God's servant brings justice to the nations; the "villages that Kedar inhabits" (42:11) rejoice, and Kedar was a son of Ishmael (Gen 25:13).
  5. Isa 29:12: "the book is given to one who cannot read, saying, 'Read this'; he says, 'I cannot read,'" which parallels Muhammad's first revelation ("Iqra'!" "I am not a reader").
  6. Deut 33:2 / Hab 3:3: God "shone forth from Mount Paran," where Ishmael lived, which they identify with Mecca.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The Qur'an claims Muhammad is described in the Torah and Gospel that 7th-century Jews and Christians possessed (7:157).
  • P2. Those books are substantially the Bible we have (2A, P3; 2B-1).
  • P3. Every passage proposed as a prophecy of Muhammad, read in context, refers to someone else or to no future prophet at all.
  • C. Either 7:157 is false, or the description was removed from every manuscript, which collides with the timing trap and with 7:157's own present tense ("they find him written with them").

Evidence for each premise

Claimed text What the context shows Rating of the Muslim claim
Deut 18:15–18 "From among you, from your brothers": in Deuteronomy "your brothers" means fellow Israelites (Deut 17:15: the king must be "from among your brothers," explicitly not "a foreigner"). Deut 34:10: "no prophet has arisen in Israel like Moses." The NT applies it to Jesus (Acts 3:22). WEAK
John 14–16, Paraclete Every Greek manuscript reads parakletos; none reads periklytos. The Paraclete is "the Holy Spirit" (14:26), invisible ("the world neither sees him," 14:17), already "dwells with you" (14:17), sent to the disciples "not many days from now" (Acts 1:5; 2:1–4). Muhammad was visible and came 600 years later. WEAK
Song 5:16 Machamaddim is a plural adjective, "desirable things," and the same root appears for "precious things" elsewhere (1 Kgs 20:6; Hos 9:6). It's a love poem's description of the beloved. WEAK: drop it
Isa 42 Kedar appears among the nations who praise God (42:10–12), not as the servant's origin. The servant is "a covenant for the people, a light for the nations" (42:6), "will not cry aloud" (42:2), and "a bruised reed he will not break" (42:3); Matt 12:18–21 applies it to Jesus. WEAK–MODERATE (Kedar is real, but it doesn't identify the servant)
Isa 29:12 Part of an oracle of judgment: the "vision of all this" has become like a sealed book that neither the literate nor the illiterate can read (29:11–12), because Israel's heart is far from God (29:13). WEAK
Deut 33:2 / Hab 3:3 (Paran) Paran is a wilderness between Sinai and Canaan (Num 10:12; 13:3, 26), far from Mecca. See 2B-15. WEAK

A notable early Muslim witness: Ibn Ishaq's biography of Muhammad (8th c., via Ibn Hisham) quotes John 15:23–16:1 from a Palestinian Syriac/Aramaic version, rendering the Paraclete as al-Munhamanna (from Syriac menahhemana, "comforter") and identifying it with Muhammad (Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad, 1955, pp. 103–104; analyzed by Sean W. Anthony, "Muḥammad, Menaḥem, and the Paraclete," Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies, 2016). This shows early Muslims treated the Gospel of John's text as genuine and looked for Muhammad in it.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "The Paraclete 'will guide you into all truth' and 'will not speak on his own authority' (John 16:13), which describes a prophet." Answer: The same verses say he "will glorify me [Jesus], for he will take what is mine and declare it to you" (16:14). Muhammad's message denied Jesus' death and sonship, so it doesn't glorify Jesus in John's sense. And the Paraclete is sent "in my name" (14:26) and "dwells with you and will be in you" (14:17), which fits the Spirit, not a man.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "The prophecies were removed from the Bible."

  • Close (R1): 7:157 says they find him written with them, present tense. A removed prophecy can't be found.
  • Their comeback: "Some remained, like the Paraclete, and were distorted in meaning."
  • Close (R2): Then show me the Paraclete passage read in context, and let's see if it fits Muhammad. (It doesn't: see the table.) And if the remnant only fits when you change parakletos to periklytos, you are changing every manuscript to fit your theory.

2. "Deut 18: Jesus isn't like Moses; Muhammad is."

  • Close (R1): Deuteronomy defines the likeness itself: Moses knew God "face to face" and did "signs and wonders" (Deut 34:10–11). The Qur'an says Muhammad was refused signs (2G).
  • Their comeback: "Moses and Muhammad both brought law, led a state, married, and died naturally."
  • Close (R2): Those similarities fit many leaders. The text's own criteria are "from among your brothers" (Israel) and signs and intimacy with God. And Jesus, like Moses, was a mediator of a covenant (Jer 31:31; Luke 22:20), was saved from a king's massacre as a baby (Exod 1–2; Matt 2), and fed the people in the wilderness.

Boomerang check

"Christians do the same: they read Jesus into Old Testament texts." Answer: A fair challenge. Some Christian prophecy claims are also weak (e.g., using Hos 11:1 as a straightforward prediction rather than a typological pattern). Apply the same test to both: context, specificity, and checkable fulfillment. That's why 1C rates Christian prophecy MODERATE and relies most on Isa 53 and the "before AD 70" point of Dan 9.

Strength rating

Why: Each proposed text fails on its own context, and the manuscript evidence for parakletos is unanimous. The argument requires no disputed hadith. The only escape ("it was removed") contradicts 7:157's present-tense wording.

Audience How it lands Adjust

Educated Sunni Often know the Paraclete argument is weak Focus on 7:157's claim and its testability.
Quranists 7:157 and 61:6 are Qur'anic Very effective.
Cultural Muslims Heard "the Bible predicts Muhammad" Read John 14:16–26 together.

Trap questions

  1. "7:157 says they find Muhammad written in what they have. Which passage did 7th-century Christians find him in?"
  2. "In John 14, who is the Helper, according to verse 26?"
  3. "Jesus says the Helper 'dwells with you and will be in you.' How could that be someone born 600 years later?"
  4. "In Deuteronomy 17:15, does 'from among your brothers' include foreigners?"

30-second version

"The Qur'an says Muhammad is written in the Torah and Gospel that Christians have. So let's look. In John 14, the Helper is named: 'the Holy Spirit.' He's invisible, and he was already with the disciples. When we read each proposed prophecy in context, none of them is Muhammad."

2-minute version

"I really respect that the Qur'an makes a testable claim. 7:157 says Jews and Christians find Muhammad written in the Torah and Gospel they have. So we can check. The most popular passage is John 14–16, the Helper, or Paraclete. But verse 26 tells us who he is: 'the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name.' Jesus says the world can't see him, and that he already 'dwells with you and will be in you.' A few weeks later the Spirit came at Pentecost. Some say the Greek word was originally 'praised one,' but there isn't a single manuscript that reads that way.

Or take Deuteronomy 18, 'a prophet like me from among your brothers.' In Deuteronomy, 'your brothers' means fellow Israelites; the very previous chapter uses the same phrase to rule out a foreign king. I've looked at every passage that's proposed, and none of them fits. So I'm left with a question: if Muhammad isn't in the Bible Christians had, what does Qur'an 7:157 mean?"

2B-5

The Missing Injil

1 card1 strong

New terms

Euangelion: Greek for 'good news, gospel'; the source of the Arabic word Injil.

Argument2B-5STRONG

The Missing Injil

no historical trace of a lost book; the Qur'an treats the Injil as present

Name + thesis

Many Muslims say the true Injil was a book revealed to Jesus that has since been lost. But no historical source mentions such a book; the earliest Christians used "gospel" for the message about Jesus; and the Qur'an itself treats the Injil as present among Christians in Muhammad's day and even refers to its contents.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 5:46–47: "We gave him [Jesus] the Injil, in which was guidance and light... Let the People of the Injil judge by what Allah has revealed therein."
  • Qur'an 48:29: "...their description in the Torah; and their description in the Injil is as a seed which sends forth its shoot, then strengthens it, so it grows firm and stands upon its stalk, delighting the sowers."
  • Qur'an 9:111: "Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and wealth for that they will have Paradise. They fight in the cause of Allah, kill and are killed. A true promise binding on Him in the Torah, the Injil, and the Qur'an."
  • Mark 1:1: "The beginning of the gospel (euangelion) of Jesus Christ, the Son of God."
  • Mark 4:26–28: "The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground... the earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear."
  • 1 Cor 15:1–4: "the gospel I preached to you... that Christ died for our sins... that he was buried, that he was raised."

Their best case (steelman)

Shabir Ally and other Muslim scholars argue: Jesus preached "the gospel of the kingdom" (Mark 1:14–15), a message from God. That message is the Injil. Its words survive partly within the canonical Gospels, mixed with later material written by others. The Qur'an says God gave the Injil to Jesus (5:46), so it was his revelation, not a biography written by others. And 57:27 says, "We gave him the Injil," which fits a revealed book.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. If Jesus received a distinct written Injil, we would expect some trace of it: quotations, references, or a community that used it.
  • P2. There is no such trace. The earliest Christian sources use euangelion for the proclamation about Jesus' death and resurrection (1 Cor 15:1–4; Mark 1:1), and by the 2nd century for the four written Gospels.
  • P3. The Qur'an treats the Injil as accessible to "the People of the Injil" in Muhammad's day (5:47; 7:157) and cites its content (48:29), which matches a parable in our Gospels.
  • C. The "lost Injil" theory has no evidence and contradicts the Qur'an's own picture. The Injil the Qur'an refers to is the Gospel Christians had.

Evidence for each premise

  • The word. Arabic Injil comes from Greek euangelion, probably by way of Ethiopic (Ge'ez) wangel (Arthur Jeffery, The Foreign Vocabulary of the Qur'an, 1938, pp. 71–72, reporting Nöldeke's view that the Ethiopic form is almost conclusive evidence the word came from Abyssinia). The Qur'an uses the Christians' own word for their Gospel.
  • 48:29 describes the Injil's image of believers as a seed that grows by stages, delighting the sowers. That closely matches Mark 4:26–29 (the seed growing by itself) and the mustard seed (Mark 4:30–32). Ibn Kathir reads 48:29 as the Injil's description of the Companions but does not name a Gospel passage (Ibn Kathir on 48:29), so the link to Mark 4 is our comparison. Present it as a question, not as something Muslim commentators concede.
  • No trace. Early Christian writers (Papias, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus) quote and discuss written Gospels; none mentions a book revealed to Jesus. Neither do Jewish or pagan critics of Christianity (Celsus, c. 175; Porphyry, 3rd c.).
  • 9:111 claims the Injil contains a promise of Paradise for those who "kill and are killed" fighting in God's cause. No such promise exists in the Gospels, or in any early Christian text. This is a testable claim the Muslim must explain.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "The gospel Jesus preached was a revelation from God, and fragments of it survive in the Gospels." Answer: Then what did that preaching contain? According to every Gospel, Jesus taught that "the Son of Man must suffer many things... and be killed, and after three days rise again" (Mark 8:31), and that he came "to give his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). If the fragments are trustworthy, they include the cross. And the Qur'an never says the Injil was lost; it says Christians have it.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "The real Injil was lost."

  • Close (R1): Where does the Qur'an say that? It calls Christians "the People of the Injil" and tells them to judge by it (5:47).
  • Their comeback: "It was lost after Muhammad, or corrupted before."
  • Close (R2): Either way you face the timing trap (2B-1). And if God commanded Christians to judge by a book that had already vanished, he commanded the impossible.

2. "The Gospels are biographies by others, so they can't be the Injil."

  • Close (R1): The Qur'an is also full of narratives about prophets, written in the third person ("Remember when Jesus son of Mary said...," 61:6). Narrative form doesn't disqualify revelation.
  • Their comeback: "The Qur'an is God's speech; the Gospels are human speech about Jesus."
  • Close (R2): That's the question, not the answer. And 48:29 describes the Injil's content. Where does that parable exist, if not in the Gospels?

Boomerang check

"Christians also have 'lost books': Q (the hypothetical Gospel source), or Paul's lost letter to the Corinthians (1 Cor 5:9)." Answer: True. But Christians don't claim God commanded people to judge by those books, or that they are the main revelation of their faith. Q is a scholarly hypothesis about sources, not a missing scripture. The Islamic claim is that the central revelation to Jesus vanished while God commanded people to follow it.

Strength rating

Why: There is no historical evidence for a lost revealed Injil. The Qur'an's own language assumes the Injil is present (5:47, 7:157) and alludes to its content (48:29). The best Muslim reply (fragments survive) brings back the cross.

Audience How it lands Adjust

Quranists Must rely on the Qur'an's own description Use 5:47, 48:29, and 9:111.
Cultural Muslims May never have thought about it Show 48:29 next to Mark 4.

Trap questions

  1. "What did the Injil given to Jesus say? Where can I read it?"
  2. "If it was lost, how could the Christians of Muhammad's day judge by it (5:47)?"
  3. "48:29 describes a parable in the Injil about a seed. Where is that parable, if not in the Gospels?"
  4. "9:111 says the Injil promises Paradise to those who kill and are killed. Where is that in any Gospel?"

30-second version

"The Qur'an never says the Injil was lost. It tells Christians to judge by it, and it even quotes its parable of the growing seed, which is in Mark 4. The Injil the Qur'an knew is the Gospel we have."

2-minute version

"Many Muslims tell me the real Injil was a book God gave Jesus, and it was lost. I've looked for any trace of it, and there isn't one: no early Christian, Jewish, or Roman writer mentions it. The earliest Christians used the word 'gospel' for the good news about Jesus: that he died for our sins and rose again. That's how Paul uses it, within about 20 years of Jesus.

And the Qur'an doesn't say it was lost. It calls Christians 'the People of the Injil' and tells them to judge by it. In 48:29 it even describes the Injil's picture of believers as a seed that sprouts, grows, and delights the sower. That's the parable Jesus tells in Mark 4. So the Qur'an seems to know the Gospels Christians had. If that's the Injil, I'd love to read it with you."

Further reading

  • Arthur Jeffery, The Foreign Vocabulary of the Qur'an (Baroda, 1938)
  • Gabriel Said Reynolds, The Qur'an and the Bible (Yale, 2018), on 48:29 and 9:111
  • Shabir Ally, lectures on "the Injil of Jesus" (the fragments view)
  • Martin Hengel, The Four Gospels and the One Gospel of Jesus Christ (Trinity Press, 2000)
2B-6

"Allah Founded Christianity"

1 card1 strong

New terms

Shubbiha lahum: "It was made to appear so to them" (4:157): the phrase behind the Islamic belief that Jesus was not crucified.

Makr: Plan, stratagem, scheme. In 3:54 and 8:30 God is 'the best of planners' (khayr al-makirin). Not properly translated 'deceiver.'

Substitution theory: The classical Islamic view that God cast Jesus' likeness onto someone else, who was crucified in his place.

Argument2B-6STRONG

"Allah Founded Christianity"

on the majority substitution reading; still forceful on the others

Name + thesis

If, as most classical commentators held, God made someone else look like Jesus so that people believed Jesus was crucified (4:157), then God himself caused the belief that founded Christianity. The disciples, Jesus' mother, the Romans, and the Jews all believed what God made them see, and for 600 years no correction came. On the Qur'an's own account, the faith in a crucified and risen Christ was produced by God's act.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 4:157: "and [for] their saying, 'We killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of Allah.' They did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them (wa lakin shubbiha lahum). Those who differ about it are in doubt about it; they have no knowledge of it except following conjecture."
  • Qur'an 3:54: "And they planned, and Allah planned, and Allah is the best of planners (wa makaru wa makara llahu, wa llahu khayru l-makirin)."
  • Qur'an 3:55: "I will take you and raise you to Myself and purify you from those who disbelieve, and make those who follow you superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection."
  • Qur'an 8:30: the same phrase, khayr al-makirin, used of God's plan protecting Muhammad.

Their best case (steelman)

  1. The verse is ambiguous. Shubbiha lahum can mean "it was made to seem so to them" (the matter was obscured), not necessarily that someone was transformed into Jesus' likeness. Modern Muslim scholars (Mahmoud Ayoub; see Todd Lawson, The Crucifixion and the Qur'an, 2009) note a range of readings.
  2. The deceivers were the Jews, not God. God thwarted a murder plot; the confusion is the plotters' own.
  3. God didn't found Christianity; Paul did. The disciples remained true monotheists ("we are Muslims," 3:52), and Paul later invented the cross-centered religion.
  4. Makr is not "deceit." It means a plan or stratagem; God's plan was to rescue his prophet, which is good.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. On the majority classical reading of 4:157, God caused another person to look like Jesus, so that witnesses believed Jesus was crucified.
  • P2. The witnesses included Jesus' own followers, who sincerely believed and proclaimed that he had died and risen (1 Cor 15:3–8; the minimal facts in 1C).
  • P3. That proclamation is the origin of Christianity.
  • P4. God gave no correction for about 600 years, while 3:55 promises that Jesus' followers would be "superior... until the Day of Resurrection."
  • C. On the Qur'an's own account, God caused the belief from which Christianity arose and let it stand for six centuries.

Evidence for each premise

  • The substitution reading is mainstream. Al-Tabari's tafsir on 4:157 reports several versions: the likeness was cast on everyone in the house, or on one companion left behind (both from Wahb ibn Munabbih); or a disciple volunteered to take it in exchange for paradise (Qatada, al-Suddi, Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Ishaq, who names him Sarjis); Mujahid says simply that they crucified a man other than Jesus. Ibn Ishaq also mentions a claim that Judas was the one made to look like Jesus. Al-Tabari himself prefers Wahb's accounts, in which even the disciples could not tell what had happened, which is this card's point in its strongest form. Ibn Kathir (on 4:158) gives a report from Ibn Abbas in which the youngest of the twelve volunteered, and says its chain is "sound to Ibn Abbas," adding that al-Nasa'i has it in similar wording.
  • Translation of makr. Translate honestly: "best of planners" or "best of schemers," not "best of deceivers." Arabic makr can be good or bad; the force of the argument doesn't depend on mistranslation.
  • The disciples' belief: the 1 Cor 15:3–7 creed dates within a few years of the cross and names Cephas (Peter), the Twelve, and James, not Paul alone.
  • No early non-crucifixion Christianity. The only early alternatives (Basilides, reported by Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.24.4; the Nag Hammadi Second Treatise of the Great Seth) are Gnostic, deny Jesus' real body, and post-date the crucifixion proclamation (2B-14).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: the ambiguity of shubbiha lahum. Answer: On every reading, the result is that people saw what looked like Jesus' crucifixion and believed it. Whether God transformed a substitute or merely "made it appear so," the appearance came from God and produced the faith of the disciples. So the argument's core survives any reading. (The Ahmadiyya view, that Jesus was put on the cross but survived, faces a different problem: 4:157 says "nor did they crucify him.")

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "God only deceived the plotters, not the disciples."

  • Close (R1): The disciples believed he died too, and preached it within days (Acts 2:23–24). If God intended only the enemies to be fooled, why did the effect fall on his own prophet's followers?
  • Their comeback: "The disciples fled; they didn't witness it."
  • Close (R2): The women and John are reported present (Mark 15:40; John 19:25–26). And the disciples' belief rested on the appearances afterward. Who appeared to them, if Jesus had already been taken up?

2. "Paul invented the cross, not the disciples."

  • Close (R1): The creed Paul "received" names Peter and James as witnesses (1 Cor 15:3–7), and Paul says, "Whether it was I or they, so we preach" (15:11).
  • Their comeback: "The disciples were true Muslims (3:52; 61:14)."
  • Close (R2): Then show one early source where the disciples deny the crucifixion. There is none. See 2B-8.

3. "God's plan (makr) was good: he saved Jesus."

  • Close (R1): Agreed that makr needn't mean evil. The question is the effect: God's plan produced the universal belief that Jesus died.
  • Their comeback: "God is not responsible for people's misunderstandings."
  • Close (R2): He is, if he produced the appearance that caused them. 4:157 says "it was made to appear so to them" (passive: someone made it appear). Who, other than God?

Boomerang check

"The Bible says God sends deception too: 2 Thess 2:11 ('God sends them a strong delusion'), 1 Kgs 22:19–23 (a lying spirit in the prophets' mouths)." Answer: This is a fair challenge, so take it seriously.

  • 2 Thess 2:10–12: the delusion is a judgment on those who "refused to love the truth" and "had pleasure in unrighteousness." It confirms people in a lie they have already chosen.
  • 1 Kgs 22: God reveals the lying spirit to Ahab through the true prophet Micaiah (22:19–23). Ahab is told exactly what is happening and chooses to ignore it.
  • 4:157 is different: it makes the innocent (Jesus' faithful followers and mother) believe something false, with no warning for 600 years, and the result is the founding of a world religion. In the Bible, judicial hardening falls on those who reject revealed truth; in the 4:157 scenario, the deception falls on those who loved the truth.

Strength rating

Why: The substitution reading is the majority classical view, and every reading of shubbiha lahum leaves the appearance of crucifixion in place. The Muslim's best moves (the disciples fled; Paul invented it) collide with the 1 Cor 15 creed. The boomerang (2 Thess 2; 1 Kgs 22) has a clear answer.

  3. "If God made them believe it, and they preached it, who started Christianity?"
  4. "Why would God wait 600 years to correct it?"

30-second version

2-minute version

"Can I ask about 4:157? It says they didn't crucify Jesus, 'but it was made to appear so to them.' Many of your classical scholars explain that God put Jesus' likeness on someone else. Think about what follows. Jesus' mother, the women at the cross, and his disciples would all have believed they saw him die. They weren't plotters; they loved him. Then they said they saw him risen, and they preached it. That preaching became Christianity.

So if that's what happened, God's own action produced the faith of Jesus' followers, and he let it stand for 600 years. That's hard for me to square with a God of truth. The simpler explanation is that they saw what really happened: Jesus died for our sins, and God raised him."

Further reading

  • Gabriel Said Reynolds, "The Muslim Jesus: Dead or Alive?," Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 72.2 (2009)
  • Mahmoud Ayoub, "Towards an Islamic Christology II: The Death of Jesus, Reality or Delusion," Muslim World 70 (1980)
  • Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, tafsir on 4:157
  • David Wood, Acts 17 Apologetics materials on Qur'an 4:157 (popular; check claims against the above)
2B-7

The Failed Promise

1 card1 moderate

New terms

Ebionites: Early Jewish-Christian groups that kept the Mosaic law and rejected Paul; most reports say they denied the virgin birth.

Arianism: The 4th-century teaching of Arius that the Son is a created, though pre-existent and worshiped, divine being.

Al-hawariyyun: The Qur'an's word for Jesus' disciples (3:52; 61:14).

Argument2B-7MODERATE

The Failed Promise (3:55 and 61:14)

depends on who counts as Jesus' "followers"

Name + thesis

The Qur'an promises that Jesus' followers would be "above those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection" (3:55), and says the believers who helped Jesus "became dominant" (61:14). If Jesus' true followers held the Qur'an's view of Jesus (a human prophet, not crucified), history shows no such group ever became dominant. The only followers of Jesus who prevailed were those who confessed his death, resurrection, and deity.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 3:55: "O Jesus, I will take you and raise you to Myself... and make those who follow you (alladhina ttaba'uka) above those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection."
  • Qur'an 61:14: "O you who believe, be helpers of Allah, as Jesus son of Mary said to the disciples (al-hawariyyun), 'Who are my helpers for Allah?' The disciples said, 'We are the helpers of Allah.' And a faction of the Children of Israel believed and a faction disbelieved. So We supported those who believed against their enemy, and they became dominant (fa-asbahu zahirin)."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. Christians in general are the followers in 3:55. Some classical commentators applied 3:55 to Christians staying above Jews until the Last Day: al-Tabari records this view from Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Kathir notes that Christians historically dominated Jews, though both prefer the reading that the followers are Muslims (al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir on 3:55). So the verse was fulfilled.
  2. Muslims are Jesus' true followers. Following Jesus means following the prophet he foretold (61:6). Muslims became dominant.
  3. There were early monotheist Christians: the Ebionites (Jewish Christians who rejected Paul) and the Arians (who denied Jesus was equal to God). Arians dominated parts of the Roman world in the 4th century.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. 3:55 and 61:14 promise that the believers who followed Jesus would prevail, continuously, "until the Day of Resurrection."
  • P2. If those believers held the Qur'anic view of Jesus (human prophet; not crucified; virgin-born), there must be a historical community holding that view that prevailed.
  • P3. No such community is attested. The Ebionites denied the virgin birth (in most reports); the Arians affirmed the crucifixion and worshiped Christ as a pre-existent divine being; neither prevailed long-term.
  • C. Either the promise failed, or Jesus' "followers" in 3:55 are the Christians who confessed the cross, which concedes that the cross-believing church was the true continuation of Jesus' disciples.

Evidence for each premise

  • Ebionites: Irenaeus (Against Heresies 1.26.2; c. 180) says they used only Matthew and rejected Paul. He and others report they held Jesus was the natural son of Joseph (Against Heresies 3.21.1; 5.1.3), which contradicts the Qur'an's virgin birth (19:20; 3:47). Origen distinguishes two groups, one of which accepted the virgin birth (Against Celsus 5.61). There's no evidence any Ebionite group denied the crucifixion. They were a small, marginal movement.
  • Arians: Arius (d. 336) held the Son was a created being, but pre-existent, the agent of creation, and worshiped; he affirmed the crucifixion and resurrection. Arianism dominated some Germanic kingdoms until the 6th–7th centuries, then disappeared.
  • The dominant church from the 1st century onward confessed the death and resurrection of Jesus (1 Cor 15:3–7) and worshiped him as Lord (Phil 2:6–11).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "3:55 means Christians in general, and they have indeed been above the Jews." Answer: That reading concedes the point: the "followers of Jesus" whom God made superior were the Christians who believed in the crucifixion and deity. Then God promised supremacy to people teaching (on the Muslim view) the unforgivable sin of shirk (4:48), with no indication that they were in error.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Muslims are the true followers."

  • Close (R1): 3:55 promises superiority "until the Day of Resurrection," starting with Jesus. Who were his followers from AD 33 to 610?
  • Their comeback: "A small, hidden remnant of true believers."
  • Close (R2): A hidden remnant is the opposite of "dominant" (zahirin, 61:14). Name one early source showing them.

2. "The Arians were the true monotheists."

  • Close (R1): Arius taught the Son existed before creation, created the world, was worshiped, and died on the cross and rose. Is that the Qur'an's Jesus?
  • Their comeback: "At least they rejected the Trinity."
  • Close (R2): They rejected equality, not Jesus' worship or crucifixion. The Qur'an condemns both (4:157; 5:72).

Boomerang check

"Jesus promised he would return soon (Mark 9:1; 13:30), and it didn't happen. That's your failed promise." Answer: A serious objection. Mark 9:1 is followed immediately by the Transfiguration (9:2–8), which the Gospel presents as the disciples "seeing the kingdom come with power." Mark 13:30 ("this generation") most plausibly refers to the events of AD 70 described earlier in the chapter (13:1–23), which happened within that generation. Christians debate the details, but the texts have plausible readings that fit history. Qur'an 3:55 has no reading in which a Qur'anic-Christian community prevailed.

Strength rating

Why: The historical point is solid: no early community held the Qur'anic Jesus and prevailed. But the Muslim can read "followers" as Christians in general (with classical support), or as Muslims. Each move has a cost, but the argument depends on interpretation, so MODERATE.
