2C-1

The Hadith Dilemma

1 card1 moderate

New terms

Sunna: The normative example of Muhammad (words, deeds, approvals), known through hadith and community practice.

Quranists (Qur'aniyyun): Muslims who accept the Qur'an alone and reject hadith as a source of religious authority.

Tawatur: Mass transmission: a report passed on by so many people in every generation that collusion in falsehood is considered impossible.

Mufassal: 'Fully detailed' or 'made distinct': the Qur'an's description of itself (6:114).

Argument2C-1MODERATE

The Hadith Dilemma

decisive against Quranists' consistency; Sunnis have a strong answer

Name + thesis

The Qur'an calls itself "fully detailed" (6:114) and "a clarification of all things" (16:89). Yet it doesn't say how many times to pray each day, how to perform the prayer, or what percentage to give in zakat. Muslims need the Sunna, known through hadith and practice, to fulfill the Qur'an's most basic commands. So either the Qur'an is not as complete as it claims, or the Quranists are right and nearly all Muslims practice a religion the Qur'an doesn't define.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 6:114: "Shall I seek a judge other than Allah, when it is He who has sent down to you the Book fully detailed (mufassalan)?"
  • Qur'an 16:89: "We have sent down to you the Book as a clarification of all things (tibyanan li-kulli shay')."
  • Qur'an 12:111: "...a detailed explanation of all things (tafsila kulli shay')."
  • Qur'an 59:7: "Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it."
  • Qur'an 4:80: "He who obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah."

Their best case (steelman)

The Sunni answer (strong): (1) The Qur'an itself commands obedience to the Messenger (4:59; 4:80; 33:21; 59:7), so the Sunna is part of what the Qur'an "details": it points to its own explanation. (2) "All things" means all things of guidance in principle (al-Shafi'i, al-Risala). (3) The prayer was not learned from 9th-century books; it was transmitted by the living practice of the whole community from Muhammad onward (tawatur 'amali, mass-transmitted practice), and later recorded in hadith. Hadith collections didn't create the prayer; they documented it.

The Quranist answer: the Qur'an is sufficient; the details of prayer can be derived from the Qur'an (e.g., 11:114; 17:78; 24:58) or are left flexible. Hadith are unreliable human reports compiled two centuries later.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The Qur'an claims to be fully detailed and a clarification of all things (6:114; 16:89; 12:111).
  • P2. Essential practices it commands (the five daily prayers, their form; zakat rates; many hajj rites) are not specified in it.
  • P3. Either those practices are specified elsewhere (Sunna), or they are left undefined (Quranism).
  • C. If elsewhere, then "fully detailed" must be read as "detailed with the help of an outside source." If undefined, then 1,400 years of Muslim practice goes beyond the Qur'an. Either way, the Qur'an's self-description needs qualification, and the Sunni Muslim relies on hadith literature compiled two centuries after Muhammad for the content of his religion.

Evidence for each premise

  • The Qur'an mentions prayer times in general terms (11:114; 17:78; 2:238, "the middle prayer"), but never states "five" or describes the units (rak'at).
  • Hadith collections were compiled in the 9th century: al-Bukhari (d. 870), Muslim (d. 875), Abu Dawud (d. 889), al-Tirmidhi (d. 892). Earlier written material existed (Malik's Muwatta', d. 795; scholars' notebooks).
  • Jonathan Brown (a Muslim scholar) explains the Sunni method and the role of practice (Hadith, 2nd ed., 2017; Misquoting Muhammad, 2014).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: the Sunni practice-transmission answer. Answer: Concede it's a good answer for the prayer's basic form. The dilemma then has two real uses: (1) Against Quranists: their position makes the Qur'an insufficient to define the religion it commands. (2) Against the "Qur'an alone is perfectly clear" rhetoric: the Sunni Muslim admits the Qur'an needs the Sunna, which is known through human transmission and graded by human scholars. That's an important admission when he insists the Bible is unreliable because it was transmitted by humans.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. (Sunni) "The Qur'an commands following the Sunna, so it's complete."

  • Close (R1): Then you accept that the Qur'an's meaning depends on reports transmitted and graded by humans. Fine. Then the Bible's human transmission isn't, by itself, a reason to reject it.
  • Their comeback: "Hadith are verified by isnad criticism, the most rigorous system ever."
  • Close (R2): It's a serious system, and Christians should respect it. But it's still human judgment two centuries later, and Sunni scholars themselves disagree on many gradings. Apply the same humility to the Bible's manuscripts, which are far earlier.

2. (Quranist) "The Qur'an is sufficient; hadith are unreliable."

  • Close (R1): Then how many times a day do you pray, and how? Where does the Qur'an say?
  • Their comeback: "The details are flexible; God gave principles."
  • Close (R2): Then the religion of Muhammad's community, practiced by nearly all Muslims, goes beyond the Qur'an. Who preserved the true religion between Muhammad and you?

Boomerang check

"Christians also need tradition to know how to worship; the Bible doesn't specify the liturgy." Answer: True, and Christian traditions differ on the role of tradition (Catholic and Orthodox vs. Protestant). But the Bible doesn't claim to be a "detailed explanation of all things." It claims sufficiency for salvation and godliness (2 Tim 3:15–17), and leaves worship forms largely open (Col 2:16–17). The Qur'an's claim is stronger, so the problem is sharper.

Strength rating

Why: Against Quranists, it's strong. Against Sunnis, the practice-transmission answer is good, so the argument's real value is the admission it draws out: Sunni Islam depends on human transmission and grading. MODERATE overall. Don't say "they need 9th-century hadith even to know how to pray"; that overstates it.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Quranists Direct hit Ask how they pray.
Sunni (all schools) They'll give the Sunna answer Use it to establish one standard on human transmission.
Twelver Shia Rely on Imami hadith (al-Kafi etc.) Same as Sunni.

Trap questions

  1. "Where does the Qur'an say to pray five times a day?"
  2. "If the Qur'an is 'a clarification of all things,' why do we need hadith?"
  3. "If hadith transmitted by humans can be trusted, why can't biblical manuscripts?"

30-second version

"The Qur'an says it explains all things, but it doesn't say how many times to pray or how. You need the Sunna for that, passed on by people and graded by scholars. If human transmission is reliable for the Sunna, why not for the Bible?"

2-minute version

"Here's a question I've wondered about. The Qur'an calls itself 'fully detailed' and 'a clarification of all things.' But it doesn't tell you to pray five times a day, or how many units each prayer has. For that, Muslims rely on the Sunna, which was passed on by the community and recorded in hadith collections compiled about 200 years after Muhammad. I know the Sunni answer: the Qur'an itself says to follow the Messenger, and the prayer was passed on by everyone's practice. That's reasonable. But it means Islam depends on human transmission too. So when people tell me the Bible can't be trusted because humans copied it, I wonder why the same reasoning doesn't apply to the Sunna."

Further reading

  • Al-Shafi'i, al-Risala, tr. Joseph Lowry (NYU Press, 2013)
  • Aisha Musa, Hadith as Scripture (Palgrave, 2008): on Quranist debates

2C-2

Abrogation vs. Unchangeable Words

1 card1 weak

New terms

Naskh: Abrogation: the doctrine that some Qur'anic rulings or verses were superseded by later ones.

Naskh al-tilawa: Abrogation of a verse's recitation (it is no longer in the Qur'an) while, in some cases, its ruling remains.

Argument2C-2WEAK

Abrogation vs. Unchangeable Words

as a contradiction; the related preservation point is stronger, see 2F

Name + thesis

The Qur'an teaches that God abrogates and replaces verses (2:106; 16:101), yet also that "no one can change His words" (6:115; 10:64). As a contradiction, this has a good Muslim answer. Its real value is what abrogation implies for the claim that the Qur'an is preserved exactly as revealed.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 2:106: "We do not abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten (ma nansakh min ayatin aw nunsiha) except that We bring forth one better than it or similar to it."
  • Qur'an 16:101: "When We substitute a verse in place of another... they say, 'You are only an inventor.'"
  • Qur'an 87:6–7: "We will make you recite, and you will not forget, except what Allah wills."
  • Qur'an 6:115: "None can alter His words."
  • Qur'an 10:64: "There is no change in the words of Allah."

Their best case (steelman)

"No one can change His words" means no creature can. Abrogation is God's own act: the Author revising his own law for his people's good, as a legislator amends rulings over time. There's no contradiction. (Some modern Muslims, e.g., Muhammad Asad, also read aya in 2:106 as "message," referring to earlier scriptures, and deny abrogation within the Qur'an.)

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The Qur'an teaches that God abrogates verses, including by causing them to be forgotten (2:106; 87:7).
  • P2. Classical Islamic scholarship recognizes verses whose recitation was abrogated though their ruling remained (naskh al-tilawa duna l-hukm), such as the stoning verse (Sahih al-Bukhari 6829 (in-book 86/55), Umar on the stoning verse; Sahih Muslim 1691a (in-book 29/21), Ibn Abbas reporting Umar's sermon) and the ten/five sucklings (Sahih Muslim 1452a (in-book 17/30), narrated by Aisha).
  • C. The Qur'an as recited today is not identical to everything that was revealed as Qur'an. That complicates the claim that it is perfectly preserved and complete (see 2F), even if it doesn't create a formal contradiction with 6:115.

Evidence for each premise

  • Muslim 1452 (Aisha): "ten known sucklings" was abrogated by "five," and "the Messenger of Allah died while it was among what was recited of the Qur'an."
  • Bukhari 6829 / Muslim 1691 (Umar): the stoning verse was revealed in the Book of Allah, and "I fear that people will say, 'We do not find stoning in the Book of Allah.'"
  • Classical works on abrogation (e.g., Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam, d. 838; al-Nahhas, d. 949) list many abrogated verses; estimates range from about twenty (al-Suyuti) to well over a hundred in earlier works.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Fatal for the contradiction form: "No creature can change God's words" removes the contradiction. Concede it.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Abrogation is God's prerogative."

  • Close (R1): Agreed. I'm not saying abrogation contradicts 6:115. I'm asking about Muslim 1452: a verse "recited of the Qur'an" when Muhammad died, and not in the Qur'an today.
  • Their comeback: "Its recitation was abrogated; that's still God's act."
  • Close (R2): After Muhammad's death, no further revelation came. So who removed it from recitation, and when? That leads to 2F.

Boomerang check

"Christians believe God changed his law too (the old covenant to the new)." Answer: Yes, and Christians openly say so (Heb 8:13). But Christians don't claim the Old Testament text was removed or forgotten. The text remains; its application changed. That's a parallel to naskh al-hukm (abrogation of the ruling), not to the removal of recitation.

Strength rating

Why: As a contradiction, it's easily answered: drop that form. The useful point (removed recitations) belongs in 2F, where it is rated with the preservation evidence.

Audience notes

Quranists Many deny intra-Qur'anic abrogation Not useful.

  2. "What does Aisha mean in Muslim 1452 by 'among what was recited of the Qur'an' when the Prophet died?"

30-second version

"I don't think abrogation contradicts 'no one can change His words'; that means no creature. My question is different: Aisha said a verse was still recited when Muhammad died, and it isn't in the Qur'an today. What happened to it?"

2-minute version

"Some Christians argue that abrogation contradicts the Qur'an's statement that no one can change God's words. I don't think that works; God can revise his own rulings. But it raises a different question. According to Sahih Muslim, Aisha said that the verse on five sucklings was still being recited as Qur'an when Muhammad died. It's not in the Qur'an today. And Umar said the stoning verse was revealed in the Book of Allah. If those verses were part of the Qur'an at Muhammad's death, how can we say the Qur'an we have is everything that was revealed?"

Further reading

  • David S. Powers, "The Exegetical Genre nasikh al-Qur'an wa mansukhuhu," in Andrew Rippin (ed.), Approaches to the History of the Interpretation of the Qur'an (Oxford, 1988)
  • Muhammad Asad, The Message of the Qur'an (1980), note on 2:106
2C-3

The 4:82 Test

1 card1 weak

New terms

Ikhtilaf: Disagreement or inconsistency; in 4:82, the 'contradiction' a non-divine book would contain.

Argument2C-3WEAK

The 4:82 Contradictions

the classic candidates all have standard harmonizations, and the boomerang is severe

Name + thesis

The Qur'an says that if it were from other than God, people would find "much contradiction" in it (4:82). Christians often cite apparent contradictions. Honestly rated, the usual candidates have harmonizations of exactly the kind Christians use for the Bible. The strongest "4:82 case" isn't a pair of verses at all; it's the Islamic Dilemma.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 4:82: "Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an? If it had been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction (ikhtilafan kathiran)."
  • Qur'an 41:9–12: the earth created "in two days"; its mountains and provisions "in four days"; the heavens completed "in two days."
  • Qur'an 7:54 (also 10:3; 11:7; 25:59): "created the heavens and the earth in six days."
  • Qur'an 32:11: "The angel of death will take you." 6:61: "Our messengers take him." 39:42: "Allah takes the souls at the time of their death."

Their best case (steelman)

  • 41:9–12: the "four days" include the first two (cumulative: "in four days in all"), so 2 + 2 + 2 = 6. This is the standard classical reading (e.g., Ibn Kathir on 41:10).
  • Who takes souls? God takes them through the angel of death, who works with assisting angels: one action, described at three levels of agency, as a king "builds" a palace through workers.
  • 4:82 itself: "ikhtilaf" can mean inconsistency in style, quality, or message, not just strict logical contradiction.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. 4:82 sets a test: a non-divine book would contain much contradiction.
  • P2. The commonly cited candidates (41:9–12 vs. 7:54; 32:11 vs. 6:61 vs. 39:42; 32:5 vs. 70:4 on the length of a "day"; 2:256 vs. 9:29) have harmonizations accepted by classical commentators.
  • P3. Christians harmonize biblical tensions in the same ways.
  • C. These verse-pair "contradictions" don't carry weight in debate. The serious 4:82 question is whether the Qur'an's major claims cohere: affirming the Torah and Gospel while contradicting them (2A), and claiming perfect preservation while reporting lost verses (2C-2; 2F).

Evidence for each premise

Candidate Muslim harmonization Verdict
41:9–12 (8 days?) vs. 7:54 (6 days) "Four days" includes the first two WEAK: drop
32:11 / 6:61 / 39:42 (who takes souls) Levels of agency WEAK: drop
32:5 (a day = 1,000 years) vs. 70:4 (50,000 years) Different events or "days" WEAK: drop
2:256 ("no compulsion in religion") vs. 9:29 (fight the People of the Book until they pay jizya) Different contexts; jizya isn't conversion WEAK–MODERATE: belongs in 2I, not here
6:14, 6:163 (Muhammad "first of the Muslims") vs. 7:143 (Moses "first of the believers") vs. 2:131–132 (Abraham a Muslim) "First of my community / my time" WEAK
Iblis: an angel or a jinn? The angels are told to bow and all do "except for Iblees" (2:34), angels never disobey Allah (66:6), yet 18:50 says Iblis "was of the jinn" and made of fire (7:12) Iblis was never an angel; he was among them and was commanded too ("when I commanded you," 7:12), so "except" is a separate exception. Ibn Kathir on 18:50 records that early commentators disagreed: al-Hasan al-Basri said Iblis was never an angel "for the blink of an eye," while a report from Ibn Abbas says he came from a tribe of angels called "the jinn." Angels are made of light and jinn of fire (Sahih Muslim 2996) WEAK: drop. Raised in GodLogic Apologetics' "Quran error found! [Iblis] Angel or jinn?" The Qur'an itself says he was a jinn and was commanded, so no contradiction is forced.
The Qur'an affirms the Torah and Gospel (5:47) yet contradicts them (4:157) Remnant, tahrif, muhaymin STRONG: see 2A

Weakest premise / hardest objection

The boomerang is the objection. Every harmonization above has a biblical twin (e.g., the two creation accounts; the differing Gospel resurrection details). If you dismiss Muslim harmonizations, you lose yours.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "The Qur'an has no contradictions."

  • Close (R1): I won't argue over verse pairs; harmonizations exist for both books. Let's apply 4:82 to the Qur'an's biggest claim about the Bible.
  • Their comeback: "That's not a contradiction within the Qur'an."
  • Close (R2): It is: the Qur'an says the Gospel Christians have contains God's guidance (5:46–47), and also denies what that Gospel says (4:157). That's ikhtilaf at the heart of the book.

Boomerang check

Severe. Muslim debaters (Shabir Ally, Paul Williams) list Bible contradictions: Judas' death (Matt 27:5 vs. Acts 1:18), Jesus' genealogies (Matt 1 vs. Luke 3), the resurrection accounts, 2 Sam 24:1 vs. 1 Chr 21:1 (God vs. Satan inciting David). The Christian answer: harmonizations (Judas hanged himself and his body fell; Matthew's genealogy through Joseph's legal line, Luke's possibly through Mary or a different line; God permitting Satan's action), plus a different view of inspiration: Christians don't claim the Bible was dictated word-for-word in one language. One standard: accept reasonable harmonizations in both books, and debate the major claims instead. See 2J on Bible contradictions.

Strength rating

Why: The classic candidates are easily harmonized, and the boomerang is heavy. Drop verse-pair contradictions from debates. Keep the reframed point: the Dilemma is the Qur'an's real 4:82 problem.

Christians in training Need to know why to avoid this Teach the boomerang.

Trap questions

  1. "If we agree to accept reasonable harmonizations in both books, can we talk about the Qur'an's claims about the Bible instead?"
  2. "Does the Qur'an affirm the Gospel and also deny what it says? Is that ikhtilaf?"

30-second version

"I don't use contradiction lists; both books have answers for those. The real 4:82 question is bigger: the Qur'an affirms the Gospel and denies what it says. That's a contradiction at the center."

2-minute version

"Some Christians bring lists of contradictions in the Qur'an. I don't, because most have reasonable explanations, the same way apparent contradictions in the Bible do. If I reject your harmonizations, I'd have to reject mine. But 4:82 invites us to reflect on the Qur'an's consistency, and I think the real issue is a big one. The Qur'an tells Christians to judge by the Gospel, and calls it guidance and light. And then it denies what the Gospel says about Jesus' death. Isn't that the kind of inconsistency 4:82 is talking about?"

Further reading

2D-1

The Deception Problem

1 card1 moderate

New terms

Mutawatir: A report transmitted by tawatur; Muslims hold the Qur'an's text is mutawatir.

Argument2D-1MODERATE

The Deception Problem

strong as an internal critique of the substitution reading; Muslims have a "single purposeful miracle" reply

Name + thesis

If God made the crucifixion of a substitute look exactly like the crucifixion of Jesus to every witness, friend and enemy, then the unanimous testimony of many eyewitnesses can be wrong because God made it wrong. But Islam's own confidence in the Qur'an's transmission, in mass-transmitted hadith, and even in Muhammad's existence rests on exactly that kind of testimony (tawatur). The substitution theory undermines the foundation of Islamic knowledge.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 4:157: "...but it was made to appear so to them (shubbiha lahum)."
  • Qur'an 15:9: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian."
  • Heb 6:18: "it is impossible for God to lie." Titus 1:2: "God, who never lies." Num 23:19: "God is not man, that he should lie."
  • John 20:27: "Put your finger here, and see my hands... Do not disbelieve, but believe." (The Christian God invites the senses to verify.)

Their best case (steelman)

  1. A single, purposeful miracle to save a prophet from murderers is not a general policy of deception. God normally upholds the reliability of testimony.
  2. God guarantees the Qur'an (15:9), so its transmission is protected whatever happened with Jesus.
  3. The witnesses were few and confused. The disciples fled (Mark 14:50); "those who differ about it are in doubt" (Qur'an 4:157). It wasn't the kind of clear, mass, firsthand testimony tawatur requires.
  4. Parity: any theism faces this. The Christian God could deceive; Christians just trust he doesn't. Muslims trust Allah the same way.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. On the substitution reading, God caused many witnesses (Roman soldiers, Jewish leaders, crowds, Jesus' mother and friends) to perceive and report falsely that Jesus was crucified.
  • P2. If God does this, then unanimous, sincere, multiple eyewitness testimony is not a reliable guide to what happened, at least in matters God cares about.
  • P3. Islam relies on precisely such testimony for its foundations: the tawatur (mass transmission) of the Qur'an, the mutawatir hadith, and the historical existence and career of Muhammad.
  • C. The substitution reading undercuts the epistemic basis Muslims use to trust the Qur'an and the Sunna. A Muslim must either drop the substitution reading or accept that tawatur is not trustworthy.

Evidence for each premise

  • Tawatur in Islamic thought: knowledge transmitted by so many that collusion in falsehood is impossible is treated as certain ('ilm daruri) by Sunni theologians and jurists (e.g., al-Ghazali in al-Mustasfa, as modern studies of his epistemology note). The Qur'an's text is held to be mutawatir.
  • The crucifixion's witnesses were public and varied: Roman executioners (whose job was to verify death), Jewish authorities, passersby (Mark 15:29), women followers (Mark 15:40–41), and John (John 19:26, 35). It was a public execution at Passover.
  • The founding of Christianity followed directly from these perceptions (2B-6).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "A single, purposeful miracle doesn't make testimony generally unreliable." Answer: (1) This wasn't a minor event; it determined the faith of Jesus' followers and, on the Islamic view, created the world's largest false religion. If God would mislead the faithful on that, what principle tells us he wouldn't elsewhere? (2) The Muslim's guarantee (15:9) is known through the Qur'an, whose text is known through tawatur, so appealing to 15:9 to rescue tawatur is circular. (3) The parity reply misreads Christianity: the Bible grounds God's truthfulness in his nature ("it is impossible for God to lie"), and never presents God as making his faithful people perceive a false event. See 2D-2 on how Ash'ari theology handles God's truthfulness.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "God only deceived the enemies."

  • Close (R1): The effect fell on Jesus' mother and disciples too. And the appearances afterward convinced the disciples he had risen. Were those also illusions?
  • Their comeback: "We don't know the details; God knows best."
  • Close (R2): Then on the Islamic account, we don't know whether God has done something similar with any other event, including the Qur'an's transmission.

2. "The disciples fled; there was no tawatur."

  • Close (R1): The Romans and the Jewish authorities saw it, and so did many in Jerusalem at Passover. Roman, Jewish, and Christian sources all report it (2B-14).
  • Their comeback: "Hostile sources don't count."
  • Close (R2): Then the Qur'an's own transmission, which you defend partly by the absence of hostile contradiction, faces the same rules. One standard.

Boomerang check

"The Bible says God sends delusion (2 Thess 2:11) and a lying spirit (1 Kgs 22)." Answer: See 2B-6: in both cases God's action is a judicial hardening of people who have already rejected revealed truth, and in 1 Kgs 22 God openly announces it through his prophet. Neither involves God making his faithful followers perceive a false event.

"Christianity also depends on testimony." Yes, and Christianity affirms that testimony is reliable, because God is truthful and made our senses to know the world. That's why the Christian position is consistent and the substitution theory isn't.

Strength rating

Why: The internal tension is real and follows from the majority substitution reading. But the Muslim "single purposeful miracle" and "15:9 guarantee" replies are coherent enough to keep this at MODERATE. It's very effective with thoughtful Muslims, especially those who value tawatur.

Ash'ari God may do whatever he wills Connect to 2D-2.
Quranists Still rely on the Qur'an's transmission Same point, without hadith.
Cultural Muslims Never considered it Use the simple question: "Would God fool Jesus' mother?"

Trap questions

  1. "How do you know the Qur'an you have is the one Muhammad recited?"
  2. "If God made everyone at the cross see something false, how do you know he didn't do that elsewhere?"
  3. "Would God make Jesus' own mother believe her son died, when he hadn't?"

30-second version

"If God made everyone, including Jesus' mother and disciples, see a crucifixion that didn't happen, then even unanimous eyewitnesses can be wrong because of God. But you trust the Qur'an because of unanimous transmission. The substitution theory saws off the branch it sits on."

2-minute version

"I want to ask about how we know things. You trust the Qur'an because so many people, generation after generation, passed it on that they couldn't all be wrong. That's tawatur, and it's a good principle. But think about 4:157 as many scholars explain it: God made someone else look like Jesus, so that everyone present, the soldiers, the priests, the crowd, Jesus' own mother, saw what looked like Jesus dying. If God did that, then a whole crowd of sincere eyewitnesses can be completely wrong, because God made them wrong. So how can we trust testimony at all, including the testimony that gave us the Qur'an? I believe in a God who cannot lie, who invited Thomas to touch his wounds. What happened at the cross was real."

Further reading

  • Todd Lawson, The Crucifixion and the Qur'an (2009)
  • Bernard Weiss, "Knowledge of the Past: The Theory of Tawatur According to Ghazali," Studia Islamica 61 (1985)
  • C.A.J. Coady, Testimony: A Philosophical Study (Oxford, 1992)
2D-2

The Islamic Euthyphro

1 card1 moderate

New terms

Euthyphro dilemma: From Plato: is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good?

Ash'ari: The Sunni theological school of al-Ash'ari (d. 935), dominant at al-Azhar; stresses God's absolute will and holds that good and evil are known through revelation.

Maturidi: The Sunni theological school of al-Maturidi (d. 944), dominant among Hanafis; holds that reason can know basic good and evil.

Athari: 'Traditionalist': Sunni theology that affirms God's attributes as revealed, without philosophical interpretation (Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ibn Taymiyya); the creed of most Salafis.

Voluntarism: The view that God's will, not his nature, is the ultimate ground of what is good.

Occasionalism: Al-Ghazali's view (and that of many Ash'aris) that created things have no causal power; God directly creates each effect.

Husn and qubh: 'Goodness and badness': the debate over whether they are known by reason ('aqli) or only by revelation (shar'i).

Hikma: Wisdom; in Maturidi and Athari theology, God always acts for wise purposes.

Argument2D-2MODERATE

The Islamic Euthyphro

applies mainly to strict Ash'ari theology; Maturidis and Atharis have different answers

Name + thesis

Classical Ash'ari theology holds that good and evil are known only by God's command, that God is not bound by any moral standard, and (with al-Ghazali) that God directly creates every event with no real natural causes. If so, morality is arbitrary, the regularity of nature has no ground, and even God's truthfulness has no moral basis. Christianity grounds goodness, order, and truth in God's unchanging nature, and so avoids all three problems.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 2:253; 22:18: "Allah does what He wills" (yaf'alu ma yasha'). 21:23: "He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned."
  • Qur'an 16:90: "Allah commands justice and good conduct... and forbids immorality and bad conduct." (Implies knowable standards.)
  • Gen 18:25: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?"
  • Ps 119:68: "You are good and do good." 1 John 1:5: "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all."
  • Heb 6:18: "it is impossible for God to lie."

Their best case (steelman)

Ash'aris (al-Ash'ari, al-Juwayni, al-Ghazali): God is utterly sovereign. Nothing is "good" independently of him; "good" means what God commands. Human reason can't judge God. Yet God's truthfulness isn't arbitrary: lying is an imperfection (naqs), and God is free of imperfection, so his speech is necessarily true. And nature's regularity is God's custom ('ada), which he reliably maintains.

Maturidis: reason can know basic good and evil (husn and qubh 'aqli), and God always acts with wisdom (hikma). No arbitrariness.

Atharis / Ibn Taymiyya: God acts for wise purposes; created things have real causal powers (asbab) that God gives them. They reject both pure voluntarism and full occasionalism.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. On strict Ash'ari voluntarism, an act is good only because God commands it, and God is not bound by goodness. (Some Ash'aris said it would not be unjust for God to punish the obedient forever, because they defined injustice as acting on what belongs to another or disobeying one who must be obeyed, neither of which can apply to God, as Ibn Taymiyya reports in his treatise on God's justice.)
  • P2. On al-Ghazali's occasionalism, created things have no real causal power; God directly creates the burning when fire touches cotton (The Incoherence of the Philosophers, 17th discussion).
  • P3. If both hold, then (a) morality is grounded in will alone, so "God is good" says only "God does what God wills"; (b) the regularity of nature is grounded in a custom God may break at any time; (c) God's truthfulness has no moral ground.
  • C. Strict Ash'ari theology struggles to ground objective morality, scientific induction, and trustworthy revelation. Christianity grounds all three in God's nature (TAG, 1A).

Evidence for each premise

  • Al-Ghazali's cotton example: "the connection between what is habitually believed to be a cause and what is habitually believed to be an effect is not necessary" (Tahafut al-Falasifa, 17th discussion; tr. Michael Marmura, 2000).
  • Ash'ari ethics: good and bad are shar'i (known by revelation), not 'aqli (known by reason). See George Hourani, Reason and Tradition in Islamic Ethics (Cambridge, 1985).
  • The tension in practice: the Qur'an appeals to moral standards its hearers recognize (16:90; 7:28, "Allah does not command immorality"), which fits the Maturidi view better.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "The Christian faces the same dilemma: is it good because God commands it?" Answer: No. Christians reject both horns: good is grounded in God's nature, which is necessarily good, and his commands express that nature. Notice that the Ash'ari answer about truthfulness (lying is an imperfection God can't have) is itself an appeal to God's nature. That concedes the Christian solution for one attribute, and invites the question why it shouldn't apply to goodness and justice too.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "God's custom keeps nature regular."

  • Close (R1): A custom that God may break at will gives no ground for expecting regularity, only a hope that he won't break it.
  • Their comeback: "God promised order (e.g., 35:43, 'you will never find any change in the way of Allah')."
  • Close (R2): Good: then regularity rests on God's faithfulness to his word, which is the Christian answer (Gen 8:22). But on strict voluntarism, why is keeping a promise good?

2. "God is not questioned about what He does (21:23)."

  • Close (R1): Agreed that creatures can't put God on trial. The question is whether "God is just" means anything more than "God does what he does."
  • Their comeback: "It means God acts according to his own wisdom."
  • Close (R2): That's the Maturidi answer: God's actions follow his wise nature. I agree, and I think it leads to the Christian view of God's character.

Boomerang check

"Christian voluntarists (William of Ockham) said the same." True: Ockham held a strong divine-command view, and some Reformed thinkers lean voluntarist. Answer: The mainstream Christian tradition (Augustine, Aquinas, most Reformed theology) grounds goodness in God's nature. A Christian voluntarist faces the same problems; that's why this card targets a view, not a religion.

"God commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son." Christians read Gen 22 as a test that God himself stops, pointing to his own provision ("God will provide the lamb," 22:8), not as God commanding evil for its own sake.

Strength rating

Why: The problems for strict Ash'ari voluntarism and occasionalism are well known and discussed within Islamic thought itself. But Maturidis and Atharis have different, stronger answers, and many modern Ash'aris soften the view. Use it only after finding out which tradition your partner follows.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Ash'ari (dominant at al-Azhar; much of North Africa and Southeast Asia) Strong; they know these doctrines Use al-Ghazali's own words.
Maturidi (South Asia, Turkey, Central Asia) Already hold reason knows good Use it to agree that goodness is grounded in God's nature, then ask about love (2D-3).
Athari / Salafi Reject Ash'ari kalam Don't use this; they'll agree with your critique.
Twelver Shia Hold rational ethics (like the Mu'tazila) Not applicable.
Cultural Muslims Unfamiliar with kalam Use the simple question: "Is something good because God commands it?"

Trap questions

  1. "Is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it's good?"
  2. "Could God command cruelty and make it good?"
  3. "If fire doesn't really cause burning, why do scientists expect it to?"
  4. "Why is it impossible for God to lie, on your view?"

30-second version

"If good just means 'whatever God commands,' then 'God is good' means 'God does what he does.' Christians say goodness is God's nature, so his commands are good because he is good. That makes morality, science, and God's word all trustworthy."

2-minute version

"Here's an old question: is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it's good? Some Muslim theologians, the Ash'aris, said good just means what God commands, and God isn't bound by anything. Al-Ghazali even said fire doesn't cause burning; God creates the burning each time. I respect how seriously they take God's sovereignty. But if goodness is just God's will, then saying 'God is good' doesn't say much, and if nature has no real order, science has no foundation. The Christian answer is that goodness, order, and truth flow from God's own character. He commands justice because he is just. He upholds nature because he is faithful. He can't lie because he is truth. That's a God you can trust completely."

Further reading

  • Al-Ghazali, The Incoherence of the Philosophers, tr. Michael E. Marmura (BYU Press, 2000), 17th discussion
  • George F. Hourani, Reason and Tradition in Islamic Ethics (Cambridge, 1985)
  • Ulrich Rudolph, Al-Maturidi and the Development of Sunni Theology in Samarqand (Brill, 2015)
  • Robert M. Adams, Finite and Infinite Goods (Oxford, 1999): the Christian "nature" view
2D-3

Tawhid and Love

1 card1 moderate

New terms

Tawhid: The absolute oneness of God, the central doctrine of Islam.

Al-Wadud: 'The Loving': one of the names of God in the Qur'an (85:14; 11:90).

Sifat (dhatiyya / fi'liyya): God's attributes: attributes of essence (eternal: life, knowledge, power, etc.) vs. attributes of action (creating, providing).

Kalam nafsi: In Ash'ari theology, God's eternal 'inner speech,' distinct from the created sounds and letters of recitation.

Argument2D-3MODERATE

Tawhid and Love

philosophical; depends on how Muslims define God's eternal attributes

Name + thesis

Islam teaches that God is eternally loving (al-Wadud), hearing (al-Sami'), and speaking (al-Mutakallim), and that these are eternal attributes, not later additions. But love, hearing, and speech are relational: they need an object. Before creation, a God who is one person alone had no one to love, hear, or speak to. The Trinity answers the question: the Father, Son, and Spirit have loved and spoken within the one God from eternity.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 85:14: "He is the Forgiving, the Loving (al-Wadud)." 11:90: "my Lord is Merciful and Loving."
  • Qur'an 112:1–4: "Say: He is Allah, the One (Ahad)... He neither begets nor is born, and there is none comparable to Him."
  • John 17:24: "you loved me before the foundation of the world." 17:5: "the glory that I had with you before the world existed."
  • John 1:1: "the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
  • 1 John 4:8: "God is love."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. Attributes of essence vs. action (sifat dhatiyya vs. sifat fi'liyya). Ash'aris hold that God's essential attributes (life, knowledge, power, will, hearing, sight, speech) are eternal, while his actions (creating, providing) occur in time. God's hearing is eternal but relates to sounds only when they exist (ta'alluq). Love may be an eternal will to benefit that relates to creatures when they exist.
  2. Maturidis hold God's "bringing into being" (takwin) is eternal too: God is eternally Creator, even before creation exists.
  3. Atharis affirm God loves "in a way befitting His majesty" without asking how (bila kayf), and hold God has always been able to speak and love, exercising these when he wills (Ibn Taymiyya).
  4. Love doesn't need an eternal object: God's self-sufficiency (al-Ghani) means he doesn't need anyone, and his love for creation is a free gift, which is more gracious, not less.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Islam affirms that God is eternally loving, hearing, and speaking (essential attributes).
  • P2. Love, hearing, and speech are relational; in their full sense they require a subject and an object.
  • P3. If God is a single person, then before creation these attributes had no object other than God himself, so they were either (a) unexercised potentials, (b) self-directed, or (c) dependent on creation.
  • P4. (a) implies God changed when he created; (b) reduces love to self-love; (c) makes God dependent on creation. Each conflicts with God's perfection and self-sufficiency.
  • C. Only a God in whom there are eternal, real relations of love and communication (the Trinity) is both eternally loving and self-sufficient.

Evidence for each premise

  • The Islamic debate itself shows the problem is felt: the doctrine of eternal speech (kalam nafsi, the eternal "inner speech" of God, in Ash'ari theology) required elaborate explanations of how God's eternal speech could include commands like "O Moses" before Moses existed (VERIFY in al-Juwayni, al-Irshad).
  • Ash'ari reinterpretation of love: many Ash'aris interpret God's love as his will to bestow favor and reward (iradat al-in'am, iradat al-thawab), not a real affective attribute, as both they and their Athari critics report. That suggests eternal love proper was hard to fit.
  • The Christian answer is stated in John 17:24, before creation, and is central to the doctrine of the Trinity (Augustine, On the Trinity, books 8–9: the lover, the beloved, and the love).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "Love as a disposition or will needs no eternal object." Answer: Then God's love before creation is love for no one, a disposition never exercised. That means God was not actually loving until creation, and the "Loving" is a title earned by creating. The Christian claim is stronger: God is love (1 John 4:8), not just disposed to it.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "God loved himself."

  • Close (R1): Is self-love the highest form of love? The Qur'an praises love that gives to others (e.g., 76:8).
  • Their comeback: "God's self-love is perfect, not selfish."
  • Close (R2): In the Trinity, God's love is perfect and other-directed: the Father loves the Son, without any creature. That's the best of both.

2. "God's love was eternal in his knowledge of future creatures."

  • Close (R1): Loving the idea of a future person isn't loving a person. And that makes the eternal object of God's love something other than God.
  • Their comeback: "God's knowledge is eternal; so is his love for what he knows."
  • Close (R2): Then from eternity God's love depended on creatures, at least as known. In the Trinity, it depends on no one but God.

Boomerang check

"If God needs three persons to be loving, then God is dependent on the persons." Answer: The persons aren't parts God depends on; each is fully God, and the one God is this eternal communion. God depends on nothing outside himself, which is the Islamic intuition too.

"Muslim: the Trinity is 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 gods." See 2J.

Strength rating

Why: The question is real and was felt within Islamic theology (eternal speech, the meaning of love). But sophisticated Muslim responses exist (the essence/action distinction, ta'alluq, bila kayf), so the argument persuades rather than proves.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Athari / Salafi Affirm real love and speech Ask whom God spoke to before creation.
Ash'ari Have developed answers Engage ta'alluq and the essence/action distinction.
Maturidi Hold eternal takwin Ask: eternally creating what?
Cultural Muslims Moved by the question Keep it simple and devotional.

Trap questions

  1. "Before God created anything, was he loving? Whom did he love?"
  2. "Was God al-Wadud before creation, or did he become loving?"
  3. "If God's speech is eternal, whom was he speaking to?"

30-second version

"Was God loving before he created anything? If God is one person alone, there was no one to love. Christians believe the Father, Son, and Spirit have loved each other forever. God didn't need us in order to love. He created to share it."

2-minute version

"One of the names of God in the Qur'an is al-Wadud, the Loving. I love that. But I've wondered: was God loving before he made anything? Love always has someone it loves. If God is a single person, then before creation there was no one, so either God wasn't yet loving, or he needed creation to be who he is. Neither seems right for a perfect God.

The Christian answer is beautiful. Jesus prayed, 'Father, you loved me before the foundation of the world.' Within the one God, the Father, the Son, and the Spirit have always known and loved each other. So God has always been love, and he didn't need us. He created and redeemed us to share a love that was already perfect. That's the love he offers you."

Further reading

  • Michael Reeves, Delighting in the Trinity (IVP, 2012)
  • Nabeel Qureshi, No God but One (2016), part 2
  • Al-Juwayni, A Guide to Conclusive Proofs for the Principles of Belief (al-Irshad), tr. Paul Walker (Garnet, 2000)
  • Jon Hoover, Ibn Taymiyya's Theodicy of Perpetual Optimism (Brill, 2007): on Ibn Taymiyya's view of God's eternal activity
2D-4

The Uncreated Qur'an and the Logos

1 card1 moderate

New terms

Mihna: The 'inquisition' (833–c. 848) in which Abbasid caliphs enforced the doctrine that the Qur'an is created; Ahmad ibn Hanbal resisted.

Mu'tazila: A rationalist school of Islamic theology that held the Qur'an is created and that good and evil are known by reason.

Logos: Greek 'Word': John's title for the eternal Son (John 1:1).

Kalima: 'Word': the Qur'an calls Jesus 'a word from Him' (3:45) and 'His word' (4:171).

Argument2D-4MODERATE

The Uncreated Qur'an vs. "The Logos Is Shirk"

Name + thesis

Sunni Islam holds that the Qur'an is God's eternal, uncreated speech, existing with God before creation, and, in Ash'ari terms, "neither God nor other than God." Christians hold that the Word (Logos) was eternally with God and is God (John 1:1). If an eternal Word alongside God isn't shirk in Islam, why is it shirk in Christianity? The Qur'an itself calls Jesus "a word from Him."

Key texts

  • John 1:1, 14: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us."
  • Qur'an 3:45: "O Mary, Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him (bi-kalimatin minhu), whose name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary."
  • Qur'an 4:171: "The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, was only a messenger of Allah and His word (kalimatuhu), which He directed to Mary, and a spirit from Him (ruhun minhu)."
  • Qur'an 85:21–22: "it is a glorious Qur'an, in a preserved tablet (lawh mahfuz)."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. The Qur'an is an attribute, not a person. God's speech is an attribute like knowledge. Nobody worships it, prays to it, or says it became flesh.
  2. "His word" for Jesus means Jesus was created by God's word "Be!" (3:59: "the example of Jesus is like Adam: He created him from dust, then said to him 'Be,' and he was"). Jesus is the product of the word, not the word itself.
  3. The mihna proves the opposite of your point: Ahmad ibn Hanbal suffered precisely to defend God's attributes against those who denied them, while still rejecting any partner with God.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Sunni orthodoxy (Athari and Ash'ari) holds that the Qur'an, God's speech, is eternal and uncreated, and Ash'aris say God's attributes are "neither God nor other than God" (la huwa wa la ghayruhu).
  • P2. So Sunni Islam already affirms an eternal, uncreated reality that is in some sense distinct from God's essence, yet not a second god.
  • P3. Christians affirm the eternal Word, distinct from the Father as a person, yet one God with him, not a second god (John 1:1).
  • C. The principle "an eternal Word alongside God is shirk" condemns Sunni orthodoxy along with Christianity. The real question is not whether God has an eternal Word, but whether that Word is personal and became flesh in Jesus, which the Qur'an itself hints at by calling Jesus "His word."

Evidence for each premise

  • The mihna (833–c. 848/851): the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun imposed the Mu'tazili doctrine that the Qur'an was created; Ahmad ibn Hanbal refused and was flogged. The Mu'tazila argued that an uncreated Qur'an would be a second eternal beside God, compromising tawhid, essentially the objection Muslims bring against the Logos (W. Montgomery Watt, The Formative Period of Islamic Thought, 1973).
  • John of Damascus (d. c. 749), in his Disputation between a Saracen and a Christian (attribution debated: Sidney Griffith doubts John wrote it and suggests Theodore Abu Qurrah's circle), presses exactly this: is God's Word created or uncreated? If uncreated, the Muslim must accept an eternal Word with God.
  • The Ash'ari formula la huwa wa la ghayruhu tries to hold unity and distinction together, which is what the doctrine of the Trinity also does, with different terms.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "The Qur'an is not a person and isn't worshipped." Answer: Granted: the analogy isn't identity. Its point is narrow: Islam already accepts an eternal, uncreated Word that is distinct from God's essence without being a second god. So "eternal Word = shirk" isn't a principle Sunnis can use. The disagreement is whether God's eternal Word is personal and incarnate, and that's a question about Jesus (the Gospels, the resurrection), not about logic.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Jesus is 'a word' because God said 'Be' (3:59)."

  • Close (R1): Every creature came by God's "Be." Why is only Jesus called "His word" and "a spirit from Him"?
  • Their comeback: "Because of his miraculous birth."
  • Close (R2): Adam had a more miraculous origin (no father or mother) and isn't called "His word." The title points beyond the manner of birth.

2. "Attributes aren't persons."

  • Close (R1): Agreed: Christians don't say the Son is an attribute. But the attribute analogy shows that eternal distinction in God isn't automatically shirk.
  • Their comeback: "Three persons is still three gods."
  • Close (R2): Only if "person" means a separate being. See 2J on "1+1+1=3."

Boomerang check

"Then you admit the Trinity is like Ash'ari attribute theory, which is just philosophy." Answer: The Trinity is revealed in Scripture (Matt 28:19; John 1:1; 2 Cor 13:14), not derived from philosophy. The comparison only shows that both traditions faced the same question: how can God's Word be eternal without being a second god?

Strength rating

Why: The parallel is real and was recognized early (the Mu'tazila; John of Damascus). But the disanalogies (person vs. attribute; worship; incarnation) are real too. Use it to remove the charge that the Logos doctrine is automatically shirk, then move to the evidence about Jesus.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Athari / Salafi Strongly hold the uncreated Qur'an (Ahmad ibn Hanbal) Very effective; ask about kalimatuhu (4:171).
Ash'ari Know la huwa wa la ghayruhu Engage the formula.
Twelver Shia Many hold the Qur'an is created (Mu'tazili influence) Not applicable.
Quranists Varied Focus on 3:45 and 4:171.

Trap questions

  1. "Is the Qur'an created or uncreated? Has it always existed with God?"
  2. "Is the Qur'an God, or other than God?"
  3. "Why does the Qur'an call Jesus, and only Jesus, 'His word' and 'a spirit from Him'?"

30-second version

"You believe the Qur'an is God's eternal, uncreated Word, with God before creation, yet not a second god. Christians believe the eternal Word was with God and is God, and became flesh in Jesus. And the Qur'an calls Jesus 'His word.'"

2-minute version

"Can I ask about something Ahmad ibn Hanbal suffered for? He insisted the Qur'an is God's uncreated speech: eternal, with God before anything was made. Some Muslims at the time said that made the Qur'an a second eternal being beside God. But Sunni Islam said no: God's Word is eternal without being a second god.

That's very close to what John's Gospel says: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.' The difference is that the Gospel says this Word is personal and 'became flesh' in Jesus. And the Qur'an itself calls Jesus 'His word' and 'a spirit from Him.' I'd love to look at those verses with you and ask what they might mean."

Further reading

  • W. Montgomery Watt, The Formative Period of Islamic Thought (Edinburgh, 1973)
  • Nimrod Hurvitz, The Formation of Hanbalism: Piety into Power (Routledge, 2002)
  • Daniel J. Sahas, John of Damascus on Islam (Brill, 1972)
  • Harry A. Wolfson, The Philosophy of the Kalam (Harvard, 1976), on the Trinity and the attributes
2E

Jesus vs. Muhammad in the Qur'an

1 card1 strong

New terms

'Isma: The doctrine that prophets are protected from sin (or from major sin).

Dhanb: Sin, fault; used in the Qur'an of Muhammad (40:55; 47:19; 48:2).

Istighfar: Asking God's forgiveness.

Argument2ESTRONG

Jesus vs. Muhammad in the Qur'an

the texts are clear; what they imply about rank is debated

Name + thesis

Read on its own terms, the Qur'an gives Jesus titles and qualities it gives no one else, including Muhammad: born of a virgin, "a word from God," "a spirit from Him," pure and sinless, a worker of creative miracles, raised to God, and a sign of the Hour. Muhammad, by contrast, is told to ask forgiveness for his sins and says he doesn't know what will be done with him. Why would the final prophet be presented as lesser than the one before him?

Key texts

  • Qur'an 3:45: "a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, distinguished (wajih) in this world and the Hereafter, and among those brought near (al-muqarrabin)."
  • Qur'an 19:19: "I am only the messenger of your Lord to give you a pure boy (ghulaman zakiyya)."
  • Qur'an 40:55: "So be patient; indeed the promise of Allah is truth. And ask forgiveness for your sin (wa-staghfir li-dhanbika)." 47:19: "ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and women." 48:2: "that Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin and what will follow."
  • Qur'an 46:9: "Say: I am not something new among the messengers, nor do I know what will be done with me or with you."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. Every prophet has his distinctions (2:253: "Those messengers, We favored some above others"). Jesus' virgin birth doesn't make him greater any more than Adam's birth without parents makes Adam greater (3:59).
  2. Dhanb for prophets means minor lapses or "what would be a fault in someone of your rank," not sin. The doctrine of 'isma (prophetic protection from sin) governs these verses. Some commentators read 47:19 and 48:2 as addressed to the community through the Prophet.
  3. Muhammad has unique honors: the Seal of the Prophets (33:40), a mercy to the worlds (21:107), intercession on Judgment Day, and the Qur'an, the greatest miracle.
  4. 46:9 is early (Meccan); later verses (48:2) show assurance.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The Qur'an attributes to Jesus a unique set of titles and qualities (word from God, spirit from Him, pure, virgin-born, creating life, raised to God, sign of the Hour).
  • P2. The Qur'an never attributes these to Muhammad, and repeatedly tells Muhammad to seek forgiveness for his dhanb (sin).
  • P3. Hadith add that Satan touches every newborn except Mary and her son (Sahih al-Bukhari 3431 (in-book 60/102), narrated by Abu Hurayra).
  • C. On the Qur'an's own portrait, Jesus stands apart from all prophets, including Muhammad, which fits the Christian claim about Jesus far better than the Islamic claim that Muhammad is the greatest prophet.

Evidence for each premise

Quality Jesus Muhammad
Birth Virgin birth (3:47; 19:20) Ordinary birth
Title "A word from Him" (3:45); "His word and a spirit from Him" (4:171) "Messenger of Allah and Seal of the Prophets" (33:40)
Purity "A pure boy" (19:19); untouched by Satan at birth (Bukhari 3431) Told to "ask forgiveness for your sin" (40:55; 47:19; 48:2)
Miracles Creates birds from clay, heals the blind and leper, raises the dead "by Allah's permission" (3:49; 5:110) Signs refused in the Qur'an (17:59; 17:90–93; 29:50); the Qur'an itself as the sign (29:51)
Knowledge Knows "what you eat and store in your houses" (3:49) "I do not know what will be done with me or with you" (46:9)
End Raised to God (3:55; 4:158) Died and was buried in Medina
Future "A sign ('ilm) of the Hour" (43:61, majority reading) —
Return Will "descend amongst you... as a just ruler" (Bukhari 2222), "as a just judge" (Muslim 155), and "judge mankind justly" (Bukhari 3448) Does not return
Title "Messiah" Al-Masih (3:45; 4:171; 11 times) Never

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: 'isma and the meaning of dhanb. Answer: The Qur'an uses dhanb for real sins elsewhere (e.g., 3:135; 12:29, Joseph telling Potiphar's wife to "ask forgiveness for your sin"). 'Isma is a later theological doctrine read back into the verses; the verses themselves draw no distinction. And even granting "minor lapses," the Qur'an never says Jesus needed forgiveness at all.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Adam was born without a father or mother, so the virgin birth doesn't make Jesus greater" (3:59).

  • Close (R1): True. But Adam isn't called "a word from God," "a spirit from Him," the Messiah, or a sign of the Hour, and Adam sinned (20:121).
  • Their comeback: "These are honors, not divinity."
  • Close (R2): Agreed: the Qur'an's honors don't prove divinity. They raise the question why this prophet is so unique. The Gospels answer it.

2. "Muhammad is the Seal of the Prophets, so he is the greatest."

  • Close (R1): "Seal" means last, not greatest. And the Qur'an's portrait of the last prophet includes repeated calls to seek forgiveness.
  • Their comeback: "Hadith call him the master of the children of Adam."
  • Close (R2): That's hadith, not the Qur'an. On the Qur'an's own terms, who is more exalted?

3. "Jesus comes back as a Muslim, to break the cross" (Bukhari 2222).

  • Close (R1): Look at the role the hadith gives him: he descends to judge mankind justly (Bukhari 3448; Muslim 155). Muhammad doesn't come back at all. In Scripture the Judge of all the earth is God (Gen 18:25; Ps 96:13), and Jesus claims that role: "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father" (John 5:22–23; Matt 25:31–32).
  • Their comeback: "A judge here means a just ruler who applies the Shari'a, not God."
  • Close (R2): Then ask why, of all prophets, Islam's end of history centers on Jesus. And "breaking the cross" assumes the cross never happened, which history says it did (2B-14).

Boomerang check

"The Bible says Jesus 'learned obedience' (Heb 5:8), was baptized for repentance (Matt 3), and called himself not good ('Why do you call me good?', Mark 10:18)." Answer: Hebrews says the same Jesus was "without sin" (Heb 4:15). Jesus' baptism was to "fulfill all righteousness" (Matt 3:15), identifying with sinners. Mark 10:18 is a question that invites the man to see who Jesus is ("No one is good except God alone"), not a confession of sin. The Bible consistently presents Jesus as sinless (2 Cor 5:21; 1 Pet 2:22; John 8:46). The Qur'an presents Muhammad as needing forgiveness.

Strength rating

Why: The Qur'anic texts are clear and widely acknowledged. The Muslim answers ('isma; different honors for different prophets) concern what the portrait implies, so present the conclusion as a question.

Educated Sunni Will cite 'isma Show 12:29 and 3:135 for dhanb.

Trap questions

  1. "Who does the Qur'an call 'a word from Him' and 'a spirit from Him'?"
  2. "Is Jesus ever told in the Qur'an to ask forgiveness for his sins? Is Muhammad?"
  3. "Why would the Qur'an call Jesus, and not Muhammad, the Messiah?"
  4. "Who in the Qur'an gives life to the dead?"
  5. "In the hadith, who comes back at the end of the world to judge mankind: Jesus or Muhammad?" (Bukhari 3448)

30-second version

"In the Qur'an, Jesus is born of a virgin, called God's word and a spirit from him, is pure, raises the dead, and is raised to God. Muhammad is told to ask forgiveness for his sins. On the Qur'an's own terms, who is greater?"

2-minute version

"I've made a little comparison from the Qur'an alone, and I'd love your thoughts. Jesus is born of a virgin. He's called 'a word from God' and 'a spirit from Him.' He's called the Messiah, and 'a pure boy.' He creates birds from clay, heals the blind, raises the dead. He's raised up to God, and he's a sign of the Last Hour. Muhammad, whom I respect as an important figure in history, is told several times to ask forgiveness for his sin, and says, 'I don't know what will be done with me.'

I'm not trying to insult Muhammad. I'm asking: why does the Qur'an portray Jesus as so unique? The Gospel's answer is that Jesus is the eternal Word who became flesh to save us. Would you read one of the Gospels with me to see who he claimed to be?"

2F

Preservation: One Standard

1 card1 strong

New terms

Mushaf: A written copy of the Qur'an (a codex).

Uthmanic rasm: The consonantal skeleton of the Qur'an standardized under the caliph Uthman (c. 650).

Ahruf (seven): The 'seven modes' in which, according to hadith, the Qur'an was revealed; their exact meaning is debated among Muslim scholars.

Palimpsest: A manuscript whose original text was scraped off and written over; the lower text can often be recovered.

Qurra': Qur'an reciters; also the transmitters of the canonical readings.

This section is about fairness, not about proving the Qur'an "corrupt." Both the Qur'an and the New Testament are well preserved by the standards of ancient texts. What Islamic sources show is that the popular claim, "the Qur'an has been preserved letter for letter with no variants, unlike the Bible," is false. A Muslim who rejects the Bible for variants and lost passages must apply the same standard to the Qur'an.

Argument2FSTRONG

One Standard for Preservation

against the "perfect, letter-for-letter preservation" claim; not evidence that the Qur'an's text is unreliable overall

Name + thesis

Sunni hadith collections themselves report that verses were lost or forgotten, that companions' codices differed, and that Uthman standardized one text and burned the others. Canonical readings still differ in wording. Early manuscripts (the Sana'a palimpsest) show a non-Uthmanic text. The Qur'an's transmission is strong, but it is not the flawless, variant-free exception it is often claimed to be, and it must be judged by the same standards as the Bible.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 15:9: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian."
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 4987, narrated by Anas ibn Malik: Uthman had Hafsa's sheets copied, sent a copy to each province, "and ordered that all other Qur'anic material, whether written in fragmentary manuscripts or whole copies, be burnt."
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 4988 (in-book 66/10), narrated by Zayd ibn Thabit: "I missed one verse of Surat al-Ahzab when we copied the Qur'an... we searched for it and found it with Khuzayma ibn Thabit."
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 6829 (in-book 86/55), Umar on the stoning verse: Umar: "I am afraid that after a long time has passed, people may say, 'We do not find the verses of stoning in the Book of Allah.'"
  • Sahih Muslim 1452a (in-book 17/30), narrated by Aisha: Aisha: "ten known sucklings" was abrogated by "five," and "the Messenger of Allah died while it was among what was recited of the Qur'an."
  • Sahih Muslim 1050 (in-book 12/156), Abu Musa al-Ash'ari to the reciters of Basra: Abu Musa: "We used to recite a surah which resembled Bara'a in length and severity, which I have forgotten, except that I remember from it: 'If the son of Adam had two valleys of wealth...'". He also mentions a second forgotten surah that resembled one of the Musabbihat (surahs that open by glorifying God).

Their best case (steelman)

  1. Abrogation (naskh) explains the missing verses. God himself removed the recitation of some verses (2:106; 87:7). Nothing was lost against his will.
  2. The seven ahruf. Muhammad said the Qur'an was revealed in "seven modes" (Sahih al-Bukhari 4992 (in-book 66/14), narrated by Umar); variant readings are divinely sanctioned, not corruption.
  3. Uthman preserved, not altered. He standardized the text on the Quraysh dialect to stop disputes; the content was agreed by the Companions.
  4. Oral transmission by thousands (tawatur) guarantees the text independently of manuscripts.
  5. The Birmingham folios (parchment radiocarbon-dated 568–645 (95.4% probability; University of Oxford, 2015)) match the Uthmanic text, showing it existed within decades of Muhammad.
  6. Shia "tahrif" reports are rejected by mainstream Shia scholars.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The claim that the Qur'an was preserved letter for letter without variants, unlike the Bible, is widely made in dawah.
  • P2. Islamic sources (sahih hadith; classical works on the readings; early manuscripts) report verses lost or removed from recitation, differing Companion codices, an official standardization with burning of alternatives, and continuing variant readings.
  • P3. Christians openly acknowledge NT variants, which are visible because no one burned the alternatives.
  • C. Both texts are substantially preserved; neither is variant-free. A Muslim who rejects the Bible because of variants must, on the same standard, reject the Qur'an. On a fair standard, he should accept both as substantially preserved, which returns him to 2A.

Evidence for each premise

1. Lost or removed verses (Sunni sources): the stoning verse (Bukhari 6829; Muslim 1691); the sucklings (Muslim 1452); the forgotten surah like Bara'a (Muslim 1050). Ibn Majah 1944 reports that the sheet with the stoning and adult-suckling verses was eaten by a domestic animal after Muhammad's death (graded hasan in the Darussalam edition on sunnah.com, though other scholars dispute it). Al-Qurtubi (on 33:1) dismisses the domestic-animal story as an invention of heretics, so expect a Muslim to reject it; lead with the sahih reports instead.

2. Companion codices: Ibn Mas'ud, whom Muhammad named among the four from whom to learn the Qur'an (Bukhari 4999), reportedly didn't include surahs 113–114 in his codex (Bukhari 4977, where Ubayy is asked about Ibn Mas'ud's view; Musnad Ahmad 21189, with a chain graded sahih by Darussalam, says Ibn Mas'ud "scrapes them out of the mushaf"; the narrator Sufyan explains that Ibn Mas'ud took them for protective prayers because he never heard them recited in prayer). His codex is reported to have had different readings (e.g., 5:89, "three days consecutively").

3. Surah al-Ahzab: Ubayy ibn Ka'b swore that al-Ahzab "was equal to Surat al-Baqara, or longer" (it now has 73 verses). That report is in Musnad Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Hibban, and its chain is graded sahih in the Dorar hadith encyclopedia. Aisha is reported to have said it was recited as 200 verses in the Prophet's time, but that chain runs through Ibn Lahi'a, whom hadith critics often weaken, and the modern editor of al-Suyuti calls it unsound. Al-Qurtubi gives both reports (on 33:1) and explains that God "raised" the rest, i.e., abrogation; al-Suyuti gives both in his section on abrogation (Mu'tarak al-Aqran, vol. 1, p. 95).

4. Canonical readings differ in wording, not only pronunciation. Hafs (most common today) vs. Warsh (North and West Africa): | Verse | Hafs | Warsh | Effect | |---|---|---|---| | 2:132 | wa-wassa ("and he enjoined") | wa-awsa (same root, different form) | minor | | 3:146 | qātala ("fought") | qutila ("was killed") | changes meaning | | 2:184 | fidyatun ta'amu miskinin ("one poor person") | fidyatu ta'ami masakina ("poor persons") | changes meaning | (Checked: al-Qurtubi on 2:132 and 2:184 gives the Medinan reading, which Warsh transmits from Nafi', against the other readers; al-Tabari on 3:146 lists qutila for readers of Hijaz and Basra and qātala for readers of Hijaz and Kufa, and he prefers qutila. For depth: Shady Nasser, The Transmission of the Variant Readings of the Qur'an, Brill, 2013.)

5. The Sana'a palimpsest: the lower (erased) text, parchment radiocarbon-dated c. 578–669 (95%; Sadeghi & Bergmann, 2010), is a non-Uthmanic Qur'an with variants in words and phrases, and some differences in surah order (Behnam Sadeghi and Mohsen Goudarzi, "Ṣan'ā' 1 and the Origins of the Qur'ān," Der Islam 87, 2012). It confirms the Qur'an existed early, and that it circulated in more than one textual form before standardization.

6. Shia tahrif reports: al-Kulayni's al-Kafi (10th c.) has a report, through Hisham ibn Salim from Ja'far al-Sadiq, that "the Qur'an that Gabriel brought to Muhammad was 17,000 verses" (today's Qur'an has about 6,236), which the modern Shia hadith scholar Asif Mohseni grades reliable (mu'tabar), and Mirza Husayn Nuri al-Tabarsi wrote Fasl al-Khitab fi Tahrif Kitab Rabb al-Arbab (1875) arguing the Qur'an was altered. Be fair: mainstream Shia scholars (al-Saduq, al-Sharif al-Murtada, al-Tusi, and in modern times Abu al-Qasim al-Khoei, al-Bayan) reject tahrif of the Qur'an.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "All the missing verses were abrogated by God (naskh al-tilawa)." Answer: (1) That's an explanation, not a denial: the Qur'an as recited today is not everything that was revealed as Qur'an. (2) Muslim 1452 says the sucklings verse was still recited when Muhammad died; revelation ended at his death, so its removal from recitation occurred after revelation ended. (3) Uthman's burning of other codices removed evidence that would let us check. The NT's variants survive because no one did that. Don't overclaim: the Qur'an's text is remarkably stable from the Uthmanic recension onward.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "The seven ahruf were revealed; the variants are from God."

  • Close (R1): Then the Qur'an was revealed in multiple wordings. Which one is on the preserved tablet (85:22)?
  • Their comeback: "All of them."
  • Close (R2): Then when Uthman burned the others, he destroyed revealed ahruf. And the canonical qira'at (fixed by Ibn Mujahid in the 10th century) aren't the same as the seven ahruf; scholars disagree about what the ahruf were.

2. "Oral transmission guarantees the text."

  • Close (R1): Oral transmission is valuable. But the sahih reports above are oral transmission, reporting verses lost and forgotten.
  • Their comeback: "Those were abrogated."
  • Close (R2): Then the claim isn't "nothing was lost," but "everything lost was meant to be lost." That's a theological claim, and Christians can make the same one about the Bible's variants. One standard.

3. "The Birmingham manuscript proves perfect preservation."

  • Close (R1): It proves the Uthmanic text existed early. It doesn't tell us what the burned codices contained.
  • Their comeback: "It matches today's Qur'an."
  • Close (R2): And Codex Sinaiticus matches today's New Testament on the crucifixion, centuries before Muhammad. If early agreement proves preservation, it proves it for both.

Boomerang check

"The Bible's textual problems are far worse: Mark 16:9–20, John 7:53–8:11, 1 John 5:7." Answer: Agree that these are real variants, then compare honestly (table below). The NT has more variants because it has more manuscripts and no one destroyed the alternatives. Christians print the doubtful passages in brackets. The question for both books isn't "variants or none" but "can the original be reconstructed, and does any core teaching depend on doubtful readings?" For the NT, the answers are yes and no.

Strength rating

Why: The evidence comes from Sunni sahih collections, classical Islamic scholarship, and peer-reviewed manuscript research. It decisively refutes the perfect-preservation claim. It does not show the Qur'an is badly preserved, so don't claim that.

Trap questions

  1. "Why did Uthman burn the other copies of the Qur'an?"
  2. "In Muslim 1452, Aisha says a verse was still recited when the Prophet died. Where is it now?"
  3. "Do Hafs and Warsh have the same wording in 3:146?"
  4. "If variants don't make the Qur'an unreliable, why do they make the Bible unreliable?"

30-second version

"Your own hadith say verses were lost, codices differed, and Uthman burned the alternatives. Hafs and Warsh still differ in wording. I don't think that means the Qur'an is unreliable. I think both books are well preserved. But then the Bible can't be rejected for having variants either."

2-minute version

"Muslims often tell me the Qur'an was preserved perfectly, letter for letter, unlike the Bible. I've been reading your sources, and they tell a more complicated story. Sahih al-Bukhari says Uthman made an official copy and ordered the others burned. Umar said the verse on stoning was revealed but people wouldn't find it in the Book. Aisha said in Sahih Muslim that a verse was still being recited when the Prophet died, and it's not in the Qur'an today. And the readings of Hafs and Warsh still differ in some words.

I'm not saying this to attack the Qur'an. I think it's remarkably well preserved. My point is that we should use one standard. The New Testament has variants too, which we know about because no one burned the other copies. If the Qur'an can be substantially preserved with variants, so can the Bible. And then we're back to what the Bible actually says about Jesus."

Bible vs. Qur'an: an honest comparison of textual transmission

Question New Testament Qur'an
Time from composition to earliest substantial manuscripts Fragments within ~100–150 years; complete NT ~250–300 years Fragments within decades (Birmingham, Sana'a); complete codices within ~1–2 centuries
Central control of the text? None; copied freely across regions and churches Yes: Uthman's official recension, other codices burned

2G

Was Muhammad a Prophet?

5 cards4 moderate1 weak

New terms

Aya (pl. ayat): 'Sign' or 'miracle,' and also a verse of the Qur'an.

Satanic Verses (gharaniq incident): The early report that Muhammad briefly recited verses praising three Meccan goddesses, later retracted as from Satan.

Al-watin: The aorta or main artery (69:46).

I'jaz: The inimitability of the Qur'an, held by Muslims to be its central miracle.

Sarfa: 'Turning away': the view of some Muslim theologians (e.g., al-Nazzam) that the Arabs could have imitated the Qur'an but God prevented them.

Argument2GMODERATE

Refused Signs vs. Later Miracle Reports

Name + thesis

When Muhammad's opponents demanded miracles, the Qur'an repeatedly declined: Muhammad is "only a warner," and the Qur'an itself is the sign. Yet hadith collected two centuries later attribute hundreds of miracles to him. The Qur'an's own picture of a prophet without miracles fits poorly with the later miracle tradition, and it contrasts sharply with Jesus.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 17:59: "Nothing has prevented Us from sending signs (ayat) except that the former peoples denied them."
  • Qur'an 17:90–93: the opponents demand a spring, a garden, a house of gold, an ascent to heaven; the answer: "Say, 'Exalted is my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?'"
  • Qur'an 29:50–51: "They say, 'Why are no signs sent down to him from his Lord?' Say, 'The signs are only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner.' Is it not sufficient for them that We sent down to you the Book?"
  • Qur'an 6:37: "They say, 'Why has no sign been sent down to him?' Say, 'Allah is able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know.'"
  • Qur'an 54:1: "The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split (inshaqqa l-qamar)."
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 3636 (in-book 61/140), narrated by Ibn Mas'ud: "The moon was split into two parts during the lifetime of the Prophet, and he said, 'Bear witness.'"

Their best case (steelman)

  1. The refused signs were specific, demanded signs given as conditions for belief. God refuses to perform on demand, but Muhammad performed other miracles.
  2. 54:1 records a real miracle, with mass-transmitted (mutawatir) reports.
  3. The Qur'an is the greatest miracle (its inimitability, see the literary challenge card).
  4. Jesus also refused signs to those who demanded them (Mark 8:11–12; Matt 12:39).

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The Qur'an repeatedly answers demands for signs by pointing to the Qur'an itself and to Muhammad's role as a warner (6:37; 13:7; 17:59; 17:90–93; 29:50–51).
  • P2. It never narrates a miracle performed by Muhammad (54:1 is disputed: many commentators read it as past, some as a sign of the Hour).
  • P3. The extensive miracle tradition appears in hadith and biography written down one to two centuries later.
  • C. The earliest source, the Qur'an, presents a prophet without miracles; the miracle stories are later. By contrast, Jesus' miracles are reported in the earliest sources and even acknowledged by his opponents (Mark 3:22; b. Sanhedrin 43a, "practiced sorcery").

Evidence for each premise

  • 13:7: "the disbelievers say, 'Why has a sign not been sent down to him?' You are only a warner."
  • 54:1: the context (54:1–2, "if they see a sign, they turn away and say, 'passing magic'") supports a past event for many commentators; others note the verse begins "the Hour has drawn near," and no astronomical record anywhere (India, China, Rome) reports the moon split. Treat the dispute honestly.
  • Jesus' opponents attributed his miracles to Beelzebul (Mark 3:22) or sorcery (b. Sanhedrin 43a), conceding that unusual works occurred.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "Jesus also refused to give signs on demand." Answer: True (Mark 8:12). But he did perform many works, reported in the earliest sources, and he pointed to them (Matt 11:4–5; John 10:37–38). The Qur'an points away from Muhammad's works to the book. The contrast isn't "signs on demand" but "works recorded in the earliest source."

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "The moon-splitting is mutawatir."

  • Close (R1): It's reported by several Companions. But the event would have been visible to half the world. Why does no other culture record it?
  • Their comeback: "It was night only in some places, and brief; others weren't watching."
  • Close (R2): Possible. Then rest the case on the Qur'an's own repeated statements that Muhammad is "only a warner," which are clear.

Boomerang check

"Your miracle reports are also from believers." Answer: Yes, but much earlier (Mark within ~40 years; Paul's references within ~20, e.g., 2 Cor 12:12 on the apostles' own signs), and acknowledged by opponents. Apply the same criteria (earliness, multiple attestation, hostile acknowledgment) to both.

Strength rating

Why: The Qur'anic pattern is clear, but the Muslim distinction between "demanded signs" and other miracles is reasonable, and 54:1's reading is disputed.

Sunni Hold to the hadith miracles Ask about 29:50–51.

  1. "When people asked Muhammad for a sign, what did the Qur'an tell him to say?"
  2. "Does the Qur'an ever describe Muhammad healing someone or raising the dead?"
  3. "Who in the Qur'an raises the dead and heals the blind?"

30-second version

"When people asked Muhammad for a miracle, the Qur'an said he was 'only a warner' and the book was enough. The miracle stories come from hadith centuries later. Jesus' miracles are in the earliest sources."

2-minute version

"I've noticed something in the Qur'an. When people demanded a sign from Muhammad, the answer was, 'I am only a human messenger,' and, 'Isn't the Book enough?' The Qur'an tells of Jesus healing the blind and raising the dead, but it never describes Muhammad doing anything like that. The stories of Muhammad's miracles come from collections written much later. I'm not saying that to belittle him. I'm saying the Qur'an itself seems to present him as a warner, not a miracle-worker, while it presents Jesus as one who gives life. Why do you think that is?"

Further reading
