  • Craig Keener, Miracles: The Credibility of the New Testament Accounts (Baker, 2011)
Argument2GMODERATE

The Satanic Verses

the chains are disputed; early acceptance was wide

Name + thesis

Early Islamic sources report that Muhammad once recited verses praising the pagan goddesses al-Lat, al-'Uzza, and Manat as intercessors, then retracted them as inserted by Satan. 22:52 says Satan interferes in every prophet's recitation. If the incident occurred, Muhammad couldn't reliably tell revelation from Satan's suggestion, even briefly.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 53:19–23: "Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other? ... They are nothing but names you have named."
  • The reported verses (al-Tabari, Tarikh and Tafsir on 22:52; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat): "These are the exalted cranes (al-gharaniq al-'ula), whose intercession is hoped for."
  • Qur'an 22:52: "We did not send before you any messenger or prophet except that when he recited [or: desired], Satan threw into his recitation (umniyyatihi); but Allah abolishes what Satan throws in; then Allah makes precise His verses."
  • Qur'an 17:73–74: "they were about to tempt you away from what We revealed to you, so that you would invent about Us something else... if We had not strengthened you, you would almost have inclined to them a little."
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 4862 (in-book 65/383), narrated by Ibn Abbas: when Muhammad recited Surat al-Najm (53) and prostrated, "the Muslims, the pagans, the jinn, and the humans prostrated with him."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. The chains are weak. All the reports are mursal (missing the Companion link) or weak; none is in Bukhari or Muslim. Al-Albani wrote a treatise rejecting them (Nasb al-Majaniq).
  2. It contradicts 'isma (prophetic protection) and 53:3–4: "Nor does he speak from desire. It is only a revelation revealed."
  3. Bukhari 4862 has no satanic verses: the pagans prostrated because of the surah's power.
  4. Umniyya in 22:52 can mean "desire," not "recitation."

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The incident is reported in several of the earliest Islamic biographical and exegetical sources (Ibn Ishaq via al-Tabari; al-Waqidi via Ibn Sa'd; Musa ibn 'Uqba; all surveyed in Shahab Ahmed, Before Orthodoxy: The Satanic Verses in Early Islam, Harvard, 2017).
  • P2. Shahab Ahmed showed that the story was widely accepted by early Muslim scholars and only later rejected on theological grounds (Before Orthodoxy: The Satanic Verses in Early Islam, Harvard, 2017).
  • P3. Ibn Hajar (d. 1449), a leading hadith critic, judged that the multiple mursal chains, three of them with sound narrators, indicate the story has a basis (asl) (Fath al-Bari, on Surat al-Hajj, vol. 8, pp. 439–440 in common editions).
  • P4. 22:52 and 17:73–74 fit the story, and Bukhari 4862 (pagans prostrating) is otherwise puzzling.
  • C. It is historically plausible that Muhammad briefly proclaimed Satan's words as revelation. That conflicts with Deut 18:20 and undermines confidence in his discernment.

Evidence for each premise

  • Why would early Muslims invent it? The criterion of embarrassment: a story damaging to Muhammad, accepted by early pious scholars.
  • The chains: honestly, they are mursal; none reaches a Companion with a connected chain. That's why the rating is MODERATE.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: the chain grading. Answer: Concede it. In hadith-science terms the story is weak. The historical case rests on its wide early attestation and on Ibn Hajar's judgment, not on a sahih chain. Present it as "reported by the earliest biographers and accepted by many early scholars," not as "in Bukhari."

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "It's not in Bukhari, so it's fake."

  • Close (R1): Bukhari includes only what met his criteria, and he wrote over two centuries later. Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabari are earlier or equally respected sources for history.
  • Their comeback: "Al-Albani refuted it."
  • Close (R2): And Ibn Hajar, the greatest commentator on Bukhari, thought it had a basis. Muslim scholars disagree; it's not settled.

Boomerang check

"Peter said Satan's thoughts and Jesus rebuked him: 'Get behind me, Satan' (Mark 8:33)." Answer: Peter was a disciple, not a prophet delivering revelation; Jesus immediately corrected him. The question here is whether a prophet proclaimed Satan's words as revelation. Deut 18:20 addresses exactly that.

Strength rating

Why: Early and widely attested, accepted by many early scholars, with support from Ibn Hajar; but every chain is mursal, and many Muslims reject it. MODERATE. Never present it as sahih.

  1. "What does 22:52 mean when it says Satan threw something into every prophet's recitation?"
  2. "Why did the pagans prostrate with Muhammad at the end of Surat al-Najm?"
  3. "Why would early Muslim historians record a story so embarrassing to the Prophet?"

30-second version

"Early Muslim historians like al-Tabari report that Muhammad once recited verses praising pagan goddesses, then said Satan had inserted them. The chains are weak, but even Ibn Hajar thought it had a basis, and 22:52 seems to refer to it."

2-minute version

"This is a sensitive topic, and I want to be careful. Some of the earliest Muslim historians, like Ibn Ishaq as preserved by al-Tabari, report that Muhammad once recited verses honoring the three goddesses of Mecca, and then said Satan had put those words in his mouth. Many later scholars rejected the story because the chains are incomplete. But Ibn Hajar, the great commentator on Bukhari, thought it had some basis. And 22:52 says Satan throws something into every prophet's recitation. If that happened, I'd find it hard to trust that every other verse was from God. What do you make of 22:52?"

Further reading

  • Al-Tabari, The History of al-Tabari, vol. 6, tr. W.M. Watt and M.V. McDonald (SUNY, 1988)
  • Muhammad Nasir al-Din al-Albani, Nasb al-Majaniq li-Nasf Qissat al-Gharaniq (the Muslim rejection)
Argument2GWEAK

The Aorta Test (69:44–46)

different Arabic word; reads a "test" into a warning

Name + thesis

Popular Christian apologetics argues: the Qur'an says that if Muhammad fabricated revelation, God would cut his aorta (al-watin); and a hadith reports Muhammad saying, as he died from poison, that he felt his aorta being cut. So, by the Qur'an's own test, he was a false prophet.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 69:44–46: "And if he had made up about Us some false sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand; then We would have cut from him the aorta (al-watin)."
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 4428 (in-book 64/450), narrated by Aisha; Bukhari introduces it with 'Yunus said, from al-Zuhri' (a suspended, mu'allaq, chain): "O Aisha! I still feel the pain caused by the food I ate at Khaybar, and at this time I feel as if my abhar (aorta) is being cut from that poison."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. Different words: the Qur'an says al-watin; the hadith says al-abhar.
  2. The verse describes swift divine punishment of a fabricator, not a slow death from poison years later.
  3. The chain in Bukhari is suspended ("Yunus said, from al-Zuhri"), though Bukhari's confidently worded suspended reports are generally treated as authentic.
  4. Dying of poison made him a martyr in Muslim tradition.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. 69:46 says a fabricating prophet would have his watin cut.
  • P2. Muhammad reportedly felt his abhar being cut by poison.
  • P3. If watin and abhar refer to the same vessel, the hadith describes the Qur'an's punishment.
  • C. (Weakly) Muhammad met the Qur'an's penalty for fabrication.

Evidence for each premise

  • Arabic lexicons describe both watin and abhar as a main artery, the aorta or a vessel connected with the heart (Lane's Arabic-English Lexicon describes both as the aorta).
  • But the verse is a hypothetical warning of immediate seizure ("We would have seized him by the right hand"), and the poisoning was about three years after Khaybar.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Fatal: the vocabulary differs, and the verse describes immediate divine action, not a poisoning by a Jewish woman years earlier. A Muslim can easily say the argument reads a literal test into rhetoric.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Different words."

  • Close (R1): They may denote the same vessel. But concede that this is uncertain.
  • Their comeback: "Then the argument fails."
  • Close (R2): Agree that it doesn't prove anything. Move to stronger ground.

Boomerang check

"Jesus died a violent death, so by your logic he was cursed." Answer: Deut 21:23 says one hanged on a tree is cursed, and Paul embraces this: Christ "became a curse for us" (Gal 3:13), bearing the curse in our place. The Christian claim includes the violent death; it isn't a test he failed.

Strength rating

Why: Different words, a strained reading of a hypothetical warning, and an easy Muslim reply. Drop it from debates, and know how to answer Christians who use it.

  1. (None recommended.)

30-second version

2-minute version

"You may have heard Christians argue that Muhammad failed the 'aorta test' of 69:46. I don't use that argument. The Qur'an and the hadith use different Arabic words, and the verse describes God immediately seizing a fabricator, not a poisoning years later. I'd rather talk about the questions where the evidence is strong, like what the Qur'an says about the Gospel."

Further reading

  • David Wood, "The Death of Muhammad" (popular presentation; read critically)
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 4428 with Ibn Hajar's commentary
Argument2GMODERATE

The Literary Challenge (2:23)

as a reply: literary excellence doesn't establish divine origin

Name + thesis

The Qur'an challenges doubters to "produce a surah like it" (2:23). But the challenge has no objective criteria, its judges are its believers, Arabic grammar itself was later codified from the Qur'an, and a Muslim theological school (the doctrine of sarfa) held that the Arabs could have matched it but were prevented by God. Literary brilliance, even if granted, doesn't prove divine authorship.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 2:23: "If you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it and call your witnesses other than Allah, if you are truthful." (Also 10:38; 11:13; 17:88; 52:34.)

Their best case (steelman)

The Qur'an's style (nazm) is unique: neither poetry (shi'r) nor rhymed prose (saj'), with unmatched eloquence, sound, and meaning. Arab poets of the time, masters of the language, couldn't meet it; some converted. Al-Baqillani (d. 1013) and 'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani (d. 1078) built a theory of inimitability (i'jaz). Fourteen centuries of attempts have failed.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. A test for divine origin must have clear criteria and impartial judges.
  • P2. The challenge specifies neither, and its judges are, in practice, believers.
  • P3. Uniqueness of style is common to great works (Homer, Shakespeare, the Psalms); it shows genius, not necessarily divinity.
  • P4. Some Muslim theologians (al-Nazzam, d. c. 845, and others) held the doctrine of sarfa: the Arabs could have produced something like it but God prevented them.
  • C. The literary challenge doesn't establish that the Qur'an is from God.

Evidence for each premise

  • Circularity: classical Arabic grammar was systematized by Sibawayh (d. c. 796) and others using the Qur'an as a primary model. Measuring the Qur'an by standards drawn from the Qur'an guarantees it wins.
  • Attempts existed: Musaylima (d. 632) and others composed verses; Islamic sources ridicule them, but the judges were Muslims.
  • Sarfa shows that inimitability was debated within Islam itself (Richard C. Martin, "The Role of the Basrah Mu'tazilah in Formulating the Doctrine of the Apologetic Miracle," Journal of Near Eastern Studies 39.3, 1980, pp. 175–189).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "Arab masters of language admitted they couldn't match it." Answer: That's evidence of its power, which many non-Muslim Arabists also acknowledge. But by the same reasoning, the King James Bible or the Psalms could be called inimitable. Literary greatness is not a revealed seal.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Then produce a surah."

  • Close (R1): Who will judge, and by what criteria? If the judges are those who already believe it's inimitable, no entry can win.
  • Their comeback: "Arabic experts, Muslim or not."
  • Close (R2): And if they rank a new composition highly, would you accept that the Qur'an is human? If not, it's not a test.

Boomerang check

"Then the Bible's beauty proves nothing either." Answer: Agreed. Christians don't argue the Bible is divine because of its style. The case for Christianity rests on history (the resurrection, 1C), not literary inimitability.

Strength rating

Why: The challenge is unfalsifiable as usually framed, and Islam's own sarfa debate shows it's contestable. But the Qur'an's literary power is real and respected, so engage it respectfully. MODERATE.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Arabic speakers Feel the Qur'an's beauty deeply Acknowledge its beauty first.
Non-Arab Muslims Usually can't evaluate the Arabic themselves Ask how they know it's inimitable.

Trap questions

  1. "What are the exact criteria for a surah 'like it'? Who judges?"
  2. "If an Arabic expert judged a new text equal to the Qur'an, would you change your mind?"
  3. "Do you read Arabic well enough to judge? If not, how do you know?"

30-second version

"The Qur'an's Arabic is beautiful; I don't deny it. But the challenge has no criteria and no neutral judges, and some Muslim theologians said the Arabs could have matched it if God hadn't stopped them. Beauty shows genius, not God."

2-minute version

"I respect how much the Qur'an's language means to you, and even non-Muslim scholars praise it. But I have a question about the challenge in 2:23. What exactly would count as a surah 'like it,' and who decides? If the judges are people who already believe nothing can match it, then nothing ever will. Some early Muslim theologians even said the Arabs could have produced something like it, but God prevented them. That's interesting, because it means the inimitability wasn't in the text itself. Great writing is a gift, but Shakespeare's genius doesn't make his plays revelation. I think the question of whether a book is from God is better answered by testing its claims, like what it says about Jesus."

Further reading

  • Richard C. Martin, "Inimitability," in Encyclopaedia of the Qur'an (Brill)
  • Al-Baqillani, I'jaz al-Qur'an (10th–11th c.): the classical Muslim case for inimitability
  • Navid Kermani, God Is Beautiful: The Aesthetic Experience of the Quran (Polity, 2015)
Argument2GMODERATE

"Scientific Miracles" in the Qur'an

strong on method; whether a verse is an "error" depends on how its Arabic is read

Name + thesis

Popular dawah says the Qur'an foretold modern science, above all embryology (23:12–14). But the verses use the everyday language of the ancient world, the classical commentators read them in pre-modern ways, and each "miracle" is announced only after scientists discover the fact. A prediction that no one can read until after the discovery predicts nothing. Hold Christians to the same standard: Job 10:10–11 uses similar poetic pictures of the womb, and the case for Christianity doesn't rest on it.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 23:13–14: "Then We placed him as a sperm-drop in a firm lodging. Then We made the sperm-drop into a clinging clot, and We made the clot into a lump [of flesh], and We made [from] the lump, bones, and We covered the bones with flesh."
  • Qur'an 86:6–7: "He was created from a fluid, ejected, emerging from between the backbone and the ribs."
  • Qur'an 22:5: "We created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then from a clinging clot, and then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed."
  • For the one standard, Job 10:10–11: "Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews."

Their best case (steelman)

The Qur'an describes stages of the embryo: a "clinging" thing ('alaqah) that looks like a leech, a "chewed lump" (mudghah) with marks like teeth, then bones, then flesh. No one in 7th-century Arabia had a microscope. The leading embryology textbook, Keith Moore's The Developing Human, was even reissued "with Islamic Additions" by Abdul Majeed al-Zindani, a leader of the "scientific miracles" movement (al-i'jaz al-'ilmi). Maurice Bucaille's The Bible, the Qur'an and Science (1976) spread the case worldwide.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. A scientific prophecy proves foreknowledge only if its meaning could be known before the discovery.
  • P2. The classical commentators read these verses in pre-modern ways (a blood clot; fluid from the man's backbone and the woman's ribs), and no one drew a modern fact from them in advance.
  • P3. The language matches what ancient people could already see and say (miscarried embryos at every stage; poetic pictures like Job 10:10–11).
  • P4. Where the verses are specific, they fit ancient ideas better than modern embryology (86:7; "bones, then flesh").
  • C. These verses don't show scientific foreknowledge.

Evidence for each premise

  • How the classical commentators read 86:7: Ibn Kathir explains "between the backbone and the ribs" as "the backbone (or loins) of the man and the ribs of the woman, which is referring to her chest," and quotes Ibn Abbas saying the same (Tafsir Ibn Kathir on 86:7). Sperm is made in the testes, not between the backbone and the ribs. Modern readers have to give the verse a new meaning to rescue it.
  • How they read "clot": On 23:14 Ibn Kathir says the drop "becomes a red clot," and quotes Ikrimah: "This is blood." The "leech" reading came later, after embryology.
  • "Bones, then We covered the bones with flesh": In the embryo, bone and muscle come from the same blocks of tissue (somites), which divide into the parts that become the skeleton and the parts that become muscle, and they develop side by side. There's no stage of bare bones later wrapped in flesh. Muslim apologists answer that cartilage forms before muscle surrounds it; that is a new reading, which is the point.
  • The method runs backward: Every "miracle" is announced after scientists discover the fact, and none has ever led to a discovery. If the Qur'an taught embryology, Muslim scholars reading it for 1,200 years would have known it.
  • Some Muslims reject it too: the Apostate Prophet channel's video "Muslim YouTuber Ali Dawah ADMITS Scientific Miracles are NONSENSE" shows a well-known Muslim speaker distancing himself from the genre.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "How could a 7th-century man know the embryo passes through a leech-like stage?" Answer: Miscarriages at every stage were seen in every culture, and the Arabic 'alaqah ordinarily meant blood or a leech, which an early embryo or a clot resembles to the naked eye. The verse describes nothing invisible. And the classical reading was "a red clot... blood," which is not what an embryo is.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "'Alaqah means 'clinging thing,' which is exactly what the embryo does in the womb."

  • Close (R1): Then why did Ibn Kathir, quoting Ikrimah, say it was blood? If the meaning were plain, the early commentators would have seen it.
  • Their comeback: "The word has many meanings, and Allah knew all of them."
  • Close (R2): Then any verse can be stretched to fit any discovery, after the fact. A test that can't fail isn't evidence.

2. "86:7 means the fluid comes from the region between the backbone and the ribs, where the testes first form in the embryo."

  • Close (R1): That's not what Ibn Abbas or Ibn Kathir said: the man's backbone and the woman's chest. The new reading exists only because the old one failed.
  • Their comeback: "Ibn Kathir wasn't a scientist."
  • Close (R2): Neither was the first audience. If a verse needs modern science to be understood, it couldn't have been a sign to the people who first heard it.

3. "Christians say the Bible has science in it too."

  • Close (R1): Some do, and I'd give them the same answer. Job 10:10–11 pictures the womb with milk, cheese, skin, and bones. It's poetry, not a textbook, and I don't argue that it proves the Bible is from God.
  • Their comeback: "Then you have no argument either."
  • Close (R2): My argument is history, not science claims: the resurrection (1C), and the Qur'an affirming the Torah and Gospel (2A).

Boomerang check

"The Bible has scientific errors too: the mustard seed is 'the smallest of all seeds' (Matt 13:32), and the sun 'rises.'" Answer: Scripture speaks in the everyday language of its hearers (see 2J on contradictions). That's exactly why Christians shouldn't sell "scientific miracles," and why the same honesty should be applied to the Qur'an. Hold both books to one standard.

Strength rating

Why: The method argument is strong, and the classical commentary on 86:7 and on "clot" is clear. But Arabic words have ranges of meaning, and apologists can keep reinterpreting, so any single "error" claim stays debatable. Use this as a reply, not your opening. MODERATE.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Young Muslims raised on dawah videos Often the main reason they feel sure Be gentle. Let Ibn Kathir do the talking.
Educated or scholarly Muslims Some already distrust the "scientific miracles" genre Agree quickly and move to the Islamic Dilemma (2A).

Trap questions

  1. "Before modern embryology, did any Muslim scholar describe the embryo from these verses in a way we'd now call scientific?"
  2. "Ibn Kathir says 86:7 means the man's backbone and the woman's chest. Was he wrong?"
  3. "If a verse can only be understood after science, how was it a sign to the people who first heard it?"

30-second version

"Ibn Kathir explains 86:7 as fluid from 'the backbone of the man and the ribs of the woman,' and on 23:14 he quotes Ikrimah that the 'clot' is blood. The modern readings only appeared after scientists found the facts. A prophecy you can only read after the discovery isn't a prophecy. And I'd say the same to a Christian claiming science in Job."

2-minute version

"I've looked into the embryology verses, and I want to be fair. The Qur'an describes the womb in vivid language: a drop, a clinging clot, a lump, bones, and flesh. But Job in the Bible does something similar: 'You poured me out like milk and curdled me like cheese; you clothed me with skin and flesh and knit me together with bones.' That's beautiful poetry, and I'd never say it proves the Bible is from God.

Here's my problem with the miracle claim. Ibn Kathir, one of your greatest commentators, says 86:7 means the fluid comes from the man's backbone and the woman's chest. On 23:14 he quotes Ikrimah: the clot 'is blood.' The leech reading and the new reading of 86:7 only appeared after modern science. If a verse can only be understood after the discovery, it can't prove anything. So I'd rather test the Qur'an where it makes clear claims, like what it says about the Torah and the Gospel. Can we look at that together?"

Further reading

  • Tafsir Ibn Kathir on 23:12–14 and 86:5–7 (abridged English, Darussalam)
  • Maurice Bucaille, The Bible, the Qur'an and Science (1976): the book that popularized the Muslim case
  • Taner Edis, An Illusion of Harmony: Science and Religion in Islam (Prometheus, 2007)
  • Videos on this topic: Testify, "There Are NO 'SCIENTIFIC MIRACLES' in the Quran"; Apostate Prophet, "Muslim YouTuber Ali Dawah ADMITS Scientific Miracles are NONSENSE | David Wood & Apostate Prophet"; GodLogic Apologetics, "Scientific Miracles In the Quran? | Young Muslim vs GodLogic!"
2H

Salvation and God's Character

3 cards3 moderate

New terms

Mizan: The scales on which deeds are weighed on the Day of Judgment.

Sirat: The bridge over Hell that all must cross on the Day of Judgment.

Shafa'a: Intercession, especially Muhammad's intercession on the Day of Judgment.

Atonement: God's provision for reconciling sinners to himself; in Christianity, through Christ's death in our place.

Argument2HMODERATE

Assurance of Salvation

a clear contrast; Muslims value "hope and fear" as a virtue

Name + thesis

The Qur'an and hadith present a believer, even Muhammad, as unable to know his eternal destiny. The Gospel gives assurance: whoever trusts Christ "has eternal life" now and can know it. This is less a refutation than an invitation, and often the most powerful point in a real conversation.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 46:9: "Say: I am not something new among the messengers, nor do I know what will be done with me or with you."
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 1243 (in-book 23/6), narrated by Umm al-Ala': Muhammad: "By Allah, though I am the Messenger of Allah, I do not know what Allah will do with me."
  • Qur'an 19:71–72: "There is not one of you except he will come to it (wariduha). This is upon your Lord an inevitability decreed. Then We will save those who feared Allah."
  • Qur'an 7:8–9: "those whose scales are heavy, they are the successful; and those whose scales are light, they are the ones who lost themselves."
  • John 5:24: "whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life."
  • 1 John 5:13: "I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. 46:9 is Meccan; later verses give assurance (48:2; 9:100 on the Companions promised gardens), and hadith name ten Companions promised Paradise.
  2. Hope and fear (khawf wa raja') together are a spiritual virtue; certainty breeds complacency.
  3. 19:71 means passing over the bridge (sirat) above Hell; the righteous cross safely (19:72).
  4. Christians also say "work out your salvation with fear and trembling" (Phil 2:12), and some Christians doubt their salvation.
  5. God is the Most Merciful; his mercy "encompasses all things" (7:156), and Muhammad will intercede.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. In Islam, final salvation depends on God's will and the weighing of deeds; the believer, even the Prophet in some texts, cannot be certain of it.
  • P2. In the Gospel, salvation is a gift received by faith in Christ's finished work, and the believer can know he has eternal life (John 5:24; 1 John 5:13; Rom 8:1).
  • C. The Gospel offers what Islam cannot: assurance grounded not in our deeds but in what God has done.

Evidence for each premise

  • Even Muhammad's deeds wouldn't save him without mercy: "No one's deeds will admit him to Paradise." They said, "Not even you?" He said, "Not even me, unless Allah covers me with mercy" (Sahih al-Bukhari 6463; Sahih Muslim 2816).
  • Rom 8:1: "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus."
  • Phil 2:12–13 continues: "for it is God who works in you," so fear and trembling is reverence, not uncertainty.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "Assurance leads to complacency; fear keeps us obedient." Answer: The New Testament grounds obedience in gratitude, not fear: "We love because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19); "the grace of God... training us to renounce ungodliness" (Titus 2:11–12). Assurance doesn't mean license (Rom 6:1–2).

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "The Prophet and the ten companions were promised Paradise."

  • Close (R1): Then why did Muhammad say, "I do not know what Allah will do with me" (Bukhari 1243)? And what about you?
  • Their comeback: "I hope in God's mercy."
  • Close (R2): Hope is good. Jesus offers more: "whoever believes has eternal life." Would you like to know you're forgiven?

Boomerang check

"Some Christians lose assurance, and some traditions (Catholic, Orthodox) don't teach certainty." Answer: True. Christians disagree on some aspects of assurance. But the NT texts themselves (John 5:24; 1 John 5:13) offer it, grounded in Christ's work rather than in our deeds.

Strength rating

Why: The texts are clear, but this is a contrast of theological visions, not a logical refutation. Its power is pastoral. MODERATE as an argument; often the most effective conversation point.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Devout Muslims Often deeply moved; many carry real anxiety Ask gently, listen.
Sufi-inclined Muslims Emphasize God's love Use God's love in Christ (Rom 5:8).
Cultural Muslims Unsure about everything Offer the gospel simply.

Trap questions

  1. "If you died tonight, do you know whether you'd go to Paradise?"
  2. "Why did Muhammad say he didn't know what God would do with him?"
  3. "What would you do if you could know you were forgiven?"

30-second version

"Muhammad said, 'I do not know what Allah will do with me.' Jesus said, 'Whoever believes has eternal life.' I don't hope I'm forgiven because of my deeds; I know it, because of what Jesus did."

2-minute version

"Can I ask you a personal question? Do you know whether you'll be accepted by God on the Day of Judgment? I ask because Muhammad himself said, 'By God, though I am the Messenger of God, I do not know what will be done with me.' That's honest, and if salvation depends on our deeds, it's the only honest answer.

The Gospel is different. Jesus said, 'Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life; he does not come into judgment.' That's not because Christians are better. It's because Jesus paid for our sins on the cross. So I don't just hope; I know I'm forgiven. And God offers that to you too."

Further reading

  • Nabeel Qureshi, Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus (Zondervan, 2014)
  • Mark Durie, Liberty to the Captives (Deror, 2010)
  • Al-Ghazali, The Remembrance of Death and the Afterlife (Book 40 of the Ihya'), tr. T.J. Winter (Islamic Texts Society, 1989): Islamic hope and fear
Argument2HMODERATE

Justice, Mercy, and the Atonement

Name + thesis

A just judge can't simply acquit the guilty, and a merciful God wants to forgive. Islam affirms both justice and mercy but has no mechanism that reconciles them: God simply forgives whom he wills. The cross shows how God can be "just and the justifier" (Rom 3:26), and the Qur'an itself records God ransoming Abraham's son with "a great sacrifice" (37:107).

Key texts

  • Qur'an 6:164 (also 17:15; 35:18; 53:38): "No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another."
  • Qur'an 3:129: "He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills."
  • Qur'an 37:107: "And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice (wa fadaynahu bi-dhibhin 'azim)."
  • Prov 17:15: "He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORD."
  • Rom 3:25–26: God put Christ forward "as a propitiation by his blood... so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus."
  • Isa 53:6: "the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. God is not a human judge. Sin is against God; he can waive what is owed to him, as a creditor forgives a debt.
  2. Substitution is unjust: punishing an innocent person for the guilty violates 6:164.
  3. 37:107 is a ram replacing a son in a test, not atonement for sin.
  4. Repentance suffices: "Allah loves those who repent" (2:222); the scales and God's mercy handle the rest.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. God is perfectly just: he doesn't declare the guilty innocent without dealing with guilt (Prov 17:15).
  • P2. God is perfectly merciful: he desires to forgive.
  • P3. Forgiving without any satisfaction of justice compromises justice; punishing everyone compromises mercy.
  • P4. At the cross, God himself, in the person of the Son, bears the penalty, so justice is satisfied and mercy is given (Rom 3:26).
  • C. The cross uniquely reconciles God's justice and mercy.

Evidence for each premise

  • Sin wrongs others, not only God; a judge who waives the murderer's penalty doesn't only forgive "his own debt."
  • The substitute is not a third party: in Christian theology, God himself bears the cost (2 Cor 5:19, "in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself"). That answers the injustice objection: no innocent outsider is coerced.
  • Ransom in the Qur'an: 37:107 uses fida' (ransom) and calls the sacrifice 'azim ("great"). The Torah's version points forward: "God will provide for himself the lamb" (Gen 22:8); John the Baptist: "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!" (John 1:29).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "Punishing an innocent person is itself unjust (6:164)." Answer: 6:164 forbids forcing one person's guilt on another. In the Gospel, the Son freely lays down his life (John 10:18), and he is God himself, so this is God bearing the cost of his own forgiveness, the way a forgiving person absorbs the cost of a wrong rather than demanding repayment.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "God just forgives; he doesn't need payment."

  • Close (R1): Would a human judge be just if he let a murderer go because he felt merciful?
  • Their comeback: "God is not bound by human standards."
  • Close (R2): Then "God is just" means nothing we can understand (see 2D-2). The Bible says God is just in a way we can understand, and that's why the cross was needed.

Boomerang check

"The Old Testament also says each person dies for his own sin (Ezek 18:20; Deut 24:16)." Answer: These forbid human courts from punishing children for parents. The same Old Testament has the sacrificial system (Lev 16, the Day of Atonement) and Isa 53, where the servant bears others' sins. Both principles stand: no forced transfer of guilt; God's provision of a substitute.

Strength rating

Why: A strong theological argument with clear biblical texts, but Muslims have a coherent alternative (God's sovereign forgiveness), so it persuades rather than proves.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Thoughtful Muslims The justice question resonates Use the judge analogy.
Ash'aris "God isn't bound" Connect to 2D-2.
All 37:107 is a powerful bridge Use Abraham and the ram, especially around Eid al-Adha.

Trap questions

  1. "Would a judge be just if he let a guilty man go free just because he was kind?"
  2. "In 37:107, who provided the 'great sacrifice,' and why was a ransom needed?"
  3. "How can God be both perfectly just and perfectly merciful?"

30-second version

"A just judge can't just let the guilty go. A loving God wants to forgive. At the cross God does both: he pays the penalty himself. Even the Qur'an says God ransomed Abraham's son with a great sacrifice."

2-minute version

"Here's something I've thought about a lot. We both believe God is perfectly just and perfectly merciful. But how can he be both? If a judge lets a guilty man go because he feels kind, he's not just. If he punishes everyone, where's the mercy?

At Eid al-Adha you remember how God ransomed Abraham's son with 'a great sacrifice.' The son was spared because something died in his place. Christians believe that was a picture of what God would do. Jesus is 'the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.' On the cross God himself paid the penalty, so he can forgive us and still be just. That's the heart of the Gospel."

Further reading

  • John Stott, The Cross of Christ (IVP, 1986)
  • Fleming Rutledge, The Crucifixion (Eerdmans, 2015)
Argument2HMODERATE

God's Love for Sinners

watch the boomerang: Ps 5:5 and Ps 11:5

Name + thesis

The Qur'an repeatedly says what God does not love: transgressors, disbelievers, wrongdoers. His love is conditional on obedience ("follow me; Allah will love you," 3:31). The Gospel announces that God loved us while we were still sinners and enemies (Rom 5:8, 10).

Key texts

  • Qur'an 2:190: "Allah does not love transgressors." 3:32: "Allah does not love the disbelievers." 3:57: "Allah does not love the wrongdoers."
  • Qur'an 3:31: "Say: If you love Allah, follow me; Allah will love you and forgive your sins."
  • Qur'an 2:222: "Allah loves those who repent and loves those who purify themselves."
  • Rom 5:8: "God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." 5:10: "while we were enemies we were reconciled to God."
  • John 3:16: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. "Does not love" means disapproval of their actions, not hatred of people as such.
  2. God's mercy encompasses all things (7:156); he is al-Rahman, the Most Merciful, and calls sinners to repent (39:53: "do not despair of the mercy of Allah").
  3. The Bible says God hates evildoers: "you hate all evildoers" (Ps 5:5); "his soul hates the wicked" (Ps 11:5).

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. In the Qur'an, God's love (hubb) is expressed toward the righteous, the repentant, and the obedient, and explicitly withheld from disbelievers and wrongdoers.
  • P2. In the Gospel, God's love takes the initiative toward sinners and enemies before they repent, and is demonstrated by the cross.
  • C. The Gospel reveals a love that seeks the unlovely, which is good news for sinners, not just for the righteous.

Evidence for each premise

  • 39:53 shows real mercy: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah." Acknowledge it.
  • The difference: in the Qur'an, mercy is extended to sinners who repent; in the Gospel, love goes out to sinners in order to bring them to repentance (Luke 15; Luke 19:10, "the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost").

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: the boomerang. Ps 5:5 and Ps 11:5 say God hates evildoers. Answer: The Bible holds both together: God's holy hatred of sin and wrath against the wicked, and his love that sent the Son for those under that wrath (John 3:16, 36; Eph 2:3–5, "children of wrath... But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead"). The difference isn't that the Bible lacks wrath; it's that the Bible shows God's love reaching across the wrath at the cost of his Son.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "God is the Most Merciful; he loves everyone."

  • Close (R1): The Qur'an says he doesn't love the disbelievers (3:32). Mercy, yes; love, not stated.
  • Their comeback: "Mercy is love."
  • Close (R2): Then where in the Qur'an does God love sinners before they repent, and pay a price to win them?

Boomerang check

See the hardest objection (Ps 5:5; 11:5).

Strength rating

Why: The Qur'anic texts are clear, and the Rom 5:8 contrast is powerful. But the boomerang (Ps 5:5) requires a careful answer, and Muslims rightly point to God's mercy in the Qur'an. MODERATE.

God didn't wait for us to become lovable. He came looking for us, like a father running to his lost son. That's the love that changed my life."

2I

Hard Ethics

3 cards1 strong2 moderate

New terms

Uswa hasana: 'Excellent example': the Qur'an's description of Muhammad (33:21).

Jizya: The poll tax paid by non-Muslim subjects (dhimmis) under Islamic rule (9:29).

Ridda: Apostasy: leaving Islam.

Jihad: 'Striving'; in Islamic law, especially armed struggle in the way of God.

These are the topics most likely to turn a conversation into a fight. Rules: quote primary sources exactly; present the real debate, including Muslim reformist views; never exaggerate; apply the boomerang check honestly (the Old Testament has hard texts too); and remember the goal is the person, not the point.

Argument2IMODERATE

Aisha's Age

the sources are sahih; the moral argument depends on contested premises about historical context

Name + thesis

Sahih hadith report that Muhammad married Aisha when she was six and consummated the marriage when she was nine. Muslims hold Muhammad to be "an excellent example" for all time (33:21). The question is not whether the 7th century had different customs, but whether a timeless moral example can be culturally relative.

Key texts

  • Sahih al-Bukhari 5133 (in-book 67/69), narrated by Aisha: "The Prophet married her when she was six years old and he consummated his marriage when she was nine years old, and then she remained with him for nine years (i.e., till his death)." (Also Sahih Muslim 1422.)
  • Qur'an 33:21: "There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example (uswa hasana)."
  • Qur'an 65:4: the waiting period ('idda) for divorced women includes "those who have not menstruated" (wa-lla'i lam yahidna), which classical commentators applied to young wives who had not yet menstruated (al-Tabari on 65:4: such girls, divorced after consummation, wait three months).

Their best case (steelman)

  1. Historical context: marriage around puberty was common in the ancient and medieval world, including among Christians and Jews; no contemporary, including Muhammad's many enemies, objected.
  2. Aisha became a great scholar and spoke of her marriage with affection.
  3. Some modern Muslims argue she was older (around 18–19), based on her sister Asma's age and other chronological reports. (Mainstream Sunni scholarship generally accepts the hadith ages.)
  4. Judging the past by today's standards is anachronistic ("presentism").

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Sahih hadith, accepted by mainstream Sunni scholarship, report that Muhammad consummated his marriage with Aisha when she was nine.
  • P2. Muslims regard Muhammad as an excellent moral example for all people and times (33:21).
  • P3. If his example is timeless, it can't be excused as merely the custom of his time; if it's culturally relative, then his example isn't timeless in this area.
  • C. The Muslim must either defend this marriage as a timeless model, or accept that Muhammad's conduct is not a universal moral standard, which weakens the claim that he is the perfect example.

Evidence for each premise

  • The hadith are in both Bukhari and Muslim, narrated by Aisha herself through several chains.
  • Classical scholars didn't regard the ages as problematic and accepted them. The "older Aisha" view is a modern revision, not the traditional position (Jonathan Brown discusses the debate, Misquoting Muhammad, 2014, ch. 4).
  • These texts still shape law debates: in Yemen in 2009–2010, clerics opposing a bill to set the minimum marriage age at 17 cited Aisha's marriage.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "Presentism: you're judging a 7th-century man by 21st-century norms." Answer: That's a fair point about historical judgment, and Christians should acknowledge it. But it collides with the claim of a timeless example. The question is put to the Muslim's own claim, not to the 7th century. Also avoid labels like "pedophile" in conversation; they shut down discussion and invite a debate about definitions instead of the real question.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "It was normal at the time."

  • Close (R1): I accept that it was more common then. Is Muhammad's example for his time, or for all times?
  • Their comeback: "For all times, in principle; specific customs vary."
  • Close (R2): Then some of his actions are not examples to follow. How do you decide which ones?

2. "She was really 18 or 19."

  • Close (R1): That contradicts Aisha's own words in Bukhari and Muslim. Are you willing to reject those sahih reports?
  • Their comeback: "Hadith can contain errors in numbers."
  • Close (R2): Then sahih hadith can be wrong on clear factual matters. That has consequences for the rest of the Sunna.

Boomerang check

"The Bible allowed marrying young girls too: Num 31:18 ('all the young girls who have not known man... keep alive for yourselves'); and Mary was probably a young teenager." Answer: (1) Mary's age is not stated in the Bible; traditions vary. (2) Num 31:18 is a hard text about captives in war; it does not present any specific marriage as a moral model, and the Bible nowhere holds up an Israelite soldier as "an excellent example for all time." The difference is the claim of a perfect, timeless model. (3) Christians should admit that the Old Testament records hard practices it doesn't endorse as ideals (e.g., polygamy).

Strength rating

Why: The sources are sahih, and the tension with 33:21 is real. But the moral argument relies on judgments about historical context that thoughtful people dispute, and it is extremely sensitive. Use it rarely, gently, and only as a question about the "perfect example."

30-second version

Many Muslims explain that this was normal in that culture, and historically there's something to that. But the Qur'an calls Muhammad 'an excellent example' for believers. If his example is for all times, then the custom of his time can't be the full explanation. That's the question I struggle with. Jesus, I believe, is the perfect example in a way that never needs excusing. Can I tell you why?"

Further reading

  • Kecia Ali, Marriage and Slavery in Early Islam (Harvard, 2010)
  • Paul Copan, Is God a Moral Monster? (Baker, 2011): for the Old Testament boomerang
Argument2IMODERATE

The Warfare Passages

context matters on both sides; classical law is the decisive evidence

Name + thesis

The Qur'an commands fighting polytheists and the People of the Book (9:5; 9:29), and classical Islamic law developed a standing doctrine of offensive jihad and the subjugation of non-Muslims. The Old Testament also contains war commands, but they were limited to a specific time and place and are not a continuing command for God's people; Jesus explicitly rejected the sword as the means of his kingdom.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 9:5: "When the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, and capture them, besiege them, and sit in wait for them at every place of ambush. But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, let them go."
  • Qur'an 9:29: "Fight those who do not believe in Allah or the Last Day... from among those who were given the Scripture, until they give the jizya willingly while they are humbled (wa hum saghirun)."
  • Qur'an 2:190: "Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress."
  • Deut 20:16–18: "in the cities of these peoples that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance, you shall save alive nothing that breathes."
  • John 18:36: "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting." Matt 26:52: "Put your sword back into its place."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. Context: 9:1–13 concerns specific polytheist tribes that broke treaties; 9:6 commands granting asylum to those who seek it; 2:190 forbids aggression.
  2. 9:29 concerns hostile Byzantine forces (the Tabuk campaign), not all Christians everywhere.
  3. Jizya was a tax in place of military service, often lighter than the Muslims' zakat; non-Muslims were protected (dhimmis).
  4. The Old Testament is worse: it commands killing women and children (1 Sam 15:3).
  5. Modern Muslim scholars (e.g., the Marrakesh Declaration of January 2016, signed by some 250 Muslim scholars and leaders) reject offensive jihad and affirm religious minorities' rights.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The Qur'an contains commands to fight non-Muslims until they submit or pay jizya "while humbled" (9:29).
  • P2. Classical Sunni and Shia jurisprudence treated offensive jihad to expand Muslim rule as a communal obligation (fard kifaya) and codified the subordinate status of dhimmis (Ibn Rushd, Bidayat al-Mujtahid, book of jihad: "scholars agree that the jihad is a collective, not a personal, obligation").
  • P3. The Old Testament's war commands were tied to the conquest of Canaan in a specific era and were never made a standing command for Israel's relations with all nations, let alone for the church; Jesus and the apostles forbade spreading the faith by force.
  • C. Islam's sources and classical law contain a continuing warfare ethic in a way the New Testament does not.

Evidence for each premise

  • Classical consensus: Islamic jurists divided the world into dar al-Islam and dar al-harb and regarded jihad as a means of extending Muslim rule (Rudolph Peters, Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam, 2nd ed., 2005; Majid Khadduri, War and Peace in the Law of Islam, 1955).
  • Old Testament limits: Deut 20:10–15 commands offering peace to distant cities; the "devote to destruction" (herem) commands are confined to the Canaanite nations (Deut 20:16–18); Gen 15:16 presents the conquest as judgment delayed for centuries; ancient Near Eastern war rhetoric uses hyperbole (Josh 10:40 "left none remaining" vs. Judg 1:21, 27–36, many remained) (Copan and Flannagan, Did God Really Command Genocide?, 2014).
  • New Testament: the church's weapons are "not of the flesh" (2 Cor 10:4); Christians are to love enemies (Matt 5:44).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: the boomerang. 1 Sam 15:3 ("put to death both man and woman, child and infant") is, on its face, harsher than Qur'an 9:5. Answer: Don't minimize it; Christians should feel its weight. The honest answer: (1) it is a specific, one-time judgment on a specific people (Amalek, for its earlier attack on Israel, Exod 17; Deut 25:17–19), not a law for later generations; (2) the hyperbole point (Amalekites appear again in 1 Sam 27:8; 30:1); (3) Christians are never commanded to repeat it, and the New Testament forbids it. The question is not which book has harder passages, but which has standing commands to fight for religion, and which founder modeled warfare for his followers.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "9:29 is only about the Byzantines at Tabuk."

  • Close (R1): The verse's wording is general ("those who were given the Scripture"), and classical jurists applied it generally.
  • Their comeback: "Classical jurists were influenced by empire; the Qur'an is defensive."
  • Close (R2): I'm glad many Muslims read it that way today. But which interpretation is more faithful to Muhammad's own practice and the Companions' conquests?

2. "The Bible is more violent."

  • Close (R1): The Old Testament contains hard war texts, and I won't deny it. Were they commands for all time?
  • Their comeback: "God commanded them, so they reflect God's will."
  • Close (R2): God's will for that time and place, as judgment on specific nations. Jesus told Peter to put away his sword. What did Muhammad tell his followers?

Boomerang check

See the hardest objection (1 Sam 15:3; Deut 20:16–18). Also be honest about Christian history (the Crusades, wars of religion): these happened, and they were contrary to Jesus' teaching. The question is which actions follow the founder's example.

Strength rating

Why: The Qur'anic texts and classical law are clear, but context debates are real on both sides, the Old Testament boomerang is heavy, and many modern Muslims sincerely reject offensive jihad. MODERATE, and handle with care.

The Old Testament has hard passages about war, and I take them seriously; they were limited to a particular time and judgment. Jesus, though, told Peter to put away his sword and said his kingdom isn't of this world. The early Christians spread their faith by preaching and dying, not by fighting. The Qur'an says, in 9:29, to fight the People of the Book until they pay jizya while humbled, and classical Islamic law treated that as a lasting rule. I'm glad many Muslims today read it differently. But whose example shows us God's way: the one who conquered, or the one who died for his enemies?"

Further reading

  • Rudolph Peters, Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam (2nd ed., Markus Wiener, 2005)
  • David Cook, Understanding Jihad (2nd ed., University of California Press, 2015)
  • Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan, Did God Really Command Genocide? (Baker, 2014)

Argument2ISTRONG

Apostasy

the classical legal consensus is well documented; modern reformist views exist

Name + thesis

Sahih hadith command the execution of those who leave Islam, and all the classical Sunni schools and Twelver Shia law prescribed death for the male apostate. Jesus commanded no penalty for leaving his community, and the New Testament's strongest response is exclusion from fellowship.

Key texts

  • Sahih al-Bukhari 6922, narrated by Ikrima from Ibn Abbas: "Whoever changes his religion, kill him (man baddala dinahu fa-qtuluhu)."
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 6878 (in-book 87/17), narrated by Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: the blood of a Muslim may be shed only in three cases, including "one who leaves his religion and separates from the community."
  • Qur'an 2:256: "There is no compulsion in religion."
  • Qur'an 4:137: "Those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then increased in disbelief: Allah will not forgive them." (No earthly penalty stated.)
  • John 6:66–67: "many of his disciples turned back... So Jesus said to the Twelve, 'Do you want to go away as well?'"
  • 1 Cor 5:12–13: "God judges those outside. 'Purge the evil person from among you.'" (Exclusion, not death.)

Their best case (steelman)

  1. The hadith concern treason, not belief: in 7th-century Arabia, leaving the community meant joining its enemies.
  2. The Qur'an prescribes no earthly penalty for apostasy (4:137; 2:217), and 2:256 forbids compulsion.
  3. Modern Muslim scholars (e.g., Mohammad Hashim Kamali, Freedom of Expression in Islam, 1997; Abdullah Saeed and Hassan Saeed, Freedom of Religion, Apostasy and Islam, 2004) argue against capital punishment for apostasy alone.
  4. Christians executed heretics (e.g., Michael Servetus in Geneva, 1553), and the Old Testament prescribes death for enticing others to idolatry (Deut 13:6–10).

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Sahih hadith command death for those who change their religion (Bukhari 6922; 6878).
  • P2. The classical schools of Sunni law (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) and Twelver Shia law prescribed death for the adult male apostate, with differences on women and repentance periods.
  • P3. Jesus and the apostles prescribed no civil penalty for leaving the faith; the church's discipline was exclusion.
  • C. Classical Islam coerces belief by law in a way Jesus never did, which conflicts with 2:256 and with the freedom the Gospel assumes.

Evidence for each premise

  • The classical consensus is documented across the madhhabs (Rudolph Peters and Gert De Vries, "Apostasy in Islam," Die Welt des Islams 17, 1976–77; Wael Hallaq, Shari'a, 2009).
  • Reformist dissent is real and growing, but it is a minority position historically.
  • Deut 13 was civil law for theocratic Israel and is never applied to the church in the NT; Christians who executed heretics acted against Christ's teaching (Matt 13:24–30, the wheat and weeds left until harvest).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: Christian history and Deut 13. Answer: Admit it plainly: Christians have persecuted and killed dissenters, and that was wrong by Jesus' own standard. The question is what the founders commanded. Jesus asked the Twelve, "Do you want to go away as well?" Muhammad, in sahih hadith, said, "Whoever changes his religion, kill him."

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "It's about treason, not belief."

  • Close (R1): Bukhari 6922 says "whoever changes his religion." And Ibn Abbas applied it to people Ali had executed for heresy, not for treason.
  • Their comeback: "Context: leaving Islam then meant joining the enemy."
  • Close (R2): If so, the classical jurists, who lived much closer to that context, misunderstood it for 1,200 years. And what would happen to an ex-Muslim in many countries today?

2. "2:256: no compulsion."

  • Close (R1): I agree with 2:256. How do you reconcile it with Bukhari 6922?
  • Their comeback: "2:256 is about entering Islam, not leaving."
  • Close (R2): Then belief is free to enter but not to leave. Is that freedom?

Boomerang check

Deut 13:6–10 and Christian persecution of heretics: see the hardest objection. Be honest; don't minimize.

Strength rating

Why: The hadith are sahih, and the classical consensus is documented by Muslim and non-Muslim scholars alike. Modern reformist views exist and should be acknowledged.
