  • Verdict: In Scripture, the true Messiah has complete authority over the powers of darkness, and they have none over him.

Key texts

  • Qur'an 17:47–48: "the wrongdoers say, 'You follow not but a man affected by magic (rajulan mas-hura).' Look how they strike for you comparisons; but they have strayed."
  • Qur'an 25:8–9: the same charge, rejected the same way.
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 5763 (Aisha): "A man called Labid bin al-A'sam... worked magic on Allah's Messenger till Allah's Messenger started imagining that he had done a thing that he had not really done."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. The magic affected his body and worldly matters, not revelation. Classical scholars (such as al-Mazari and Ibn Hajar) explain that it affected things like his sense of having done ordinary tasks, never his prophetic message. Ibn Hajar quotes al-Mazari: the "innovators" denied this hadith, claiming it lowers the station of prophethood, but it concerns "worldly matters for which he was not sent" (Fath al-Bari, vol. 10, pp. 226–227).
  2. The disbelievers' charge was permanent insanity, a claim that the Qur'an came from madness. A temporary illness from magic is different, just as prophets could fall sick.
  3. Allah cured him and revealed the cause, which shows his protection (the hadith continues with the angels revealing the magic and the cure).
  4. Prophets suffered physical attacks, including Jesus, who was beaten.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The Qur'an rejects the charge that Muhammad was "a man bewitched" (17:47–48; 25:8–9).
  • P2. Sahih al-Bukhari 5763 says a sorcerer bewitched him so that he imagined doing things he hadn't done.
  • P3. A prophet whose perception of his own actions can be altered by a sorcerer gives grounds to doubt what he perceived and reported.
  • C. Either the sahih hadith is wrong (and the hadith collections are unreliable at their highest grade), or the Qur'an's denial fails.

Evidence for each premise

The hadith's content. Bukhari 5763 is narrated from Aisha, graded sahih, and also in Sahih Muslim. It describes an effect on Muhammad's perception: he thought he had done things he hadn't. That's not a bodily illness like a fever.

Some Muslims rejected the hadith for this reason. The Hanafi jurist Abu Bakr al-Jassas (d. 981) argued that the report contradicts the Qur'an's denial and must be rejected (Ahkam al-Qur'an, on 2:102; modern studies list him among scholars who rejected the report; VERIFY the passage). That shows the tension is real and recognized within Islam.

Contrast with Jesus. Jesus says the ruler of this world "has no claim on me" (John 14:30). Demons begged him for mercy (Mark 5:7); no sorcerer ever affected him.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "It affected only worldly matters." "Ibn Hajar and others say the magic never touched revelation. The Qur'an was protected."

Answer: The hadith itself doesn't make that distinction; it says he imagined doing things he hadn't done. If his perception of his own actions could be altered, how was the boundary known? Rated MODERATE because the Muslim answer is coherent and widely accepted; present this as a question, not a knockout.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "It was only a physical illness."

  • Close (R1): The hadith says he imagined he had done things he hadn't. That's a mental effect, not a fever.
  • Their comeback: "Ibn Hajar limited it to worldly matters."
  • Close (R2): That's his interpretation, not the hadith's wording. And al-Jassas thought the hadith contradicted the Qur'an.

2. "The Qur'an's 'bewitched' means insane."

  • Close (R1): The word is mas-hur, "affected by magic" (from sihr), the same root as in the hadith.
  • Their comeback: "The disbelievers meant permanently deluded."
  • Close (R2): The Qur'an rejects that they were right in any sense: "they have strayed." Bukhari says that, in fact, he was affected.

3. "Allah protected him by revealing the cure."

  • Close (R1): The hadith describes a period in which he was affected before the cure was revealed.
  • Their comeback: "Prophets can be harmed."
  • Close (R2): Harmed in body, yes. But a prophet whose mind a sorcerer controls, even briefly, is what the Qur'an says he was not.

Boomerang check

"Paul had a 'messenger of Satan' (2 Cor 12:7), and Jesus was tempted." Paul's thorn was a weakness he endured; it never altered his perception, and God's purpose was to keep him humble (2 Cor 12:7–9). Jesus was tempted but never overcome (Heb 4:15; Matt 4:1–11). Neither text says anyone's mind was controlled by sorcery.

Strength rating

MODERATE. The hadith is sahih and the tension with 17:47 and 25:8 is real (al-Jassas felt it), but the "worldly matters only" answer is standard and coherent.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Sunni Muslims Accept Bukhari; may not know this hadith Read Bukhari 5763 together on sunnah.com.
Quranists Reject the hadith Use it to show why they distrust Bukhari, then turn to 2C-1.
Ex-Muslims Often cite it Make sure they also know the Muslim answer.

Trap questions

  1. "In Qur'an 25:8, what do the disbelievers say about Muhammad, and does the Qur'an agree?"
  2. "What does Bukhari 5763 say happened to Muhammad's perception?"
  3. "If a sorcerer could make him think he'd done things he hadn't, how do we know where it stopped?"

30-second version

"The Qur'an says Muhammad's enemies called him 'a man bewitched,' and it says they were wrong (25:8–9). But Sahih Bukhari says a sorcerer did bewitch him, so that he imagined doing things he hadn't done (Bukhari 5763). Even the Muslim scholar al-Jassas saw the problem. Jesus said Satan 'has no claim on me' (John 14:30)."

2-minute version

"There's a hadith I'd like your view on. Qur'an 25:8 and 17:47 report that the disbelievers said, 'You follow only a man bewitched,' and the Qur'an says they've strayed.

But in Sahih al-Bukhari, Aisha says a man called Labid worked magic on the Prophet, 'till he started imagining that he had done a thing that he had not really done.' That's in Bukhari and Muslim, the most trusted collections.

I know many scholars say it only affected worldly things, not revelation. But the hadith doesn't say that, and the scholar al-Jassas rejected the hadith because he thought it contradicted the Qur'an. Compare Jesus: demons begged him for mercy, and he said 'the ruler of this world has no claim on me.' That's the kind of authority I'd expect from God's final messenger."

Further reading

  • Sahih al-Bukhari 5763 with Ibn Hajar's commentary (Fath al-Bari)
  • Jonathan A. C. Brown, Misquoting Muhammad (Oneworld, 2014): how Muslim scholars handled hadith that seemed to conflict with the Qur'an
Argument2MWEAK

Muhammad's Despair at the Pause in Revelation

the suicide detail is an unconnected addition; use only the sahih core

Name + thesis

Drop this as a knockout. Popular videos claim that "Bukhari says Muhammad tried to commit suicide." The core account of the first revelation (Muhammad's fear, Khadija's reassurance) is sahih. But the detail about going to throw himself from mountains is introduced with "as we have heard" (fima balaghana), a report that most Muslim hadith scholars identify as an unconnected addition by the transmitter al-Zuhri. Use the core, not the addition.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • True prophets also felt terror at God's call (Isa 6:5; Jer 1:6), so fear alone proves nothing.
  • The test of a prophet is his message and its fruit (Deut 13:1–5; Deut 18:20–22; Gal 1:8).
  • Verdict: Scripture judges a prophet by whether his message agrees with God's prior revelation, not by his emotional reaction.

Key texts

  • Sahih al-Bukhari 3: after the first revelation, Muhammad came home "with his heart beating severely... and said, 'I fear that something may happen to me.'"
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 6982: "the Divine Inspiration was also paused for a while and the Prophet became so sad, as we have heard, that he intended several times to throw himself from the tops of high mountains."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. The suicide detail isn't part of the connected chain. "As we have heard" marks it as al-Zuhri's unconnected report (a balagh); Ibn Hajar identifies it as one of al-Zuhri's unconnected reports (Fath al-Bari on 6982).
  2. Even if true, it shows sincerity. A deceiver wouldn't be distressed; his grief shows he took the experience seriously.
  3. Biblical prophets despaired too: Elijah asked to die (1 Kgs 19:4), and Jonah said "it is better for me to die than to live" (Jonah 4:3).

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The sahih core (Bukhari 3) records Muhammad's fear after his first experience.
  • P2. The suicide detail (Bukhari 6982) is introduced as hearsay from a later transmitter and is not part of the connected chain.
  • P3. Prophets in Scripture also experienced fear and despair.
  • C. This report can't carry an argument against Muhammad; at most it opens a conversation about how Muhammad first interpreted his experience.

Evidence for each premise

The wording matters. Bukhari's text itself says "as we have heard," signaling a report outside the main chain. Ibn Hajar treats this as al-Zuhri's addition, found in Ma'mar's version, and the Dorar hadith encyclopedia grades this part weak (Fath al-Bari on 6982). Citing it as "Bukhari says" without that caveat will lose you credibility with an informed Muslim.

The usable point. The sahih core shows that Muhammad's first reaction was fear: "I fear that something may happen to me" (Bukhari 3). Early biographies report that he feared he was possessed or a poet (Ibn Ishaq, Sira, Guillaume trans. p. 106; VERIFY page). That raises a fair question about how the experience was first understood, without relying on the disputed addition.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "It's in Sahih al-Bukhari." Answer: It's in the book, but not as part of a connected, sahih chain; Bukhari's own wording flags it. Be the one who points that out, and you'll earn trust.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "It's in Bukhari, so it's sahih."

  • Close (R1): Bukhari includes material beyond his connected chains, including chapter headings and side reports. "As we have heard" marks this one.
  • Their comeback: "Then why use it?"
  • Close (R2): I don't, except to show that I won't misuse your sources. The sahih part is enough for a fair question.

2. "Elijah and Jonah despaired too."

  • Close (R1): Agreed, and that's why emotional despair proves nothing either way.
  • Their comeback: "Then drop it."
  • Close (R2): I have. Let's talk about the test that matters: whether the message agrees with the earlier Scripture (2B-9).

Boomerang check

"Christians cite Muhammad's emotions but ignore Elijah's." Fair. That's why this card is WEAK. Judge prophets by their message (Deut 13; Gal 1:8), not their moods.

Strength rating

WEAK as an argument. The famous detail rests on an unconnected report, and biblical prophets also despaired. Drop it; use 2B-9 and 2G instead.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Informed Muslims Will immediately cite "as we have heard" Don't use it.
Christians who saw it in a video May think it's a knockout Show them the wording and the caveat.

Trap questions

  1. "What does the phrase 'as we have heard' in Bukhari 6982 tell us about where that part came from?"
  2. "Elijah asked to die. Does that make him a false prophet?"

30-second version

"I'd avoid the 'Muhammad tried to commit suicide' argument. That detail in Bukhari 6982 is marked 'as we have heard,' and most hadith scholars treat it as an unconnected addition. The better question is the one that matters for any prophet: does his message agree with God's earlier word? (Deut 13; Gal 1:8)."

2-minute version

"You might hear Christians say Bukhari records Muhammad trying to kill himself. I don't use that argument, and here's why. The main account of the first revelation is sahih: he came home terrified and said, 'I fear something may happen to me.' But the detail about the mountains is introduced with 'as we have heard,' which marks it as a side report, and Muslim scholars treat it as unconnected.

Besides, biblical prophets despaired too. Elijah asked God to take his life. So emotions don't decide whether someone is a prophet. What decides it is the message: does it agree with what God already revealed? That's the conversation I'd rather have."

Further reading

  • Sahih al-Bukhari 3 and 6982 with Ibn Hajar's commentary
  • Ibn Ishaq, The Life of Muhammad, trans. A. Guillaume (Oxford, 1955)

Part 3

Other Worldviews and Traditions

3A

Atheism and Naturalism

1 card1 moderate

New terms

Naturalism: The view that nature (matter, energy, and physical law) is all that exists.

Problem of evil: The objection that the existence or amount of suffering is incompatible with, or makes unlikely, an all-good, all-powerful God.

For full cards on the objections skeptics raise most (the problem of evil, animal suffering, hell, and "scholars say the Gospels are anonymous"), see 1E.

Worldview3AMODERATE

Atheism and Naturalism

TAG and the cumulative case are strong in conversation; not academic consensus

Name + thesis

Atheism denies God; naturalism adds that nature is all there is. Naturalism can't account for the logic, scientific regularity, moral obligation, and reliable reason it uses to argue, so it borrows from the Christian worldview it denies.

What they believe (steelman)

Best case (Graham Oppy, J.L. Mackie, Sean Carroll): the universe is a self-contained physical system; science explains what can be explained; God adds no explanatory power and faces the problem of evil (why would a good, all-powerful God allow so much suffering?) and divine hiddenness (why isn't God more evident? J.L. Schellenberg). Morality is grounded in human well-being or is a useful construction. Atheism is simply the absence of belief, so the burden of proof is on the theist.

TAG internal critique

Use 1A (TAG) first.

  • Logic: universal, unchanging, normative laws of thought don't fit a universe of matter in motion.
  • Induction: naturalism has no reason to expect the future to resemble the past (Hume).
  • Morality: evolution explains moral feelings, not moral truth (Street's dilemma).
  • Reason: naturalism plus unguided evolution undermines trust in reason (Plantinga's EAAN, 1B).

Then the cumulative case (1B): the universe's beginning, contingency, fine-tuning, consciousness, the applicability of mathematics; and the resurrection (1C).

Key texts

  • Ps 14:1: "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God.'"
  • Rom 1:20–21: "his invisible attributes... have been clearly perceived... although they knew God, they did not honor him."

Weakest premise / hardest objection

The problem of evil. Answer: (1) Calling evil "evil" assumes an objective moral standard, which atheism struggles to ground (so the argument presupposes a moral law-giver). (2) The logical problem has been widely judged answered by the free-will defense (Plantinga, God, Freedom, and Evil, 1974; even Mackie conceded that the problem of evil does not show theism's central doctrines to be logically inconsistent, The Miracle of Theism, 1982, p. 154). (3) The evidential problem is real; Christianity answers it with a God who enters suffering on the cross and promises its end (Rev 21:4). Don't answer grief with arguments; answer it with presence.

Boomerang check

"Atheism is a lack of belief; you have the burden of proof." Answer: Fine for agnostics (3B). But anyone who claims naturalism (that nature is all there is) makes a claim and has a burden too.

Trap questions

  1. "On your view, why do the laws of logic hold everywhere?"
  2. "Is anything really wrong, even if everyone approved of it?"
  3. "Why should we trust a brain shaped for survival to tell us the truth about God?"

30-second version

"To argue against God you use logic, trust nature to be regular, make moral claims, and rely on your reason. Those make sense if a rational God made the world. What makes sense of them on your view?"

Bridge to the gospel

The atheist's moral outrage at evil is a clue: it points to a moral law, and to a Lawgiver who doesn't stand far off but suffers with and for us at the cross.

Further reading

  • Greg Bahnsen, Always Ready (1996)
  • Alvin Plantinga, Where the Conflict Really Lies (2011)
  • Graham Oppy, Atheism: The Basics (Routledge, 2018): the best atheist introduction
  • Timothy Keller, The Reason for God (Dutton, 2008)
3B

Agnosticism

1 card1 moderate

New terms

Agnosticism: Not knowing (soft) or holding that one cannot know (hard) whether God exists.

Worldview3BMODERATE

Agnosticism

the critique is strong against "strong" agnosticism; respect honest seekers

Name + thesis

"Soft" agnosticism ("I don't know whether God exists") is an honest starting point. "Hard" agnosticism ("No one can know") is a claim to know something important about God, that he can't be known, which undercuts itself. Either way, neutrality is not possible: everyone lives as if God exists or as if he doesn't.

What they believe (steelman)

Best case (T.H. Huxley coined the term in 1869; Bertrand Russell; many thoughtful people today): the evidence is balanced or insufficient; intellectual honesty requires withholding judgment; religions disagree, so how could anyone be sure?

TAG internal critique

  • Hard agnosticism is self-refuting: "God, if he exists, can't be known" claims knowledge of God's nature (that he is unknowable or unwilling to reveal himself).
  • TAG (1A): the agnostic uses logic, induction, and moral judgment every day. Reasoning itself depends on the God he's unsure about.
  • Neutrality is impossible in practice: you either pray or don't, worship or don't, live accountable to God or not. "Not deciding" is a decision (Pascal, Pensées, the wager, fragment 233 in Brunschvicg's numbering, 418 in Lafuma's).
  • If God has spoken (the resurrection, 1C), the question is historical and can be investigated.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

"So many religions disagree; how can anyone know?" Answer: Disagreement doesn't mean no one is right. People disagree about history and medicine too. Test the claims, starting with the most testable: did Jesus rise from the dead?

Trap questions

  1. "Do you mean you don't know, or that no one can know? How would you know that?"
  2. "If God did exist and wanted to be known, what kind of evidence would you accept?"
  3. "Have you examined the evidence for the resurrection?"

30-second version

"Not knowing is a fine place to start. But if God exists, the stakes are too high to stay there. Would you look at the evidence for the resurrection with me? If Jesus rose, we're not left guessing."

Bridge to the gospel

Jesus promised: "If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God" (John 7:17). Invite the agnostic to read a Gospel with the prayer, "God, if you're there, show me."

Further reading

  • Timothy Keller, Making Sense of God (Viking, 2016)
  • Blaise Pascal, Pensées
  • Rebecca McLaughlin, Confronting Christianity (Crossway, 2019)
3C

Judaism

1 card1 moderate

New terms

Rabbinic Judaism: The Judaism shaped by the rabbis after the Temple's destruction (AD 70), centered on Torah study, prayer, and the Talmud.

Tanakh: The Hebrew Bible: Torah (Law), Nevi'im (Prophets), Ketuvim (Writings).

Mashiach: Hebrew 'anointed one,' Messiah.

Approach with special respect. Christianity is rooted in the faith of Israel; Jesus, his apostles, and the first church were Jewish. Remember the long history of Christian mistreatment of Jews, and never speak of "the Jews" as Christ-killers (Acts 2:23 and Acts 4:27–28 implicate Jews and Gentiles together, and every sinner).

Worldview3CMODERATE

Judaism

Isaiah 53 and Daniel 9 are strong texts with real interpretive debates

Name + thesis

The Hebrew Scriptures promise a Messiah who would suffer for the people's sins (Isa 53) and come before the Second Temple's destruction (Dan 9:26). They also teach that atonement requires a sacrifice (Lev 17:11). Since AD 70 there has been no Temple and no sacrifice. Jesus fulfills these Scriptures: the suffering servant, the Messiah who came before AD 70, and the final atonement.

What they believe (steelman)

Best case (Rashi; modern rabbis such as Tovia Singer; scholars like Jon Levenson): the servant of Isa 53 is the nation Israel, suffering among the nations (Isa 41:8; 49:3). The Messiah will be a human king who rebuilds the Temple, gathers the exiles, and brings world peace (Isa 2:4; Ezek 37), which Jesus did not do. God is absolutely one (Deut 6:4); worshiping a man is idolatry. After the Temple's destruction, prayer, repentance, and good deeds replace sacrifice (Hos 14:2, "we will offer the bulls of our lips"; the Talmud, b. Berakhot 17a, where Rav Sheshet prays that the fat and blood he lost by fasting be counted as a sacrifice).

TAG internal critique

TAG's internal critique matters less here; Judaism shares the God of the Bible. The issues are internal to the Hebrew Scriptures:

  • Atonement: "it is the blood that makes atonement for the soul" (Lev 17:11). The Day of Atonement (Lev 16) required the Temple. Since AD 70, rabbinic Judaism has had no sacrifice. Hos 14:2 is a call to sincere repentance, not a cancellation of Lev 17.
  • Isaiah 53: the servant suffers for "my people" (Isa 53:8), is innocent (Isa 53:9), and is "cut off" for their transgressions. See 1C.
  • Daniel 9:26: the anointed one is "cut off" before "the city and the sanctuary" are destroyed. That points to someone before AD 70.
  • One God, more than one person: the Hebrew Scriptures hint at plurality within God (Gen 1:26; Ps 110:1; Isa 9:6, "Mighty God"; Dan 7:13–14), which the New Testament explains.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

"Jesus didn't fulfill the messianic prophecies of peace and the Temple." Answer: Christians believe the Messiah comes twice: first to suffer (Isa 53; Zech 12:10), then to reign (Isa 2; Zech 14). The Hebrew Scriptures themselves present both a suffering and a reigning figure; some rabbinic traditions even spoke of two messiahs (Messiah ben Joseph, who is killed, and Messiah ben David, who reigns; b. Sukkah 52a).

Boomerang check

"Christians changed the meaning of Jewish texts (e.g., Isa 7:14, almah, 'young woman,' not 'virgin')." Answer: A fair point to discuss. Almah means a young woman of marriageable age; the Septuagint, translated by Jews before Christ, rendered it parthenos ("virgin"). Concede the debate is real, and rely more on Isa 53 and Dan 9.

Trap questions

  1. "Without the Temple, how is atonement made according to Leviticus 17:11?"
  2. "In Isaiah 53:8, the servant is 'stricken for the transgression of my people.' Can the people be stricken for themselves?"
  3. "Daniel 9 says the anointed one is 'cut off' before the sanctuary is destroyed. Who came before AD 70?"

30-second version

"Leviticus says atonement requires blood, and Daniel says the Messiah would come and be 'cut off' before the Temple's destruction. The Temple fell in AD 70. Jesus came before that, and died as the final atonement Isaiah 53 describes."

Bridge to the gospel

Read Isaiah 53 together, slowly, without saying who it's about, and ask, "Who is this?"

Further reading

  • Michael L. Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, 5 vols. (Baker, 2000–2010)
  • Darrell Bock and Mitch Glaser (eds.), The Gospel According to Isaiah 53 (Kregel, 2012)
  • Jon D. Levenson, Inheriting Abraham (Princeton, 2012): a Jewish scholar's perspective
  • Daniel Boyarin, The Jewish Gospels (New Press, 2012): a Jewish scholar on the Son of Man
3D

Hinduism

1 card1 moderate

New terms

Brahman: In Hinduism, ultimate reality; in Advaita, impersonal pure consciousness.

Atman: The self or soul; in Advaita Vedanta, ultimately identical with Brahman.

Maya: In Advaita Vedanta, the appearance or illusion of a world of many distinct things.

Karma: The principle that actions produce corresponding consequences, in this life or future lives.

Samsara: The cycle of death and rebirth.

Moksha: In Hinduism, liberation from samsara.

Bhakti: Loving devotion to a personal God in Hinduism.

Worldview3DMODERATE

Hinduism

Hinduism is very diverse; the critique must fit the school

Name + thesis

Hinduism is a family of traditions, not one system. In its monist form (Advaita Vedanta), ultimate reality is impersonal and distinctions are illusion, which undermines logic and morality. In its devotional forms (bhakti), God is personal, but grace is limited by karma. The gospel offers a personal God who forgives completely, in history, through Christ.

What they believe (steelman)

Best case:

  • Advaita Vedanta (Shankara, 8th c.): Brahman, pure consciousness, alone is real; the individual self (atman) is ultimately identical with Brahman; the world of distinctions is maya (appearance). Liberation (moksha) is realizing this identity.
  • Vishishtadvaita / Dvaita (Ramanuja, Madhva): God (Vishnu/Krishna) is personal and distinct from souls; liberation comes through devotion (bhakti) and God's grace.
  • Karma and samsara: actions produce consequences across lifetimes (samsara, the cycle of rebirth).
  • Pluralism: many paths lead to the same truth ("Truth is one; the wise call it by many names," Rig Veda 1.164.46).

TAG internal critique

  • Advaita: if distinctions are ultimately unreal, then so are true and false, good and evil; the claim "all is Brahman" can't be ultimately true (see the monism card in 1A).
  • Karma: it explains suffering as deserved (from past lives), which, applied consistently, blames victims and offers no forgiveness, only payment. And the cycle has no first life to explain the first karma (an infinite regress).
  • Pluralism: "all paths are one" contradicts the paths themselves (Advaita and Dvaita disagree with each other about whether God is personal).
  • Bhakti: devotional Hinduism is closest to Christianity in its longing for a personal, gracious God; ask what grounds that grace and how sin is dealt with.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

"Christianity is just one path among many." Answer: Christianity's central claim is a historical event (the resurrection), not a mystical experience. Paths that contradict each other can't all be true; the question is which is true.

Boomerang check

"Christians believe in an eternal hell, which is harsher than karma." Answer: A serious point. Christianity offers forgiveness (karma does not), and hell is the just consequence of rejecting God, not a cycle of payment. Speak about it with humility and sorrow.

Trap questions

  1. "If all distinctions are illusion, is the difference between cruelty and kindness an illusion?"
  2. "Under karma, can a sin ever be forgiven, or must it always be paid?"
  3. "If Advaita and Dvaita contradict each other, can both be true?"

30-second version

"Karma says every wrong must be paid. The gospel says God himself paid it, in Jesus, so you can be forgiven. And God isn't an impersonal force; he's a Father who loves you."

Bridge to the gospel

Many Hindus are drawn to Jesus' person and teaching; meet them there. The avatar idea can be a bridge, with care: Jesus is not one of many appearances, but the one God become fully and permanently human, once for all (Heb 9:26; John 1:14).

Further reading

  • Vishal Mangalwadi, The World of Gurus (rev. ed., 1992)
  • Timothy C. Tennent, Christianity at the Religious Roundtable (Baker, 2002)
  • Gavin Flood, An Introduction to Hinduism (Cambridge, 1996): a scholarly overview
3E

Buddhism

1 card1 moderate

New terms

Anatta: Buddhism's doctrine of 'no-self': there is no permanent, unchanging self.

Dukkha: Suffering or unsatisfactoriness, the first of Buddhism's Four Noble Truths.

Nirvana: In Buddhism, the cessation of craving and suffering, and release from rebirth.

Dependent origination: The Buddhist teaching that all phenomena arise in dependence on causes and conditions.

Worldview3EMODERATE

Buddhism

Name + thesis

Buddhism teaches that suffering (dukkha) comes from craving, and that there is no permanent self (anatta). But without a self, it's hard to say who is reborn, who is enlightened, or who is responsible for karma; and without a personal ground of reality, compassion and moral obligation lack a foundation. The gospel affirms real persons, real guilt, and real forgiveness from a personal God.

What they believe (steelman)

Best case: the Buddha's Four Noble Truths: (1) life involves suffering; (2) suffering arises from craving; (3) suffering can cease (nirvana); (4) the Eightfold Path leads there. All things are impermanent and arise in dependence on causes (dependent origination); there is no permanent self, only a stream of changing processes. Theravada emphasizes the individual path; Mahayana emphasizes the compassionate bodhisattva; many Buddhists are agnostic about a creator.

TAG internal critique

  • No-self and karma: if there is no continuing self, who inherits the karma, and who is reborn? Buddhists answer with "continuity without identity" (a flame lighting another flame), but then the one who suffers for past karma isn't the one who did it, which seems unjust.
  • Compassion without a ground: why is compassion better than cruelty, if reality is an impersonal process? (TAG's moral argument, 1A.)
  • Logic and impermanence: the claim "all things are impermanent" is itself presented as a permanent truth.
  • Craving vs. sin: Buddhism diagnoses desire; the Bible diagnoses disordered desire (sin against a personal God), which can be forgiven, not merely extinguished.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

"Ultimate reality is beyond concepts; your objections are conceptual." Answer: Then the Buddha's own teachings, which are conceptual, can't be ultimately true either. Christianity affirms a God who is beyond full comprehension yet has spoken truly.

Boomerang check

"Christians also say the self must die (Gal 2:20, 'I have been crucified with Christ')." Answer: Paul's next words: "it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me... I live by faith." The Christian self is not extinguished but redeemed and given new life.

Trap questions

  1. "If there is no self, who is reborn, and who reaches nirvana?"
  2. "Why is compassion better than cruelty, if reality is impersonal?"
  3. "Is 'all things are impermanent' itself impermanent?"

30-second version

"The Buddha saw that life is full of suffering and that our desires are often the problem. I agree. But Jesus offers more than the end of desire. He offers forgiveness, a new self, and a life of love with a personal God."

Bridge to the gospel

Start with suffering, which Buddhists take seriously. Show the God who entered suffering at the cross, and promises to wipe away every tear (Rev 21:4).

Further reading

  • Keith Yandell and Harold Netland, Buddhism: A Christian Exploration and Appraisal (IVP, 2009)
  • Walpola Rahula, What the Buddha Taught (1959): a classic Buddhist presentation
  • Ravi Zacharias, The Lotus and the Cross (Multnomah, 2001)
3F

Mormonism (LDS)

1 card1 strong

New terms

Book of Mormon: LDS scripture published by Joseph Smith in 1830, presented as a record of ancient peoples in the Americas.

Exaltation: In LDS teaching, the highest state of salvation, in which the faithful become like God.

Book of Abraham: LDS scripture Joseph Smith produced from Egyptian papyri acquired in 1835.

Latter-day Saints are often kind, family-centered, and morally serious. Engage them as friends. Use their own sources, especially the Church's official Gospel Topics essays, which are candid about several issues.

Worldview3FSTRONG

Mormonism (LDS)

the Book of Abraham and the God-as-exalted-man doctrine are documented in LDS sources

Name + thesis

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints teaches that God the Father was once a man who progressed to godhood, and that faithful humans may become gods. It rests on Joseph Smith's scriptures, including the Book of Abraham, whose source papyri were recovered and identified as ordinary Egyptian funerary texts. TAG adds that a God who is one of many, embodied, and progressing within an eternal universe can't ground logic or morality.

What they believe (steelman)

Best case: Joseph Smith (1805–1844) restored the true church after a great apostasy. The Book of Mormon is "another testament of Jesus Christ," confirmed by the witness of the Holy Spirit (Moroni 10:4–5, "a burning in the bosom"). God the Father has "a body of flesh and bones" (Doctrine and Covenants 130:22). Through obedience and temple ordinances, humans may progress to exaltation. The Book of Abraham (in the Pearl of Great Price) is inspired scripture; even if not a literal translation of the papyri, it may have been revealed with them as a "catalyst."

TAG internal critique

  • God's nature: LDS teaching: "As man now is, God once was: as God now is, man may be" (Lorenzo Snow; see also Joseph Smith's King Follett discourse, 1844). A God who was once a man is finite and contingent, subject to an eternal universe and its laws. That God can't be the ground of logic and morality (TAG, 1A); he is under them.
  • The Bible: "Before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me" (Isa 43:10); "I am God and not a man" (Hos 11:9); God is spirit (John 4:24).
  • The Book of Abraham: the papyri Joseph Smith used were rediscovered in 1966 (Metropolitan Museum of Art). Egyptologists identify them as funerary texts (the Book of Breathings, Book of the Dead), unrelated to Abraham. The Church's essay "Translation and Historicity of the Book of Abraham" (2014) acknowledges that the fragments never mention Abraham and that scholars identify them as standard funerary texts, and proposes that the papyri prompted revelation "even if that revelation did not directly correlate to the characters on the papyri."
  • Book of Mormon history: no archaeological evidence confirms its peoples, cities, or wars in the Americas; DNA studies link Native Americans to Asian populations. The Church's own essay "Book of Mormon and DNA Studies" (2014) acknowledges that "the majority of Native Americans carry largely Asian DNA."

Weakest premise / hardest objection

"The Holy Spirit confirms the Book of Mormon to me" (Moroni 10:4). Answer: Feelings are real but must be tested by Scripture and facts (1 John 4:1; Gal 1:8). Muslims, Hindus, and others report similar inner confirmation for contradictory beliefs. If the Book of Abraham's source can be checked, and it fails, that's evidence a feeling can't override.

Boomerang check

"Christians also rely on faith, and the Bible has archaeological gaps." Answer: True, some details lack confirmation. But the Bible's peoples, places, and rulers are widely attested (e.g., Pilate, Caiaphas, Hezekiah, the Assyrian kings). The Book of Mormon's are not attested at all.

Trap questions

  1. "Was God the Father once a man? Who was God before him?"
  2. "What do the Joseph Smith papyri actually say, according to Egyptologists and the Church's own essay?"
  3. "Isaiah 43:10 says no god was formed before or after the LORD. How does that fit with exaltation?"

30-second version

"The Bible says God was never a man and no god was formed before or after him (Isa 43:10; Hos 11:9). And the Book of Abraham papyri, now recovered, turn out to be Egyptian funeral texts. I'd love to show you the God who has always been God, and who became man to save us."

Bridge to the gospel

LDS friends value Jesus and grace (2 Nephi 25:23, "after all we can do"). Show the grace that needs no "after all we can do": Eph 2:8–9; Rom 4:5.

Further reading

  • The Church's Gospel Topics essays (churchofjesuschrist.org), especially "Translation and Historicity of the Book of Abraham" and "Book of Mormon and DNA Studies"
  • Richard Mouw, Talking with Mormons (Eerdmans, 2012): a respectful approach
  • Robert M. Bowman Jr., Jesus' Resurrection and Joseph's Visions (Hill, 2020)
  • Francis J. Beckwith, Carl Mosser, and Paul Owen (eds.), The New Mormon Challenge (Zondervan, 2002)
3G

Jehovah's Witnesses

2 cards1 strong

New terms

New World Translation (NWT): The Bible translation published by the Watch Tower Society (Jehovah's Witnesses).

Watch Tower Society: The governing organization of Jehovah's Witnesses.

Worldview3GSTRONG

Jehovah's Witnesses

the texts on Jesus' deity are clear; the Watchtower's prophetic record is documented

Name + thesis

Jehovah's Witnesses teach that Jesus is a created being, the archangel Michael, and that the Holy Spirit is an impersonal force. They depend on the Watch Tower Society as God's channel, whose publications predicted events that didn't happen. The biblical texts on Jesus' deity, read in Greek, and the Society's own record, undermine both claims. TAG adds that their unitarian God faces the one-and-many problem (1A).

What they believe (steelman)

Best case: Jehovah alone is God (Deut 6:4). Jesus is "the firstborn of all creation" (Col 1:15), the first thing God created, through whom he made everything else; "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28); John 1:1 should read "the Word was a god" (New World Translation), because the Greek theos lacks the article. The Trinity is a 4th-century pagan corruption. God guides his people through the Governing Body of the Watch Tower Society.

TAG internal critique

  • John 1:1: the lack of the article before theos marks the Word's nature ("the Word was God" in quality), not "a god" (see E.C. Colwell's rule and Daniel Wallace, Greek Grammar Beyond the Basics, 1996, on qualitative nouns). The NWT doesn't translate other anarthrous theos uses as "a god" (e.g., John 1:6, 12, 18).
  • Jesus as Creator: "All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made" (John 1:3); if Jesus were created, he would have made himself. The NWT adds "other" to Col 1:16 ("all other things").
  • Worship: the Father commands angels to worship the Son (Heb 1:6); Jesus is called God by the Father (Heb 1:8).
  • The Watchtower's record: the 1920 booklet Millions Now Living Will Never Die pointed to 1925 for the resurrection of the patriarchs; the 1966 book Life Everlasting in Freedom of the Sons of God pointed to 1975 as the end of 6,000 years of human history, and in 1980 the Society acknowledged that "considerable expectation was aroused regarding the year 1975." Deut 18:22 is the test for those who speak in God's name.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

"Col 1:15: Jesus is the 'firstborn of all creation.'" Answer: "Firstborn" (prototokos) means preeminent heir: God calls David his "firstborn" though he was the youngest son (Ps 89:27). Col 1:16–17 says all things were created through him and he is "before all things."

Boomerang check

"Christians predicted the end too (date-setters)." Answer: Yes, and they were wrong, but they weren't the official voice of the church claiming to be God's sole channel. The Watch Tower Society claims that role, which is why Deut 18:22 applies.

Trap questions

  1. "In John 1:3, if all things were made through Jesus, was Jesus made through himself?"
  2. "Why does the NWT add 'other' in Colossians 1:16?"
  3. "In Hebrews 1:6, whom does God command the angels to worship?"
  4. "What did the Society teach about 1925?"

30-second version

"John says all things were made through the Word, so the Word can't be a created thing. And God tells the angels to worship the Son (Heb 1:6). Would God command the angels to worship another angel?"

Bridge to the gospel

Jehovah's Witnesses usually know their Bibles and value careful reading. Read John 1, Colossians 1, and Hebrews 1 slowly, in their translation and then in others.

Further reading

  • Robert M. Bowman Jr., Jehovah's Witnesses (Zondervan, 1995)
  • Ron Rhodes, Reasoning from the Scriptures with the Jehovah's Witnesses (Harvest House, rev. 2009)
  • Raymond Franz, Crisis of Conscience (1983): a former Governing Body member's account
Defense3G

"Jehovah is God's true name, and the churches took it out of the Bible."

The objection (best form)

"God has a personal name, Jehovah (Ps 83:18), and Jesus made it known (John 17:6). Most Bibles hide it behind 'LORD.' The New World Translation restores it, even in the New Testament."

Answer

  • Agree first: God has a personal name. The Hebrew Bible writes it with four letters, YHWH, thousands of times, and God explains it to Moses: "I AM WHO I AM" (Exod 3:14–15). Honoring the name is common ground.
  • "Jehovah" is a blend, not the original sound. Before Jesus' time, Jews stopped saying the name aloud out of reverence and said Adonai ("my Lord") instead. The Mishnah (about AD 200) records Abba Saul counting "one who pronounces the Name by its letters" among those with no share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10.1). Medieval Jewish scribes (the Masoretes) wrote the vowels of Adonai under YHWH as a reminder to say "Lord." Read together, letters and vowels give "Yehowah," which first appeared in English as "Iehouah" in William Tyndale's 1530 Pentateuch (Exod 6:3) and later became "Jehovah." Most scholars think the original sounded like "Yahweh." "Jehovah" is a respectful form, not something to divide over. Wes Huff walks through this history in "What is the name of God? Where did 'Jehovah' come from?"
  • The real question is whose name it is. When the New Testament writers quoted YHWH passages in Greek, they wrote "Lord" (Kyrios) and applied them to Jesus. "Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved" (Rom 10:13, quoting Joel 2:32) points back to "Jesus is Lord" (Rom 10:9). Isaiah's "To me [YHWH] every knee shall bow" (Isa 45:23) becomes "at the name of Jesus every knee should bow" (Phil 2:10–11).
  • No Greek manuscript of the New Testament contains the name. The New World Translation inserts "Jehovah" 237 times in the New Testament. Its own appendix explains this as restoring what it believes scribes replaced with "Lord," and admits the major manuscripts lack it. Putting "Jehovah" where the Greek says "Lord" breaks exactly the links that identify Jesus with YHWH, as in Rom 10:9–13.

30-second version

"You're right that God has a personal name, YHWH, and we should honor it. 'Jehovah' is a later blend of those letters with the vowels of 'Adonai.' But look at what the apostles did with the name: 'Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved' (Rom 10:13) is about Jesus, the Lord of verse 9. The name you love is the name Jesus bears."

3H

Secular Humanism and Relativism

1 card1 strong

New terms

Relativism: The view that truth or morality is relative to individuals or cultures.

Secular humanism: A non-religious worldview affirming human reason, ethics, and flourishing without God.

Worldview3HSTRONG

Secular Humanism and Relativism

relativism is self-refuting; humanism borrows its values

Name + thesis

Relativism says there is no objective truth or morality, a claim that presents itself as objectively true. Secular humanism affirms human dignity, rights, and reason without God, but those values arose from, and depend on, the Christian belief that humans are made in God's image.

What they believe (steelman)

Best case: humans can be good without God; morality is grounded in human flourishing, reason, and empathy (Steven Pinker, Enlightenment Now, 2018; the Humanist Manifesto III, 2003). Relativists add that moral and religious claims are cultural, so tolerance requires not judging others.

TAG internal critique

  • Relativism is self-refuting: "There is no absolute truth" is an absolute claim. "You shouldn't judge" is a judgment. "Tolerance is the highest virtue" is an objective moral claim.
  • Humanism's borrowed capital: human equality and dignity were not obvious to the ancient world (Aristotle defended natural slavery). Historians, including non-Christians (Tom Holland, Dominion, 2019), trace them to the Christian claim that all humans bear God's image (Gen 1:27) and that Christ died for all.
  • Grounding: on naturalism, humans are one species among many; why are they of equal and infinite worth? (TAG's moral argument, 1A.)

Weakest premise / hardest objection

"You don't need God to be good." Answer: Agreed: many humanists are kind and just. The question is whether human dignity is real or a useful fiction without God (see the moral argument card in 1B).

Boomerang check

"Christians have been intolerant and cruel." Answer: True, and Christians must repent of it. But you can only condemn it as truly wrong if objective morality exists. And the reformers who opposed slavery and cruelty (William Wilberforce, the abolitionists) often did so from Christian conviction.

Trap questions

  1. "Is it absolutely true that there is no absolute truth?"
  2. "Is it wrong for me to judge you for judging others?"
  3. "Why are all humans equal in worth, on your view?"

30-second version

"If there's no objective truth, then 'there's no objective truth' isn't objectively true. And human dignity, which humanists rightly value, comes from the Christian belief that every person is made in God's image."

Bridge to the gospel

Affirm the humanist's best values (justice, compassion, dignity) and show their source and fulfillment in the God who became human.

Further reading

  • Tom Holland, Dominion: How the Christian Revolution Remade the World (Basic, 2019)
  • Glen Scrivener, The Air We Breathe (Good Book Company, 2022)
  • Francis J. Beckwith and Gregory Koukl, Relativism: Feet Firmly Planted in Mid-Air (Baker, 1998)
3I

New Age

1 card1 moderate

New terms

Pantheism: The view that God and the universe are identical.

Panentheism: The view that the universe is within God, while God is more than the universe.

Monism: The view that all reality is ultimately one, with distinctions being secondary or illusory.

Worldview3IMODERATE

New Age Spirituality

diffuse beliefs; the monism critique is strong where monism is held

Name + thesis

New Age spirituality blends pantheism ("all is God"), the divine self ("you are God"), and personal experience as the final authority. If all is one, the distinctions between good and evil, true and false, and Creator and creature disappear, and with them the possibility of real love, morality, and truth.

What they believe (steelman)

Best case (Eckhart Tolle, The Power of Now, 1997; Deepak Chopra; popular spirituality): the universe is a unified, conscious energy; each person is divine; spiritual growth is awakening to that truth; all religions point to it; "my truth" is valid for me.

TAG internal critique

  • Monism undermines logic and morality (the monism card in 1A).
  • "You are God" can't explain ignorance: how does the infinite God forget it is God and need to be reminded by a bestselling author?
  • "My truth": relativism refutes itself (3H).
  • Love requires an other: if all is one, there is no one to love. The triune God grounds both unity and real relationship.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

"Christianity is too narrow; spirituality should be inclusive." Answer: Jesus welcomed everyone, including outcasts and sinners, but he also said, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life" (John 14:6). Inclusive doesn't mean every path is true; it means everyone is invited.

Boomerang check

"Christians talk about being 'one with Christ' too." Answer: Christian union is relationship, not identity: believers share Christ's life while remaining themselves (John 17:21–23, "even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you").

Trap questions

  1. "If you are God, why did you need to discover it?"
  2. "If all is one, is there any real difference between love and cruelty?"
  3. "Can someone else's truth be false?"

30-second version

"If all is one, there's no one to love and no difference between good and evil. The Christian God is one, yet Father, Son, and Spirit are distinct and love each other. And he invites you into that love, not to dissolve into him."

Bridge to the gospel

New Age seekers often long for transcendence and connection. Point to the God who is both far above us and personally near (Acts 17:27–28).

Further reading

  • Douglas Groothuis, Unmasking the New Age (IVP, 1986)
  • Vishal Mangalwadi, When the New Age Gets Old (IVP, 1992)
  • Ross Douthat, Bad Religion (Free Press, 2012), on American spirituality
3J

Roman Catholicism

6 cards4 strong1 moderate

New terms

Magisterium: The teaching authority of the Roman Catholic Church (the pope and the bishops in communion with him).

Papal infallibility: The Catholic dogma (Vatican I, 1870) that the pope cannot err when he defines a doctrine of faith or morals ex cathedra.

Ex cathedra: "From the chair": a pope's solemn definition of doctrine for the whole church.

Development of doctrine: John Henry Newman's theory (1845) that church teaching grows over time like an acorn into an oak, making explicit what was there from the start without contradicting it.

Invincible ignorance: In Catholic teaching, not knowing the truth of the gospel or the Church through no fault of your own; Rome teaches such people may still be saved.

Immaculate Conception: The Catholic dogma (1854) that Mary was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her conception.

Assumption: The Catholic dogma (1950) that Mary was taken body and soul into heaven at the end of her earthly life.

Purgatory: In Catholic teaching, a state of purification after death for those who die in God's grace but are not yet fully purified.

Catholics confess the Trinity, the deity of Christ, his virgin birth, his atoning death, and his bodily resurrection. Treat them as people who share much of the faith, and argue as a brother or sister would. The question in every card is the apostolic one (1D): does Scripture teach this? Catholic sources are quoted from the Church's own documents (the Council of Trent, Vatican I, papal definitions, and the Catechism of the Catholic Church, "CCC") so you never misrepresent what Catholics actually hold.

Argument3JMODERATE

The Rock Is Christ, Not a Papal Office

who the "rock" is is honestly debated; the card wins either way because succession and infallibility are absent from Scripture

Name + thesis

The papacy. Jesus built his church on the rock of Peter's confession, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God," that is, on Christ himself, the only foundation (1 Cor 3:11). And even on the reading that Peter is the rock, Scripture never teaches that Peter had successors, that the bishop of Rome holds his office, or that this bishop is infallible, all of which Catholics must believe (Vatican I, 1870). Either way, the papacy has no apostolic basis.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "No one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ" (1 Cor 3:11).
  • "The Rock was Christ" (1 Cor 10:4); Peter himself calls Jesus "a living stone" and the "chosen and precious" cornerstone (1 Pet 2:4–8; Isa 28:16).
  • "Who is a rock, except our God?" (Ps 18:31; Deut 32:4).
  • The church is built on "the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone" (Eph 2:20), and Peter calls himself "a fellow elder" (1 Pet 5:1).
  • Verdict: Scripture consistently names God in Christ as the rock and foundation. It never mentions a successor to Peter, Rome, or infallibility.

Key texts

  • Matt 16:15–18: "'But who do you say that I am?' Simon Peter replied, 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.'... 'And I tell you, you are Peter (Petros), and on this rock (petra) I will build my church.'"
  • Matt 16:23: "Get behind me, Satan! You are a hindrance to me."
  • Vatican I, Pastor Aeternus (1870), ch. 4: when the Roman pontiff speaks ex cathedra to define a doctrine of faith or morals, he possesses infallibility, and such definitions are "irreformable of themselves, and not from the consent of the church."
  • John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew 54.3: "upon this rock will I build my Church; that is, on the faith of his confession."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. Peter is the rock. "You are Peter, and on this rock" is a wordplay pointing to Peter. In Aramaic, which Jesus probably spoke, both words would be Kepha (John 1:42, "Cephas"). In ordinary Greek of the time, petros and petra overlapped in meaning; Petros is masculine simply because it's a man's name. Many Protestant scholars agree the rock is Peter (e.g., D. A. Carson, R. T. France).
  2. The keys echo Isa 22:22, where the king's steward receives "the key of the house of David," an office with successors.
  3. Peter leads throughout: named first in every list (Matt 10:2), preaching at Pentecost (Acts 2), told to "feed my sheep" (John 21:15–17) and "strengthen your brothers" (Luke 22:32).
  4. The early church honored Rome. Irenaeus (c. 180) says every church must agree with Rome because of its preeminent authority (Against Heresies 3.3.2).
  5. A church needs a visible head to stay one.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Christ built his church on the rock of the truth Peter confessed, which is Christ himself (Matt 16:16–18; 1 Cor 3:11; 1 Cor 10:4; 1 Pet 2:4–8).
  • P2. Even if Peter is the rock, Scripture never teaches successors to his role, never links it to Rome, and never teaches that anyone is infallible.
  • P3. A doctrine binding on all Christians must be taught by the apostles (1D; Jude 3).
  • C. The papacy as defined by Vatican I is not an apostolic doctrine.

Evidence for each premise

Line 1: the rock is the confession and the Christ it confesses.

  • The subject of the passage is who Jesus is. Jesus asks, "Who do you say that I am?" (Matt 16:15). The Father reveals the answer to Peter (Matt 16:17): Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. That revealed truth is what the church rests on. (The cross comes next: from verse 21 Jesus begins to teach that he must die and rise.)
  • The wording shifts. Jesus says "you are Petros, and on this petra." Protestants have long read the change from a man's name to "this bedrock" as pointing from Peter to the truth he confessed.
  • Scripture's "rock" is God. The Old Testament repeatedly calls God the Rock (Deut 32:4; Ps 18:2, 31; Isa 44:8). The New Testament applies this to Christ (1 Cor 10:4; Rom 9:33). Peter himself, writing later, calls Jesus the stone and cornerstone and calls believers "living stones" built on him (1 Pet 2:4–8). He never calls himself the rock.
  • Five verses later, the "rock" stumbles. When Jesus predicts his death, Peter rebukes him, and Jesus says, "Get behind me, Satan! You are a hindrance (literally, a stumbling stone) to me" (Matt 16:22–23). The church's foundation is what Peter confessed, not Peter's reliability.
  • Early witnesses read it this way too (witnesses, not authorities, 1D). John Chrysostom: "on the faith of his confession" (Homilies on Matthew 54.3). Augustine said he had often explained the rock as Christ, "whom Peter confessed," and left readers to choose between that and Peter (Retractations 1.21; wording varies by translation). Calvin: Christ builds on the confession "because it is the only foundation" (Institutes 4.6.6).

Line 2 (the fallback): even if Peter is the rock.

  • The text is silent about succession. It says nothing about successors, Rome, or infallibility. Peter's foundational role belongs with the apostles' (Eph 2:20; Rev 21:14: twelve foundations, not one), and foundations aren't relaid.
  • Isaiah 22 cuts both ways. The steward who received the key was warned that the peg would "give way" and fall (Isa 22:25).
  • Peter's actual conduct. Paul corrected him publicly over the gospel itself (Gal 2:11–14). In Acts 15 Peter speaks, but James gives the decision ("my judgment is," Acts 15:19). Peter calls himself "a fellow elder" (1 Pet 5:1).
  • Silence where it should speak. Paul's letter to the Romans greets many believers in Rome and never mentions Peter (Rom 16). Paul's list of the leaders Christ gave the church has no chief bishop (Eph 4:11).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: Kepha and the wordplay. "In Aramaic Jesus said Kepha both times (John 1:42). The Greek shift to Petros is only because a man's name needs a masculine form. The natural reading of 'this rock' is Peter."

Answer: That's a fair point, and many Protestant scholars accept it, so don't stake everything on Petros versus petra. Two replies:

  1. Even read as Peter, the rock is Peter the confessor of Christ. The blessing follows his confession and rests on it, and Scripture interprets the foundation for us: "no one can lay a foundation other than... Jesus Christ" (1 Cor 3:11). The apostles are a foundation only with Christ as the cornerstone (Eph 2:20).
  2. Then switch to Line 2. Granting that Peter is the rock, there is still no successor, no Rome, and no infallibility in the text. On the early church: concede the honor of Rome (the capital, where Peter and Paul died), but honor isn't jurisdiction. When Pope Victor tried to excommunicate the Asian churches over the date of Easter (c. 190), Irenaeus himself rebuked him (Eusebius, Church History 5.24). Papal infallibility wasn't defined until 1870.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Petros and petra are the same word in Aramaic."

  • Close (R1): Possibly. But the rock is still tied to the confession Peter has just made, and Scripture names the one foundation: Christ (1 Cor 3:11; 1 Pet 2:4–8).
  • Their comeback: "Jesus said 'you are Peter, and on this rock.' The rock is Peter."
  • Close (R2): Then let's grant it. Where does the text say "and on your successors in Rome"? And Jesus gave the same binding and loosing to all the disciples (Matt 18:18).

2. "The keys imply an office with successors (Isa 22:22)."

  • Close (R1): That steward's peg would "give way" and fall (Isa 22:25), and the binding and loosing is shared with all the disciples (Matt 18:18).
  • Their comeback: "The keys themselves were given to Peter alone."
  • Close (R2): And Peter used them: he opened the door of the kingdom to Jews at Pentecost (Acts 2) and to Gentiles at Cornelius's house (Acts 10; Acts 15:7). Scripture shows the keys used, never handed on.

3. "Feed my sheep" (John 21).

  • Close (R1): Jesus restores Peter three times after his three denials. Peter himself later applies "shepherd the flock" to all elders (1 Pet 5:1–2).
  • Their comeback: "It's still unique to Peter."
  • Close (R2): Unique to Peter, yes. Transferable to a bishop in Rome? The text is silent.

4. "Without a pope there's no unity."

  • Close (R1): The church's unity is in Christ and the apostolic gospel (Eph 4:3–6), not in a single bishop.
  • Their comeback: "Look at Protestant divisions."
  • Close (R2): The papacy hasn't guaranteed unity either: during the Western Schism (1378–1417), up to three men claimed to be pope at once.

Boomerang check

"Protestants have no visible authority, so anything goes." Protestant churches have elders and confessions, all tested by Scripture (Acts 17:11; Titus 1:9). A teacher's authority is real when it serves the word, not when it is placed above it.

"You're just avoiding the plain meaning of Matthew 16." We hold both readings open honestly. The confession reading has strong scriptural support (1 Cor 3:11; 1 Cor 10:4; 1 Pet 2:4–8) and early witnesses, and the argument against the papacy doesn't depend on it.

Strength rating

MODERATE. The confession-and-Christ reading has strong scriptural support and early witnesses (Chrysostom, Augustine), but the Aramaic and wordplay arguments give the Catholic reading real force, so who the "rock" is remains honestly debated. The card as a whole is strong in practice because it doesn't need to win that debate: succession, Rome, and infallibility are simply absent from Scripture.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Catholic apologists Will raise Kepha and Isa 22 Lead with the confession and 1 Cor 3:11; fall back to Line 2 without hesitation.
Cultural Catholics Often assume the pope is "like a prophet" Read Matt 16:13–23 together, including verse 23; then 1 Pet 5:1.
Orthodox Agree with you against papal supremacy Use common ground, then turn to 3K.

Trap questions

  1. "What question was Jesus asking in Matthew 16, and what was Peter's answer?" (Matt 16:15–16)
  2. "Who does Paul say is the only foundation of the church?" (1 Cor 3:11)
  3. "Five verses after 'on this rock,' what does Jesus call Peter?" (Matt 16:23)
  4. "Where does Scripture mention Peter's successors, or Rome?"

30-second version

"Jesus asked, 'Who do you say that I am?' and Peter answered, 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.' That truth is the rock: Paul says no one can lay any foundation but Jesus Christ (1 Cor 3:11). Five verses later Jesus calls Peter 'Satan' for resisting the cross. And even if Peter were the rock, the Bible never mentions a successor, Rome, or an infallible pope."

2-minute version

"Let's read Matthew 16 together. Jesus asks his disciples, 'Who do you say that I am?' Peter answers, 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.' Jesus says that truth was revealed by the Father, and then: 'You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church.'

I believe the rock is that confession, and really the Christ it confesses. Scripture consistently calls God the Rock, Paul says 'the Rock was Christ' and that no one can lay any foundation other than Jesus Christ, and Peter himself later calls Jesus the cornerstone and believers living stones. Even early Christians like John Chrysostom read it as 'the faith of his confession.' And just five verses later, when Peter tries to stop Jesus from going to the cross, Jesus calls him 'Satan.' The church can't rest on Peter's reliability; it rests on Christ.

But suppose you're right that Peter is the rock. The text still says nothing about successors, nothing about Rome, and nothing about infallibility, which the Catholic Church defined in 1870. Peter called himself 'a fellow elder.' The foundation was laid once, and Christ is the cornerstone."
