Argument3JSTRONG

The Unchanging Church Has Changed

Rome's own highest documents supply both sides of the dilemma; the death-penalty and religious-liberty examples are MODERATE on their own

Name + thesis

The "unchanging" Church. Rome offers one main reason to trust it over your own reading of the Bible: its teaching never changes, and Vatican I (1870) forbids ever giving a defined dogma a different meaning from the one the Church first declared. But Rome's own documents reverse themselves. In 1442 an ecumenical council (one of the councils Rome counts as speaking for the whole Church) taught that pagans, Jews, heretics, and schismatics who die outside the Catholic Church go into eternal fire. Today the Catechism says "the plan of salvation also includes" Muslims, who "together with us" adore the one God (CCC 841). So either the council was wrong, or the meaning has changed. Either way the "unchanging Church" claim fails, and the only fixed rule left is the faith "once for all delivered" in Scripture (Jude 3). By that rule, Rome has missed the gospel on both sides: first too narrow (salvation requires submission to the pope), now too wide (people who deny the Son adore the same God).

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "Contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints" (Jude 3). Delivered once and finished, not still unfolding into new dogmas.
  • "Even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed" (Gal 1:8). The apostles put even themselves under the gospel already preached, so no later authority can revise it.
  • "You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men... making void the word of God by your tradition" (Mark 7:8, 13). Jesus judged a religious tradition by Scripture, not the other way around.
  • "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings" (Heb 13:8–9).
  • "There is salvation in no one else" (Acts 4:12). "Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life" (1 John 5:12). "No one who denies the Son has the Father" (1 John 2:23).
  • Verdict: The apostolic gospel was finished, never needed revising, and gives one unchanging line on salvation: whoever has the Son has life. Scripture never moved. Rome did.

Key texts

  • Boniface VIII, Unam Sanctam (18 November 1302): the Church is the one "outside of which there is neither salvation nor forgiveness of sins," and "we declare, say, define, and pronounce that it is altogether necessary for salvation for every human creature to be subject to the Roman Pontiff." (Translated from the Latin.)
  • Council of Florence, Bull of union with the Copts (Session 11, 4 February 1442): the Church "firmly believes, professes, and preaches that none of those outside the Catholic Church, not only pagans but also Jews, heretics, and schismatics, can share in eternal life, but they will go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels, unless they are joined to it before the end of their life." It adds that no one, "even if he has shed his blood for the name of Christ, can be saved unless he has remained in the bosom and unity of the Catholic Church." (Translated from the Latin.)
  • Vatican I, Dei Filius (1870), ch. 4: the meaning of the dogmas "that holy mother Church has once declared must be kept forever," and must never be abandoned "under the pretense or name of a deeper understanding." Canon 4.3 pronounces anathema (formal condemnation) on anyone who says that, as knowledge advances, a dogma may be given "a sense different from the one the Church has understood and understands." (Translated from the Latin.)
  • Vatican II, Lumen Gentium 16 (1964), quoted in CCC 841: "The plan of salvation also includes those who acknowledge the Creator, in the first place amongst whom are the Muslims; these profess to hold the faith of Abraham, and together with us they adore the one, merciful God, mankind's judge on the last day."
  • CCC 847: those who "through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel of Christ or his Church," but seek God sincerely and follow their conscience, "may achieve eternal salvation."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. Development isn't change. John Henry Newman (An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine, 1845) argued that doctrine grows like an acorn into an oak: the same life, more fully expressed. Vincent of Lérins (c. 434) allowed growth "in the same doctrine, in the same sense, and in the same meaning" (Commonitory 23.54), and Vatican I uses his words. Protestants accept development too: "Trinity" and Nicaea's "of one substance" are not words in the Bible.
  2. "No salvation outside the Church" always had a qualifier. Trent (1547) said justification can't happen without baptism "or the desire for it" (Session 6, ch. 4). Aquinas taught "baptism of desire" (Summa Theologiae III, q. 68, a. 2). In 1863 Pius IX taught that people in "invincible ignorance" (not knowing the truth through no fault of their own) who live honest lives "are able to attain eternal life" (Quanto Conficiamur Moerore 7). Vatican II only spells this out. And Rome still teaches that anyone who knows the Catholic Church is necessary and refuses to enter it "could not be saved" (CCC 846).
  3. Rome itself rejected the harsh reading. In 1949 the Holy Office (Rome's doctrinal office) corrected Fr. Leonard Feeney of Boston, who read Florence literally. Its letter, approved by Pius XII, said that in invincible ignorance "God accepts also an implicit desire."
  4. Not everything a pope says is infallible. Only ex cathedra definitions (the pope formally defining a doctrine for the whole Church) and solemn conciliar definitions are irreformable. Earlier teaching on the death penalty and religious liberty can be refined. The Vatican's doctrinal office called the 2018 death-penalty revision "an authentic development of doctrine that is not in contradiction with the prior teachings of the Magisterium."
  5. History favors Rome. Newman wrote, "To be deep in history is to cease to be a Protestant" (Essay, Introduction, 5). Irenaeus (c. 180) listed Rome's bishops back to the apostles (Against Heresies 3.3.3).
  6. Protestants change far more. Thousands of denominations disagree, and Protestant churches have reversed themselves on contraception (the Anglican Lambeth Conference, 1930) and divorce.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Rome teaches that a defined dogma can never be given a different sense from the one the Church declared (Vatican I, Dei Filius ch. 4 and canon 4.3), and it offers this unchanging teaching as the reason to trust it over private reading of Scripture.
  • P2. Rome solemnly taught that everyone outside the Catholic Church, naming pagans, Jews, heretics, and schismatics, goes into eternal fire unless joined to it before death, and that being subject to the pope is necessary for salvation for every human creature (Florence, 1442; Unam Sanctam, 1302).
  • P3. Rome now teaches that the plan of salvation includes Muslims, who adore the one God "together with us"; that baptized non-Catholics are "members of Christ's body"; and that people may be saved without knowing the gospel (Lumen Gentium 16; Unitatis Redintegratio 3; CCC 841, 847).
  • P4. So either the sense of P2 has changed (which P1 forbids), or P2 was wrong (so solemn definitions can err), or P2 "always meant" P3 (so even a defined dogma can't be understood without a later interpreter).
  • C. On every option, Rome's claim to be an unchanging, self-interpreting authority fails. The only fixed rule is the apostolic word (Jude 3; Gal 1:8), and by it both the old position and the new one miss the gospel: "Whoever has the Son has life" (1 John 5:12).

Evidence for each premise

Rome's own dilemma. This works like the Islamic Dilemma (2A): the opponent's own authorities supply both sides. Rome says its dogmas never change their meaning (Vatican I). Then put two of its official texts side by side:

  • 1442 (Florence): pagans, Jews, heretics, and schismatics who die outside the Catholic Church go into eternal fire. Even someone who sheds their blood for Christ can't be saved outside its unity.
  • 1964 to today (Vatican II and the Catechism): Muslims "together with us... adore the one, merciful God," and "the plan of salvation also includes" them (CCC 841). Baptized Protestants "justified by faith in Baptism are members of Christ's body" and are "correctly accepted as brothers" (Unitatis Redintegratio 3).

Either Florence was wrong, or the meaning has changed. Both options deny what Rome says about itself. The third option, that Florence "always meant" what Vatican II says, leads to the next point.

The infallible interpreter needs an interpreter. Rome's main case against Scripture alone is that the Bible's words can be read many ways, so Christians need an infallible interpreter. But Florence's words are plain: "not only pagans but also Jews." If those words actually meant "only those who knowingly reject the Church," then a solemn definition can't be understood without a later pope explaining it. And a later pope's words can be read many ways too. The problem Rome says Scripture has hasn't been solved; it has been moved. The 1949 letter to Boston was needed precisely because a Catholic priest believed what the council said. Wes Huff puts it this way: the claim of unbroken, unchanged teaching sounds good on paper but doesn't survive inspection.

Exhibit 2: religious liberty. In 1832 Gregory XVI called the idea that freedom of conscience must be guaranteed for everyone an "absurd and erroneous opinion, or rather insanity" (deliramentum, Mirari Vos 14, translated from the Latin). In 1864 Pius IX's Syllabus of Errors condemned the statement "Every person is free to embrace and profess the religion he, led by the light of reason, thinks true" (proposition 15), and condemned allowing other faiths public worship in Catholic countries (propositions 77–78). In 1965 Vatican II declared that "the human person has a right to religious freedom" (Dignitatis Humanae 2). Catholics themselves can't agree whether this is a contradiction. Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre's Society of St. Pius X has long insisted it is; other Catholic scholars defend continuity. A Church whose members can't agree whether it has reversed itself can't offer "unchanging teaching" as its credential.

Exhibit 3: the death penalty. The 1990s Catechism said Church teaching "does not exclude recourse to the death penalty, if this is the only possible way of effectively defending human lives against an unjust aggressor" (CCC 2267, as issued under John Paul II). In 2018 Pope Francis replaced that text: the death penalty is now "inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person." The new paragraph itself admits that the death penalty "was long considered an appropriate response." The Vatican insists the change is "not in contradiction" with earlier teaching. If moving from "allowed in rare cases" to "an attack on human dignity" isn't a contradiction, the word has lost its meaning.

Exhibit 4: the papacy itself grew (Wes Huff's history points, with sources):

  • Rome was first led by a group of elders. The Shepherd of Hermas (Rome, early 2nd century) speaks of "the presbyters who preside over the Church" (Vision 2.4.3), in the plural. 1 Clement (c. 96) is sent by "the church of God which sojourns at Rome," never names its author or a single bishop, and uses "episcopate" and "presbyters" for the same office (chs. 42, 44).
  • Ignatius is silent where he'd be loudest. Around 110, Ignatius wrote seven letters insisting on obedience to bishops: "Let no man do anything connected with the Church without the bishop" (Smyrnaeans 8). He names the bishops of Ephesus (Onesimus), Magnesia (Damas), and Tralles (Polybius). His letter to Rome praises the church there but names no bishop at all. As Wes says, from the strongest champion of bishops in the early church, that silence is the elephant in the room.
  • Catholic historians agree. Eamon Duffy (Saints and Sinners: A History of the Popes, Yale, 1997, p. 2) says all the indications are that Rome had no single bishop for almost a century after the apostles died. Jesuit scholar Francis Sullivan writes that scholars hardly doubt Rome was still led by a group of presbyters for at least part of the second century (From Apostles to Bishops, 2001, introduction).
  • The Petrine claim appears in the 250s, and was resisted. One of the earliest clear records of a bishop of Rome resting his authority on succession from Peter is Stephen (c. 256). Bishop Firmilian of Caesarea protested his "folly": Stephen "so boasts of the place of his episcopate, and contends that he holds the succession from Peter" (Cyprian, Letters 74.17 in the Ante-Nicene Fathers numbering).
  • Nicaea treated Rome as one regional church among others. Canon 6 (325) confirms Alexandria's authority over Egypt "since the like is customary for the Bishop of Rome also": a regional custom, not universal rule. The bishop of Rome, Sylvester, didn't even attend. Eusebius says his age kept him away, and two of his presbyters came in his place (Life of Constantine 3.7). As Wes points out, no one treated his absence as a problem.
  • A council condemned a pope as a heretic. The Sixth Ecumenical Council (Constantinople III, 680–681) anathematized Pope Honorius I for supporting the "one will in Christ" heresy. Pope Leo II confirmed it, saying Honorius "did not attempt to sanctify this Apostolic Church with the teaching of Apostolic tradition, but by profane treachery permitted its purity to be polluted" (as quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia, "Pope Honorius I"). The early church didn't think a bishop of Rome couldn't err in doctrine.
  • The full claim came late. Wes dates explicit claims of Rome's universal supremacy to Damasus (366–384), Leo the Great (440–461), and Gelasius (492–496). Papal infallibility wasn't defined until 1870.

Even Newman had to give up the old test. The classic Catholic rule was Vincent of Lérins's: hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all" (Commonitory 2.6). Newman admitted the rule "is more serviceable in determining what is not, than what is Christianity" (Essay, Introduction, 8), and built his theory of development to explain changes the old rule couldn't. Historian Owen Chadwick traces how the older Catholic conviction that doctrine never changes gave way to Newman's idea (From Bossuet to Newman, 1957). Wes's point: the bishops at Trent would not have accepted Newman's theory. The claim moved from "we never change" to "our changes are developments."

The gospel never moved. Here is the deepest point. Rome swung from one side of the apostolic line to the other. In 1302, salvation required being subject to the Roman pontiff, which Scripture never says. Today, Muslims who deny that Jesus is the Son of God "adore the one, merciful God" with Catholics, which Scripture denies: "No one who denies the Son has the Father" (1 John 2:23; see 2M). The apostles' line has never changed in any century: salvation is in Christ alone (Acts 4:12), received through faith (Rom 4:5), and "whoever has the Son has life" (1 John 5:12).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "Development, not contradiction." "An acorn becomes an oak without becoming a different tree. The Church has always taught that people can be saved through invincible ignorance or implicit desire (Trent, Aquinas, Pius IX). Vatican II just made it explicit. You're calling growth a reversal."

Answer: Concede what is true: doctrine can be clarified, and Trent and Pius IX did speak of desire and invincible ignorance. Then apply a fair test of real development: it makes explicit what was already taught, and it never says the opposite of an earlier definition. Nicaea passes that test, because "of one substance" can be checked against John 1:1 and John 20:28. Now compare Florence with the Catechism. Florence named whole groups ("not only pagans but also Jews") and said even someone who dies for Christ can't be saved outside the Church's unity. The Catechism says Muslims adore the one God with Catholics and are included in the plan of salvation. An acorn keeps its species. This changes direction. Two more points:

  1. Who decides what counts as development? Only Rome. So the test is circular: Rome checks Rome and always passes.
  2. The desire Trent meant was desire for baptism. Trent spoke of people who want baptism and die before receiving it. Stretching that to an "implicit desire" in people who explicitly reject the Trinity is exactly the change being debated.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Florence only meant people who knowingly reject the Church."

  • Close (R1): The text names whole groups, pagans and Jews, and says even a martyr for Christ can't be saved outside its unity. Nothing in it limits it to people who know better.
  • Their comeback: "Pius IX and the 1949 letter show the Church always read it that way."
  • Close (R2): Then the plain words of a solemn definition didn't mean what they said until later popes explained them. So who explains the later popes? That's the very problem Rome says Scripture has, and the infallible interpreter hasn't solved it.

2. "Those weren't infallible statements."

  • Close (R1): Fine. Then which statements are? Rome has never published an official list of infallible teachings, and Catholic theologians disagree about many, including Unam Sanctam's "we define."
  • Their comeback: "Theologians agree on the main ones, like the two Marian dogmas."
  • Close (R2): So Catholics are told to submit to the Magisterium because Scripture is unclear, yet can't say for sure which magisterial teachings can never change. Every word of Scripture, by contrast, is God-breathed (2 Tim 3:16) and fixed.

3. "Protestants change far more."

  • Close (R1): Protestants do disagree, and churches do err, but we have never claimed an infallible church. We claim an unchanging Scripture and a church always being reformed by it. Rome claims it can't err when it defines doctrine. That's why a reversal counts against Rome in a way it doesn't count against us.
  • Their comeback: "Then you have no way to settle disputes."
  • Close (R2): We settle them the way the apostles did: "examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so" (Acts 17:11). Jesus settled disputes with "Have you not read?" (Matt 19:4; Matt 22:31).

4. "To be deep in history is to cease to be a Protestant."

  • Close (R1): Newman wrote that in the same book where he admitted that Vincent's "always, everywhere, by all" test couldn't establish Catholic doctrine. That's why he needed a theory of development. Wes Huff says the opposite happened to him: his study of history is what made him a convinced Protestant.
  • Their comeback: "Irenaeus lists Rome's bishops back to Peter."
  • Close (R2): Irenaeus says Rome was founded by both Peter and Paul, and that the apostles handed the office of bishop to Linus (Against Heresies 3.3.2–3). So in his list Peter isn't the first pope. He wrote around 180, when Catholic historians like Duffy and Sullivan say Rome had only recently come under a single bishop. The earlier Roman sources (Hermas, 1 Clement) speak of presbyters in the plural.

5. "The papacy was there in seed form: Clement corrected Corinth, and Ignatius says Rome 'presides over love.'"

  • Close (R1): 1 Clement comes from "the church of God which sojourns at Rome," not from a pope, and never names its author. Ignatius honors the Roman church, but unlike his letters to Ephesus, Magnesia, and Tralles, he names no bishop there.
  • Their comeback: "Silence isn't evidence."
  • Close (R2): It is when the writer would certainly have spoken. Ignatius is the early church's strongest champion of bishops ("nothing... without the bishop," Smyrnaeans 8). If Rome had a supreme bishop, he's the one writer we'd expect to mention him.

6. "Honorius didn't speak ex cathedra."

  • Close (R1): Granted. Catholic scholars say his letter wasn't a formal definition. But an ecumenical council and a later pope condemned a pope as a heretic, which shows the early church didn't think a bishop of Rome couldn't err in doctrine.
  • Their comeback: "Infallibility only covers ex cathedra definitions."
  • Close (R2): And that limit was defined in 1870. That's the point: the conditions that protect the claim were written long after the cases that challenge it.

Boomerang check

"You're cherry-picking a few obscure statements." These aren't obscure. They are an ecumenical council (Florence), a papal bull that ends "we define," a constitution of Vatican II, and the official Catechism. Read them side by side with your friend.

"The Trinity developed too, so your faith changed as well." The doctrine of the Trinity puts into words what Scripture already says (Matt 28:19; John 1:1; 2 Cor 13:14), and anyone can check Nicaea against the text. Protestants don't claim Nicaea's bishops were infallible, only that they were right because Scripture says so. As Wes Huff puts it, tradition has a voice and a vote, but Scripture has the veto.

"So you think Catholics can't be Christians." No. Wes Huff says plainly that many Catholics are genuine believers, saved in spite of Rome's official teaching, not because of it. Luther granted that "much that is Christian and good" remained under the papacy (Concerning Rebaptism, 1528), and Calvin spoke of churches among them where "Christ lies hid, half buried" (Institutes 4.2.12). The aim is to lead friends to the unchanging word, not to win a point.

Strength rating

STRONG. The core dilemma uses Rome's own highest-level documents: an ecumenical council, a solemn papal definition, Vatican I, Vatican II, and the Catechism. The best Catholic reply ("it always meant that") gives up the key point: the plain meaning of a solemn definition can't be trusted without a later interpreter. Taken alone, the religious-liberty and death-penalty examples are MODERATE, because Catholics can call the earlier teaching non-infallible. Use them to support the main example, not to replace it. Catholic historians largely concede the early-papacy evidence.

Trap questions

  1. "Does your Church teach that a dogma's meaning can ever change?" (Vatican I says never.)
  2. "What did the Council of Florence say happens to Jews and pagans who die outside the Catholic Church?"
  3. "Does CCC 841 sound like the same teaching?"
  4. "If an infallible definition needs a later pope to explain it, who explains the later pope?"
  5. "Which bishop does Ignatius greet in his letter to the Romans?"
  6. "How many bishops of Rome attended the Council of Nicaea?" (None. Sylvester sent presbyters.)

30-second version

"Vatican I says a dogma's meaning can never change. But in 1442 the Council of Florence taught that pagans, Jews, heretics, and schismatics who die outside the Catholic Church go into eternal fire. Today the Catechism says the plan of salvation includes Muslims who adore the one God with Catholics (CCC 841). Either the council was wrong or the meaning changed. Scripture never moved: 'Whoever has the Son has life' (1 John 5:12)."

2-minute version

"Can I show you something that really bothers me? Catholics are told to trust the Church over their own reading of the Bible, because the Church's teaching never changes. Vatican I even says a dogma's meaning can never be changed in the name of deeper understanding.

But in 1442 the Council of Florence said that pagans, Jews, heretics, and schismatics who die outside the Catholic Church go into eternal fire, and that even someone who dies for Christ can't be saved outside it. In 1302 a pope defined that being subject to the pope is necessary for every human being's salvation. Now the Catechism says the plan of salvation includes Muslims, who adore the one God together with Catholics. Those can't both be the unchanging meaning. Either the council was wrong, or the meaning changed.

And if the answer is 'Florence always meant what Vatican II says,' then even an infallible definition needs a later pope to tell you what it means. So the Church hasn't solved the problem it says the Bible has.

The papacy itself grew too. The early Roman church was led by a group of elders. Even Catholic historians admit there was no single bishop at Rome for decades after the apostles.

Meanwhile one thing hasn't changed in two thousand years: 'Whoever has the Son has life.' That's where I want to stand, on the word that never moves."

Argument3JSTRONG

Justified by Faith Alone

the Pauline texts are explicit; James 2 has a clear answer

Name + thesis

Justification. Scripture teaches that God declares sinners righteous through faith alone, apart from works, because Christ's righteousness is credited to them. The Council of Trent condemned this teaching. On the central question of how a sinner is made right with God, Rome's official position contradicts the apostolic gospel. Wes Huff names the real divide: Rome agrees that grace, faith, and Christ are necessary; the Reformation says, from Scripture, that they are sufficient.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "We hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law" (Rom 3:28).
  • "To the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness" (Rom 4:5).
  • "By grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works" (Eph 2:8–9).
  • "...not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ" (Phil 3:9).
  • Verdict: Paul repeatedly excludes works from the ground of justification. Good works follow as fruit (Eph 2:10).

Key texts

  • Gal 2:16: "a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ."
  • Council of Trent, Session 6 (1547), Canon 9: "If anyone says that the sinner is justified by faith alone, meaning that nothing else is required to cooperate in order to obtain the grace of justification... let him be anathema."
  • Trent, Session 6, Canon 24: anathematizes anyone who says good works are only the fruits and signs of justification and not a cause of its increase.
  • Trent, Session 6, ch. 7: justification "is not remission of sins merely, but also the sanctification and renewal of the inward man"; its instrumental cause is "the sacrament of baptism"; and "we are not only reputed, but are truly called, and are just." Canon 11 condemns the view that we are justified by Christ's righteousness credited to us alone, without grace poured into the heart. Canon 32 teaches that the good works of the justified truly merit an increase of grace and eternal life.
  • CCC 1129: "for believers the sacraments of the New Covenant are necessary for salvation." CCC 2010: "we can then merit for ourselves and for others the graces needed for our sanctification, for the increase of grace and charity, and for the attainment of eternal life."
  • James 2:24: "You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. James 2:24 is the only place "faith alone" appears in the Bible, and it denies it.
  2. "Works of the law" in Paul means the Mosaic law (circumcision, food laws), not all good works. Paul opposes Jewish boundary markers, not grace-enabled obedience.
  3. Catholics believe salvation is by grace. Trent itself says nothing before justification merits it (Session 6, ch. 8). Works done in grace are God's work in us (Phil 2:13).
  4. Judgment is according to works (Rom 2:6–7; Matt 25:31–46; 2 Cor 5:10).
  5. Justification is real transformation, not a legal fiction: God makes us righteous, not just declares us so.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Scripture teaches that a sinner is justified before God through faith, apart from works (Rom 3:28; 4:4–5; Gal 2:16; Eph 2:8–9; Phil 3:9).
  • P2. The Council of Trent anathematizes those who teach justification by faith alone (Session 6, Canon 9) and teaches that works increase justification (Canon 24).
  • P3. James 2 addresses a different question (the evidence of genuine faith), so it doesn't contradict P1.
  • C. Rome's official doctrine of justification departs from the apostolic gospel (Gal 1:8–9).

Evidence for each premise

"Works" in Paul is broader than the Mosaic law. In Rom 4:4–5 the contrast is between working and believing, wages and gift. Abraham is Paul's example, and he lived before the law (Rom 4:10, 13). In Eph 2:8–9 and Titus 3:5 ("not because of works done by us in righteousness") the works excluded are any works at all.

Justification is a verdict. "Justify" is the opposite of "condemn" (Deut 25:1; Rom 8:33–34). Judges don't make people righteous; they declare them so. God credits righteousness to the ungodly who believe (Rom 4:5–6), because Christ was made sin for us "so that in him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Cor 5:21).

Necessary or sufficient? (Wes Huff's key.) Rome doesn't deny grace, faith, or Christ. It calls them necessary, and then adds more that is necessary: the sacraments are "necessary for salvation" (CCC 1129), grace is poured in at baptism (Trent, Session 6, ch. 7), and the good works of the justified "merit... the attainment of eternal life" (CCC 2010; Trent, Canon 32). Scripture says more than "necessary." It says "sufficient":

  • Grace is sufficient: "if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace" (Rom 11:6). God "saved us... not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began" (2 Tim 1:9).
  • Christ's work is sufficient: "By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified" (Heb 10:14), so "there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Rom 8:1).
  • We bring nothing to add: "Those who are in the flesh cannot please God" (Rom 8:8), and "without faith it is impossible to please him" (Heb 11:6). Salvation has to come entirely from Christ.
  • Faith is sufficient because of what it holds. The Reformers didn't make faith a work that earns. Melanchthon wrote to Johannes Brenz (May 1531) that faith justifies not because it is a new work of the Spirit in us, but because it lays hold of Christ, for whose sake we are accepted. Luther pictured faith as a marriage (The Freedom of a Christian, 1520): it joins the soul to Christ like a bride to her bridegroom, so Christ takes her sins, death, and damnation, and she receives his grace, life, and salvation. Calvin: faith "consists in the knowledge of God and Christ, not in reverence for the Church" (Institutes 3.2.3).

Declared righteous first, then made holy. Trent says God declares just only those who are actually just inside: "truly called, and are just" (Session 6, ch. 7). Scripture separates the verdict from the lifelong change. "You were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified" (1 Cor 6:11) names them as distinct. And it speaks of justification as finished: "since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God" (Rom 5:1); "we have now been justified by his blood" (Rom 5:9); "those whom he justified he also glorified" (Rom 8:30). God "justifies the ungodly" (Rom 4:5), so the verdict comes to people who are not yet righteous in themselves. As Wes puts it, holiness is the effect of justification, not its cause: it is received, not achieved.

James answers a different question. James asks what kind of faith saves: "Can that faith save him?" (James 2:14). His test is "Show me your faith" (James 2:18). Abraham was credited righteous in Gen 15:6, decades before he offered Isaac in Gen 22. That offering showed his faith was real and fulfilled the earlier verdict ("the Scripture was fulfilled," James 2:23). Paul and James agree: faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone (Gal 5:6; Eph 2:10).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: James 2:24. "Scripture says 'not by faith alone.' You add 'alone' to Paul and remove it from James."

Answer: James uses "justified" in the sense of "shown to be righteous," as in Luke 7:35 ("wisdom is justified by all her children") and James's own "show me" (James 2:18). The faith James rejects is a faith of words without deeds (James 2:15–16), even the demons' kind of belief (James 2:19). Paul rejects works as the ground of the verdict. James rejects empty faith as evidence of it. Both texts are honored without contradiction.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "'Works of the law' means circumcision and food laws."

  • Close (R1): Then why does Paul make the contrast work-versus-gift (Rom 4:4–5) and use Abraham, who lived before Moses? Why does Eph 2:9 say simply "not a result of works"?
  • Their comeback: "Ephesians means works done without grace."
  • Close (R2): Paul says the opposite: the good works God prepared come after salvation (Eph 2:10). They are its result, not its cause.

2. "Catholics believe in grace, not earning."

  • Close (R1): Agreed, and that's common ground. The question is whether grace-enabled works become part of the ground of justification. Trent says they increase it (Canon 24) and anathematizes faith alone (Canon 9). This was John MacArthur's central objection to the 1994 "Evangelicals and Catholics Together" statement (Reckless Faith, 1994): shared language about grace isn't a shared gospel while Trent's canons stand.
  • Their comeback: "You're misreading Trent."
  • Close (R2): Read the canon aloud together. Then ask whether the thief on the cross (Luke 23:43) was justified by faith with no works.

3. "Judgment is according to works."

  • Close (R1): Yes: works are the evidence at judgment (Matt 7:16–20), not the ground of acceptance. Those in Christ face no condemnation (Rom 8:1).
  • Their comeback: "Then works don't matter."
  • Close (R2): They matter enormously, as fruit. "Faith apart from works is dead" (James 2:26). A living tree bears fruit; the fruit doesn't make it alive.

4. "Justification includes sanctification. It's a lifelong process" (Trent, Session 6, ch. 7).

  • Close (R1): Scripture names them separately: "you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified" (1 Cor 6:11). And it speaks of justification as already done: "since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God" (Rom 5:1).
  • Their comeback: "Then a justified person can live however they like."
  • Close (R2): No. Everyone God justifies, he also sanctifies (Rom 6:22; Phil 1:6). But the change is the fruit of a finished verdict, not part of its ground. If it were part of the ground, no one could have "no condemnation" now (Rom 8:1) until the change was complete.

Boomerang check

"So Protestants think Catholics deny grace." No. As Wes Huff says, both sides agree that grace, faith, and Christ are necessary. The disagreement is whether they are sufficient: does Christ's finished work, received by faith, settle your standing with God, or does it need sacraments, merit, and (if needed) purgatory to complete it?

"Faith alone leads to lawless living." Paul faced that charge and rejected it: "Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!" (Rom 6:1–2). The faith that justifies unites us to Christ, and union with Christ produces new life (Rom 6:4; 2 Cor 5:17).

Strength rating

STRONG. The key Pauline texts are explicit; Trent's canons are clear and official; and James 2 has a well-grounded answer in its own context.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Devout Catholics Feel accused of believing in earning Affirm their belief in grace, then show Trent Canon 9.
Catholic apologists Will use James 2 and the "works of the law" argument Use Rom 4:4–5 and Gen 15/22 timing.
Cultural Catholics Often hope they've "been good enough" Lead with assurance: Rom 5:1; 1 John 5:13.

Trap questions

  1. "When was Abraham counted righteous, Genesis 15 or Genesis 22?"
  2. "In Romans 4:5, whom does God justify: the godly who work, or the ungodly who believe?"
  3. "What good works had the thief on the cross done, and where did Jesus say he'd be that day?" (Luke 23:43)

30-second version

"Paul says God 'justifies the ungodly' who trust him, apart from works (Rom 4:5), and that we're saved by grace through faith, 'not a result of works' (Eph 2:8–9). James agrees that real faith always shows itself in works (James 2:18). Works are the fruit of salvation, not its root. That means you can know you're forgiven today (Rom 5:1)."

2-minute version

"I know Catholics believe salvation is by God's grace, and I'm glad we agree there. The question is what God's verdict rests on.

Paul gives Abraham as the example. God counted him righteous in Genesis 15, when he simply believed the promise. Paul says, 'to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness' (Rom 4:5). That's not someone who has earned it; it's someone who trusts.

James 2 is often quoted against this, but James is asking whether a faith with no deeds is real. Abraham's offering of Isaac in Genesis 22, decades later, showed his faith was real. Paul and James agree: faith alone saves, but saving faith is never alone.

The Council of Trent condemned 'justification by faith alone.' I can't follow it there, because Paul says that if we add anything to the gospel of grace, we've changed it (Gal 1:8–9). And the good news is that you can know you have peace with God now (Rom 5:1)."

Further reading

  • R. C. Sproul, Faith Alone: The Evangelical Doctrine of Justification (Baker, 1995)
  • John MacArthur, Reckless Faith (Crossway, 1994), on Evangelicals and Catholics Together; and Faith Works: The Gospel According to the Apostles (Word, 1993)
  • Thomas R. Schreiner, Faith Alone (Zondervan, 2015)
  • The Council of Trent, Session 6 (decree and canons on justification), read in full
  • Catholic side: Jimmy Akin, The Drama of Salvation (Catholic Answers, 2015)
  • Primary texts: Martin Luther, The Freedom of a Christian (1520); John Calvin, Institutes 3.2 (on faith) and 3.11 (on justification)
  • Videos on this topic: A Messenger of Truth, "What are Works of the Law?" and "What Works Prove We are Saved?"; Wes Huff, "6 reasons why I'm not Roman Catholic" (sufficiency starts 2 min 31 s in; justification starts 34 min 55 s in)
Argument3JSTRONG

The Mass and Christ's Once-for-All Sacrifice

Hebrews is explicit that no further offering for sin remains

Name + thesis

The sacrifice of the Mass. The Catholic Church teaches that the Mass is a true, propitiatory sacrifice in which Christ is offered "in an unbloody manner." Hebrews teaches that Christ offered himself once for all, that his sacrifice was finished, and that "there is no longer any offering for sin."

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily... since he did this once for all when he offered up himself" (Heb 7:27).
  • "By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified" (Heb 10:14).
  • "Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin" (Heb 10:18).
  • "It is finished" (John 19:30).
  • Verdict: Scripture presents the Lord's Supper as a remembrance and proclamation of a finished sacrifice (1 Cor 11:24–26), not as the offering of a sacrifice.

Key texts

  • Heb 9:25–26: "Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly... he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself."
  • Council of Trent, Session 22 (1562), Canon 1: anathema to anyone who says that in the Mass "a true and proper sacrifice is not offered to God"; Canon 3: anathema to anyone who says it is not a propitiatory sacrifice.
  • CCC 1367: "The sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice... the same Christ who offered himself once in a bloody manner on the altar of the cross is contained and is offered in an unbloody manner."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. It's not a new sacrifice. The Mass doesn't repeat Calvary; it re-presents (makes present) the one sacrifice (CCC 1366–1367). Hebrews denies repetition, which Catholics also deny.
  2. Jesus said, "This is my body" (Matt 26:26), and "unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you" (John 6:53).
  3. Malachi 1:11 foresees "a pure offering" among the nations.
  4. Paul compares the Lord's table to altars (1 Cor 10:16–21).
  5. The early church spoke of the Eucharist as a sacrifice (Didache 14; Ignatius, Smyrnaeans 7).

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Catholic dogma teaches that the Mass is a true and proper, propitiatory sacrifice offered to God (Trent, Session 22, Canons 1 and 3).
  • P2. Scripture teaches that Christ's sacrifice was offered once, perfected believers for all time, and left "no longer any offering for sin" (Heb 7:27; 10:10–18).
  • P3. Scripture describes the Lord's Supper as remembrance and proclamation (Luke 22:19; 1 Cor 11:24–26), never as a propitiatory offering.
  • C. The sacrifice of the Mass is not an apostolic doctrine and obscures the finished work of Christ.

Evidence for each premise

Hebrews' whole argument is "once, finished." The old priests stood daily, offering repeatedly; Christ "sat down" because his work was done (Heb 10:11–12). The words "once for all" (ephapax) recur (Heb 7:27; 9:12; 10:10). The conclusion is explicit: where sins are forgiven, "there is no longer any offering for sin" (Heb 10:18).

"Do this in remembrance of me." Jesus commands remembrance (Luke 22:19). Paul says that in eating and drinking "you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes" (1 Cor 11:26). The Supper points back to a finished death; it doesn't offer that death to God again.

John 6 explains itself. Jesus says, "whoever believes has eternal life" (John 6:47) and "whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst" (John 6:35). Coming and believing are the eating and drinking. He adds, "the words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life" (John 6:63). John 6 is also before the Last Supper was instituted.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "re-presentation, not repetition." "Catholics agree the sacrifice happened once. The Mass makes that one sacrifice present."

Answer: Then ask why the Mass must be offered to God as propitiatory, offered daily for the living and the dead (Trent, Session 22, ch. 2). Hebrews contrasts Christ with priests who offer continually (Heb 10:11–12), and says nothing remains to be offered (Heb 10:18). Scripture has no category of an ongoing, unbloody offering of Christ. The apostolic Supper is a meal of remembrance and fellowship (1 Cor 10:16), not a priestly sacrifice.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "This is my body" is literal.

  • Close (R1): Jesus was physically present, holding the bread, when he said it. He also called himself the door and the vine (John 10:9; 15:1). And he called the cup "the fruit of the vine" after blessing it (Matt 26:29).
  • Their comeback: "Those are obvious metaphors; the Eucharist isn't."
  • Close (R2): Even granting a real presence, which many Protestants affirm in a spiritual sense, the issue is sacrifice. Hebrews says no offering for sin remains (Heb 10:18).

2. Malachi 1:11's "pure offering."

  • Close (R1): The New Testament applies sacrifice language to believers' praise, lives, and gifts (Rom 12:1; Phil 4:18; Heb 13:15–16; 1 Pet 2:5). That fulfills Malachi without a propitiatory Mass.
  • Their comeback: "The fathers read Malachi of the Eucharist."
  • Close (R2): As witnesses, they show an early interpretation; they aren't apostles. Scripture itself interprets Christian sacrifice as praise and self-offering.

3. "The early church called it a sacrifice."

  • Close (R1): Didache 14 calls the thanksgiving meal a "sacrifice" while connecting it to confession and to Malachi; thanksgiving was a sacrifice (Heb 13:15). That isn't Trent's propitiatory sacrifice.
  • Their comeback: "Later fathers were more explicit."
  • Close (R2): Doctrine developing later isn't apostolic doctrine (1D).

Boomerang check

"Protestants ignore John 6 and the real presence." Many Protestants (Lutherans, and the Reformed in a spiritual sense) affirm Christ's real presence in the Supper. This card targets the propitiatory sacrifice, which is the point Hebrews addresses directly.

Strength rating

STRONG. Trent's canons and the Catechism are explicit, and Hebrews 7–10 is explicit that the sacrifice is finished with no remaining offering for sin. The "re-presentation" reply is coherent, but Scripture never states it.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust

Catholic apologists Will cite John 6 and Malachi Use John 6:35, 47, 63 and Heb 10:18.
Cultural Catholics Often think the Mass is how they "keep forgiven" Lead with assurance: Heb 10:14, 17–18.

Trap questions

  1. "Hebrews says the old priests stood daily, but Christ sat down. Why did he sit down?" (Heb 10:11–12)
  2. "What does Hebrews 10:18 say remains after sins are forgiven?"
  3. "In John 6, what does Jesus say we must do to have eternal life?" (John 6:47)

30-second version

"Hebrews says Jesus offered himself 'once for all,' and 'by a single offering he has perfected for all time' those who are his (Heb 10:14). Then it says there's 'no longer any offering for sin' (Heb 10:18). The Lord's Supper proclaims a finished sacrifice (1 Cor 11:26). You don't need it offered again; it's done (John 19:30)."

2-minute version

"I love the Lord's Supper too. Jesus told us to do it in remembrance of him, and when we do we proclaim his death until he comes.

But the Catholic Church teaches that the Mass is itself a propitiatory sacrifice offered to God; Trent says so, and so does the Catechism. When I read Hebrews, I see the opposite emphasis. The old priests stood every day offering sacrifices that could never take away sins. Jesus offered himself once, and then he sat down, because the work was finished. 'By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.' And then: 'Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.'

That's the best news there is. You don't need a sacrifice offered for you again and again. Jesus said 'It is finished,' and he meant it."

Further reading

  • John MacArthur, The MacArthur New Testament Commentary: Hebrews (Moody, 1983), on Heb 7–10
  • James R. White, The Roman Catholic Controversy (Bethany House, 1996), chapter on the Mass
  • The Council of Trent, Session 22; CCC 1356–1372
  • Catholic side: Brant Pitre, Jesus and the Jewish Roots of the Eucharist (Image, 2011)
Argument3JSTRONG

The Marian Dogmas Have No Apostolic Basis

the Immaculate Conception and Assumption have no scriptural text; perpetual virginity is MODERATE

Name + thesis

The Marian dogmas. Rome requires belief that Mary was conceived without original sin (defined 1854) and was assumed body and soul into heaven (defined 1950), and it teaches her perpetual virginity. Scripture teaches none of these. Mary is "blessed among women," and the Bible shows her as a humble believer who needed a Savior.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • Mary herself says, "my spirit rejoices in God my Savior" (Luke 1:47).
  • "All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Rom 3:23); the only exception Scripture names is Christ (Heb 4:15; 2 Cor 5:21).
  • Jesus redirects praise of his mother: "Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!" (Luke 11:27–28).
  • Joseph "knew her not until she had given birth to a son" (Matt 1:25), and Jesus' brothers and sisters are named (Mark 6:3).
  • Verdict: No text teaches an immaculate conception or a bodily assumption, and the natural reading of Matt 1:25 and Mark 6:3 counts against perpetual virginity.

Key texts

  • Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus (1854): Mary was preserved free from all stain of original sin from the first instant of her conception; anyone who thinks otherwise "has suffered shipwreck in the faith."
  • Pius XII, Munificentissimus Deus (1950): Mary, "having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory"; whoever denies it "has fallen away completely from the divine and Catholic Faith."
  • Luke 1:28: "Greetings, O favored one (kecharitomene), the Lord is with you!"

Their best case (steelman)

  1. Kecharitomene (Luke 1:28) is a perfect participle: "having been graced," implying a completed, lasting state of grace from the start.
  2. Mary is the new Ark (compare Luke 1:39–56 with 2 Sam 6). The ark was holy and kept pure; so was the one who carried the Word made flesh.
  3. Revelation 12 shows "a woman clothed with the sun" in heaven, giving birth to the Messiah.
  4. "Saved" can mean preserved. God saved Mary by preventing sin, so Luke 1:47 still applies.
  5. "Brothers" can mean cousins or relatives (Gen 13:8, where Lot is Abraham's nephew), and "until" doesn't always imply change afterward (2 Sam 6:23).

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The Catholic Church requires belief in the Immaculate Conception and the Assumption as revealed dogma (1854; 1950).
  • P2. A revealed dogma must be taught by the apostles (1D).
  • P3. No apostolic writing teaches either dogma; Scripture's statements about universal sin and Mary's need of a Savior point the other way.
  • C. These dogmas are not apostolic, and binding them on consciences adds to the faith once delivered (Jude 3).

Evidence for each premise

Kecharitomene doesn't carry the weight. The same verb appears in Eph 1:6 ("his grace, with which he has blessed [echaritosen] us in the Beloved"), applied to all believers. A perfect participle shows that Mary had been favored, not when or how. The angel explains the favor himself: she will bear the Son of God (Luke 1:30–31).

The Assumption has no early witness. Scripture records no event. Most accounts of Mary's departure (the Transitus narratives) can't be dated much before the 5th century, though Stephen Shoemaker argues a few were composed by the 3rd century; they also disagree with one another (Ancient Traditions of the Virgin Mary's Dormition and Assumption, Oxford, 2002). None is apostolic. Epiphanius (c. 377) says no one knows how Mary's life ended (Panarion 78.11 and 78.23; section numbers vary by edition).

Revelation 12's woman flees into the wilderness and is protected for 1,260 days (Rev 12:6, 14) and has other offspring persecuted by the dragon (Rev 12:17). The image fits Israel and the people of God (compare Gen 37:9–10).

Jesus' family. The Gospels mention his mother and his brothers together (Mark 3:31–32; John 2:12; Acts 1:14). John says "not even his brothers believed in him" (John 7:5). Paul names "James the Lord's brother" (Gal 1:19). Greek has a word for cousin (anepsios, Col 4:10), which the New Testament never uses for these men.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: perpetual virginity. "'Brothers' had a broad range in Jewish usage, and Mary's question 'How will this be, since I am a virgin?' (Luke 1:34) suggests a vow."

Answer: Concede the range of adelphos, which is why this part is MODERATE. But the natural reading of "until" (Matt 1:25) with repeated references to Jesus' brothers with his mother is a family. Luke 1:34 is naturally read as "I have not yet known a man," since she was only betrothed. Keep the focus on the two dogmas that Rome requires (1854, 1950), which have no text at all.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Mary is the new Ark, so she was sinless."

  • Close (R1): The parallels are interesting, but a parallel isn't a doctrine. Scripture never calls Mary an ark, and the ark itself was made by human hands from ordinary acacia wood (Exod 25:10).
  • Their comeback: "The typology is clear in Luke 1."
  • Close (R2): Even granting typology, Luke records Mary calling God "my Savior" (Luke 1:47). Typology can't override a direct statement.

2. "Saved by prevention" (Luke 1:47).

  • Close (R1): Scripture never describes salvation as prevention from ever sinning. Salvation is from sins committed (Matt 1:21). Mary even offered the sin offering after childbirth (Luke 2:22–24; Lev 12:6–8).
  • Their comeback: "That was ritual purity, not moral sin."
  • Close (R2): Then show the text that says Mary had no sin. Romans 3:23 states the rule, and Scripture names only one exception: Christ.

3. "Tradition and the sense of the faithful testify to it."

  • Close (R1): Then admit it isn't in Scripture. Can a doctrine be required for salvation that the apostles never taught?
  • Their comeback: "Doctrine develops (Newman)."
  • Close (R2): Development clarifies what was taught; it can't add new facts about history, like a bodily assumption no apostle records (1D; Jude 3).

Boomerang check

"Protestants dishonor Mary." We call her blessed, as Scripture does (Luke 1:42, 48). We honor her by imitating her faith ("let it be to me according to your word," Luke 1:38) and her pointing to her Son: "Do whatever he tells you" (John 2:5).

Strength rating

STRONG for the Immaculate Conception and the Assumption: they are required dogmas with no apostolic text. MODERATE for perpetual virginity, where adelphos gives Catholics a real (if strained) answer.

Audience notes

Catholic apologists Will use kecharitomene and Ark typology Use Eph 1:6 and Luke 1:47.
Hispanic or Filipino Catholics Marian devotion may be central to family identity Focus on Jesus' words in Luke 11:27–28 and John 2:5.

Trap questions

  1. "What does Mary call God in Luke 1:47?"
  2. "Which apostle records Mary's assumption into heaven?"
  3. "When a woman praised Mary to Jesus, what did he say?" (Luke 11:27–28)

30-second version

"I love that Scripture calls Mary blessed. But she herself calls God 'my Savior' (Luke 1:47), and no apostle mentions an immaculate conception or an assumption into heaven. Those were defined in 1854 and 1950. Mary's last recorded words to us are 'Do whatever he tells you' (John 2:5). That's the honor she wants."

2-minute version

"I want to be careful, because I know how much Mary means to you, and she should mean a lot to every Christian. Scripture says all generations will call her blessed.

But the Catholic Church requires two beliefs about her that I can't find anywhere in Scripture: that she was conceived without original sin, defined in 1854, and that she was taken body and soul into heaven, defined in 1950. Pius XII said anyone who denies the Assumption has fallen away from the faith. That's a serious thing to bind on people if the apostles never taught it.

And Scripture points the other way. Mary rejoices in 'God my Savior.' Paul says all have sinned, and the only exception the Bible names is Jesus. When a woman praised Mary's womb, Jesus said, 'Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it.' Mary's own instruction is the best one: 'Do whatever he tells you.'"

Further reading

  • Tim Perry, Mary for Evangelicals (IVP Academic, 2006)
