  • Stephen J. Shoemaker, Ancient Traditions of the Virgin Mary's Dormition and Assumption (Oxford, 2002): a scholarly history of the early accounts
  • Catholic side: Brant Pitre, Jesus and the Jewish Roots of Mary (Image, 2018)
  • Videos on this topic: Testify, "Why I Don't Believe Mary Was Immaculately Conceived," "Why I Can't Accept the Assumption of Mary," and "I Looked Into Marian Apparitions. I Have Questions."
Defense3J

"Purgatory is in Scripture (1 Corinthians 3:15; 2 Maccabees)."

The objection (best form)

"Paul says a believer 'will be saved, but only as through fire' (1 Cor 3:15). And 2 Maccabees chapter 12 praises prayer for the dead so that they might be loosed from sin. Purgatory purifies those who die in grace but aren't yet perfect (CCC 1030–1031)."

Answer

  • 1 Corinthians 3 is about workers and their work. The fire tests the work built on the foundation, "the Day will disclose it" (1 Cor 3:13). The builder suffers loss of reward, not purification of sins. The context is church leaders building on Christ (1 Cor 3:5–10).
  • 2 Maccabees isn't Scripture. It's not in the Hebrew Bible Jesus called Scripture (Luke 24:44), and Jewish tradition never received it. Even on its own terms, it describes prayer for soldiers who died wearing idolatrous amulets, a mortal sin in Catholic terms, which purgatory doesn't cover.
  • Scripture says Christ's work is complete. "By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified" (Heb 10:14). "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Rom 8:1). To be away from the body is to be "at home with the Lord" (2 Cor 5:8), and the thief went to paradise "today" (Luke 23:43).

30-second version

"First Corinthians 3 is about fire testing a builder's work for reward, not purging sin. And Scripture says Jesus 'perfected for all time' those who are his (Heb 10:14), so the believer who dies is 'at home with the Lord' (2 Cor 5:8). Jesus didn't promise the thief purgatory; he said 'today you will be with me in paradise.'"

3K

Eastern Orthodoxy

4 cards3 strong

New terms

Proskynesis / latreia: Greek words for bowing or veneration (proskynesis) and worship or service (latreia). Nicaea II allowed the first toward icons and reserved the second for God.

Iconoclasm: Opposition to religious images; especially the 8th–9th century Byzantine movement against icon veneration.

Theosis: "Deification": the Orthodox understanding of salvation as union with God and participation in his life.

Ecumenical council: A council claiming to speak for the whole church, such as Nicaea (325) or Chalcedon (451).

Orthodox Christians hold the Nicene faith, love the Scriptures in their liturgy, and often know church history well. Many converts to Orthodoxy come from evangelical churches, so expect careful arguments. Two cards here (prayers to saints, and tradition) apply to Roman Catholics too. As always, the test is the apostolic one (1D).

Argument3KSTRONG

Holy Tradition Needs a Judge: Scripture

rests on Mark 7 and on councils that contradicted each other

Name + thesis

Holy Tradition. Orthodoxy teaches that Scripture lives within Holy Tradition: the councils, fathers, liturgy, and icons together carry the apostolic faith. But Scripture never presents tradition as a co-equal or containing authority, and the history of councils shows that tradition itself needs a judge. The only judge the apostles left is Scripture.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • Jesus condemned "the tradition of men" when it set aside God's command (Mark 7:8–13).
  • "See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition... and not according to Christ" (Col 2:8).
  • Even the apostle Paul's teaching was tested by Scripture (Acts 17:11).
  • Verdict: Tradition is welcome as a servant of Scripture and rejected where it adds to or overrides it.

Key texts

  • 2 Thess 2:15: "hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter."
  • Mark 7:8: "You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men."
  • Second Council of Nicaea (787): required the veneration of icons and anathematized those who refuse it.
  • Council of Hieria (754): a council of over 300 bishops that called itself the Seventh Ecumenical Council and condemned the veneration of icons.

Their best case (steelman)

  1. Scripture is part of Tradition, not opposed to it. The church wrote, received, and canonized the Scriptures, and reads them in the liturgy.
  2. Tradition is the life of the Holy Spirit in the church (Ware), promised by Jesus (John 16:13).
  3. Paul commands holding to unwritten tradition (2 Thess 2:15; 1 Cor 11:2).
  4. Without tradition, Scripture becomes private opinion, as Protestant division shows.
  5. The church recognizes a council as ecumenical by reception: the whole church, over time, accepts it as true.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Tradition can conflict with God's word (Mark 7:8–13), so any tradition needs a standard above it.
  • P2. Councils that claimed the same ecumenical authority have contradicted each other (Ephesus 449 vs. Chalcedon 451; Hieria 754 vs. Nicaea II 787).
  • P3. "Reception" is decided only after the fact and has no standard of its own; the only fixed, God-breathed standard is Scripture (2 Tim 3:16).
  • C. Tradition must be judged by Scripture, not Scripture by tradition.

Evidence for each premise

Rival councils. The Second Council of Ephesus (449), called by the emperor, endorsed Eutyches; Chalcedon (451) overturned it, and Pope Leo called Ephesus II a "robbery" synod. Hieria (754) condemned icons with imperial backing and over 300 bishops; Nicaea II (787) reversed it and anathematized the iconoclasts. Each side claimed the Spirit and the fathers. The church needed a test outside the councils themselves.

"Reception" is circular. A council is ecumenical if the church receives it; the true church is the one that receives the true councils. Orthodox sources themselves note that the bishops have never set out a universal definition of what makes a council ecumenical, and some Orthodox writers call the reception theory circular (OrthodoxWiki, "Ecumenical Councils").

Paul's traditions were his own apostolic teaching (2 Thess 2:15; 1 Cor 11:2, 23), and when he names their content, it is what Scripture contains: the Lord's Supper (1 Cor 11:23–26) and the gospel (1 Cor 15:1–4).

Scripture is sufficient. John MacArthur's case for the sufficiency of Scripture (Our Sufficiency in Christ, 1991) makes the same point from 2 Pet 1:3 and 2 Tim 3:16–17: God has given everything needed for life and godliness in Christ and his word, so tradition can serve Scripture but never complete it.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "Your canon and creeds come from tradition." "You accept the Nicene Creed and the 27-book New Testament because of the councils and fathers."

Answer: We accept the creed because it summarizes Scripture (John 1:1–3; Col 2:9; Heb 1:3), and the canon because the churches received those books as God's word (1D). Recognizing truth is different from creating it. And Orthodoxy itself has never fixed one Old Testament canon for all its churches, which shows that tradition doesn't settle even this cleanly.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "The Spirit guides the church into all truth" (John 16:13).

  • Close (R1): Jesus spoke that promise to the apostles in the upper room, and it was fulfilled in the apostolic teaching and writings (John 14:26).
  • Their comeback: "It extends to the church through the ages."
  • Close (R2): Then which church? Rome, Constantinople, and the Oriental Orthodox each claim it, with contradicting councils. The apostles' writings are the one thing all agree came from the Spirit.

2. "Reception settles which councils are true."

  • Close (R1): Received by whom, and by what standard? Hieria was widely received for decades in the East.
  • Their comeback: "The church eventually rejected it."
  • Close (R2): On what basis? The Nicaea II fathers argued from Scripture and the fathers. So Scripture was being used as the judge, which is the point.

3. "Protestants have their own traditions."

  • Close (R1): Yes, and they're fallible and must be tested by Scripture too. That is exactly the principle.
  • Their comeback: "Then you're your own magisterium."
  • Close (R2): Every believer, Orthodox included, has to judge which church and councils to trust. The question is what standard they use, and Scripture alone is God-breathed (2 Tim 3:16).

Boomerang check

"Scripture alone ignores the church." Not at all. We need the church's teaching, preaching, and history (Eph 4:11–13). We just don't place them on the same level as the word of God (Mark 7:13).

Strength rating

STRONG. Mark 7 gives a clear principle, and the history of contradicting councils is undisputed. The Orthodox reply ("reception") is real but has no standard that doesn't already presuppose the conclusion.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Orthodox converts from evangelicalism Know the arguments; often left over Protestant division Grant the problem; show that councils divide too.
Cradle Orthodox (Greek, Russian, Arab, Ethiopian) Faith tied to culture and liturgy; little debate experience Start with shared love of Scripture in the liturgy.
Catholics Agree with Orthodoxy here The same card applies; add Vatican I.

Trap questions

  1. "When two councils both claiming to be ecumenical contradicted each other, how did the church decide?"
  2. "What did Jesus use to judge the Pharisees' ancient tradition?" (Mark 7:13)
  3. "Can you name a tradition that's binding, isn't in Scripture, and goes back to the apostles verifiably?"

30-second version

"Councils have contradicted each other. Hieria condemned icons in 754, and Nicaea II required them in 787, and both claimed to speak for the church. Jesus showed that even ancient tradition has to be tested by God's word (Mark 7:13). Scripture is the one standard the apostles left that everyone agrees came from God."

2-minute version

"I appreciate how seriously Orthodoxy takes continuity with the early church. I want that too.

But here's my problem with putting tradition on the level of Scripture. Tradition has disagreed with itself. In 449 a large council backed by the emperor approved a heretic, and two years later Chalcedon overturned it. In 754 a council of over 300 bishops condemned icons and called itself ecumenical, and in 787 another council reversed it and anathematized them. How did the church tell which was right? By arguing from Scripture and earlier teaching.

Jesus did the same with the Pharisees. Their tradition was old and claimed to come from Moses, and he said it 'made void the word of God.' So I treasure tradition as a servant. But only Scripture is God-breathed, and it's the judge."

Further reading

  • Robert Letham, Through Western Eyes: Eastern Orthodoxy, A Reformed Perspective (Mentor, 2007)
  • John MacArthur, Our Sufficiency in Christ (Word, 1991); and his chapter on the sufficiency of the written word in Don Kistler (ed.), Sola Scriptura! The Protestant Position on the Bible (Soli Deo Gloria, 1995)
  • James J. Stamoolis (ed.), Three Views on Eastern Orthodoxy and Evangelicalism (Zondervan, 2004): Orthodox and evangelical contributors in dialogue
  • Orthodox side: Timothy (Kallistos) Ware, The Orthodox Church (Penguin, rev. ed.)
  • Videos on this topic: Wes Huff, "What really led to the Council of Nicaea?"
Argument3KSTRONG

Icon Veneration and the Second Commandment

the Greek Old Testament forbids the very act Nicaea II requires

Name + thesis

Icons. The Second Council of Nicaea (787) requires Christians to venerate icons by bowing, kissing, and burning incense before them, and it distinguishes this "veneration" (proskynesis) from "worship" (latreia). But the Second Commandment forbids both. In the Greek Old Testament the early church read, God says of images, "you shall not bow down to them (proskyneseis) or serve them (latreuseis)."

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "You shall not make for yourself a carved image... You shall not bow down to them or serve them" (Exod 20:4–5).
  • Hezekiah destroyed the bronze serpent, an image God himself had commanded, because the people burned incense to it (2 Kgs 18:4; Num 21:8–9).
  • When John fell down before an angel, the angel said, "You must not do that!... Worship God" (Rev 22:8–9); Peter refused Cornelius's bowing (Acts 10:25–26).
  • Verdict: Scripture forbids bowing to images, even holy ones, and forbids proskynesis to creatures.

Key texts

  • Exod 20:5 (Septuagint): ou proskyneseis autois oude me latreuses autois, "you shall not bow down to them nor serve them."
  • Second Council of Nicaea (787), definition: images are to be given "honorable veneration" (timetike proskynesis), not "true worship" (latreia), which belongs to God alone; "the honor paid to the image passes to its prototype."
  • 2 Kgs 18:4: Hezekiah "broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for until those days the people of Israel had made offerings to it."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. The incarnation changed things. God made himself visible in Christ (John 1:14; Col 1:15), so depicting Christ confesses the incarnation (John of Damascus).
  2. God commanded images in the tabernacle and temple: cherubim over the ark, and woven into the curtains (Exod 25:18–22; Exod 26:1).
  3. Veneration isn't worship. Bowing to honor someone is biblical: Jacob bowed to Esau (Gen 33:3), and people bowed to kings.
  4. The honor passes to the person depicted, as kissing a photograph of your mother honors her, not the paper.
  5. The early church used images, as in the Dura-Europos church (3rd century) and the catacombs.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The Second Commandment forbids bowing down to and serving images (Exod 20:4–5), and in Greek it forbids exactly proskynesis and latreia.
  • P2. Nicaea II requires proskynesis toward images: bowing, kissing, incense, and candles.
  • P3. Scripture shows that a God-commanded image becomes forbidden once it receives veneration (2 Kgs 18:4), and that proskynesis toward creatures is refused (Acts 10:25–26; Rev 22:8–9).
  • C. Icon veneration as Nicaea II requires it contradicts Scripture.

Evidence for each premise

The distinction is not in the text. Nicaea II's defense rests on separating proskynesis (allowed) from latreia (forbidden). But Exod 20:5 in the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament the early church used, forbids both words. The commandment doesn't say "don't worship images"; it says "don't bow to them."

Cherubim, not veneration. God commanded the cherubim, but they were in the Most Holy Place, seen only by the high priest once a year (Heb 9:7), and no one bowed to them. The bronze serpent shows what happens when a holy image becomes an object of devotion: a righteous king destroyed it (2 Kgs 18:4), and Scripture praises him for it (2 Kgs 18:3, 5).

Bowing before a creature in worship contexts is refused. Bowing before a king as a social custom (Gen 33:3) is not the same as bowing in prayer before an image in a sanctuary with incense. When Cornelius bowed before Peter in a religious context, Peter refused (Acts 10:25–26). When John bowed before a glorious angel, the angel refused (Rev 22:8–9).

God chose how to reveal himself. Moses reminded Israel: "you saw no form on the day that the LORD spoke to you... beware lest you act corruptly by making a carved image for yourselves" (Deut 4:15–16). Even after the incarnation, the apostles never commanded or described any images of Christ. "We walk by faith, not by sight" (2 Cor 5:7).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: the incarnation. "God forbade images because he had not yet been seen. In Christ he was seen. To refuse icons is to deny that the Word became flesh."

Answer: The question is not whether Christ was visible (he was) but whether we are commanded or permitted to bow to images. The apostles, who saw Christ, never made or venerated images, and the New Testament repeats the warning: "Little children, keep yourselves from idols" (1 John 5:21). An image of Jesus can depict his humanity, but the person it claims to depict is also God, whose divinity no image can show. Veneration of the image remains bowing to a made thing, which the commandment forbids.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "God commanded the cherubim."

  • Close (R1): God commanded them, and no one bowed to them. When God's own commanded image, the bronze serpent, received offerings, Hezekiah destroyed it and Scripture praised him (2 Kgs 18:3–4).
  • Their comeback: "Israel worshiped the serpent; we only venerate."
  • Close (R2): The text says they "made offerings to it," that is, burned incense, which is exactly what is done before icons.

2. "Veneration is not worship."

  • Close (R1): Read Exod 20:5 in the Septuagint: it forbids proskynesis, the very word Nicaea II uses for "veneration."
  • Their comeback: "Proskynesis has a range of meanings."
  • Close (R2): It does, and in the commandment, directed at images, it is forbidden. The council chose the forbidden word.

3. "The honor passes to the prototype."

  • Close (R1): Israel at Sinai said the same: the golden calf was proclaimed "a feast to the LORD" (Exod 32:5). Intention didn't make it acceptable.
  • Their comeback: "The calf was a false image; icons depict true persons."
  • Close (R2): The bronze serpent was a true, God-given image. It was still destroyed once it was venerated.

Boomerang check

"Protestants use pictures and crosses too." Art, illustrations, and a plain cross aren't the issue. The issue is bowing to images, kissing them in devotion, and burning incense before them, and requiring others to do so under anathema. A children's Bible illustration isn't venerated.

Strength rating

STRONG. The Septuagint wording, 2 Kgs 18:4, and the refusals of proskynesis in Acts 10 and Rev 22 directly address the practice. The incarnation argument has a clear answer.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust
Orthodox converts Have heard the "cherubim" and "incarnation" defenses many times Lead with the Septuagint of Exod 20:5 and 2 Kgs 18:4.
Cradle Orthodox Icons are part of home and family life Speak gently; focus on what God asks, not on criticism of their family.
Catholics Statues and images play a similar role The same argument applies.

Trap questions

  1. "What Greek word does the Septuagint use in Exodus 20:5 for what we must not do to images?"
  2. "Why did Hezekiah destroy the bronze serpent, an image God himself commanded?" (2 Kgs 18:4)
  3. "Where do the apostles command or practice bowing before images of Christ?"

30-second version

"The Second Commandment, in the Greek Bible the early church read, says of images, 'you shall not proskyneseis,' that is, not bow or venerate. That's the exact word the council used for venerating icons. And when people burned incense to the bronze serpent God had commanded, Hezekiah destroyed it, and Scripture praised him (2 Kgs 18:4)."

2-minute version

"I understand that icons are about honoring Christ and the saints, not about worshiping wood and paint. I want to take that seriously.

But here's what troubles me. The council that required icon veneration distinguished proskynesis, veneration, from latreia, worship. The Second Commandment in the Greek Old Testament, the Bible the early church read, forbids both: 'you shall not proskyneseis to them, nor latreuseis to them.' The commandment doesn't only forbid worshiping images; it forbids bowing to them.

Scripture even gives a test case. God commanded Moses to make the bronze serpent. Centuries later the people burned incense to it, and King Hezekiah broke it in pieces, and Scripture praises him for it. If a God-given image had to go once people venerated it, I can't see how we're commanded to venerate images now. Jesus said the Father seeks those who worship in spirit and truth (John 4:23–24)."

Further reading

  • Edwyn Bevan, Holy Images (Allen & Unwin, 1940): history of images in worship
  • Robert Letham, Through Western Eyes (Mentor, 2007), chapter on icons
  • Orthodox side: John of Damascus, On the Divine Images (St Vladimir's Seminary Press)
  • Videos on this topic: Testify, "Why I Can't Accept Eastern Orthodox Icon Veneration"
Argument3KSTRONG

Praying to Saints and to the Theotokos

one Mediator; Scripture never shows prayer to the departed

Name + thesis

Prayer to the saints. Orthodox and Catholic Christians ask the departed saints, above all Mary the Theotokos ("God-bearer"), to pray for them, and their liturgies address Mary directly: "Most Holy Theotokos, save us." Scripture never shows a believer praying to anyone in heaven except God, forbids seeking the dead, and gives believers direct access to the Father through the one Mediator, Christ.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "There is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim 2:5).
  • "Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace" (Heb 4:16); Christ "always lives to make intercession" for us (Heb 7:25).
  • "There shall not be found among you... one who inquires of the dead" (Deut 18:10–12); "Should they inquire of the dead on behalf of the living? To the teaching and to the testimony!" (Isa 8:19–20).
  • Jesus taught us to pray "Our Father in heaven" (Matt 6:9).
  • Verdict: Every prayer in Scripture to a heavenly being is addressed to God. No text commands, models, or permits prayer to the departed.

Key texts

  • 1 Tim 2:5: "one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus."
  • Orthodox Paraklesis to the Theotokos (refrain): "Most Holy Theotokos, save us."
  • Rev 5:8: the elders hold "golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints."
  • 1 Kgs 8:39: "you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind."
  • Catechism of the Catholic Church 2683: the saints' "intercession is their most exalted service to God's plan. We can and should ask them to intercede for us and for the whole world."
  • CCC 956: the saints "do not cease to intercede with the Father for us, as they proffer the merits which they acquired on earth through the one mediator between God and men, Christ Jesus."
  • Martyrdom of Polycarp 17 (c. 155–160): "Him indeed, as being the Son of God, we adore; but the martyrs, as disciples and followers of the Lord, we worthily love."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. Asking the saints is like asking a friend to pray for you (James 5:16). Death doesn't separate members of Christ's body (Rom 8:38–39).
  2. The saints are alive: "He is not God of the dead, but of the living" (Matt 22:32).
  3. The saints in heaven know and pray: the martyrs cry out about earthly events (Rev 6:9–10), and the elders offer "the prayers of the saints" (Rev 5:8).
  4. "Save us" means "help save us" by her prayers, as Paul says he may "save some" (1 Cor 9:22).
  5. The early church asked martyrs to pray for them, as inscriptions in the catacombs show.
  6. Honor, not worship. Catholics and Orthodox distinguish dulia (the honor given to saints) and hyperdulia (the higher honor given to Mary) from latria (worship, which belongs to God alone). The Catechism says devotion to Mary "differs essentially from the adoration" given to God (CCC 971).

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Scripture gives believers one Mediator and direct access to the Father (1 Tim 2:5; Heb 4:16; Heb 7:25).
  • P2. Scripture forbids seeking the dead (Deut 18:10–12; Isa 8:19–20) and never models prayer to anyone in heaven but God.
  • P3. Hearing the silent prayers of millions at once requires knowledge of hearts that Scripture ascribes to God alone (1 Kgs 8:39).
  • C. Prayer to the saints and to Mary isn't apostolic and attributes to creatures what belongs to God.

Evidence for each premise

No example in Scripture. From Genesis to Revelation, believers pray to God. Not one apostle prays to Abraham, Moses, Elijah, or Mary, though they knew Mary personally. After the ascension, the church prays to God, with Mary present among them (Acts 1:14).

Asking a friend isn't the same. James 5:16 is about believers on earth whom we can actually speak to. Praying to the departed requires that they hear silent prayers from millions of people in many languages at once. Scripture says God alone knows all hearts (1 Kgs 8:39; Jer 17:10). To assume a creature can do this ascribes a divine attribute to that creature.

Revelation doesn't show what's claimed. In Rev 5:8 the elders hold prayers; Revelation never says anyone on earth prayed to them. In Rev 6:9–10 the martyrs pray to God about justice; no one prays to them.

"Save us." Hymns addressing Mary as "our life, our sweetness and our hope" (the Latin Salve Regina) and "save us" give her titles Scripture gives to Christ alone (Col 3:4; 1 Tim 1:1; Acts 4:12).

In Scripture, every believer is a saint (Wes Huff's first point). Paul writes to all the believers in Rome as "called to be saints" (Rom 1:7), and to the Corinthians as "called to be saints together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Cor 1:2). The saints the New Testament asks us to pray for are living believers we can actually talk to: "making supplication for all the saints" (Eph 6:18). Honoring the heroes of the faith is good (Heb 11). But "saint" in the Bible isn't a special class of the dead in heaven.

Prayer is worship, so the line between honor and worship breaks down (Wes Huff's main point). Every prayer in Scripture is addressed to God, even complaint (Ps 13; Hab 1:2–4), bargaining (Gen 18:23–33), and raw grief. Scripture treats prayer itself as an offering of worship: "Let my prayer be counted as incense before you" (Ps 141:2), and in heaven the prayers of the saints rise like incense to God (Rev 5:8; Rev 8:3–4). Wes grants that the honor-versus-worship distinction makes sense on paper. In practice it collapses: speaking to someone unseen and trusting them to hear and help you anywhere in the world is the very act Scripture reserves for God, and in popular devotion it often slides into asking the saints instead of God. The Catechism also says the saints offer God "the merits which they acquired on earth" for us (CCC 956). That is far more than a friend's prayer.

History: remembering came first, praying to them came later. The earliest account of a martyr being honored draws the line clearly. The church at Smyrna wrote of Christ, "Him indeed, as being the Son of God, we adore; but the martyrs, as disciples and followers of the Lord, we worthily love" (Martyrdom of Polycarp 17), and it gathered to "celebrate the anniversary of his martyrdom" (ch. 18): remembrance and imitation, not prayer to him. Requests to the martyrs show up in Christian graffiti in Rome from around the mid-3rd century, and the practice spread in the 4th and 5th centuries. Even then, Cyril of Jerusalem's liturgy (c. 350) still speaks to God: it remembers the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs "that at their prayers and intercessions God would receive our petition" (Catechetical Lectures 23.9). Wes dates the shift from praying for the dead to praying to them to this period (Cyril, John Chrysostom, Gregory of Nazianzus). Early isn't the same as apostolic: no apostle ever did it (1D).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: "God of the living" (Matt 22:32). "The saints aren't dead; they're alive in Christ. Asking them to pray isn't necromancy."

Answer: Agreed, they are alive with Christ (Phil 1:23). But being alive doesn't mean they are present to hear us or appointed to receive our requests. Moses and Elijah were alive at the Transfiguration (Matt 17:3), yet no one in Scripture prays to them. Deut 18 forbids inquiring of the dead, and Isa 8:19–20 directs God's people instead "to the teaching and to the testimony." The question isn't whether the saints are alive, but whether God has told us to address them. He hasn't; he has told us to come to him (Heb 4:16).

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "It's just like asking a friend to pray."

  • Close (R1): My friend is here and hears me. Can Mary hear the silent prayers of millions at once? Scripture says only God knows all hearts (1 Kgs 8:39).
  • Their comeback: "God reveals the prayers to them."
  • Close (R2): Where does Scripture say that? And why go through anyone when Christ invites us to come boldly ourselves (Heb 4:16)?

2. "Revelation shows saints offering prayers" (Rev 5:8).

  • Close (R1): It shows prayers rising to God. It never shows anyone praying to the elders.
  • Their comeback: "If they offer our prayers, we can ask them."
  • Close (R2): That's an inference the apostles never drew. In the same book, John is twice told not to bow before a heavenly being (Rev 19:10; 22:8–9).

3. "'Save us' only means 'pray for us.'"

  • Close (R1): Then why not say "pray for us"? Scripture reserves "save" and "our hope" in this sense for God (Acts 4:12; 1 Tim 1:1).
  • Their comeback: "Paul says he saves some" (1 Cor 9:22).
  • Close (R2): Paul does that by preaching the gospel to the living. He never asks anyone to pray to him.

4. "We don't worship the saints. It's honor (dulia), not worship (latria)."

  • Close (R1): That's the official teaching (CCC 971). But Scripture never makes that distinction for prayer. Every prayer in the Bible goes to God, and Scripture treats prayer itself as worship, like incense (Ps 141:2; Rev 8:3–4).
  • Their comeback: "Asking isn't worshiping. You ask people for things all the time."
  • Close (R2): Asking someone standing in front of you is conversation. Kneeling and speaking to someone unseen, trusting them to hear your heart and help you anywhere on earth, is what Scripture calls prayer, and Scripture directs it to God alone. As Wes Huff puts it, the distinction may hold on paper, but in practice it collapses.

5. "The saints in heaven are holier, so their prayers are more powerful" (James 5:16).

  • Close (R1): James's example of powerful prayer is Elijah, "a man with a nature like ours" (James 5:17), praying to God while on earth. James tells us to pray like Elijah, not to Elijah. And every believer is a saint (1 Cor 1:2).
  • Their comeback: "But the saints in glory are closer to God."
  • Close (R2): Every believer has been "brought near by the blood of Christ" (Eph 2:13) and may draw near with confidence (Heb 4:16; Heb 10:19–22). No one is closer to the Father than the Son, and he "always lives to make intercession" for us (Heb 7:25).

Boomerang check

"Protestants ask each other to pray, so they accept intercession." Yes, among the living, as Scripture commands (James 5:16; Eph 6:18). The issue is praying to departed saints, which Scripture never models.

"Protestants dishonor the saints." We honor them the way Scripture does, and the way the church at Smyrna honored Polycarp: we remember them and imitate their faith. "Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God... imitate their faith" (Heb 13:7; see Heb 11).

Strength rating

STRONG. 1 Tim 2:5, Heb 4:16, Deut 18, and the complete absence of any biblical example make the scriptural case clear. The "living saints" reply is answered by asking for a command or example.

Audience notes

Audience How it lands Adjust

Defense3K

"We become partakers of the divine nature (theosis)."

The objection (best form)

"Salvation is theosis, union with God by grace: 'he became man so that we might become god' (Athanasius, On the Incarnation 54). Peter says we become 'partakers of the divine nature' (2 Pet 1:4). Western ideas of legal justification miss this."

Answer

  • Scripture does promise real union with God. Believers are united to Christ (Rom 6:5; John 17:21–23), indwelt by the Spirit (Rom 8:9), and will be like Christ when he appears (1 John 3:2). That should be affirmed gladly.
  • 2 Pet 1:4 explains itself: we share God's nature by "having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire." The next verses list virtues: faith, virtue, knowledge, self-control, love (2 Pet 1:5–7). It is about moral likeness, not sharing God's essence.
  • The foundation is still justification. Union with Christ begins with being declared righteous through faith (Rom 5:1; Rom 8:30). Transformation follows. John MacArthur presses this point in Faith Works (1993): justification is God's once-for-all legal declaration, and sanctification flows from it, never the reverse. Orthodoxy often treats salvation as a lifelong cooperation (synergy) without a settled verdict, but Scripture gives the believer peace with God now (Rom 5:1) and no condemnation (Rom 8:1).
  • The essence-energies framework (Gregory Palamas, 14th century) used to explain theosis isn't taught in Scripture; it's a later theological system.

30-second version

"Peter's 'partakers of the divine nature' means sharing God's holiness, 'having escaped the corruption in the world' (2 Pet 1:4). That's real and beautiful. But it rests on a finished verdict: 'since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God' (Rom 5:1). Transformation flows from acceptance, not toward it."

3L

Gnosticism

2 cards2 strong

New terms

Gnosticism: A family of 2nd-century movements teaching salvation through secret knowledge, a lesser creator god, and a Christ who only seemed to have a body.

Gnosis: Greek for "knowledge"; in Gnosticism, the secret saving knowledge of one's divine origin.

Demiurge: In Gnostic teaching, the lesser, ignorant god who made the material world (in some texts named Yaldabaoth).

Nag Hammadi library: A collection of 13 Coptic codices, copied in the 4th century and found in Egypt in 1945, containing many Gnostic texts.

Ancient Gnosticism was a family of 2nd-century movements (Sethian, Valentinian, and others) teaching that salvation comes through secret knowledge (gnosis), that the material world was made by a lesser, ignorant god, and that Christ was a spiritual revealer who only seemed to have a body. It returns today in popular books and documentaries ("the lost gospels the church suppressed"), in some New Age spirituality, and in the claim that the Council of Nicaea chose the Bible. The apostles were already warning against its early forms.

Argument3LSTRONG

The "Lost Gospels" Are Late and Secondary

dating of the Nag Hammadi texts is mainstream scholarship

Name + thesis

The Gnostic gospels. The Gospels of Thomas, Judas, Mary, and Philip were written in the 2nd and 3rd centuries, generations after the apostles, and depend on ideas foreign to 1st-century Judaism. The four canonical Gospels were written within the lifetime of eyewitnesses. The church didn't suppress the "real" Jesus; it kept the earliest witnesses to him.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • Luke wrote from those "who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word" (Luke 1:2).
  • "That which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes... and touched with our hands" (1 John 1:1).
  • Paul warns Timothy against "what is falsely called knowledge (gnosis)" (1 Tim 6:20).
  • Verdict: The apostolic Gospels claim eyewitness testimony; the apostles already warned against "knowledge" that departs from it.

Key texts

  • Nag Hammadi library: 13 leather-bound Coptic codices found in Upper Egypt in 1945, copied in the 4th century.
  • Gospel of Thomas, saying 114: "every woman who makes herself male will enter the kingdom of heaven."
  • Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.31.1 (c. 180): mentions a "Gospel of Judas" used by a Gnostic sect.
  • 1 Tim 6:20: "Avoid the irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge."

Their best case (steelman)

  1. Thomas may be early. Some scholars date a core of the Gospel of Thomas to the late 1st century, and some of its sayings parallel the Synoptics independently.
  2. History is written by the winners. The orthodox party suppressed rival Christianities; early Christianity was diverse (Walter Bauer, Bart Ehrman's Lost Christianities).
  3. The canon was decided late, and Constantine's Council of Nicaea (325) chose four Gospels for political reasons.
  4. The Gnostic texts preserve a spiritual, inward Jesus that appeals to modern seekers more than a Jesus of law and blood sacrifice.

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. The canonical Gospels were written in the 1st century, within living memory of the eyewitnesses (see 1C).
  • P2. The Gnostic gospels were composed in the 2nd–3rd centuries and presuppose 2nd-century Gnostic systems.
  • P3. Earlier sources rooted in eyewitness testimony are better historical evidence than later, dependent ones.
  • C. The Gnostic gospels are not a better or equal source for the historical Jesus, and the church's preference for the four Gospels was historically sound.

Evidence for each premise

Dates. The Nag Hammadi codices were copied in the 4th century. The Gospel of Judas survives in Codex Tchacos, carbon-dated to roughly AD 220–340, and Irenaeus knew of it c. 180, so it was written in the 2nd century. The Gospel of Mary is known from a 5th-century Coptic copy and 3rd-century Greek fragments. The Gospel of Thomas has Greek fragments from about AD 200 (Oxyrhynchus papyri 1, 654, 655); most scholars date it to the 2nd century, and it appears to know the Synoptic Gospels in their edited forms (Simon Gathercole, The Composition of the Gospel of Thomas, Cambridge, 2012).

Nicaea didn't choose the canon. The Council of Nicaea (325) dealt with Arius and the date of Easter; its canons say nothing about which books belong in the Bible. Irenaeus already insisted on exactly four Gospels around 180 (Against Heresies 3.11.8). Athanasius's Festal Letter 39 (367) lists the 27 New Testament books.

The content is foreign to Jesus' world. Jesus was a Jew who affirmed the Creator, creation, and marriage (Mark 10:6–9). Gnostic texts treat the creator as an inferior or evil being and the body as a prison. Thomas 114's call for women to "become male" reflects Gnostic ideas about matter and gender, not anything in Jesus' recorded teaching.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: Thomas's early core. "Some of Thomas's sayings may preserve early, independent tradition."

Answer: Possibly, for a few sayings, and that's an honest scholarly debate. But a few early sayings in a 2nd-century collection don't make the collection an eyewitness Gospel. Thomas has no narrative, no crucifixion, and no resurrection, and where it differs from the Synoptics it tends toward Gnostic ideas. The case for the canonical Gospels doesn't depend on Thomas being late.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "History is written by the winners."

  • Close (R1): Then look at the sources apart from who "won." The canonical Gospels are 1st-century; the Gnostic texts are 2nd–3rd century. That's a dating question, not a political one.
  • Their comeback: "Early Christianity was diverse."
  • Close (R2): There was diversity, and the New Testament records it, warning against false teachers from the start (1 John 4:1–3; Gal 1:6–9). The earliest sources already define the gospel as Jesus' death and bodily resurrection (1 Cor 15:3–5).

2. "Constantine and Nicaea picked the Bible."

  • Close (R1): Read Nicaea's canons: they deal with church order and Arius, not the canon. Irenaeus defended the four Gospels 145 years earlier.
  • Their comeback: "It was still decided by the church later."
  • Close (R2): The church recognized books that were already being read as apostolic (1D). Lists differed at the edges (Hebrews, Revelation), but no Gnostic gospel was ever seriously considered.

3. "The Gnostic Jesus is more spiritual."

  • Close (R1): That's a preference, not evidence. And the Gnostic Jesus offers secret knowledge to a spiritual elite, while the biblical Jesus offers forgiveness to sinners (Luke 5:32).
  • Their comeback: "Inner enlightenment is better than blood sacrifice."
  • Close (R2): Then the Gnostic gospel has nothing for the guilty, the poor, or the uneducated. Jesus came for them (Matt 11:25, 28).

Boomerang check

"The Bible was also written by people with agendas." Every author has a purpose (John 20:31). The question is evidence: date, eyewitness connection, and fit with the historical setting. On every measure the canonical Gospels are earlier and more grounded.

Strength rating

STRONG. The dating of the Nag Hammadi texts, the Gospel of Judas, and the Gospel of Mary is mainstream scholarship; the claim about Nicaea is a popular myth. Only Thomas's early core is debated, and the argument doesn't depend on it.

Skeptics influenced by Ehrman Know the "diversity" argument Grant diversity; press dates and 1 Cor 15.
New Age or "spiritual not religious" Drawn to inward, esoteric spirituality See also 3I; focus on grace for ordinary people.

30-second version

"The Gnostic gospels were written in the 2nd and 3rd centuries, long after the apostles. The four Gospels come from the 1st century, from eyewitnesses and their companions (Luke 1:2). And Nicaea never voted on the Bible; Irenaeus was defending the four Gospels in 180. The church didn't hide the real Jesus; it kept the earliest witnesses."

2-minute version

"I find the Nag Hammadi texts fascinating too, and I'd encourage anyone to read them. But when people say the church suppressed the 'real' gospels, I have to look at the dates.

The Nag Hammadi books were copied in the 300s. The Gospel of Judas was known to Irenaeus around 180 and survives in a copy from the 200s or 300s. The Gospel of Thomas has fragments from about 200, and most scholars date it to the 2nd century. Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John were written in the 1st century, when people who knew Jesus were still alive. Luke says he got his material from eyewitnesses.

And the content fits that. The Gnostic texts teach that the world was made by a lesser god and the body is a prison. Jesus, a Jew, called the Creator his Father, blessed marriage, and rose bodily from the dead. That's the Jesus the earliest sources show us."

Argument3LSTRONG

The Word Became Flesh, and Creation Is Good

the apostles address docetism and anti-creation teaching directly

Name + thesis

The heart of Gnosticism refuted by the apostles. Gnostic teachers said the material world was made by an ignorant lesser god (the demiurge), that the body is evil, and that Christ only seemed to have a body (docetism). The apostles confronted these ideas head-on: the one true God made all things good, Christ came in the flesh, and denying it is the spirit of antichrist.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist" (1 John 4:2–3; 2 John 7).
  • "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14); "Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have" (Luke 24:39).
  • "God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good" (Gen 1:31); "by him all things were created" (Col 1:16; John 1:3).
  • Those who forbid marriage and foods are "devoted to deceitful spirits," for "everything created by God is good" (1 Tim 4:1–4).
  • Verdict: The apostles name and reject each core Gnostic belief.

Key texts

  • 1 John 4:2–3: "every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God."
  • Col 2:8–9: "See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit... For in him the whole fullness (pleroma) of deity dwells bodily."
  • Apocryphon of John (Nag Hammadi): the world is made by Yaldabaoth, an arrogant, ignorant lesser being.

Their best case (steelman)

  1. The world is full of suffering. A good God wouldn't make a world like this, so the maker must be lesser or flawed.
  2. Spirit is higher than matter. Our true self is a divine spark trapped in the body, longing to return home.
  3. Christ came to awaken us, not to die as a sacrifice. Salvation is knowledge of who we really are.
  4. Paul himself contrasts flesh and spirit (Rom 8:5–8; Gal 5:17).

Premises → conclusion

  • P1. Gnosticism teaches that matter is evil, that the world was made by a lesser god, and that Christ only seemed to have a body.
  • P2. The apostles teach that the one God created all things good (Gen 1:31; Col 1:16; 1 Tim 4:4), that Christ came in the flesh (John 1:14; 1 John 4:2), and that he rose bodily (Luke 24:39).
  • P3. The apostolic writings come from the eyewitnesses; Gnostic texts are later (3L, previous card).
  • C. Gnosticism contradicts the apostolic faith at its core.

Evidence for each premise

The apostles saw it coming. 1 John is written against those who denied that Jesus came in the flesh (1 John 4:2–3; 2 John 7). Colossians answers a teaching of special knowledge, angels, and ascetic rules with the fullness (pleroma, a key Gnostic term later) dwelling in Christ "bodily" (Col 2:8–9, 18–23). 1 Tim 4:1–4 condemns forbidding marriage and foods, both Gnostic practices.

"Flesh" in Paul isn't the body. Paul's "flesh" against "Spirit" (Gal 5:17) means our sinful nature; his list of "works of the flesh" includes envy and strife, which aren't bodily (Gal 5:19–21). Paul expects the body to be raised and transformed, not discarded (1 Cor 15:42–44; Phil 3:21).

Suffering came through the fall, not through a flawed creator (Gen 3:17–19; Rom 8:20–22). God's answer to suffering is to redeem creation, not escape it (Rom 8:21; Rev 21:1–5).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

Hardest objection: the problem of evil. "A good, all-powerful God wouldn't make this world. Gnosticism at least explains suffering."

Answer: Gnosticism explains suffering by making God either powerless or not the creator, which leaves no one with the power to fix it. Scripture explains suffering by the fall and promises a real remedy: God himself entered the suffering world in the flesh, bore evil on the cross, and rose bodily as the first fruits of a renewed creation (1 Cor 15:20; Rev 21:4). See also the problem of evil in 1B.

Escape routes → how to close each one

1. "Paul contrasts flesh and spirit too."

  • Close (R1): Paul's "flesh" means the sinful nature; envy and divisions are "works of the flesh" (Gal 5:19–21).
  • Their comeback: "Paul says flesh and blood can't inherit the kingdom" (1 Cor 15:50).
  • Close (R2): In the same chapter he says the body is sown and raised, transformed (1 Cor 15:42–44). Mortal bodies put on immortality; they aren't discarded (1 Cor 15:53).

2. "Christ came to awaken knowledge, not to die."

  • Close (R1): The earliest Christian creed is "Christ died for our sins... was buried... was raised" (1 Cor 15:3–4), dated within a few years of the events.
  • Their comeback: "The literal reading is for beginners; the spiritual meaning is for the wise."
  • Close (R2): Jesus thanked the Father for hiding these things "from the wise and understanding" and revealing them to little children (Matt 11:25). The gospel is public, not esoteric (Acts 26:26; John 18:20).

3. "The divine spark is within you."

  • Close (R1): Scripture says we are made in God's image (Gen 1:27), but we are creatures, not fragments of God, and we are sinners (Rom 3:23).
  • Their comeback: "Sin is just ignorance."
  • Close (R2): Then Jesus didn't need to die. Scripture says he gave his life "as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45), because our problem is guilt, not just ignorance.

Boomerang check

"Christians are anti-body too (asceticism, celibacy)." Some Christians have been, and Scripture corrects them (Col 2:20–23; 1 Tim 4:3–4). The biblical view honors the body as God's creation and the Spirit's temple (1 Cor 6:19–20).

Strength rating

STRONG. The New Testament directly names and rejects docetism, anti-creation teaching, and forbidding marriage; the texts are explicit.

30-second version

The risen Jesus said, 'Touch me... a spirit does not have flesh and bones' (Luke 24:39). And God called his creation 'very good' (Gen 1:31). The answer to suffering isn't escaping the world; it's the God who entered it to redeem it."

The apostles were already answering that. John wrote that anyone who denies Jesus came in the flesh has the spirit of antichrist. And the risen Jesus ate fish in front of his disciples and told them to touch him, because a spirit doesn't have flesh and bones.

I understand why the idea of a flawed creator appeals to people who are suffering. But it leaves no one strong enough to fix the world. The gospel says the good Creator entered his broken world, took our evil on himself, and rose bodily as the beginning of a new creation."

Hebrew Israelites

1 card1 strong

New terms

Hebrew Israelites: Movements teaching that certain Black, Hispanic, and Native American peoples are the true descendants of the tribes of Israel.

Hebrew Israelite groups (some known as Black Hebrew Israelites) teach that certain Black, Hispanic, and Native American peoples are the true descendants of the twelve tribes of Israel. Camps differ widely: some are peaceful Torah-keeping communities, while others, often met in street preaching, teach that salvation is only for Israelites, deny the Trinity, and insult outsiders. Engage the person, not the camp's reputation.

Worldview3MSTRONG

Hebrew Israelites

on the gospel's inclusion of the nations and the deity of Christ; the genealogical claims are unverifiable

Name + thesis

Many Hebrew Israelite camps teach that salvation belongs only to ethnic Israel (as they define it), that Gentiles are excluded or will serve Israel, and that Jesus is not God. The apostolic Scriptures teach that in Christ the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile is broken down, that people from every nation are saved through faith, and that Jesus is Lord and God.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "There is neither Jew nor Greek... for you are all one in Christ Jesus. And if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's offspring" (Gal 3:28–29).
  • "He himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility" (Eph 2:14).
  • "God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him" (Acts 10:34–35).
  • "A great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages" (Rev 7:9).
  • Verdict: The apostles explicitly include Gentiles in salvation through faith, not ancestry.

What they believe (steelman)

Best case: God's covenant was with Israel (Amos 3:2), and Jesus said he was sent "only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel" (Matt 15:24). The curses of Deut 28, including being taken back to "Egypt in ships" and sold as slaves (Deut 28:68), fit the transatlantic slave trade, showing that its victims' descendants are the true Israel. Christianity as usually taught is a European distortion. The law must still be kept, including the Sabbath and feasts. Some camps add that Jesus was a man and that the Trinity is pagan.

TAG internal critique

  • Gentile salvation: Jesus commanded the gospel to "all nations" (Matt 28:19). The Jerusalem council received Gentiles without circumcision (Acts 15:7–11). Paul, "a Hebrew of Hebrews" (Phil 3:5), was sent to the Gentiles (Acts 9:15) and said "the same Lord is Lord of all... everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved" (Rom 10:12–13).
  • Matt 15:24 in context: Jesus then heals the Canaanite woman's daughter for her faith (Matt 15:28). His earthly mission began with Israel and then went to the nations (Acts 1:8; Rom 1:16).
  • Deut 28:68: Scripture doesn't identify this curse with any modern people, and it describes Israel being returned to Egypt. Josephus reports that after Jerusalem fell in AD 70 many captives were sent to labor in Egypt (Jewish War 6.414–418; Whiston 6.9.2: "sent them to the Egyptian mines"). Genealogical claims about modern peoples can't be established from Scripture at all.
  • True Israel is defined by faith in the Messiah: "Not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel... it is the children of the promise who are counted as offspring" (Rom 9:6–8).
  • Jesus' deity: "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28); see 1C and 2J.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

"Gentiles can only serve Israel" (Isa 60; Isa 14:1–2). Answer: The prophets promise that the nations will come to Israel's God and share in his salvation (Isa 49:6; Isa 56:6–7). The apostles apply this to Gentiles being saved and made fellow citizens with God's people (Eph 2:19), not subjects.

Boomerang check

"Christians used the Bible to justify slavery and racism." Some did, sinfully, against Scripture, which condemns man-stealing (Exod 21:16; 1 Tim 1:10) and declares all people made from one man in God's image (Acts 17:26; Gen 1:27). The answer to that sin is the gospel's equality in Christ, not a new racial exclusion.

Trap questions

  1. "In Acts 10, what did Peter conclude about people from every nation?"
  2. "Rev 7:9 describes a multitude from every nation before the throne. Who are they?"
  3. "Paul calls himself a Hebrew of Hebrews. Who did Jesus send him to?" (Acts 9:15)

30-second version

"Paul was a Hebrew of Hebrews, and Jesus sent him to the nations (Acts 9:15). Peter said God accepts people from every nation who fear him (Acts 10:34–35). And Revelation shows a multitude from every tribe and language before God's throne (Rev 7:9). In Christ, the wall is broken down (Eph 2:14). That includes you and me."

Bridge to the gospel

Many Hebrew Israelites carry real anger over the history of slavery and racism. Acknowledge it honestly. Then point to the Messiah who breaks down hostility and gives a new family, where everyone is equally a child of Abraham by faith (Gal 3:7, 29).

Oneness Pentecostalism and Biblical Unitarianism

2 cards2 strong

New terms

Modalism: The teaching that God is one person who appears in three modes or roles (Father, Son, Spirit), not three persons. Also called Sabellianism, after the 3rd-century teacher Sabellius.

Oneness Pentecostalism: A Pentecostal movement (from 1913–1916) teaching that God is one person, that Jesus is the Father, Son, and Spirit, and that baptism must be "in Jesus' name" only.

Biblical unitarianism: The belief, argued from the Bible alone, that only the Father is God and Jesus is a human Messiah.

Two groups deny the Trinity while saying they follow the Bible alone. Oneness Pentecostals believe God is one person who reveals himself as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and that Jesus is that one God. The movement split from other Pentecostals between 1913 and 1916 over baptism "in the name of Jesus" only, and its largest body today is the United Pentecostal Church International (UPCI, formed in 1945). Biblical unitarians, such as the Christadelphians and the Church of God General Conference, believe only the Father is God and Jesus is a human Messiah. Both groups love Scripture, so meet them there: Scripture alone is exactly the right test (1D).

Worldview3NSTRONG

Oneness Pentecostalism

the Father and the Son relate to each other as two persons throughout the New Testament

Name + thesis

Oneness theology teaches that God is a single person. In the UPCI's words: "There is one God, who has revealed Himself as Father; through His Son, in redemption; and as the Holy Spirit, by emanation" ("Our Beliefs"). On this view, "Son" names the human nature, born in Bethlehem, and baptism must be "in the name of Jesus" only (Acts 2:38), with speaking in tongues as the sign of salvation. But Scripture shows the Son and the Father speaking to each other, loving each other, sending and being sent, and testifying as two witnesses. It also shows the Son with the Father before the world existed. That is one God in three persons, not one person wearing three masks.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). The Word was with God (Greek pros, "face to face with").
  • "Glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed" (John 17:5).
  • "In your Law it is written that the testimony of two people is true. I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me" (John 8:17–18).
  • "We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous" (1 John 2:1).
  • Verdict: The Son is not the Father. They are two who relate to each other, before creation and after the ascension, and yet one God (Deut 6:4; John 10:30).

What they believe (steelman)

Best case: God is absolutely one (Deut 6:4), and "in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily" (Col 2:9). Jesus said, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30) and "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). Isaiah calls the Messiah "Everlasting Father" (Isa 9:6). The apostles always baptized "in the name of Jesus Christ" (Acts 2:38; Acts 8:16; Acts 10:48; Acts 19:5), which shows that the one "name" of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in Matt 28:19 is Jesus. The word "Trinity" isn't in the Bible; the doctrine came later from philosophy. Salvation, the UPCI says, means obeying the gospel "by repentance (death to sin), water baptism in the name of Jesus Christ (burial), and the baptism of the Holy Spirit with the initial sign of speaking in tongues" ("Our Beliefs").

TAG internal critique

  • Two witnesses: Under the law, one person can't be two witnesses (Deut 19:15). Jesus counts himself and the Father as the two (John 8:17–18). If they were one person, his argument would fail.
  • Before creation: The Son had glory with the Father before the world existed (John 17:5), and the Father loved him "before the foundation of the world" (John 17:24). All things were created through the Son (Col 1:16; Heb 1:2). A Son who began at Bethlehem couldn't have done that.
  • John 10:30: In "I and the Father are one," the Greek word for "one" is neuter (hen, "one thing"), not masculine (heis, "one person"), and the verb is plural (esmen, "we are"). They are one in nature and work, and they are two.
  • John 14:9 in context: Seeing the Son reveals the Father, as an exact image does (Heb 1:3). In the same chapter Jesus says he is going to the Father (John 14:12, 28) and will ask the Father to send "another Helper" (John 14:16): three persons in one sentence.
  • Isa 9:6: "Everlasting Father" describes the Messiah's fatherly care for his people, as Eliakim would be "a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem" (Isa 22:21). It can't erase the distinction Jesus himself draws (John 8:17–18).
  • Tongues as the required sign: Paul asks, "Do all speak with tongues?" (1 Cor 12:30), and the Greek form of the question expects the answer "no." Cornelius's household received the Spirit before they were baptized (Acts 10:44–48). Salvation is "by grace... through faith" (Eph 2:8–9).
  • This view is old, and was answered long ago. Around AD 213 Tertullian wrote against Praxeas, who taught that the Father himself was born and suffered: "he put to flight the Paraclete, and he crucified the Father" (Against Praxeas 1). Historians call the view modalism.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

"The apostles baptized in Jesus' name, never in the name of the Father, Son, and Spirit" (Acts 2:38). Answer: "In the name of Jesus" means by his authority, as in "By what power or by what name did you do this?" (Acts 4:7). Luke isn't quoting a spoken formula. Jesus himself gave the words: "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matt 28:19). The early church saw no conflict. The Didache (about AD 100) says to "baptize into the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit" (Didache 7), and two chapters later speaks of those "baptized into the name of the Lord" (Didache 9). Both phrases describe the same baptism.

Boomerang check

"Trinitarians worship three gods." No. There is one God (Deut 6:4; 1 Cor 8:4). Within the one God, the Father, Son, and Spirit are distinct persons who relate to each other (Matt 3:16–17; John 17:24). Three persons in one being is not three beings. Ask which part of that the Bible denies.

Trap questions

  1. "In John 8:17–18, who are the two witnesses Jesus counts?"
  2. "In John 17:5, whose presence was the Son in before the world existed?"
  3. "At Jesus' baptism (Matt 3:16–17), who is speaking from heaven, and who is in the water?"
  4. "Paul asks, 'Do all speak with tongues?' (1 Cor 12:30). What answer does he expect?"

30-second version

"Jesus said the law needs two witnesses, and then he counted himself and the Father as the two (John 8:17–18). He prayed for the glory he had with the Father before the world existed (John 17:5). That's not one person changing masks. It's the Son and the Father, one God, before creation began."

Bridge to the gospel

Oneness believers usually love Jesus fiercely and want to honor his name above every name. Start there: you agree that Jesus is fully God (Col 2:9). Then read John 17 together and notice who is talking to whom. And show that salvation is by grace through faith in that Jesus, not proved by speaking in tongues (Eph 2:8–9; 1 Cor 12:30).

Further reading

  • Gregory A. Boyd, Oneness Pentecostals and the Trinity (Baker, 1992): by a former Oneness Pentecostal
  • James R. White, The Forgotten Trinity (Bethany House, 1998)
  • Tertullian, Against Praxeas (about AD 213)
  • From the other side: David K. Bernard, The Oneness of God (Word Aflame Press, 1983); United Pentecostal Church International, "Our Beliefs" (upci.org)

Worldview3NSTRONG

Biblical Unitarianism

the apostles place Jesus inside the identity of the one God

Name + thesis

Biblical unitarians believe only the Father is God, and Jesus is a human being, the Messiah, whom God exalted. They appeal to "the only true God" (John 17:3), "one God, the Father" (1 Cor 8:6), and "the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim 2:5). But the apostles put Jesus inside the Shema itself, apply to him Old Testament texts about the LORD alone, credit him with creating all things, and worship him together with the Father.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist" (1 Cor 8:6).
  • "At the name of Jesus every knee should bow... and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord" (Phil 2:10–11), applying the LORD's own oath: "To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear allegiance" (Isa 45:23).
  • "But of the Son he says, 'Your throne, O God, is forever and ever'" (Heb 1:8). And to the Son: "You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning" (Heb 1:10, quoting Ps 102:25).
  • Verdict: The New Testament doesn't make Jesus a second god or a mere man. It names him within the identity of the one God.

What they believe (steelman)

Best case: The Shema says the LORD is one (Deut 6:4), and Jesus affirmed it (Mark 12:29). Jesus called the Father "the only true God" (John 17:3) and "my God" (John 20:17). Paul says "one God, the Father" (1 Cor 8:6) and "one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim 2:5). Peter preached Jesus as "a man attested to you by God" (Acts 2:22), whom God made Lord and Christ (Acts 2:36). Jesus didn't know the day or the hour (Mark 13:32), and God can't be tempted (Jas 1:13) or die. On this view the Trinity came later, from Greek philosophy and church councils. The movement traces itself to the Polish Brethren's Racovian Catechism (1605) and to John Biddle in England.

TAG internal critique

  • 1 Cor 8:6 splits the Shema. In the Greek Old Testament the Shema's key words are "God" (theos) and "Lord" (kyrios): "The Lord our God, the Lord is one" (Deut 6:4). Paul gives "God" to the Father and "Lord" to Jesus, and makes Jesus the one "through whom are all things," the Creator. Unitarians quote the first half of the verse and leave out the second.
  • Texts about the LORD alone are applied to Jesus. Isa 45:23 is spoken by the LORD, who says "there is no other god besides me" (Isa 45:21), and Paul applies it to Jesus (Phil 2:10–11). Isaiah "saw his glory and spoke of him" (John 12:41), referring to Isaiah's vision of the LORD on his throne (Isa 6:1–5).
  • The Son made the world. "All things were made through him" (John 1:3); "by him all things were created" (Col 1:16); "you, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth" (Heb 1:10). A man who didn't yet exist couldn't have created the world.
  • He receives the worship due to God. "To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!" (Rev 5:13). Angels, by contrast, refuse worship (Rev 22:8–9).
  • The "human" texts describe the incarnation, which Trinitarians affirm: the Son truly became man (John 1:14; Phil 2:7). "The man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim 2:5) is the same one in whom "the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily" (Col 2:9).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

"John 17:3 calls the Father 'the only true God.'" Answer: Eternal life is knowing the Father "and Jesus Christ whom you have sent," and two verses later the Son asks for the glory he had with the Father before the world existed (John 17:5). "Only true God" contrasts the Father with idols, not with the Son. Jude calls Jesus "our only Master and Lord" (Jude 4) without denying that the Father is Lord. See the full answer in 2J.

Boomerang check

"A Jesus who is God couldn't die or not know the hour." That objection is aimed at the incarnation, not at the Trinity. Scripture says the Son "emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant" (Phil 2:7) and grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52). The real question is whether the eternal Son could take a real human nature, and John says he did (John 1:14).

Trap questions

  1. "In 1 Cor 8:6, who is the one 'through whom are all things'?"
  2. "In Isa 45:23 the LORD swears that every knee will bow to him. To whom does Paul say every knee will bow?" (Phil 2:10–11)
  3. "Heb 1:10 says, 'You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth.' Who is being spoken to?"

30-second version

"Paul takes the Shema, 'one God... one Lord,' and says the one God is the Father and the one Lord is Jesus Christ, 'through whom are all things' (1 Cor 8:6). He takes the LORD's oath, 'To me every knee shall bow' (Isa 45:23), and says every knee will bow to Jesus (Phil 2:10–11). The apostles didn't make Jesus a second god or a mere man. They put him inside the one God."

Bridge to the gospel

Biblical unitarians usually take Scripture very seriously and distrust creeds. Don't start with Nicaea. Start with 1 Cor 8:6 and Hebrews 1, and let the text do the work. Then show what's at stake: only God saves ("besides me there is no savior," Isa 43:11), and "there is salvation in no one else" but Jesus (Acts 4:12).

Further reading

  • Richard Bauckham, Jesus and the God of Israel (Eerdmans, 2008): how the New Testament includes Jesus in the identity of the one God
  • James R. White, The Forgotten Trinity (Bethany House, 1998)
  • From the other side: the Racovian Catechism (1605), the classic unitarian case from Scripture
  • Videos on this topic: GodLogic Apologetics, "Unitarian CHALLENGES the Trinity… Then THIS HAPPENS!" and "HEATED DEBATE! Unitarian Gets DESTROYED By Christians!"; Towards Jesus, "Sam Shamoun Vs. Otis Lewis HEATED DEBATE | Is The Bible Trinitarian or Unitarian?"
