Popular Errors Inside the Church

3 cards3 strong

New terms

Word of Faith: A movement, traced from E. W. Kenyon through Kenneth Hagin, teaching that health and wealth are always God's will and are received by faith-filled confession.

Positive confession: The Word of Faith practice of speaking what you want to receive (healing, money) as if it were already yours, believing the words release it.

Textus Receptus: "Received Text": the printed Greek New Testament from Erasmus (1516) onward, used for the King James Version.

Rapture: Believers being caught up to meet the Lord at his coming (1 Thess 4:17). Christians differ on its timing relative to the tribulation.

Not every error comes from outside the church. These three are popular among people who love the Bible: the prosperity gospel, King James Onlyism, and setting dates for Christ's return. Correct them as family: "restore him in a spirit of gentleness" (Gal 6:1), "correcting... with gentleness" (2 Tim 2:25). Use Scripture alone as the test (1D), and keep secondary questions, like the timing of the rapture or which good translation you prefer, secondary.

Worldview3OSTRONG

The Prosperity Gospel (Word of Faith)

Scripture promises believers suffering, contentment, and treasure in heaven, not guaranteed health and wealth

Name + thesis

The prosperity gospel teaches that health and wealth are always God's will for believers, released by "positive confession" and by giving as a "seed." The Lausanne Theology Working Group, meeting in Akropong, Ghana (2008–2009), defined it as "the teaching that believers have a right to the blessings of health and wealth and that they can obtain these blessings through positive confessions of faith and the 'sowing of seeds' through the faithful payments of tithes and offerings." It concluded that in its excesses "it can be soberly described as a false gospel." Scripture warns that "those who desire to be rich fall into temptation" (1 Tim 6:9) and shows the apostles poor, sick, and suffering while full of faith.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "Those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare... For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils" (1 Tim 6:9–10). Paul warns against people "imagining that godliness is a means of gain" (1 Tim 6:5).
  • "I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content... I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound... I can do all things through him who strengthens me" (Phil 4:11–13). The famous verse is about contentment in hunger and need.
  • "Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me. But he said to me, 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness'" (2 Cor 12:8–9).
  • "Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God" (Acts 14:22).
  • Verdict: God gives good gifts and sometimes heals and provides richly, but he doesn't owe health and wealth to anyone who confesses or gives enough. The treasure the gospel promises is Christ himself.

What they believe (steelman)

Best case: God is a good Father who gives good gifts (Matt 7:11). Jesus came so that we "may have life and have it abundantly" (John 10:10). John prayed "that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health" (3 John 2). "With his wounds we are healed" (Isa 53:5). "Give, and it will be given to you" (Luke 6:38). God "gives you power to get wealth" (Deut 8:18). Christ "became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich" (2 Cor 8:9). Faith speaks: whoever tells a mountain to move "and does not doubt in his heart... it will be done for him" (Mark 11:23), and "death and life are in the power of the tongue" (Prov 18:21). The movement's teachers trace back through Kenneth Hagin to E. W. Kenyon (1867–1948); today's best-known names include Kenneth Copeland, Benny Hinn, and Creflo Dollar.

TAG internal critique

  • 3 John 2 is a greeting, the ordinary good wishes that opened an ancient letter, not a promise for every believer.
  • "With his wounds we are healed" is about sin. The same verse says "he was pierced for our transgressions" (Isa 53:5), and Peter applies it to sin: "He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree... By his wounds you have been healed" (1 Pet 2:24). Full bodily healing comes at the resurrection (Rom 8:23; Rev 21:4). Meanwhile Paul left Trophimus "ill at Miletus" (2 Tim 4:20), told Timothy to take wine for "your frequent ailments" (1 Tim 5:23), and kept his own thorn (2 Cor 12:7–9).
  • 2 Cor 8:9's riches are spiritual. Paul is asking the Corinthians to give to the poor in Jerusalem (2 Cor 8:1–4, 13–14), not promising givers wealth. He describes the apostles "as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything" (2 Cor 6:10).
  • Look at Jesus and the apostles. "The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head" (Matt 8:20). Peter: "I have no silver and gold" (Acts 3:6). Paul: "in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure" (2 Cor 11:27). If wealth measured faith, the apostles would have failed.
  • Giving to get is what Simon tried. He offered money for the Spirit's power, and Peter said, "May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money!" (Acts 8:20).
  • "Positive confession" treats faith as a force and words as a formula. Scholars trace it, through Hagin and Kenyon, to the New Thought movement. Scripture teaches us to say instead, "If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that" (Jas 4:15).
  • "Little gods": Some Word of Faith teachers call believers "little gods," citing Ps 82:6 and John 10:34. But Ps 82 rebukes unjust judges: "nevertheless, like men you shall die" (Ps 82:7). And God says, "Before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me" (Isa 43:10).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

"So you're saying God wants us poor and sick?" Answer: No. God provides for his children (Matt 6:31–33), and we pray for the sick (Jas 5:14–15) and work hard (2 Thess 3:10). But God doesn't owe health and wealth on demand, and suffering isn't proof of weak faith. Of the man born blind, Jesus said, "It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him" (John 9:3).

Boomerang check

"Touch not my anointed" (Ps 105:15), so don't criticize God's preachers. Read the psalm: it's about God protecting Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob from kings who would harm them (Ps 105:9–15), not about shielding preachers from questions. The Bereans checked even Paul's preaching against Scripture and were called noble for it (Acts 17:11), and Jesus told us to recognize false prophets "by their fruits" (Matt 7:15–20).

Trap questions

  1. "Paul pleaded three times for his thorn to be removed. Did Paul lack faith?" (2 Cor 12:8–9)
  2. "Peter said, 'I have no silver and gold' (Acts 3:6). Was he outside God's will?"
  3. "In Phil 4:13, what situations does Paul say he can face through Christ?" (Phil 4:11–12)
  4. "If giving guarantees a return, how is it different from Simon trying to buy the gift of God?" (Acts 8:20)

30-second version

"Paul begged God three times to take away his thorn, and God said, 'My grace is sufficient for you' (2 Cor 12:9). Peter said, 'I have no silver and gold' (Acts 3:6). Jesus had nowhere to lay his head (Matt 8:20). If health and wealth measured faith, they'd all fail. The treasure the gospel promises is Christ himself."

Bridge to the gospel

Many people come to prosperity churches out of real poverty, sickness, or debt. Take the pain seriously and pray with them. Then offer the better hope: a Father who is with them in suffering and from whose love nothing can separate them (Rom 8:35–39), and "an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you" (1 Pet 1:4).

Further reading

  • Costi W. Hinn, God, Greed, and the (Prosperity) Gospel (Zondervan, 2019): by Benny Hinn's nephew, who grew up inside the movement
  • Lausanne Theology Working Group, "A Statement on the Prosperity Gospel" (2010, lausanne.org)
  • D. R. McConnell, A Different Gospel (Hendrickson, 1988): traces Word of Faith through Hagin to Kenyon and New Thought
  • Kate Bowler, Blessed: A History of the American Prosperity Gospel (Oxford, 2013): a historian's account
  • John MacArthur, Strange Fire (Thomas Nelson, 2013)
  • From the other side: Kenneth E. Hagin, The Midas Touch (1999)
  • Videos on this topic: A Messenger of Truth, "The Psychology of False Teachers"; Taco Talks, "Indulgences VS Prosperity Preacher?"
Worldview3OSTRONG

King James Onlyism

on the claim that only the KJV is God's word; preferring the KJV is perfectly fine

Name + thesis

The King James Version is a great translation, and Christians are free to love it and use it. King James Onlyism claims more: that the KJV alone is God's preserved word in English and that modern versions are corrupt. But Scripture never names one translation, the apostles themselves quoted a Greek translation of the Old Testament, the KJV's own translators rejected the idea in their preface, and the KJV itself has been revised and rests on a Greek text with known gaps.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever" (Isa 40:8). God promises to preserve his word, not one English edition of it.
  • Hebrews quotes Ps 40:6 from the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint): "a body have you prepared for me" (Heb 10:5), where the Hebrew reads "you have given me an open ear" (Ps 40:6). The apostles treated a translation as Scripture without making it the only one.
  • Verdict: God has preserved his word through the whole family of manuscripts and in faithful translations in many languages, not in a single English edition of 1611 or 1769.

What they believe (steelman)

Best case: God promised to keep his words: "Thou shalt keep them, O LORD, thou shalt preserve them from this generation for ever" (Ps 12:7, KJV), and "my words shall not pass away" (Matt 24:35, KJV). A preserved Bible must be available, and the KJV, translated from the Textus Receptus (the Greek text printed from Erasmus onward), was the English-speaking church's Bible for three centuries. Modern versions rest on a few old manuscripts (Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus) edited by Westcott and Hort, and they drop verses like Acts 8:37 and 1 John 5:7. Some, following Peter Ruckman, say the English even corrects the Greek. Others, like Edward F. Hills, defend the KJV as the best form of the Textus Receptus.

TAG internal critique

  • The KJV translators disagreed. Their preface, "The Translators to the Reader," says "the very meanest translation of the Bible in English, set forth by men of our profession... containeth the word of God, nay, is the word of God." They treated other faithful translations as God's word too.
  • Which King James? The 1611 edition included the 14 books of the Apocrypha. Most KJVs printed today follow the 1769 Oxford edition by Benjamin Blayney, which updated the text. If only one English text is perfect, which edition is it?
  • The Greek text behind it has known gaps. Erasmus lacked the end of Revelation and translated the last six verses back into Greek from the Latin Vulgate. That's why the KJV reads "book of life" in Rev 22:19, where the Greek manuscripts read "tree of life."
  • The apostles used a translation (Heb 10:5 quoting Ps 40:6 from the Septuagint) and never limited God's word to one language.
  • No doctrine depends on the disputed verses. The deity of Christ stands in every major translation (John 1:1; John 20:28; Titus 2:13; Heb 1:8). See 2J and 2F on textual variants.

Weakest premise / hardest objection

"Modern Bibles delete verses like Acts 8:37 and 1 John 5:7." Answer: They don't hide them; they put them in footnotes because the early Greek manuscripts don't have them. The question isn't "Did modern versions remove verses?" but "Were these words in what the apostles wrote, or added later?" The Trinity doesn't rest on 1 John 5:7; it stands on Matt 28:19, John 1:1, and the whole New Testament (2J).

Boomerang check

"Then you don't believe God preserved his word." I believe it more widely. God preserved his word in thousands of manuscripts across the world, so we can know what the apostles wrote (2F). The KJV-only view is the one that leaves Christians without God's preserved word before 1611, and leaves everyone who doesn't read English without it today.

Trap questions

  1. "Before 1611, where was God's preserved word in English? And where is it for Christians who don't speak English today?"
  2. "Which edition is perfect: the 1611 with the Apocrypha, or the 1769 text most KJVs follow?"
  3. "The KJV translators said even 'the very meanest translation' is the word of God. Were they wrong?"
  4. "Heb 10:5 quotes Psalm 40 from a Greek translation. Was its author using a corrupt Bible?"

30-second version

"I love the King James, but its own translators said even 'the very meanest translation of the Bible in English... is the word of God.' The 1611 edition included the Apocrypha, and most KJVs today follow a 1769 revision. God preserved his word in thousands of manuscripts, not in one English edition, and every faithful translation teaches that Jesus is God."

Bridge to the gospel

KJV-only believers usually want a Bible they can trust completely, and that's a good desire. Affirm it: the KJV is trustworthy. Then widen the circle: at Pentecost each person heard God's works "in his own native language" (Acts 2:8–11), and God's word still reaches the nations in their own languages.

Further reading

  • James R. White, The King James Only Controversy (Bethany House, 1995; 2nd ed. 2009)
  • Mark Ward, Authorized: The Use and Misuse of the King James Bible (Lexham, 2018)
  • "The Translators to the Reader," the preface to the 1611 King James Version
  • From the other side: Edward F. Hills, The King James Version Defended (Christian Research Press, 1956)
  • Videos on this topic: Wes Huff, "Why I don't recommend the King James Bible" and "Issues with English Bible Translations | Dr. Mark Ward"; Grace to You, "Are Bible translations reliable? | John MacArthur"; Taco Talks, "Blind Response To KJV Onlyist"
Worldview3OSTRONG

Setting Dates for Christ's Return

Jesus said no one knows the day or the hour, and every date set so far has failed

Name + thesis

Jesus will return bodily and visibly, and Christians should long for it (Acts 1:11; Titus 2:13). But he said no one knows the day or the hour (Matt 24:36), and the history of date-setting is a history of failure. William Miller set October 22, 1844. Edgar Whisenant published 88 Reasons Why the Rapture Will Be in 1988. Harold Camping predicted 1994, then May 21, 2011, then October 21, 2011. Each failure handed skeptics a weapon and wounded believers.

Scripture alone: the apostolic test

  • "But concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only" (Matt 24:36).
  • "It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority" (Acts 1:7).
  • "The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night" (1 Thess 5:2).
  • Verdict: Scripture tells believers to be ready, not to calculate.

What they believe (steelman)

Best case: Jesus gave signs to watch for: "when you see all these things, you know that he is near, at the very gates" (Matt 24:33). He rebuked those who couldn't "interpret the signs of the times" (Matt 16:3). Daniel and Revelation give numbers (Dan 8:14; Dan 9:24–27; Rev 11:3; Rev 12:6). Israel's rebirth in 1948, wars, and earthquakes fit the "birth pains" (Matt 24:7–8). And "no one knows the day or the hour" doesn't rule out knowing the year or the season.

TAG internal critique

  • "Not the day or hour, but the year" is a loophole the context closes: "You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect" (Matt 24:44), and "it is not for you to know times or seasons" (Acts 1:7).
  • The signs repeat in every age. Jesus said wars and earthquakes are "but the beginning of the birth pains," and "the end is not yet" (Matt 24:6–8).
  • Scripture's own test: "If the word does not come to pass or come true, that is a word that the LORD has not spoken; the prophet has spoken it presumptuously" (Deut 18:22). Every date-setter so far has failed it (2B-9).
  • The record: Miller's followers called October 22, 1844 the Great Disappointment. Whisenant's book sold millions of copies. Camping's Family Radio ran a large publicity campaign for May 21, 2011. All of them were confident from Scripture, and all of them were wrong.
  • The rapture debate is secondary. Bible-believing Christians differ on the timing of the rapture (before, in the middle of, or after the tribulation) and on the millennium. John MacArthur teaches a rapture before the tribulation ("Rapture and Resurrection"), while Taco Talks argues the other side ("THIS Is Proof The Rapture Doesn't Exist"). What Scripture makes plain, all of them share: Jesus returns visibly (Acts 1:11), the dead in Christ rise (1 Thess 4:16), and he will judge the living and the dead (2 Tim 4:1).

Weakest premise / hardest objection

"Jesus himself said 'this generation will not pass away until all these things take place' (Matt 24:34). He set a date and missed it." Answer: See the defense in 1E: Mark 9:1 is fulfilled at the Transfiguration six days later, "these things" in Matthew 24 begin with the temple's destruction in AD 70, and two verses later Jesus refuses to give a date (Matt 24:36).

Boomerang check

"Christians have said 'soon' for 2,000 years, which proves it's false." Peter predicted exactly that: "scoffers will come in the last days... They will say, 'Where is the promise of his coming?'" (2 Pet 3:3–4). And he explained the delay: "The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish" (2 Pet 3:9). The date-setters were wrong. Jesus, who refused to give a date, wasn't.

Trap questions

  1. "If Jesus said even the Son didn't know the day (Matt 24:36), how can a teacher today know it?"
  2. "Acts 1:7 says it's not for us to know 'times or seasons.' Does that include the year?"
  3. "By Deut 18:22, what should we conclude about a teacher whose date passes?"

30-second version

"Jesus said, 'Concerning that day and hour no one knows... but the Father only' (Matt 24:36), and 'It is not for you to know times or seasons' (Acts 1:7). Miller in 1844, Whisenant in 1988, and Camping in 2011 all set dates from the Bible, and all were wrong. Be ready every day; don't calculate."

Bridge to the gospel

Date-setting often grows out of real fear about the world, or a real longing for Jesus. Honor the longing: "Come, Lord Jesus!" (Rev 22:20). Then turn it toward faithful living now: "Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes" (Matt 24:46).

Further reading

  • Wayne Grudem, Systematic Theology (Zondervan, 1994; 2nd ed. 2020), chapters on the return of Christ and the millennium: fair to each view
  • Videos on this topic: Grace to You, "Rapture and Resurrection (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18) | John MacArthur" and "The Grim Reality of the Last Days (Mark 13:1-13) | John MacArthur"; Taco Talks, "THIS Is Proof The Rapture Doesn't Exist"; A Messenger of Truth, "Will Jesus Return on September 23rd?"

Part 4

Capstone

4A

Battle Plan: Top 10 Arguments

The ten arguments to rely on in conversations with Muslims, ranked by a combination of strength (the rating, read directly from each card, so this table can't drift from the cards) and usefulness in real conversations. Then a conversation flow that links them, and a list of arguments to drop.

The top 10, ranked

Rank Argument Section Rating Why it ranks here
1 The Islamic Dilemma 2A STRONG Rests on the Qur'an's own words plus undisputed manuscript dates; every other argument connects to it
2 The Timing Trap 2B-1 STRONG Closes the main escape ("the Bible was corrupted"); works even if the Muslim wins the 1st-century debate
3 4:157 vs. History 2B-14 STRONG Near-universal scholarly agreement, including skeptics
4 "Allah Founded Christianity" 2B-6 STRONG Follows from the majority reading of 4:157; hard to escape on any reading
5 The Missing Injil 2B-5 STRONG No trace of a lost book; the Qur'an treats the Injil as present (5:47; 48:29)
6 The Prophecy Test (7:157) 2B-4 STRONG The Qur'an makes a testable claim; every proposed text fails on context
7 The Paul Escape Collapses 2B-8 STRONG The cross predates Paul's letters (the 1 Cor 15 creed)
8 One Standard for Preservation 2F STRONG Disarms the "perfectly preserved Qur'an vs. corrupt Bible" contrast using Sunni sources
9 Jesus vs. Muhammad in the Qur'an 2E STRONG Moves the conversation from argument to the person of Jesus
10 The Deception Problem 2D-1 MODERATE Shows the substitution theory undermines tawatur; best with thoughtful Muslims

Honorable mentions (moving, but more philosophical or pastoral): Tawhid and Love (2D-3, MODERATE); Assurance of Salvation (2H, MODERATE); the Trinitarian TAG (1A, MODERATE).

Arguments to drop (or use only as questions)

Argument Section Rating Why
The aorta test (69:44–46) 2G WEAK Different Arabic word; reads a test into a warning
Verse-pair contradictions (4:82) 2C-3 WEAK Standard harmonizations exist; heavy boomerang
Abrogation as a contradiction 2C-2 WEAK "No creature can change His words" answers it
Mary, "sister of Aaron" 2B-12 WEAK Reasonable Muslim answers (Muslim 2135; Arabic idiom)
Isaac vs. Ishmael as an attack 2B-15 WEAK The Qur'an doesn't name the son
The modal ontological argument 1B WEAK Feels like a trick; doesn't distinguish Christianity
Song 5:16 and similar "Muhammad in the Bible" rebuttals beyond the main ones 2B-4 — Not worth the time; address only if raised

The conversation flow

The flow follows the curriculum: Dilemma → "Allah founded Christianity" → the deception problem → the Qur'an's own Jesus → the gospel. Each step is a question, not a speech.

1. BUILD TRUST
   "What do you love most about your faith?" Listen. Find common ground:
   one Creator, Jesus as Messiah, born of a virgin, prophets, judgment.
        │
2. THE DILEMMA (2A)
   "Can I ask about something in the Qur'an? 5:47 tells Christians to judge
    by their Gospel. Which Gospel did they have?"
        ├─ "It was corrupted" ──► TIMING TRAP (2B-1): "When? Before or after Muhammad?"
        ├─ "It was lost"     ──► MISSING INJIL (2B-5): "Then how could they judge by it?"
        └─ "Only true parts" ──► "How do you tell which, without assuming the Qur'an?"
        │
3. THE CROSS (2B-14 → 2B-6)
   "Every historian agrees Jesus was crucified. 4:157 says it was 'made to
    appear so.' Who made it appear so? What about Jesus' mother and disciples?"
        │
4. THE DECEPTION PROBLEM (2D-1)
   "If God can make a crowd of sincere witnesses see something false,
    how do we know the Qur'an was passed down accurately?"
        │
5. THE QUR'AN'S OWN JESUS (2E, 2B-13)
   "Why does the Qur'an call only Jesus 'a word from Him' and 'a spirit from
    Him'? And why does it say 'the day I die' (19:33)?"
        │
6. THE GOSPEL (4B)
   "Jesus said he came 'to give his life as a ransom for many' (Mark 10:45).
    God provided the sacrifice, as he did for Abraham's son (37:107).
    Would you read Mark's Gospel with me?"

Pacing. Rarely cover more than two steps in one conversation. Stop when the other person is engaged and thinking; arrange to meet again. The goal of each conversation is the next conversation.

4B

Conversation Guide

New terms

Honor-shame culture: A culture in which honor and shame before the community, more than individual guilt, frame morality.

Arguments are tools; people are the point. "Always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect" (1 Pet 3:15).

Questions to ask

Getting to know them

  • "What does your faith mean to you personally?"
  • "How did you come to believe? Was there a time it became your own?"
  • "What do you find most beautiful about Islam?"
  • "What do you think Christians get wrong about Muslims?"

Opening spiritual conversations

  • "Do you know whether God will accept you on the Day of Judgment?" (2H)
  • "What do you think about Jesus?"
  • "Have you ever read the Injil? Would you like to read it with me?"
  • "What would it take for you to believe that Jesus died on the cross?"

Diagnostic (to find out which tradition they follow, and so which cards fit)

  • "Do you follow a particular school or scholar?" (Athari/Salafi, Ash'ari, Maturidi, Shia, Quranist; see each card's audience notes.)
  • "How do you know which hadith are reliable?"
  • "Do you believe the Bible was changed in its words, or in its interpretation?"

Common Christian mistakes about Islam

  1. Calling Allah a moon god. This is historically baseless and offensive. Arab Christians called God Allah before Islam and still do. The issue is not the name but the identity and nature of God (Trinity, the Son, the cross).
  2. Treating all Muslims as the same. Sunni, Shia, Sufi, Quranist, Ahmadi, cultural Muslims, and converts differ greatly.
  3. Assuming they know their own sources. Many don't know the hadith or tafsir; don't shame them for it.
  4. Quoting weak hadith or fringe sites. Use sahih collections and standard tafsir, with gradings (2K).
  5. Misquoting the Qur'an. Always read the context first.
  6. Mistranslating to win a point (e.g., makr as "deceiver," 2B-6).
  7. Using arguments rated WEAK (4A).
  8. Attacking Muhammad's character first. It ends conversations. Start with the Qur'an's claims about the Bible and about Jesus.
  9. Forgetting the boomerang. If your argument works equally against the Bible, drop it or answer it.
  10. Debating without praying, and arguing without loving.

What not to say

  • "Your prophet was a pedophile / terrorist / demon-possessed." (Even where sources raise hard questions, labels shut down thought. See 2I for how to raise them.)
  • "Islam is a religion of violence," or "Muslims are terrorists."
  • "Allah is Satan" or "Allah is a moon god."
  • "You're going to hell" as an opening. (Talk about sin, judgment, and grace in the context of the gospel and relationship.)
  • Anything about Muslim women, dress, or family that you wouldn't want said about your own family.
  • Mocking prayer, fasting, or the Qur'an. (Never put a Qur'an on the floor or handle it carelessly in front of Muslims.)

Presenting the gospel to Muslims

Start from shared ground. Muslims already believe in one Creator, prophets, revelation, the virgin birth, Jesus as Messiah and "word from God," judgment day, and the need for forgiveness.

Bridges that work:

  • Abraham's sacrifice (Gen 22; Qur'an 37:107): God provided a ransom. "God will provide for himself the lamb" (Gen 22:8); "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29).
  • Adam's sin and its consequences: Muslims believe Adam was forgiven (2:37). Ask: if sin is just forgotten, why do people still die and suffer? Why the sacrificial system in the Torah?
  • Honor and shame: many Muslim cultures are honor-shame oriented. The gospel restores honor: Jesus bore our shame (Heb 12:2) and gives us the honor of being God's children (John 1:12).
  • Jesus as kalimat Allah (3:45; 4:171): "In the beginning was the Word" (John 1:1).
  • Assurance: Muslims often live with uncertainty; the gospel offers knowledge of forgiveness (1 John 5:13; 2H).
  • Dreams and visions: many Muslims who come to faith report dreams of Jesus. Take them seriously and point to Scripture (Nabeel Qureshi, Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus).

A simple outline (adapt it to the person):

  1. God is holy and just; he is also loving and merciful. How can he be both toward sinners?
  2. All have sinned (Rom 3:23); deeds can't outweigh sin (Isa 64:6; Gal 2:16).
  3. God himself provided the sacrifice: the eternal Word became man (John 1:14), lived without sin, and died in our place (Isa 53:5; 1 Pet 3:18).
  4. God raised him from the dead (1 Cor 15:3–8), vindicating him.
  5. Whoever turns from sin and trusts in Christ is forgiven and has eternal life now (John 5:24).
  6. Invitation: "Would you read the Gospel of Mark (or Luke, or John) with me?"

Practical wisdom

  • Hospitality matters. Eat together; visit during Ramadan (break the fast with friends); give gifts at Eid.
  • Same-gender conversations are often more appropriate, especially in conservative communities.
  • Give a Bible respectfully (wrapped, not on the floor); in their language if possible.
  • Think about safety. For many Muslims, considering Christ can mean loss of family, job, or worse. Be discreet; never share someone's interest without permission; connect seekers with experienced believers and churches.
  • Be patient. Many Muslim converts describe a journey of years (2I, apostasy card).

  • Gordon D. Nickel, The Quran with Christian Commentary (Zondervan, 2020)

4C

Glossary, Verse Index, and Cheat Sheet

Everything in this section except the cheat sheet is generated by the build from the cards themselves, so it updates automatically whenever a card changes.

One-page cheat sheet

The Islamic Dilemma (in one breath). The Qur'an tells Christians to judge by the Gospel they have (5:47; 5:43; 7:157; 10:94). We have that Gospel from more than 200 years before Muhammad's birth (Codex Sinaiticus, c. 330–360: the whole NT). It teaches the cross and Jesus' deity. So either the Gospel is reliable and the Qur'an is wrong (4:157), or it isn't and the Qur'an was wrong to commend it.

Five questions that carry most conversations

  1. "Which Gospel were Christians in Muhammad's day told to judge by (5:47)?"
  2. "When was the Bible corrupted: before or after Muhammad?"
  3. "In 4:157, who made it appear that Jesus was crucified?"
  4. "If God can make sincere witnesses see something false, how do we trust tawatur?"
  5. "Why does the Qur'an call only Jesus 'a word from Him' and 'a spirit from Him'?"

Key Qur'an verses

  • 5:43, 5:46–47, 5:68, 7:157, 10:94, 2:41, 3:3: the scriptures "with them"
  • 4:157: "they did not kill him, nor crucify him... it was made to appear so"
  • 3:55, 5:117, 19:33: tawaffa and "the day I die"
  • 3:45, 4:171: "a word from Him," "a spirit from Him"
  • 46:9: "I do not know what will be done with me or with you"
  • 15:9: "We will be its guardian"

Key hadith (sunnah.com numbering)

  • Sahih al-Bukhari 3635 (in-book 61/139), narrated by Ibn Umar: the Medina Torah contained the stoning verse (hidden, not changed)
  • Sunan Abi Dawud 4449 (in-book 40/99), narrated by Ibn Umar; graded hasan by al-Albani: "I believe in you and in Him who revealed you"
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 2685 (in-book 52/46), a statement of Ibn Abbas (mawquf): "they changed with their hands" (be ready for this one)
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 4987, narrated by Anas ibn Malik: Uthman burned the other copies
  • Sahih Muslim 1452a (in-book 17/30), narrated by Aisha: a verse "recited of the Qur'an" when Muhammad died
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 4625 (in-book 65/147), narrated by Ibn Abbas: Muhammad uses tawaffaytani of his own death
  • Sahih al-Bukhari 1243 (in-book 23/6), narrated by Umm al-Ala': "I do not know what Allah will do with me"

Key Bible texts

  • 1 Cor 15:3–8: the early creed (died, buried, raised, appeared)
  • Mark 2:5–10; Mark 14:61–64 with Dan 7:13–14; John 8:58; John 20:28: Jesus' deity
  • Isa 53:5–6; Dan 9:26: the suffering, cut-off Messiah
  • John 1:1, 14: the eternal Word became flesh
  • John 5:24; 1 John 5:13: assurance

Three things never to do: mistranslate, quote weak hadith as sahih, mock.

One thing always to do: move from the argument to the person of Jesus.

New World Translation (NWT) The Bible translation published by the Watch Tower Society (Jehovah's Witnesses). 3G
Nirvana In Buddhism, the cessation of craving and suffering, and release from rebirth. 3E
Normativity The 'ought' quality of logic and morality: they tell us how we should think and act, not just how we do. 1A
Occasionalism Al-Ghazali's view (and that of many Ash'aris) that created things have no causal power; God directly creates each effect. 2D-2
Oneness Pentecostalism A Pentecostal movement (from 1913–1916) teaching that God is one person, that Jesus is the Father, Son, and Spirit, and that baptism must be "in Jesus' name" only. 3N
Palimpsest A manuscript whose original text was scraped off and written over; the lower text can often be recovered. 2F
Panentheism The view that the universe is within God, while God is more than the universe. 3I
Pantheism The view that God and the universe are identical. 3I
Papal infallibility The Catholic dogma (Vatican I, 1870) that the pope cannot err when he defines a doctrine of faith or morals ex cathedra. 3J
Paraclete (parakletos) Greek for 'helper, advocate, comforter': Jesus' name for the Holy Spirit in John 14–16. 2B-4
Paran A wilderness the Bible places between Sinai and Canaan (Num 10:12; 13:26), which some Muslims identify with Mecca. 2B-15
Positive confession The Word of Faith practice of speaking what you want to receive (healing, money) as if it were already yours, believing the words release it. 3O
Presuppositionalism The apologetic method of Van Til and Bahnsen: argue at the level of ultimate commitments (presuppositions), showing that only the Christian worldview makes knowledge possible. 1A
Principle of Sufficient Reason (PSR) The principle that everything that exists has an explanation of its existence. 1B
Problem of evil The objection that the existence or amount of suffering is incompatible with, or makes unlikely, an all-good, all-powerful God. 3A
Problem of induction David Hume's point that we can't justify reasoning from past to future without assuming the very regularity we want to prove. 1A
Proskynesis / latreia Greek words for bowing or veneration (proskynesis) and worship or service (latreia). Nicaea II allowed the first toward icons and reserved the second for God. 3K
Pseudepigraphy Writing under someone else's name, such as a later author writing as an apostle. 1E
Pure act (actus purus) In Aristotelian-Thomist philosophy, a being with no unrealized potential at all: God. 1B
Purgatory In Catholic teaching, a state of purification after death for those who die in God's grace but are not yet fully purified. 3J
Qira'a (pl. qira'at) One of the recognized canonical "readings" of the Qur'an. 2A
Quranists (Qur'aniyyun) Muslims who accept the Qur'an alone and reject hadith as a source of religious authority. 2C-1
Qurra' Qur'an reciters; also the transmitters of the canonical readings. 2F
Rabbinic Judaism The Judaism shaped by the rabbis after the Temple's destruction (AD 70), centered on Torah study, prayer, and the Talmud. 3C
Raf' 'Raising': the Qur'an says God raised Jesus to himself (3:55; 4:158). 2B-13
Rapture Believers being caught up to meet the Lord at his coming (1 Thess 4:17). Christians differ on its timing relative to the tribulation. 3O
Relativism The view that truth or morality is relative to individuals or cultures. 3H
Resolution The statement a formal debate argues for or against. 2L
Ridda Apostasy: leaving Islam. 2I
Sahih "Sound": the top grade of hadith. 2A
Samsara The cycle of death and rebirth. 3D
Sarfa 'Turning away': the view of some Muslim theologians (e.g., al-Nazzam) that the Arabs could have imitated the Qur'an but God prevented them. 2G
Satanic Verses (gharaniq incident) The early report that Muhammad briefly recited verses praising three Meccan goddesses, later retracted as from Satan. 2G
Secular humanism A non-religious worldview affirming human reason, ethics, and flourishing without God. 3H
Septuagint (LXX) The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, made by Jews in the 3rd–1st centuries BC. 1C
Shafa'a Intercession, especially Muhammad's intercession on the Day of Judgment. 2H
Shubbiha lahum "It was made to appear so to them" (4:157): the phrase behind the Islamic belief that Jesus was not crucified. 2B-6
Sifat (dhatiyya / fi'liyya) God's attributes: attributes of essence (eternal: life, knowledge, power, etc.) vs. attributes of action (creating, providing). 2D-3
Sihr Arabic for "magic" or sorcery; mas-hur means "bewitched" or "affected by magic." 2M
Sirat The bridge over Hell that all must cross on the Day of Judgment. 2H
Sola scriptura "Scripture alone": the teaching that Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith, and every other authority must be tested by it. 1D
Son of Man Jesus' favorite self-title, drawn from Daniel 7:13–14, where 'one like a son of man' receives everlasting dominion and worship. 1C
Substitution theory The classical Islamic view that God cast Jesus' likeness onto someone else, who was crucified in his place. 2B-6
Sunna The normative example of Muhammad (words, deeds, approvals), known through hadith and community practice. 2C-1
Syriac Alexander Legend A Syriac Christian story of Alexander the Great and his gate against Gog and Magog, often dated c. 629–630. 2B-11
Tafsir Qur'anic commentary. 2A
TAG The Transcendental Argument for God: God must exist because logic, science, morality, and reasoning are impossible without him. 1A
Tahrif "Distortion" or corruption of scripture. 2A
Tahrif al-ma'na Corruption of the meaning (twisted interpretation, text intact). 2A
Tahrif al-nass Corruption of the text itself (the words were changed). 2A
Tanakh The Hebrew Bible: Torah (Law), Nevi'im (Prophets), Ketuvim (Writings). 3C
Tawaffa Arabic 'to take in full'; in the Qur'an usually 'to cause to die' (of God taking a soul), occasionally of sleep when sleep is named. 2B-13
Tawatur Mass transmission: a report passed on by so many people in every generation that collusion in falsehood is considered impossible. 2C-1
Tawhid The absolute oneness of God, the central doctrine of Islam. 2D-3
Tawrat / Injil The Qur'an's names for the Torah and the Gospel. 2A
Testimonium Flavianum Josephus' passage on Jesus (Antiquities 18.63–64); most scholars think it has an authentic core with later Christian additions. 2B-14
Textual criticism The scholarly method of reconstructing an original text by comparing its surviving copies. 1C
Textus Receptus "Received Text": the printed Greek New Testament from Erasmus (1516) onward, used for the King James Version. 3O
The one and the many The ancient puzzle of how unity (laws, kinds) and diversity (individual things) relate, and which is ultimate. 1A
Theodicy An account of why a good and all-powerful God permits evil. 1E
Theosis "Deification": the Orthodox understanding of salvation as union with God and participation in his life. 3K
Theotokos "God-bearer" or Mother of God: the title for Mary affirmed at the Council of Ephesus (431), meaning that the one she bore is God the Son. 2B-10
Transcendental argument An argument from the preconditions of something we already use (thought, experience, argument) to what must be true for it to be possible. 1A
Trinity The Christian doctrine that the one God exists eternally as three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. 2J
Uniformity of nature The assumption that nature behaves consistently, so that the future will resemble the past. 1A
Unitarian (theism) Belief in a God who is one person only (Judaism, Islam, Jehovah's Witnesses), as opposed to the Trinity. 1A
Uswa hasana 'Excellent example': the Qur'an's description of Muhammad (33:21). 2I
Uthmanic rasm The consonantal skeleton of the Qur'an standardized under the caliph Uthman (c. 650). 2F
Voluntarism The view that God's will, not his nature, is the ultimate ground of what is good. 2D-2
Watch Tower Society The governing organization of Jehovah's Witnesses. 3G
Word of Faith A movement, traced from E. W. Kenyon through Kenneth Hagin, teaching that health and wealth are always God's will and are received by faith-filled confession. 3O
Worldview A person's most basic beliefs about reality, knowledge, and ethics, the lens through which they interpret everything. 1A

Battle Plans for Every Conversation

One short plan for each kind of conversation. On the website, choose who you're talking with in the "Talking with" menu and only that plan (and the sections it uses) will show. Each plan puts the strongest arguments first (the ratings come straight from the cards), gives a conversation flow, and lists what to avoid. Lead with questions, not speeches, and aim for the next conversation, not a knockout. Every plan ends at the same place: the gospel (4B).

With Muslims

Your full ranked plan is 4A. The core in one line:

  1. The Islamic Dilemma (2A, STRONG): the Qur'an affirms the Gospel Christians had (5:47), and that Gospel teaches the cross.
  2. The timing trap (2B-1, STRONG): when was it corrupted, before or after Muhammad?
  3. The cross in history (2B-14, STRONG) and "Allah founded Christianity" (2B-6, STRONG).
  4. Not the same God, by Scripture's standard (2M, STRONG): 1 John 2:23.
  5. Who Jesus is in the Qur'an itself (2E), then the gospel.

Avoid: the aorta test, "sister of Aaron," verse-pair contradictions, and the suicide story in Bukhari 6982. All are rated WEAK.

With Roman Catholics

Strongest first:

  1. Justified by faith alone (3J, STRONG): Rom 4:5; Eph 2:8–9; against Trent, Session 6, Canon 9.
  2. Christ's once-for-all sacrifice (3J, STRONG): Heb 10:14, 18.
  3. The "unchanging" Church has changed (3J, STRONG): Florence (1442) against CCC 841, under Vatican I's rule that a dogma's meaning never changes.
  4. Scripture alone (1D, STRONG): Mark 7:13; Acts 17:11.
  5. Praying to the saints (3K, STRONG): 1 Tim 2:5; Heb 4:16.
  6. The Marian dogmas (3J, STRONG): Luke 1:47.
  7. The rock is Christ (3J, MODERATE): honestly debated, so lead with the confession and fall back to "no successors, no Rome."

Flow: start from shared faith (the Trinity, the cross, the resurrection) → ask, "How can someone know they're right with God?" → Rom 4:5 and Eph 2:8–9 → Heb 10:14–18 → assurance (Rom 5:1; 1 John 5:13). If authority comes up ("the Church decides, not you"), go to 1D and the "unchanging Church" card: if Rome's own definitions need reinterpreting, Scripture is the only fixed rule.

Avoid: mocking devotion, opening with "Catholics aren't Christians," and saying "Catholics worship Mary" (they deny it; say "pray to Mary" and quote the prayers).

With Eastern Orthodox Christians

Strongest first:

  1. Holy Tradition needs a judge (3K, STRONG): Mark 7:8–13; Hieria (754) against Nicaea II (787).
  2. Icons and the Second Commandment (3K, STRONG): Exod 20:5 in the Greek Old Testament; 2 Kgs 18:4.
  3. Praying to the saints and the Theotokos (3K, STRONG): 1 Tim 2:5; Heb 4:16.
  4. Scripture alone (1D, STRONG).
  5. Justification before transformation (the theosis defense in 3K): Rom 5:1.

Flow: honor their Nicene faith and their love of Scripture in the liturgy → councils that contradicted each other → Mark 7 → Exod 20:5 in the Greek Bible they revere → Heb 4:16.

Avoid: treating Orthodoxy as Roman Catholicism, and leading with the papacy (they already agree with you there).

With atheists and skeptics

Strongest first:

  1. TAG as an internal critique (1A, MODERATE): ask them to account for logic, induction, and moral obligation.
  2. The moral argument (1B, MODERATE).
  3. The resurrection by minimal facts (1C, STRONG) and New Testament reliability (1C, STRONG).
  4. The problem of evil, answered with compassion (1E, MODERATE).
  5. "Scholars say..." (1E, MODERATE): ask for the reasons behind the consensus.
  6. "The God of the Old Testament is evil" (1F, MODERATE): sort the verse with the seven moves, concede the hard cases, and ask for their standard.

Flow: "What would count as evidence for you?" → ask them to ground logic and morality (1A) → the minimal facts → suffering and the cross.

Avoid: the modal ontological argument with non-philosophers (WEAK), overclaiming science, and arguing with someone who is grieving.

With Jehovah's Witnesses

Strongest first:

  1. The Watchtower's prophetic record (3G, STRONG): 1925 and 1975, tested by Deut 18:22.
  2. Jesus is God: John 1:1; John 20:28; Heb 1:8. Use the deity defenses in 2J for "the Father is greater" and "John 17:3."
  3. Jesus receives the worship due to God: Heb 1:6; Rev 5:13–14.

Flow: read John 1 and John 20 together in their own New World Translation → ask what Thomas meant → the 1925 and 1975 predictions → Deut 18:22.

Avoid: arguing only from your own translation, and ridiculing their door-to-door effort.

With Latter-day Saints

Strongest first:

  1. The Book of Abraham, in the Church's own words (3F, STRONG): the papyri are "standard funerary texts."
  2. God was never a man: Isa 43:10; Hos 11:9; Num 23:19.
  3. Grace without "after all we can do": Eph 2:8–9 and Rom 4:5, compared with 2 Nephi 25:23.

Flow: ask about their testimony → the Gospel Topics essays → Isa 43:10 → grace.

Avoid: mocking temple garments or sacred ceremonies, and citing anti-Mormon claims you haven't checked; their own essays are stronger.

With Hebrew Israelites

Strongest first:

  1. Gentiles are saved through faith (3M, STRONG): Acts 10:34–35; Gal 3:28–29; Rev 7:9.
  2. Jesus is God (2J; 1C).
  3. Deut 28:68 in context, and Rom 9:6–8 on who true Israel is.

Flow: acknowledge the real history of slavery and racism → Paul, a Hebrew of Hebrews, was sent to the nations (Acts 9:15) → the multitude from every nation (Rev 7:9).

Avoid: genealogy debates you can't settle, and turning a street conversation into a shouting match.

With Oneness Pentecostals and biblical unitarians

Strongest first:

  1. The Son and the Father are two witnesses (3N, STRONG): John 8:17–18; John 17:5; 1 John 2:1.
  2. One God, one Lord (3N, STRONG): 1 Cor 8:6; Isa 45:23 with Phil 2:10–11; Heb 1:8–10.
  3. Salvation by grace through faith, not proved by tongues: Eph 2:8–9; 1 Cor 12:30; Acts 10:44–48.

Flow: agree that Jesus is fully God (with Oneness) or that God is one (with unitarians) → read John 17 or 1 Cor 8:6 together and ask who is speaking to whom → only God saves (Isa 43:11; Acts 4:12).

Avoid: leading with church councils and creeds; they'll hear "tradition over Scripture." Stay in the text (1D).

With fellow Christians caught in popular errors

Strongest first:

  1. Prosperity gospel: Paul's thorn and Peter's empty purse (3O, STRONG): 2 Cor 12:8–9; Acts 3:6; 1 Tim 6:9–10.
  2. King James Onlyism: the translators' own preface (3O, STRONG): "the very meanest translation... is the word of God."
  3. Date-setting: no one knows the day (3O, STRONG): Matt 24:36; Acts 1:7; and "this generation" answered (1E).

Flow: treat them as family if they trust Christ → open the text together → keep the gospel and Christ himself at the center.

Avoid: mocking preachers by name, sarcasm, and treating secondary questions (rapture timing, which good translation) as tests of salvation.

With Jewish friends

Strongest first:

  1. Isaiah 53 and Daniel 9 (3C; 1C, MODERATE).
  2. Atonement: Lev 17:11 and Heb 10:1–14; even the Talmud shows the loss of the altar was felt (b. Berakhot 17a).
  3. The suffering messiah in Jewish tradition: Messiah son of Joseph, who is killed (b. Sukkah 52a).

Flow: speak with respect for the Scriptures you share → read Isa 52:13–53:12 aloud → Dan 9:26.

Avoid: blaming Jewish people for the crucifixion (Acts 4:27–28 names Herod, Pilate, Gentiles, and Israel together), and any hint of contempt.

With Gnostic, New Age, and "spiritual" seekers

Strongest first:

  1. The "lost gospels" are late (3L, STRONG).
  2. The Word became flesh (3L, STRONG): 1 John 4:2–3; Luke 24:39.
  3. New Age monism (3I), and Hinduism or Buddhism where relevant (3D; 3E).

Flow: "What do you think is wrong with the world?" → the incarnation: God entered the world rather than offering an escape from it → grace for ordinary people, not secret knowledge for a few (Matt 11:25, 28).

Avoid: dismissing their spiritual hunger; take it seriously and point it to Christ.
